en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Sub-commentary on the Five Treatises in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
In the *Dhātukathāpakaraṇa-anuṭīkā*, the Commentary on the Beginning of the Book: Since the place, the teacher,
and the assembly for the teaching of the *Dhātukathāpakaraṇa* have already been stated in the manner previously described, [the author now provides] the indication of the time.
Showing this, he said, "Teaching the *Dhātukathā-pakarana*," and so forth.
For by the phrase "he taught it immediately after that," it is indicated that the time for teaching the *Dhātukathā* was right after the *Vibhaṅga*.
As for those who claim that "the *Kathāvatthu-pakarana* was taught after the *Vibhaṅga*," he refutes their assertion.
He said, “...in order to show [this] immediately after the analysis (vibhaṅga)...

Based on the statement beginning with “Sensual pleasures are your first army,” it can be said that the destruction of the defilements is also the shattering of the power of the Māra who is a son of the gods;
however, since it is stated [here] as “by way of causing non-occurrence, [the destruction] of the Māras of defilements and volitional formations,” [it refers to this].
The destruction of the power of the Devaputtamāra should be understood as the breaking of the strength of the assembly through the influence of the powers of patience, faith, and so forth.
"Transcending the sphere" means the transcendence of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*).

"By way of the full understanding of abandoning the origin" means by way of the clear realization of abandoning (*pahānābhisamaya*) and the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*). But is this not the breaking of the five Māras?
Considering the objection that such [qualities] might also be found among disciples, he said, "devoid of dependence on others," and so forth.

Taking the state of being heroic to be *vīriya* (energy), it was stated: "One of great energy is a Great Hero (*mahāvīra*). And this state of great energy is due to the perfection of the *vīriya-pāramitā* (perfection of energy), through the foundation of energy endowed with four factors, and by means of the attainment of the fourfold right exertion (*sammappadhāna*) which is not shared by others.
And it should be understood [in this way]. For it is precisely from that [foundation] that the non-decline of energy and the accomplishment [of the goal] are established.
Since the discourse on the Abhidhamma proceeds by taking the aggregates and so forth as its basis, support, and object, he said:
"or in the sense of being the basis for the discourse on the Abhidhamma. "From the discourse upon them" means from the state of discourse regarding those aggregates and so forth.

By this it is meant that a collection of phonemes (byañjana) supported by a specific meaning is a treatise (pakaraṇa). Alternatively, it is called *Dhātukathā* because the elements (*dhātu*) are discussed therein, or because one speaks by means of them;
thus, it is a collection of both phonemes and meanings proceeding in such a manner.
Anticipating the objection that, if this were so, all seven treatises would necessarily become *Dhātukathā*, he says: "Even though... and so forth.
In this context, "preeminent" means distinguished, because the teaching proceeds by way of variety, abundance, and completeness.
For it has been said: "The entire *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* is the matrix for the *Dhātukathā*. Therefore, he said:
"For elsewhere only a partial exposition was made."

Now, by way of those terms in which the word *dhātu* (element) is conventionally established within the Dispensation, the author demonstrates that this treatise possesses the unique character of a *Dhātukathā* (Discourse on Elements), even when compared to others, by stating:
"Or by means of aggregates, bases, and elements," and so forth. Therein, the phrase "in each case" (*tattha tattha*) refers to the aggregates, bases, and elements.

They are called "great-spheres" (*mahāvisayā*) because their sphere of application (*visaya*) is vast and follows many classifications; this refers to the elements (*dhātuyo*), and not to the aggregates and bases, because the latter consist of fewer terms.

Alternatively, that intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) by which phenomena receive their enumeration and description through inclusion, non-inclusion, association, and dissociation is the "element" (*dhātu*).

Since this element is taught here with particular emphasis, this treatise is called the *Dhātukathā* (Discourse on Elements) because it speaks of the element with distinction. For this word *dhātu* has the sense of "intrinsic nature," as in: "By way of elements, monks..."
[It is used] as in such passages as “beings come together. “Dhātubhedaṃ” means the classification of elements (dhātu). “Pakaraṇaṃ” is a remainder of the word [to be supplied].
To the question, “From where is the word *pakaraṇa* obtained? he says: “Because it occurs as a commentary on the seven treatises (*pakaraṇa*) in their proper order.

“Making the connection with that” means making the connection with that word *pakaraṇa*, [namely]: “The *Dhātukathā* itself is the treatise; thus, ‘the *Dhātukathā*-treatise’ (*dhātukathāpakaraṇaṃ*).”
“Having made a connection. “Explaining that” means the illumination of the meaning of the *Dhātukathā* treatise;

it refers to the commentary proceeding by way of illuminating the meaning. Having said, “I shall illuminate the meaning,” he says, “Listen to that,” thereby directing [the listener] toward its comprehension by means of the ear-door.
Thus he says: “The meaning is: ‘Comprehend it by listening to the words that explain it.’”
The commentary on the commencement of the work is finished.
1. Commentary on the Matrix (Mātikā). 1.
Commentary on the Matrix of Methods (Nayamātikā).
1. "In fourteen ways" means in fourteen modes; the meaning is "by means of fourteen terms.

In this context, "inclusion (saṅgaha) and non-inclusion (asaṅgaha)" constitutes one term, and likewise "association (sampayoga) and dissociation (vippayoga). However, the triads such as "associated with what is included," "dissociated from what is included," and so forth, each constitute a single term.
The analysis of the remaining terms is easily understood. "By these" refers to the various modes beginning with inclusion.

“Leading” (nayana) means causing to proceed and making known; thus, the meaning is stated in two ways: “it is caused to proceed” and “it is made known. When these very leadings are presented as headings, they are called *mātikās*.

In both senses, they are called “leadings” (*nayā*) because they comprise various methods such as grouping (*saṅgaha*), etc., by virtue of being the instruments for the activities of proceeding and making known.
Therefore, it was said in the Commentary: “By this [method] of grouping, etc...”
"By way of method. "Of the words" (*padānam*) means of the expressions that illuminate the meaning; for a word (*pada*) is so called because meaning is reached (*pajjati*) by means of it.

Furthermore, the genitive case in "of the words" (*padānam*) expresses a relationship of co-occurrence (*saṃsāmi-sambandha*), whereas in "of the treatise" (*pakaraṇassa*) it expresses a relationship between part and whole (*avayava-avayavī-sambandha*).
2. Commentary on the Internal Matrix (*abbhantara-mātikā-vaṇṇanā*)
2. "Tadatthāni" means having the meaning of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
For it is called "dependent origination" because formations and so forth arise dependently upon this; that is, each individual condition such as ignorance. Thus it is said in the *Saṅkhāra-piṭaka*:
"There are twelve conditions, twelve dependent originations. "Of these" refers to the aggregates and so forth. "Shown in such a way" refers to...

[This refers to] those things shown merely by way of enumeration, indication, and classification. But why is dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) here taken only as twelve factors? Anticipating the objection:

"Is it not the case that there, 'existence' (bhava) is taken according to its divisions such as kamma-bhava, and 'sorrow' (soka) and so forth are taken here in the text according to their own specific forms?

he says "Tattha" and so on. Therein, "Tattha" means "in that [text]"—namely, in that [passage] beginning with "By twenty-five... *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*

Regarding the statement "with a hundred words" found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: [the former] is called *bhava* (existence) because it is the state of bringing about (*bhāvana*) *kamma-bhava* (kamma-existence), while [the latter] is called *bhava* because it is the state of being (*bhavana*) *upapatti-bhava* (rebirth-existence). As for the meaning of the word:
*kamma-bhava* is *bhava* because existence (*bhavati*) arises from this; the other is *bhava* because it exists (*bhavati*) or because it is the process of existing (*bhavana*).
"By way of the state of suffering caused by that" means by way of the state of suffering caused by aging and death.
“‘All the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* [is] the matrix (*mātikā*) for the *Dhātukathā*’—this too is merely a statement of the matrix for the *Dhātukathā*.
Therefore, not accepting the statement ‘...all... the matrix... this is stated outside of the *Dhātukathā-mātikā*,’ he says ‘Alternatively (*atha vā*),’ etc.
The meaning is that it is stated as being the matrix for the *Dhātukathā*, even though it occurs in another treatise (*pakaraṇantara*). And here, of course...”
Those stated as being of the nature of a matrix (mātikā) are called "external" because they are to be understood from elsewhere due to their occurrence in other treatises;
those such as the "five aggregates," which are taken in their own form, are "internal. Therefore he said: "because they were established after being shown in their own form.
"Because not included in the matrix" means because they are not included in the matrix in its own form, and not otherwise.

For there is no meaning of a term that is not included within the *mātikā*. "By way of being scattered" means by way of being dispersed or spread out individually in such sections as the *Khandhavibhaṅga*.
3. Commentary on the *Nayamukhamātikā* (The Matrix of the Gateways of Method)

3. The "method" (*naya*) is the teaching concerning the various specific modes such as the compendium (*saṅgaha*), etc.; it is called a "door" (*dvāra*) because it is the point of departure for that teaching.

The summary list (*uddesa*) of those aforementioned phenomena—namely, the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and the formless aggregates (*arūpin-khandha*)—according to their respective suitability, constitutes the matrix (*mātikā*) which is the gateway to the methods.
Therefore he said, "of the methods," and so forth. They are "possessors of dissociation" (*viyogin*) because they have the nature of being dissociated, or because dissociation exists within them.

Likewise, the meaning is that the factors of association and dissociation, as well as the factors of inclusion and non-inclusion, have the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of occurring by way of including and not including, and by way of uniting and disuniting.

[The text] makes this same meaning clearer by means of the fourteen types of joy (*pīti*) and so forth. "By which" means by which aggregates (*khandha*), etc., [namely] the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*).
"Those four" refers to those four [categories] beginning with inclusion (saṅgaha). "Also by way of the truths, etc.

means together with the truths, the faculties, dependent origination, and so forth. "According to what is possible" means in accordance with what is applicable; the sense is that whichever term is appropriate to be stated as either "included" or "not included," that is the method.
"So too" refers to inclusion and non-inclusion. "By those which have become the includers" means by those which have become the agents of the act of including.

"By those" refers to the Truths and so forth. "Not by those which have become the included" means that inclusion and non-inclusion was not stated by means of the Truths and so forth as the instruments of the act of including;
for even there, it is shown that only the aggregates, bases, and elements serve as the instruments. [This is] by means of the aggregates and so forth alone.
"By way of inclusion" means by way of the very act of including through the aggregates (khandha) and so forth, which serve as the instruments of that inclusion.

Having thus determined the inclusion and non-inclusion—stating: "Included by inclusion by way of aggregates, not included by inclusion by way of bases (āyatana), not included by inclusion by way of elements (dhātu); those phenomena are not included by four aggregates, two bases, and eight elements"—it is said [as follows]. Therefore...

Because the Truths and so forth are stated by way of being inclusive categories (*saṅgāhakabhāva*), not by way of being included categories (*saṅgahabhāva*), whereas the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth are indeed stated by way of being included categories; therefore [this distinction is made].
But why are the Truths and so forth not stated here by way of inclusion? Because such a teaching is impossible.

For it is not possible to include the form-aggregate and so forth within the Truth of Origination and so forth, nor the perception-aggregate and so forth within the faculties and so forth, by means of the method of inclusion.

"To ask or to answer" means as follows: likewise, regarding the feeling and other aggregates that have arisen within the noble fruits (ariyaphala) and so forth, because they are not excluded from the [noble] truths, one cannot demonstrate their inclusion by asking, "By how many truths is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) comprised?
and then defining it by saying, "It is comprised by one truth," and so on. "According to what is possible" refers to those [factors] with which there is association, and those...
...dissociation, which is appropriate to that.
Matter is not dissociated from matter or from Nibbāna, nor is Nibbāna dissociated from matter. Why? Because it is impossible to conceive of them as associated.
For, since the four aggregates are mutually associated, [it follows that] even with respect to matter and Nibbāna—

There might be the suspicion that "it exists" or "it does not exist"; therefore, their dissociation from one another is stated, but not the dissociation of matter from matter or from Nibbāna, nor of Nibbāna from matter.
Since there is no suspicion of any association anywhere, dissociation is likewise not stated for matter from matter or Nibbāna, nor for Nibbāna from that [matter].
But since it is spoken of by means of the formless aggregates alone, he says, "By four indeed," and so forth. Regarding that which is without an object, such as the eye-base and so on.

"By those without an object and mixed with those without an object" means by the ear-base and so on, which are without an object, and by the mental-object-base and so on, which are mixed with those without an object.
Regarding that which is mixed, such as the mental-object-base and so on. Not by those without an object and mixed with those without an object.
The word "occurs" (*hoti*) should be supplied [to complete the sentence]. To show for whom and by what this occurs, it is said: "But for that which is without an object," and so forth.

For just as dissociation occurs for that which has an object through that which is without an object and that which is mixed with the objectless, so too does it occur through that which has an object.
It should be understood that the same applies to that which is without an object and that which is mixed with the objectless.
4. Explanation of the Matrix of Characteristics (Lakkhaṇamātikāvaṇṇanā):
"An individual application should be made: that which was stated as 'comprehension by three' and 'association by four' is prompted by a state of similarity;
and that which was stated as 'non-comprehension by three' and 'dissociation by four' is a state of dissimilarity."
Showing this meaning, he said: "Inclusion... is understood. That which is included is a similar state (*sabhāga*), such as the aggregates and so forth;
that which is not included is a dissimilar state (*visabhāga*). The same should be understood regarding association (*sampayoga*) as well.

Now, in order to demonstrate the aforementioned similarity by defining it according to its essential nature, the passage beginning with "Therein" was stated. Therein, "samānabhāvo" (the state of being the same) [is the definition].

By the statement "homogeneity in inclusion, and conjunction in simultaneous arising, etc.," it is implied that the state of being dissimilar—devoid of the qualities of being affected by change (ruppana) and so forth—is "non-homogeneity" in non-inclusion;
and the state of being distinct—characterized by different arising, etc.—is "disjunction. Since this meaning is established by the context, it was not explicitly stated.
5. Commentary on the External Matrix (Bāhiramātikāvaṇṇanā)

5. "By this manner of setting aside" means not by way of its specific form, but by the manner of setting aside—known as the enumeration of the status of the *mātikā* here—which corresponds to the table of contents (*mātikā*) in another treatise as previously described.

"Setting aside externally" refers to the subsequent inclusion of the *mātikā* established in another treatise without distinction; thus he says, "because it is set aside behind externally. "Not having set it aside here" means...
Without stating it explicitly in the form of this *Dhātukathā* (Discourse on Elements).

"Because it has been made manifest in that way" means because it has been illuminated by way of its matrix (*mātikā*). For the matrices themselves as they appear in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* have been taken up under the heading of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.

Regarding those methods by which the exposition of the *Dhātukathā* proceeds—among those methods, among the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth which are to be analyzed by them, and regarding the doors of occurrence and the characteristics of those methods—
Since that which ought to be stated by way of the summary for the *Dhātukathā* among those [treatises] already mentioned has indeed been stated,
having thus stated what was to be said by way of the summary, it was further said— "The entire *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* is the matrix (*mātikā*) for the *Dhātukathā*"—

for the purpose of showing the classification of the aggregates and so forth as wholesome and so on, as previously described. In this way, the method of setting forth the matrix should be understood here.

In the phrase “‘Gāvī’—this is what was said,” just as the word *gāvī* [is used], here in the phrase “inclusion and non-inclusion,” by means of the particle *iti*, which causes a reversal of the literal meaning (*padatthavipallāsa*), the words *saṅgaha* and *asaṅgaha*—which refer to the meaning (*atthapadatthaka*)—become words referring to the sound itself (*saddapadatthaka*). With this intention, he says:
“Because it is stated as the sound alone whose meaning is not yet determined. Thus, by way of extracting the meaning, he comments upon the word *saṅgaha*.
It shows [this]. "With its specific distinctions undetermined" means that its specific distinctions—such as genus (*jāti*), birth (*sañjāti*), and so forth—are not included.
"To be understood by way of generality" means being cognized or being spoken of by way of the generality consisting in the state of being denotable by the word "inclusion" (*saṅgaha*).

Nor should an objection be raised here that the generality is of only one form; for since that [generality] depends upon differentiation, the rule [of inclusion] depends precisely upon however many specific distinctions it may have.
“Of one’s own birth” is understood just as when it is said “dutiful to one’s mother,” it means beneficial to one’s own mother.
“Without specifying a particular dhamma” means without making a distinction among the dhammas to be asked about and answered by way of being included and so forth.
“In general” means without distinction. “Of dhammas” refers to dhammas such as the aggregates (khandhas) and so on. “The remainder, having specified” means...

The construction is as follows: the remaining twelve [questions], beginning with "Included by what is included" (*saṅgahitena asaṅgahitaṃ*), are enumerations of the methods for questioning and answering regarding phenomena, having determined the specific distinctions among the phenomena to be questioned and answered.

But is it not the case that those beginning with "Included by what is included" are also enumerations of the methods for questioning and answering regarding phenomena in a general sense, without determining the aforementioned specific distinctions?

With reference to the *codanā* (the prompting question), he says: "Included and not included," and so forth. That for which the meaning is understood but the word is not employed should be known as an elision (*lopa*);
or else this meaning may be illustrated by means of recurrence (*āvutti*) and so on. "By that" refers to the word "not included" (*asaṅgahita*), which is indicated by elision.
"Distinguished by the specific quality of being included" means distinguished by the specific quality of being included within the aggregate (*khandha*) by way of the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*).

That specific phenomenon (dhamma-viśeṣa) which has the nature of being affected by change (rūpaṇa-sabhāva), such as the sensitivity of the ear and so forth, is not included within the sense-base of the ear and so on.

"Dependent on that" means dependent upon that specific phenomenon. The method of answering questions, characterized by non-inclusion—such as [the statement] "Those phenomena are not included in how many aggregates...
[they are] not included in four aggregates," etc.—is explained further below.
When a question is answered after being asked, it is what is "indicated" (uddiṭṭha) here.
By the phrase "the instrumental case is used for specification," he clarifies that very quality of being distinguished by the aforementioned inclusion of that phenomenon.
Thus, it should be understood that the presentation of the method of questioning and answering proceeds after having determined the specific qualities of the phenomena to be questioned and answered.
But is it not the case that this meaning is already obtained by the mere phrase "included by what is included"?

It is not so obtained, because that [phrase] merely indicates the phenomena (*dhamma*) themselves. For this is an enumeration of the methods (*naya*), not an enumeration of the phenomena. Thus, in the Pāḷi, in the exposition of the terms "included by what is included" and "not included," it says:
"Those phenomena which are included by the eye-base through the inclusion of aggregates, bases... [and so on]... through the inclusion of elements."
Having said, "They are not included," he asked, "By how many aggregates... [etc. ...are those states not included?
and having replied, "Those states are not included by four aggregates, two bases, and eight elements," the second term regarding non-inclusion was taken up.
Otherwise, [if it were not so], "those states which are included by the eye-base through inclusion by way of aggregates..."
"Not included by way of inclusion in the bases (āyatana), not included by way of inclusion in the elements (dhātu)—which ones are these? Thus it would have to be demonstrated.

This is the method. To make clearer the meaning shown by the extension (atidesa) in the phrase "In those too," etc., he said "By the third term. He says this with reference to the term stated as being understood through an elliptical expression (luttaniddesa).
The designation of the instrument (karaṇaniddesa) is used in the sense of the agent (kattuatthe), [referring] to those that are included and not included.
Because it is stated that those phenomena are included or not included by means of those [other] phenomena.
For in that context, in the canonical text, inclusion and non-inclusion are stated by way of the phenomena themselves, in the phrase: "those phenomena which [are included] by those phenomena.
However, in the second and third [sections], the non-inclusion and inclusion of phenomena are stated by way of the qualifying door known as inclusion and non-inclusion.
Regarding the word "vuttā" (it is said): it is stated there that "the instrumental case is used for specification. Therefore he says: "For there... [etc. ...of another dhamma.
In that context, "by way of a different nature" means by way of a different mode characterized as being either included or not included.
"Of a different nature" refers to a different nature characterized as being either not included or included. "Among these" refers to the fourth and fifth [categories].
“By another phenomenon” (*dhammantarena*) means by a different phenomenon. “Of another phenomenon” (*dhammantarassa*) is used as a qualification for that other phenomenon;
for in this context, the specification of a particular mode is made by means of a phenomenon itself to qualify a phenomenon.
“By the first word alone” refers to the first word stated as “included” (*saṅgahitena*), etc. “By the others” refers to [the words] “associated,” “dissociated,” etc.
By the second and third words that have been stated. "In this" means among the four [cases] beginning with the eleventh.

The instrumental case should be understood as expressing a qualification (*visesana*), just as in the second and third [words], and not as expressing the agent (*kattua*), as in the fourth and fifth; such is the intended meaning. He clarifies that very point with the words "of the questions and answers," and so forth.

"From various conceptualization" (*vividhakappanato*) means from conceptualizing in various ways or manifoldly; the meaning is from conceptualizing the states of inclusion and non-inclusion, as well as the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, both separately and together.
Since that conceptualization is an analysis in the manner already described, he says: "The meaning is 'from differentiation'.
Because the factors associated with resolve (*adhimokkha*), which has the characteristic of determination, proceed by way of a mode of deciding upon the object...

These are the states spoken of by way of decision (*sanniṭṭhāna*). Having included those [states] together with the remaining states associated with the two sets of fivefold consciousness and with doubt, he says:
"All mental arousings spoken of by way of decision—all mental arousings spoken of by way of decision.
"The others" refers to contact and so forth. "Of all" refers to the eighty-nine mental arousings.
“Should be grasped” means it should be comprehended by way of inclusion and so forth. [It is grasped] by means of resolution (*adhimokkha*) with a vast objective field.
“Of others” refers to initial application (*vitakka*) and the rest. Regarding the statement [in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*]: “Resolution is resolving;
its characteristic is determination,” and in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*: “With craving as condition, there is resolution; with resolution as condition, there is existence.”
And this refers to the statement that has been made. "When the meaning exists" means when the meaning is being stated thus: "from determination... [and so on]... from the commonality.

"In those things to be mentioned" refers to those things to be mentioned for the purpose of grasping the inclusion and so forth. Contact and the others, ending with attention, have already been stated.
"Of such a kind" means because of the absence of any other dhamma—whether common, such as contact and the rest, or uncommon, such as resolution—that is similar to them.
"Is it not the case that the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) and the stability of consciousness (*cittatthiti*) are also common [to both]? True, they are common;

however, showing that there is a distinction, he says: 'But the life-faculty...,' and so forth. The construction is as follows: those whose nature is non-concentration (*asamādhisabhāva*), having not attained the state of strength (*balabhāva*), are to be expressed by the general term alone.
And those whose nature is concentration (*samādhisabhāva*) are to be expressed by both the general and specific terms."
"Unification of mind" (*cittekaggatā*). There is nothing else to be expressed by the word "distinction" (*visesa*) other than a concentration that has attained strength;
for there is nothing to be pervaded by a general term or excluded by a specific term, since only unification of mind—which is the very nature of concentration—is grasped.
A general term does not exclude what is other [than itself]... [etc. ...because it illuminates that distinction.
"Of that very same phenomenon" means of that very phenomenon of concentration which has attained strength.

"By those indicating differentiation" means it should be expressed by words such as "concentration," "strength," and so forth, which indicate specific distinctions. Words are defined as those that indicate a general characteristic while excluding what does not pertain to others.
By contrast, through the very words of general and specific characteristics that function by taking up what is to be pervaded and what is to be excluded from others—[the meaning is established].
It should not be described as having the nature of feeling (vedanā), such as pleasure and so forth.

Therefore—because one-pointedness of mind (citt'ekaggatā) is grasped by dividing it into two ways, namely, that which has the nature of non-concentration and that which has the nature of concentration—therefore [the former] would manifest only as having the nature of non-concentration, since it occurs independently of the qualifying term (*visesa-sadda*).
"The other" refers to the qualifying term, such as "the power of concentration" and so forth. "Here" means in this internal summary of the matrix (*mātikā-uddesa*).
This refers to when [the factors] such as contact are common, or when resolution (*adhimokkha*) is directed toward a broad object.

Anticipating the objection, "Is it not the case that one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*), if taken without being separated [from the other mental factors], is common just like feeling (*vedanā*)?", he says: "Or even though undivided," and so forth.
This is because of the statement: "One-pointedness of mind is the stability of the mind, the state of non-distraction; for immaterial phenomena, it is their life-span and stability."
It should be understood that the life-faculty of concentration (samādhijīvitindriya) is to be described by way of its dependence on other phenomena.
"Does not deserve" means here that it does not deserve to be mentioned in the summary (uddesa), when contact (phassa) and the rest—which ought to be stated directly—are being enumerated.
The commentary on the matrix (mātikā) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition (Niddesavaṇṇanā) 1.
The First Method: Commentary on the Terms of Comprehension and Non-comprehension 1.
Commentary on the Terms of the Aggregates (Khandha)

6. By stating, "The four aggregates are spoken of as things to be directly known," and so forth, and by stating, "The aggregate of form is to be directly known," and so forth, they are the objects characterized by direct knowledge;

thus he says, "of those directly known by way of their intrinsic nature. By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "to be fully understood, etc.," the states of being abandoned, realized, and developed are included.
By the phrase "predominance, etc.," the states of being a predominance condition, manifestation, foundation, and so forth are included.

It is like the distinction between the Truths and so forth; that is, the various modes of expression such as the Truth of Suffering and so on, are distinguished by their specific characteristics, such as being "to be directly known" (abhiññeyya) or "oppression" (pīḷana).

And it is because it is stated in this way—namely, because it is spoken of by way of the basis for what is to be directly known within the matrix of the headings of the method—that there is a commonality (sabhāgatā) among those material phenomena, the five aggregates, by virtue of their being the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), just as there is a commonality among the five aggregates by virtue of their being aggregates, but not by virtue of their being the feeling aggregate and so forth.

He states the characteristic of inclusion (*saṅgahalakkhaṇa*). "Thus" (*iti*) means "therefore," that is to say, because material phenomena (*rūpadhammā*) are similar to one another by way of their state as the aggregate of matter (*rūpakkhandhabhāva*), therefore [it is so].
This refers to grasping by way of the very object-aspect known as the state of the aggregate of matter.
However, when grasped by way of the word, it is either by way of the expression "aggregate of matter" or by way of the state of being expressible by the expression "aggregate of matter."
Now, in order to make that same meaning more evident, it is said: "The aggregate of form, etc.

By "the former" is meant the aggregate of form. In the passages beginning with "based on the aggregate of perception," one should apply the phrase "when joined with the former" and so forth as appropriate.
This concludes the answer to the fivefold inquiry regarding the aggregates in the exposition of the term "aggregate" (khandhapada) without differentiation.
He said, "It is the very last of all," referring to [the section] "immediately after the answer to the fivefold question regarding the analysis.
Commentary on the *Āyatana-pada* and following: 40.
Although the answers are similar even for the single [sections], the answers for the truths of origination and the path are as follows: "The truth of origination..."
Because it is defined thus: "The truth of the path is included by one aggregate... [etc. ...by one base and one element;
it is not included by four aggregates, eleven bases, and seventeen elements. Herein:
in this description of the terms for the faculties (*indriya-pada-niddesa*). "Of the dyads of eye, ear, eye-faculty, and pleasure-faculty": the dyad of eye and ear.
Regarding the "pair of eye-faculty and pleasure-faculty" among these pairs: for the eye, ear, and pleasure faculties, the answer in the section on single factors (*ekaka*) is identical:
"It is comprised by one aggregate, one base, and one element; it is not comprised by four aggregates, eleven bases, and seventeen elements.
However, for the pair of eye-faculty and ear-faculty, [the answer is]: "The eye-faculty..."
“The ear faculty is included within one aggregate, two bases, and two elements;
it is not included within four aggregates, ten bases, and sixteen elements. “The eye faculty and the pleasure faculty are included within two aggregates, two bases, and two elements;
they are not included within three aggregates, ten bases, and sixteen [elements].”
The answer for the pair of the eye-faculty and the pleasure-faculty (*cakkhusukhindriya-duka*) is not similar [to that] of the elements (*dhātu*).

Nor is the answer for a triad (*tika*) similar to that of pairs (*duka*), such as the pair of the eye-faculty and the ear-faculty (*cakkhusota-cakkhusukhindriya-duka*) being dissimilar to the triad of the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, and the pleasure-faculty (*cakkhusotasukhindriya-tika*).
"Here" (*idha*) refers to the description of the terms for the truths (*sacca-pada-niddesa*). "And by a triad" (*tikena ca*) refers to the triads of suffering, origin, the path, and so forth.
And: “They are comprised within the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements;
they are not uncomprised by any aggregates, any bases, or any elements”—this is the identical answer.
6. Commentary on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda).
61. By the expression "ignorance" (*avijjāvacanena*): by the mention of "ignorance" in the phrase "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise" (*avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā*).
No qualification need be made; the intention is that one should say "all consciousness" (*sabbampi viññāṇaṃ*). He states the reason for this with the words "even wholesome [consciousness], etc.
Because, by way of a response similar to the answer, all consciousness and so forth are included. "Of these" refers to the terms beginning with "consciousness. "Here" means in this [text].
In the first method, it is understood that even those things not born of kamma are included, because the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*) is also taken into account.
71. "Of phenomena in the states of being born... and so forth refers to phenomena existing in such states as being born. "Merely by way of the state of being born, etc.
means by way of the mere existence of the states of arising and so on. "Having separated" means having made a distinction from the state of existence.

In the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), those things which do not exist [as independent entities] but consist merely in the state of being the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of ultimate phenomena (*paramatthadhamma*) are the mere states of the ultimate phenomena.

Although they do not possess an ultimate intrinsic nature themselves, they are nevertheless apprehended as having the nature of "being affected by form" (*ruppana-bhāva*) because they constitute the arising and so forth of a material phenomenon (*rūpadhamma*).
Therefore, the connection is made by bringing in the phrase: "These are similar to the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), whereas birth, aging, and death belong to the immaterial (*arūpa*)."

"Each one is a separate entity" means that just as birth and the other [characteristics] are each distinct within a single material group (*rūpakalāpa*), so too they are within a single immaterial group (*arūpakalāpa*).
Therefore he said: "Just like the birth and so forth of a material group," and so on.

He said this because birth and the other characteristics—which constitute the arising and so forth of feeling and the rest, whose functions are experiencing, perceiving, and cognizing—are not grasped in that same way.

“...are ungraspable. By this, he states that there is no inclusion of birth and so forth within the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and the others. Since it is stated in such passages as, “Birth, monks, is impermanent and conditioned,” there is indeed a designation of “conditioned” (saṅkhata) for birth and the rest as well;

therefore, it is said that they are included in the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) by virtue of its function of conditioning the conditioned, [expressed as] “the conditioned... are of the same class. And for that very reason, regarding the aggregate of formations—

The state of having the ultimate meaning of non-absolutism (anekanta-paramattha) should be understood. Likewise, "twofold" means they are of two kinds by way of the arising and so forth of material and immaterial phenomena, according to the manner already stated.

"By that" means by the sense of commonality as previously described. "By those aggregates and so forth" refers to the aggregate of form, the aggregate of formations, the base of mental objects, and the element of mental objects.
The commentary on the first method, the inclusion and non-inclusion of terms, is finished.
2. The second method: Commentary on the terms "included by what is included" and "not included.
171. Regarding the phrase "included by what is included," here the words *saṅgahita* (included) and *asaṅgahita* (not included) do not have different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*).
It should be included because it is intended as that which qualifies and is qualified.

For the author says, "showing that very same [thing]...," in order to demonstrate that the very same phenomenon which was previously mentioned as being uncomprised—being distinguished by the distinction of being comprised [elsewhere]—is here questioned and answered by way of its state of being uncomprised. For those phenomena which, by way of the eye-base, are [included] in the aggregate-composition...
Included by way of the inclusion of the bases and elements, yet not included by way of the aggregates and so forth—this very non-inclusion of those same [factors] was asked and answered again.
Therefore it was said: “By the eye-base... [and so on]... nutriment.

“In all instances” means in all methods (nayā) and sections (vārā). “Of the commonality of inclusion as aggregates and so forth” refers to the general term “by inclusion as aggregates,” etc., without distinction.

Regarding the groupings of aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth that have been stated: it is said, "A general designation applies to specific instances," because [the general term] is always dependent upon a specific [context], as expressed by the words "because of the dependence on distinctions in both the questions and the answers.
It is stated that the questions and answers are for the purpose of bringing about the comprehension of those distinctions;

thus, although the enumeration of the aggregates and so forth is stated without distinction in such phrases as "by the grouping of aggregates," it is [actually understood] through the specific categories of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and the rest.
“Specific” means the enumeration of aggregates and so forth; the meaning is that they are included by way of the aggregates and so on. “Pure” means exclusive and complete;
what is meant is that they constitute the general category.
Regarding the phrase “therein,” it refers to the second method as previously established. He says, “included...,” because the general description is specified by its particularity.
"Because they have been determined. "In the three groupings" means in the three groupings such as the aggregates (khandha) and so forth.
"By others" means by the remaining two or one [of those groupings]. They would be shown by this much alone, because even by that much, the state of being included or not included is made manifest.
"Of these" refers to the phenomena spoken of by way of their state of being included or not included. "Of such a kind" refers to...

“Of those whose specific distinctions have not been determined, such as ‘the eye-base’ and ‘the ear-base,’ etc.”—“Because of impossibility” means because it is impossible to define them in the manner already stated.
The function of the matrix of methods (*nayamātikā*) is merely to show the method of inclusion (*saṅgaha*) and so forth;

however, those aggregates (*khandha*) and so on, as well as the wholesome (*kusala*) and so on, in which inclusion and the rest occur, are their objective domain (*visaya*). Therefore, without them, inclusion and the rest [would be impossible].
There is no occurrence [of such a case]. Therefore he said: "Because this matrix (mātikā) depends upon both internal and external matrices.

It should be stated as "comprehensive" (saṅgāhaka) and "non-comprehensive" (asaṅgāhaka). For whatever dhamma is mentioned here by way of being comprehensive is indeed also mentioned by way of being non-comprehensive. Thus:
"Those dhammas that are included by the inclusion of the aggregates (khandha-saṅgaha) are not included by the inclusion of the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu)," and "those dhammas..."

“Not included by way of inclusion in the aggregates, but included by way of inclusion in the bases and elements”—where there is no determination of specific phenomena to be asked about or answered, there, according to the first method and the sixth method, it is stated: “By how many aggregates is the aggregate of form included?
By one aggregate. “With how many aggregates is the aggregate of form associated? None. With four aggregates...”
And thus it is by way of the state of being questioned and answered as "dissociated. "In the others" means in the second and subsequent methods.

"Of each respective [one]" refers to that which is to be questioned and answered—having been determined in an unspecified form as "those phenomena"—by way of its definitive specification as "those very phenomena."
"In this" means in this treatise (*pakaraṇa*). "By whichever" refers to whichever inclusive category, such as the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth.
"In the aggregates and so forth" means in the aggregates, bases, and elements (*khandhāyatana-dhātu-saṅgaha*). "By that and that" refers to the inclusion within the aggregates and so forth.

"Another" means other than those respective inclusive categories. Whatever class of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) there may be—whether included or not included—that is excluded from those [categories], that very thing [is what remains].

“Those phenomena that are included by the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) through inclusion by aggregates (khandha), but not included by inclusion by bases (āyatana) or elements (dhātu)” is stated by way of being both inclusive and non-inclusive.
There is no other phenomenon [that could serve as its counterpart], because there is an absence of even a similar thing that could be inclusive of it.
However, one might think that there is inclusion by way of a partial similarity; rejecting that, he said: “And not...”
“...so... it is. With the words beginning “And that which,” he provides an alternative explanation.
And with the words beginning “If moreover,” he clarifies that very same point—that there is no inclusion by that [category]—by demonstrating the absence of such a reading.

In this context, “that very same” refers to whichever aggregate of form and so forth was stated as being the includer; that very same aggregate of form and so forth would then be included by that [includer].
If it were something to be included, then by that very fact he shows the characteristic of its non-inclusion, saying:
"For that [part] itself is neither a similar nor a dissimilar part of that. Just as the eye-base and so forth are parts of the aggregate of form and so forth which is their collection;
the aggregate of form is neither an includer nor a non-includer of the eye-base and so forth, because of the absence of the state of being either similar or dissimilar.
This same method applies to the remaining cases as well. By the phrase "contained within the aggregate" (*samudāyantogadhānaṃ*), etc., he makes the very meaning already stated even more evident.

Therein, "by which" (*yena*) refers to the distinction (*vibhāga*). "Those" (*te*) refers to the parts. "Of those" (*tesaṃ*) refers to the parts. Here, due to being contained within that [aggregate], there is an absence of distinction;

due to the absence of distinction, there is an absence of similarity and dissimilarity; and by that, there is an absence of the relationship between the subsumer (*saṅgāhaka*) and the subsumed (*asaṅgāhaka*).
It should be understood that [the term] "shown" (dassito) is used.

Just as a collection of parts is neither inclusive nor non-inclusive of its members due to the total absence of both similarity and dissimilarity, so too [the Buddha], demonstrating that it is not so for parts that possess partial similarity and dissimilarity, spoke the words beginning with "likewise" (tathā). In that context, the phrase beginning with "just as" (yathā) is as follows:
By showing an example, the meaning as previously stated is made clear.
The construction is: "By the inclusion of aggregates, [it is] inclusive and non-inclusive," and so on for the rest.

For the intention is this: it is not possible for a single part... [as before] ...to be of a different nature (visabhāga) such that the whole could be both inclusive and non-inclusive. And here, let alone inclusiveness, even non-inclusiveness—

Having taken into account the objection, "But why is it rejected?", he says, "Therefore," and so forth. Therein, "therefore" (tasmā) refers back to the matter already stated as the reason. The construction is as follows:

even though there is non-inclusiveness [of the self], it is distinct from that which is other than the self, distinct from that which is included within the self, and distinct from that which shares a portion of the nature of the self.
Furthermore, this [is explained by] "the aggregate of form" (rūpakkhandho).
This was said with reference to the three modes mentioned in the passage beginning, "It is neither included by the aggregate of form nor not included," and so forth.

As for the statement, "These have no inclusive nature (saṅgāhakatta)," it means that those things described as being the self, contained within the self, or having a portion of the same nature as the self, lack precisely the state of being inclusive because they lack any commonality (sabhāga). Therefore it was said: "For that very [self]..."
“Of the same class as that,” and so forth. “By which” means by way of being inclusive.
“Of such a kind” should be understood as not including the three aforementioned types, even though they are of a different class; this is the intended meaning.

“By that” refers to the statement beginning with “the sphere of mental objects” (*dhammāyatana*). [It refers to] the whole, of which the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and so forth are a single part.
The meaning is that the inclusion (*saṅgāhakatta*) of the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) [within the aggregate of form] is the state of the whole being included by a part;

that is to say, the inclusion of the eye-base and ear-base—which are parts of the aggregate of form, which is the whole—is the state of the part being included by the whole. If it does not show this, then what does it show?

He said: “By means of the divisions of the enumeration of the four aggregates,” and so forth. Therein, “by means of the divisions of the enumeration of the four aggregates” refers to the analysis of the enumeration of the four aggregates beginning with form (rūpa).
“Fivefold” refers to the state of being divided into five modes, namely: the inclusion of the four aggregates beginning with form and the inclusion of the consciousness aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha).

Therefore he said: “by way of being that which is to be enumerated and that which is not to be enumerated. In the phrases “by one aggregate” and so forth, the instrumental case (*karaṇatthe*) is used.
Having considered that the statement refers to the instrument (*karaṇa*) and not to the agent (*kattū*), he said: "of those independent of inclusion and non-inclusion. For this very reason, he said:
"because of the mere presence of the object as instrument (*kamma-karaṇa-matta*). As for the second and subsequent methods, they are the demonstrations of non-enumeration and so forth;

that is, the demonstrations of non-enumeration and enumeration. [Objection: But do not enumerations and so forth also exist in the second and subsequent [methods]? [Response: It is true they exist, but they are merely qualifiers (*visesana*).
The term "secondary primaries" (*appadhānāni*) is stated thus by way of those primaries that serve as the basis for what is to be qualified.

Because the agent and so forth are specified by such statements as, "Those phenomena which are included within the aggregate of form by means of the eye-base," he says, "because of the presence of the triad of agent, instrument, and object.

"In such and such a way" means in the manner of each respective category, such as the aggregate of form and so on. "The state of being or not being such-and-such an aggregate and so on" refers to similarity and dissimilarity.

The meaning is as follows: the state of being the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and so forth for material phenomena and the like is "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*); the absence of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and so forth is "heterogeneity" (*visabhāgatā*).
"In the discernment of phenomena as they have been determined" means in the investigation of phenomena according to the categories determined by the formula, "those phenomena which are phenomena.
"Of the grasper and the graspable" refers to the grasper, such as the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*), and the graspable, such as the ear-base (*sotāyatana*), and so on.
"Of that which is to be included. "The state of having the same aggregates, etc. means the state of having one and the same aggregate, etc.;

the meaning is the state of belonging to the aggregate of form, etc. "The absence of that" means the absence of that state of having the same aggregates, etc., namely, the state of belonging to a different aggregate, etc.

"This" refers to this very quality—consisting in being countable or uncountable in such and such a way in the first method—which [is applied] in the second and subsequent methods to those things already mentioned.
The presence or absence of the state of being this or that aggregate (khandha) and so forth is what is meant by the presence or absence of those respective aggregates;
this is the distinction between these two types of methods regarding their similar and dissimilar aspects.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the truth of origin, the faculty of pleasure, and so forth," the truth of the path, the faculty of suffering, and others are included. This is because [the former] lacks the quality of being inclusive.
Because there is an absence of non-inclusion for that which is distinguished by being included;
for it is not possible to say, "Those phenomena which are included by the aggregate-inclusion through the truth of origin are not included by the base-and-element inclusion," and so forth.
The indeterminate categories and others are similar to the truth of suffering. By the others means because of the absence of both inclusion and non-inclusion by the base-and-element inclusions.
The construction is "not extracted. The passage beginning with "Thus" (evam) is stated by way of concluding the meaning as it has been explained.
"Not the aggregate of form" (na rūpakkhandho) means "not every phenomenon belonging to the aggregate of form. Regarding the phrase "by the word 'aggregate'":
this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), not in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*); thus he says, "by inclusion within the word 'aggregate'."
"Meaning. For that very reason, in order to negate its status as the agent (*kattā*), it was said:
"not by the grasper (*saṅgāhaka*). Since there is no instrument (*karaṇa*) devoid of an agent, he said: "But this must be stated by supplying 'by some grasper.

The intention is that it does not apply to the graspers themselves, nor to those things to be grasped. For the phenomena belonging to the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) are... [those phenomena] which...

It is said: "They are included by way of inclusion within the aggregates. Anticipating the objection that a rule stated regarding a whole may also apply to its parts, he says, "By this method," and so forth.
He states, "The exclusion of the opposite is effected by the word *eva*," because the meaning of the word *eva* is not merely the exclusion of something else.
Therefore, he says: "The exclusion of what is other than the includer..."
[This is] the meaning of the word *eva*. And by the phrase "he looks" (*pekkhati*), he makes that same meaning even more clear.

For if the word "he" (*so*) and so forth were intended to express inclusion (*saṅgāhaka*), then in the statement "only the aggregate of form is included by the eye-base," it would follow that the eye-base itself is the includer;
thus, the intended meaning would be impossible. Therefore, [the author] now...

Contemplating that impossibility, he said, "How... and so forth; this is indeed easy to understand. "Therein" means in the phrase "by means of the eleven and a half bases and elements. The words "by the aggregate of form" (rūpakkhandhena) must be supplied for the purpose of qualifying the bases and elements.
That [aggregate] itself is not the subsumer of its own parts, nor is the collection [of parts] the subsumer of those parts.
And since this meaning has already been stated [by the words] "and it does not exist," he said: "The aggregate of form... does not exist. "By this method" means:
by this method, because there is no such inclusive nature as that which was described, whereby there could be a non-inclusion of what has already been included.
The absence of non-inclusion is stated in the Commentary [by the words] "And that... does not exist. "By way of inclusion" means...
The construction is as follows: it is not tenable to say that non-inclusion [of a part] by way of being included in a non-figurative sense implies its non-existence.
That "inclusion" refers either to inclusion of the whole by itself, or to the inclusion of parts of itself. "By that" means by the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).

"Of those" refers to the aggregate of form and its parts. Furthermore, there is dissociation from the aggregates of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and so forth, and from the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth.
"Viya" means "like," serving as a dissimilar example. [The phrase] "by these"—meaning by the aggregates of form, feeling, and so forth, and by others of a similar nature;
and [the phrase] "these and others"—the same principle applies here as well.
Precisely because it has been included therein, this is shown by what was demonstrated below. "Ettha" means in this section. "Aggahaṇe" means in the non-inclusion.

"In not being mentioned" means "there is no instruction [regarding it]"; this is the sense. "In the case of the truth of origination and so forth" means that such a reason would apply to the truth of origination, the faculty of pleasure, and so on.

Why? Because when there are categories of phenomena included within those aggregates and so forth—such as the truth of origination and the rest—there is an absence of any non-inclusion of them within the inclusion of the bases (*āyatana*) and so forth. "By the aggregate of form and so forth" means by the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, and the rest.
There is simply no inclusion; why? Because it has already been stated that "he himself is not its includer"—this is the meaning.
Even though there is a connection between the aggregate of form and so forth with one's own aggregate of form and so forth... [the text continues] ...there is no inclusion.
However, for another [aggregate], such as the aggregate of feeling and so forth, because it lacks inclusion by means of the aggregate of form and so forth, there *is* non-inclusion.

The construction (*yojanā*) is as follows: "the absence of both" means the absence of being included [in one category] and not being included [in the other]. Here, in this section, the construction is:

"of the *dhammāyatana*, the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), and so forth"—that is, because the *dhammāyatana* and so forth are subsumed under the four aggregates (*khandha*), and the life-faculty and so forth are subsumed under the two aggregates.

He says "perhaps" (*sati*) with apprehension, because they are not mentioned in the canonical text (*pāḷi*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the inclusion of] the first *dhammadhātu*, the six bases (*saḷāyatana*), and so on is intended.

And by the second [definition], the inclusion of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) and so forth within a single aggregate (*khandha*) is to be understood. For the faculty of pleasure is included within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) alone.
Regarding the phrase "of these," there is no absence of inclusion for the fourfold aggregates, the dyads of aggregates, and so on; rather, such inclusion certainly exists.

Therefore, the non-existence of that [inclusion] is not an absolute rule (*anaikantika*). "By the method stated previously" refers to the method stated in the passage beginning with "But by the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), etc."

"In that very same [place]" means in those aforementioned terms "with visibility" and "with resistance. "Taking it after having turned back" means taking it after having first turned back from what was previously stated, that is, by way of re-examination (*paccāmasana*).
"The state of being inexpressible" refers to the state of being inexpressible regarding their being comprised by a compendium or not being comprised by a compendium.
"Precisely because of the absence of non-comprehensiveness... not because of the absence of comprehensiveness": this is because they lack non-comprehensiveness.
It shows that there is likewise no state of being a unifier, and for that very reason, neither the state of being unified nor the state of not being unified [exists].
The commentary on the terms "unified by the second method" and "not unified" is concluded.
3. Third Method: Commentary on the Terms "Not Unified" and "Unified."
179. "Among those not included in the inclusion by way of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha)"—this is the locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*).

"Therefore" means because partial similarity (*ekadesasabhāgatā*) is not the same as total similarity (*samudāyasabhāgatā*); "therefore" [means] because of that. "By that" means by the aggregate of form.
"Those" refers to the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling and Nibbāna. And just as there is no inclusion due to partial dissimilarity (*visabhāgatā*), so too...
Showing that there is no lack of inclusion even by way of partial commonality, he says, "not only," and so forth.
The construction is: "they are indeed included; they are not non-included. "Those" refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling, Nibbāna, and subtle material phenomena.
"By those" refers to the consciousness aggregate, the eye-base, and so on. "Not mixed in any way" means not mixed in any manner whatsoever.
It establishes the non-existence [of Nibbāna] because it is not included by way of being unmixed. "Just as with the aggregate of form...

and so on... "it does not exist" means that just as Nibbāna is not included by any inclusion because it lacks commonality with the aggregate of form, likewise it is not included by the aggregates of consciousness, the eye-base, and so forth, through the inclusions of bases and elements; thus, there is an absence of inclusion within the aggregates.
It is stated thus because it has already been made clear.
"Of such kinds" refers to the aggregate of form, the aggregate of consciousness, the eye-base, and so forth. For it is not with reference to Nibbāna that it is said:
"Those phenomena which are not included by the aggregate of form, the aggregate of consciousness, or the eye-base under the inclusion of aggregates..."
It can be said that [they] are included by way of inclusion within the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu). Therefore it was said:

"Precisely because of the absence of being inclusive. Likewise, one cannot say, "Those phenomena which are not included by way of inclusion within the aggregates (khandha) among the indeterminate (abyākata) phenomena are included by way of inclusion within the bases and elements," and so forth;
for such a phenomenon does not exist. Thus he said: "Including Nibbāna... and so on.

The construction is: "the mention of 'in reality' (bhāvato) should be understood. Therefore he said, "For not," and so forth. "Anything" (kañci) refers to some kind of category of phenomena (dhammajāta).

"Those" (te) refers to the indeterminate phenomena (abyākatadhamma) and so on. "Of itself" (attanoti) is said with reference to the indeterminate phenomena and so on. "A single part" (ekadeso) refers to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and so on. "Sharing a portion of the nature of a single part of itself" (attekadesasabhāgo) refers to Nibbāna;
for it shares a portion of the nature of that [aggregate] by virtue of being included within the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) and the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu).

"Being a collector of what was not previously collected" means that those things such as the perception aggregate (*saññā-khandha*) and others which were not included by the collection of aggregates (*khandha-saṅgaha*) are now included by the collection of bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). Because they form a collection with aggregates that are of a different class and with nibbāna,
no phenomenon (*dhamma*) whatsoever is excluded from the phenomena base (*dhammāyatana*) by way of the collection of aggregates.

The construction is: "it is included. Regarding the phrase "included by the base of mental phenomena" (*dhammāyatana*), the meaning is that it is included by way of the enumeration of the base of mental phenomena.
[This refers to] a portion of the base of mental phenomena mixed with gross matter.
The commentary on the section concerning what is included by what was not included in the third method is finished.
4. The Fourth Method: Commentary on the Terms "Included" and "Not Included" 191.
"Of the three inclusions" refers to the inclusions of aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).
When non-inclusion is stated prior to inclusion, or inclusion is stated prior to non-inclusion, it is spoken of according to the specific manner in which inclusion and non-inclusion occur.

He said, "Because it is included... [and so on] ...it is taught. Since non-inclusion arises from the absence of inclusion, he said, "in the absence of the specific occurrence of inclusion," meaning that what is caused by inclusion is indeed a particular mode of the occurrence of inclusion itself.

[This refers to] a specific phenomenon included within the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) which has already been included by any of the three types of inclusion, such as the truth of origination (samudayasacca), and which is again [treated] in the same way.
That specific category of phenomena, such as the truth of origin and so forth, is included by what is included.
It is not excluded because of the absence of being an includer; rather, it is not excluded simply because it is not an includer.

For just as those which are not includers by means of three ways of inclusion are not mentioned here, likewise those which are not includers by means of two or even one way of inclusion are not mentioned here. "Included by them" means by those [ways of inclusion].
The phenomena are comprised by the three modes of inclusion (*saṅgaha*). "Of whom" means of whichever person who is the includer.
"By the term expressing the whole" means by that which expresses the meaning of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth without remainder.

"By that term for the aggregates and so forth"—in the phrase "it would thus go into inclusion by that," it should be construed as "by that term for the aggregates and so forth. However, not construing it in this way...
"It cannot be said that there is no other thing included [in a category] which, having been included by its own inclusive factor, would again be included by that very same factor.

Why? Because it is not the case that whatever class of phenomena included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is included by the aggregates and so forth through such factors as the truth of origination, it is included by that very same truth of origination."

The construction is as follows: it was not only that remaining dhamma of the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*)—namely, origination-truth (*samudayasacca*) and so forth—that was asked about and answered;
rather, [the question concerned] that dhamma of the aggregate of volitional formations consisting of contact (*phassa*) and the rest.
"Of what is included" means "distinguished by the state of being included. Therefore, one's own includer, such as the complete characteristic (*sakalakkhaṇa*) and so forth.
The meaning should be understood as follows: having grouped [them] together, there is nothing else that would fall under such categories as "aggregate" (*khandha*) and so forth;
that is to say, feeling (*vedanā*) is a separate aggregate and sound (*sadda*) is a separate base (*āyatana*).
[This is] by means of another aggregate or the like. "Unmixed" (*asammissa*) refers to the indeterminate (*abyākata*), the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), and so on.

“Unmixed,” like [the previous example]. For it is not the case that... “here” means that the inclusion (saṅgaha) characterized by the quality of being included—which is the state of being included of whatever dhamma is included by a dhamma distinguished by the quality of being included—is not asked about nor answered in this section.
“Inclusion” (saṅgaho va) means inclusion alone, not one that requires an agent; such is the meaning. “Not by the includer” (na saṅgāhakena)—this refers to what has been stated above.
The demonstration of what is excluded by the meaning [is as follows]. "Not indeed," and so forth, is the refutation thereof.
The commentary on the term "included by that which is included" under the fourth method is finished.
5. The fifth method: the commentary on the term "not included by that which is not included."

193. "By the method already stated" means that since the fifth method is devoid of the distinctions of inclusion and occurrence and is dependent upon specific phenomena not included [in the previous methods], therefore, whatever specific phenomenon here is not included by any [other] specific phenomenon not included, and which remains unincluded by what is unincluded, must be asked about and answered in terms of its state of being unincluded. That very [method] first...
Demonstrating what has been determined, it says: "Those phenomena not included in the aggregate of form...
[and so on]... those phenomena not included in the aggregates... [and so on]... by those phenomena," following the method stated in the fourth method.
"The demonstration of the phenomena as determined" means the demonstration of the types of phenomena determined in the Pāḷi. "Together with subtle form."
“Together with subtle form”: consciousness taken together with that subtle form; the collection of phenomena accompanied by those [is] “together with subtle form...
collection. But what are they? He says: “the truth of suffering,” and so forth. “Of some”: of Nibbāna, the eye-base, and so on. “By all three types of inclusion”:
by all three types of inclusion in their entirety. Those which do not include [everything] despite being complete types of inclusion are “complete-inclusion-non-including.”

Those things similar to the indeterminate (abyākata) dhammas—namely, those to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by cultivation, as well as those that are neither trainee (sekha) nor beyond training (aśaikṣa), and so forth—are [the objects of this category].
"The others" refers to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and the rest. "By way of their opposite" means by way of the reverse of what was stated;
the meaning is that because there exist things not included within the three groupings, they possess both inclusion and non-inclusion within the complete set of groupings.
Nirvana is included among the non-inclusive [factors]; therefore, the meaning is that it cannot be uncomprised by those [factors] that are non-demonstrable and non-reactive.

Hence he said: "And that very [factor] is not its non-compriser. The nine questions beginning with "Those phenomena which are comprised by the aggregate of feeling" and so forth are the second set of questions and the rest;
together with the first question, they make ten. The questions concerning name-and-form and so forth...
However, he said "twenty-four" because [he meant] "all together there are thirty-four.
The term "distinguishing words such as the aggregate of form" means that the words "aggregate of form" and so forth are distinguishing terms by virtue of not being inclusive [of all phenomena].

And the meaning of "in the question" is "for the purpose of questioning. Alternatively, it is because [the author] wishes to make known the entire passage beginning with "by the aggregate of form" as something intended to be conveyed.
Speech is called a "question" (pucchā) because it has the nature of an inquiry. Therefore, the *Aṭṭhakathā* says: "But here the questions... amount to thirty-four.

For these are shown by way of their characteristics; those determined phenomena are shown by that very characteristic known as "determination," which consists in being either included or not included [in a category].

“*Tadevā*” means by the word *eva*. Regarding the phrase “the term extracted from the question is not included among the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth,” the restriction “only among the aggregates and so forth” is purposeless here because there is no other alternative;
for it has already been stated that “there is no inclusion among the three. Likewise, in the expression “not included at all,” the exclusion of being included [in any category] is intended.

Because it is not intended [there]. However, by saying "that very same," he shows that what is intended is the restriction of the state of being uncomprised by that which was extracted but not comprised;
thus he says, "never," and so forth. In that context, "of another" means of that which was not extracted.
"He shows its indeterminacy" is a demonstration of the result of this restriction. One may connect the elliptical phrase "by way of restriction."
This too was stated in order to make the very same meaning established by the word *eva* even more evident;
for the rule of restriction (*niyama*) applies elsewhere than where the word *eva* occurs. "Of such a kind alone" means precisely the kind brought up in the question;
the sense is: of that very kind which was brought up in the question. "Of that" refers to what is not included. "Of another" refers to the kind not brought up in the question.
By this, he shows that it is only that which was raised in the question and not included by any of the three aggregates that is subject to questioning and answering here, and not anything else.
Therefore he said, "For that which was raised in the question," and so forth.

Furthermore, herein, through the inclusion of the bases and elements, one should understand the state of being accompanied by others for the aggregate of form and so on, and the state of being unaccompanied for the aggregate of consciousness and so on.
"The remaining three aggregates beginning with feeling, as well as Nibbāna, have no inclusion with the entire aggregate of form;
therefore, it cannot be said that they are 'included. However, since there is inclusion by way of a single part, one should understand it thus: 'they are not non-included.
The restriction "material phenomena" (*rūpadhammā*) is intended with reference to the state [of being] extracted in the question.
Showing [this], he said: "The inquiry... [and so on] ...the intention. By this it was stated: "For even feeling and the rest, though not explicitly mentioned, are indeed included.
"In this" means in this exposition of the fifth method (*naya*). "In the first method" means in the first interpretation of the meaning (*atthavikappa*).
"Likewise in the second"—this applies here as well. "By material form and consciousness" means by non-subtle material phenomena and by consciousness; this is what is meant here.
Showing the intended meaning (*adhippāya*), he said: "The meaning is 'gross'... [etc] ...". But how is it that when "material phenomena" (*rūpadhamma*) are mentioned, only gross matter is grasped?
He said: "For here, a portion of matter is included by the term 'matter'.
(196) Regarding "not included," it was stated as such in the sense of being non-inclusive, namely: "not included by the eye-base... [etc] ...".

Although it was stated by way of what is to be asked and what is to be answered that [the "rest"] is not included within the four [aggregates] beginning with feeling, the phrase "But by the eye-base," etc., was said to show that it is not the eye-base alone.
"By which phenomena" means by which among the aggregates and so forth. In the Pāḷi, he summarizes the entire collection of phenomena as those very phenomena beginning with form. Why?
He says, "The response is similar," and so forth, because he utters this as an inspired utterance (*udāna*). By the first inspired utterance.
He says this with reference to the word "two" mentioned in the phrase, "the two external derived [bases]. Of that which was not included. Of the type shown by the words "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth.

The giving of the method (*nayadāna*) is the production of the knowledge of the sequence of the Dhamma (*dhammanvaya-ñāṇa*). [This refers to] such passages as "Form is the sphere of mental objects" (*dhammāyatana*), and so on.
By way of these terms, this method consists of twenty-two terms.
The commentary on the terms "not included" and "included" by way of what is not comprised within the fifth method is finished.
6. The sixth method: Commentary on the terms of association and dissociation.
228. By the word “therein,” he shows that in the phrase “having analyzed the terms of association and dissociation,” it is the terms of association and dissociation that have been analyzed;
and he indicates that what is being referred back is that which is primary because it is what must be commented upon, rather than the terms such as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and so forth.
Having stated, “That which is obtained... should be understood,” he then says, “In the case of the aggregates of form, etc.,” and so on.
He explains that meaning. In this context, "it is not found" means that it is not possible to apprehend [it] as either "associated" or "dissociated.
Even though it is not found, it was included in the question and must therefore be answered by way of negation;
for even a negation is indeed an answer to a question. Thus, in the *Yamaka*: "For whom the aggregate of form has not arisen, for him..."

To the question, "Did the aggregate of feeling not arise?", the answer given was "It did not exist. By this, it is shown that here, among material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), the sense of association (*sampayoga*) is not applicable.
The connection is that even though the term "association" is not applicable, it has nevertheless been included [in the definition].
"In all cases" refers to the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, and so forth. "Of these" refers to material phenomena and Nibbāna.

"Dissimilarity" (*visabhāgatā*) means not having that same nature. For in the case of association (*sampayoga*), there is similarity (*sabhāgatā*) in the sense of arising together and so forth, but not the same-natured similarity as in the case of inclusion (*saṅgaha*).
Therefore, for material phenomena and Nibbāna, which lack the state of arising together and so forth, that state of arising together and so forth is said to be their "dissimilarity.
"Because of the absence of that" means because of the absence of that dissimilarity consisting of the state of arising together and so forth. Thus, dissociation (*vippayoga*) is also excluded.
Thus it is; the meaning stated as "dissimilarity" (*visabhāga*) and "separation" (*vippayoga*) is precisely this.

By the passage beginning with "In the four," he makes that very same meaning more manifest. Therein, the phrases "of those" and "by those" refer specifically to the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*).
And "dissimilarity" means that [the characteristic] does not exist in form (*rūpa*) or Nibbāna. Therefore, he said: "And not of a portion of form," and so forth. For that very reason...
