It is precisely because they share the nature of the four aggregates (*catukkhandha*).
"By means of three consciousness-elements" (*tīhi viññāṇadhātūhi*) refers to the consciousness-elements of nose, tongue, and body;

it illuminates those phenomena dissociated [from mind] which lack an object and are mixed with material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), and this is to be construed as "the existence of form" (*rūpabhava*). "By means of five" refers to the five consciousness-elements beginning with eye-consciousness.
"With one mind-element. "Not associated" means not *only* with those that are associated. For it has been said:

"When there are no dissociated [factors], there are seven associated ones, or even all seven. "By that" means by way of the negation of dissociation. "With those" means with the seven consciousness-elements.
"Illuminating the associated" means illuminating only those that are associated, not *only* with those that are associated.

This restriction is to be understood in this way. This same method applies to the remaining [factors] as well. Regarding the associated factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth: they are not to be described by way of being either associated or dissociated;

that very same sevenfold consciousness-element (*viññāṇadhātu-sattaka*) is what is meant. Those things which are not to be described by way of association are "associated-unclassifiables" (*sampayutta-navattabbāni*);

these include mental phenomena (*dhammajātāni*) belonging to different continuums (*bhinnasantānika*) and those occurring at different moments (*nānākkhaṇika*), even if they are formless (*arūpa*). All consciousness-elements, whether unmixed with objects or mixed, are associated with their respective [mental factors].

It should be understood that they are to be illustrated by such terms as the "base of mental phenomena" (*dhammāyatana*) and so forth; all consciousness-elements (*viññāṇadhātu*), whether without objects or mixed with those having objects, are to be illustrated by such terms as "non-mental-factor" (*acetasika*) and so forth; and the combination of both of these is to be illustrated by such terms as the "truth of suffering" (*dukkhasacca*) and so forth.

"If it were thus" means: if there were no dissociation (*vippayoga*) from phenomena that are either without objects or mixed [with them]. "Phenomena that are without objects or mixed" refers to both types of phenomena.

[It refers to] all consciousness elements together with the element of Nibbāna and the states associated with them. By "by the aggregates and so forth" is meant by the aggregates, bases, and elements themselves, and not by the immaterial aggregates alone.

He shows that this is not a fault because it was stated with reference specifically to the immaterial aggregates: "those states which are dissociated from those states," and so on, beginning with "mixed with the non-objective. "A portion of that" refers to [the phrase] "mixed with the non-objective," etc.

They are parts of the collection of phenomena already mentioned. "Being a collection of other parts of that same [collection]" means that, having become parts of that very aforementioned collection, they constitute the collection of other components such as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and so forth. "Due to the absence of division" means due to the absence of differentiation.

And here, "differentiation" is intended in the sense of absolute differentiation; for there is no absolute differentiation between a collection and its components, or between a generality and its particulars.

There is absolute difference [between them], because they are characterized by both difference and non-difference. Indeed, it is with reference to their absolute difference alone that it is stated in the *Saṅgaha*: “There is no distinction among the parts included within a whole.
By this [it is meant] that because of the existence of non-distinction, there is an absence of the state of being both similar and dissimilar.

“Of these” refers to all the elements of consciousness (*viññāṇadhātu*), etc., including those that are without objects (*anārammaṇa*) and those mixed with others; and these are unwholesome (*akusala*) and indeterminate (*abyākata*). “Of these” refers to wholesome (*kusala*), unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena (*dhamma*).
Therefore, because those things whose individual natures are distinct cannot constitute a whole, a part, or the like;

and because, since wholesome states and so forth are themselves the aggregates and so forth, the act of designating them as "aggregates" and so on would entail their being a whole, a part, or the like—thus, according to the method already stated, there would be no dissociation—therefore, avoiding that [fault], he says: "without designating them as aggregates and so forth," and so on.
“Of these” refers to the wholesome and so forth. Their mutual dissociation is stated in such passages as, “those states which are dissociated from wholesome states,” and so on.
“In all” means in all the questions beginning with the second.
Among the thirty-six sections of the *piṭṭhiduka*, twenty *duka* sections are found according to this method; the remainder—
"He said 'sixteen only' because it should be stated as 'sixteen. For that very reason, regarding the phrase "one hundred and twenty-three words," the construction is:
"twenty-three" here should also be stated as "twenty-one. "In all cases" means in all questions.

The aggregates of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), the base of phenomena (dhammadhātu), and the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu) are the collections of numerous phenomena belonging to a single momentary continuum and to multiple phenomena belonging to different times and different continua.

He said: "Of the continuity of time... [etc. ...of the elements. "Mixed with a single part" means that the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) and so forth are mixed with other aggregates and so on only by way of their own single parts;
they are not mixed with the bases of psychic power and so forth that lack an object, nor with material form (rūpa) and Nibbāna, which have no objects.

"By those of the same temporal continuity" means by those within the same temporal continuity—by parts belonging to the same interval of time that are devoid of distinctions in the continuity of time—such as the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) and so forth.

The construction is as follows: by certain specific portions of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) and so forth—namely, the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*), and so on—the truths of origin (*samudayasacca*) and the rest are indeed analyzed according to their states of association (*sampayoga*) and dissociation (*vippayoga*); while the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and the rest are grasped in their state of dissociation.
By those [factors], namely the truths of origin and so forth; those [factors], namely the aggregate of perception and so forth; with certain [factors] that are capable of arising simultaneously.

"By those distinguished according to their respective parts. For even though they are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) and so forth, the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*) and the others do not attain association with the truth of the path (*maggasacca*) and the others. "Of these" refers to the aggregates of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*), perception (*saññākkhandha*), and so forth.
"Arising together... [etc. ...and dissimilarity": this refers to both similarity and dissimilarity as appropriate, characterized by such states as arising together. By that aforementioned reason:
Because of the attainment of both association and dissociation.

"Composites of different times" refers to the aggregates of those [factors] whose constituent parts belong to different times. Furthermore, within a single continuum, only one factor at a time occurs.
Therefore—meaning because this is so—of those aggregates such as feeling (vedanā-khandha) and the rest, that which is to be analyzed...

Because it does not exist as a distinct portion. The faculties of pleasure and so forth are also portions of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*). Therefore, by way of not making such a distinction:
if the eye-consciousness element and so forth do not make a division of the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*) because there is no simultaneous thing to be divided, then why [is it said]:
"The eye-consciousness element... [up to] the mind-consciousness element [consists of] sixteen..."?
Having taken to heart the objection that it was stated [in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*] as “dissociated from the elements (*dhātu*)”, he said: “It is stated that the aggregates, bases...
are dissociated. “In this very way” means just as [it was explained] for consciousness analyzed by way of the analysis of elements (*dhātuvibhāga*).
“The state of being associated with those” means the state of being associated with those aggregates. For, just as [consciousness] exists within a continuity (*santāna*) of the same time...
The aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness, occurring within a single moment of consciousness, are associated with the truth of origination;
likewise, because they exist in different continua and at different times, they are dissociated from it. Thus he said: "In this way, its state of dissociation...
[etc. ...is not stated," referring to those three aggregates which are undivided due to the absence of any division based on heterogeneity.
With the words "In the case of division," etc., he makes that same point more evident. Regarding the phrase "by those devoid of division":

it is not appropriate to say that [the mind] is "dissociated" from the aggregates of feeling and so forth when they are undivided—meaning they belong to the same mental moment within a single, simultaneous continuum.
Therefore, he says: "while existing... by way of their presence. In that context, "existing," "common," and "of the same kind" [refer to these factors].
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). For existing material and immaterial phenomena are not dissimilar (*visabhāga*) to one another.
The phrase "like unarisen states" is an illustration by way of a dissimilar example.

Just as "unarisen states" refers to the future time and thus involves a distinction of time that has been touched upon, so too [this case] refers to that which does not involve such a distinction of touched-upon time; this is the meaning. It should be extracted.

What is meant is that it should be taught by means of a teaching. Association exists only between what is present and what is present, and dissociation exists only between those things fit for association;
thus, association and dissociation depend upon the state of existence. Therefore he said, "depending on the state of being present.
For this very reason he said, "of that which is non-existent," and so forth. And the word "that" is a quotation.

"By those that are indivisible" means by those that are without division due to the absence of heterogeneity (*visabhāgatā*). "In the difference of time not grasped" means in a specific time not grasped.
By the statement, "There is no association of that which does not exist...," the association of that which exists with that which exists is shown by way of elimination (*pārisesato*).
"When a difference indicative of non-existence is taken" means [the association] with those phenomena as they have been taken.

When their very specific distinctions—which indicate the non-existence of anything dissociated from them—are grasped through such statements as, "The immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*) is dissociated from one aggregate (*khandha*), ten bases (*āyatana*), and sixteen elements (*dhātu*)," then by that very distinction of being subject to change (*ruppana*) and so forth, their mutual heterogeneity is also necessarily grasped;
thus, the construction is that there is dissociation (*vippayoga*). However, when those distinctions are not grasped, by each [of those factors]...

"By way of inclusion" means that when the specific distinctions indicating non-existence as previously stated are not grasped, or when dissimilar factors are not grasped— such as in the case of [the statement]: "Feeling, perception,
and the aggregate of formations are associated with three aggregates, one base, and seven elements"— then,
because the dissimilarity has not been grasped by those respective inclusions which indicate similarity, there is indeed similarity.
And this being so, since there is similarity [between them], what is the similarity here? He says: "Because of its existence... it is. "Of that" means of the similarity.
"Therefore" means because dissimilarity is not obtained and similarity is obtained. 262.

"Like initial application" means like initial application in those mental arisings that possess both initial and sustained application; for that [initial application] is [distinguished] by being devoid of [sustained application].
And [there is] that which is without initial application and has only sustained application. Therefore he said: "They do not adhere to the arising of consciousness in other sections.
For that very reason, it is subordinate; since here the factors of the second jhāna alone are predominant, he said: "those which are predominant.

By that same [reasoning], because initial application was not included here among the arisings of consciousness with both initial and sustained application due to the inclusion of those with no initial application and only sustained application, in the triad of initial application...
And because it is precisely the second group that is intended. In the "immediately following method" refers to the exposition of the associated and dissociated terms.

"Having the same course as the truth of origination" means having a similar mode of occurrence. "Thus" (iti) means for this reason. Those states consisting of vicāra alone without vitakka are not included;
like the truth of origination, they have not ascended to the teaching. They do not have the same course as those states accompanied by both vitakka and vicāra.
The interpretation [is as follows]. For if those [states] were of the same category as those with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*), then it would have to be said:

"Those states which are associated with states that have no applied thought but have sustained thought alone (*avitakka-vicāramatta*)—those states are dissociated from none of the aggregates, from none of the bases, but are dissociated from one element. Since...

However, they share the same destination as the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*). For just as it is impossible to state a dissociation from some [factors] for those who are dissociated from what is associated with the truth of origination, so it is also with them.
Thus he will say: "The truths of origination, etc. ... The tenth... is stated;
here, in the tenth method, [it refers to] those dissociated from those [states] that are without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitakkavicāramatta*).
Dissociation from sixteen elements has been stated; and in the concluding method, the inclusion of those dissociated from them within eighteen elements has also been stated.
Therefore, he shows that they do not share the same destination as the states with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*).

"In those accompanied by applied thought" means in those together with applied thought. "Among those" refers to the factors of the second jhāna which are without applied thought but have sustained thought (*avitakka-vicāramatta*) along with applied thought.
“Without applied thought and with sustained thought only” means those [factors] mentioned among those already taken up.
“All of them” means that it is possible to say that all those factors—including applied thought—are present in the second jhāna. For it is said in the *Sampayoga-vippayoga-pada-niddesa*:
“Factors without applied thought and with sustained thought only are associated with one aggregate, with one base, and with one element, by way of some [of these].”

It has been stated. Therein, "by one aggregate" means by the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). For that is the collection, meaning the collection of phenomena (dhamma) spoken of as "states without applied thought but with sustained thought.
Anticipating the objection, "But surely applied thought (vitakka) is also included here in the compendium of phenomena, and it is associated not only with sustained thought," he says:
"For it is not [the case] for a single part thereof... etc.... By the words beginning with "Just as," etc., [he explains].
He clarifies this same point by way of the illustration of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*). Its meaning is as follows:

just as it was stated that the association with the three aggregates applies to the bases of psychic power such as the basis of zeal (*chandiddhipāda*), which are parts of the aggregate [of the bases of psychic power] but not to the aggregate itself, so too here, the association of applied thought (*vitakka*) with others does not apply to the aggregate that is "without applied thought but with sustained thought" (*avitakkavicāramatta*).

If it is argued that, in this case, one should not say, “The basis of psychic power (iddhipāda) is associated with two aggregates,” and so forth, [the author] replies, “No, it should not be said not to be so,” and says, beginning with “But as...”.
Therein, “in them” means in the bases of psychic power. “Of the aggregate” means of the aggregate of the bases of psychic power.
Their association with those aggregates, such as the feeling-aggregate, has been stated by such expressions as, “The basis of psychic power is associated with two aggregates.”

"Tenā" means "by investigation. With the words beginning with "na hi," he clarifies—by way of showing examples—the absence of anything that cannot be predicated regarding the associated nature of the states (dhammas) as they have been realized.
Some say that doubt and the delusion co-arising with it are defective in relation to delusion;
some are associated with delusion, while others are not. By the phrase "with delusion," he speaks specifically with reference to the delusion co-arising with doubt.
Thus, for this reason, the aggregate (*samudāya*) is not associated with that delusion (*moha*).
Nor is there any other state (*dhamma*) existing as a cause by which that aggregate could be called "having roots to be abandoned by vision" (*dassanena-pahātabba-hetuka*).

In this manner, the meaning is that it should be demonstrated that [the aggregates] are not to be described [as such], according to the sequence: "cultivation... [and] those that are associated. Thus.

Just as it cannot be said that there is association with the collection of causes to be abandoned by vision (*dassanena-pahātabba-hetuka-samudāya*), so too, there is no state whatsoever that could be associated with a phenomenon that is without initial application (*avitakka*)...

[and so on] ...there is none. Therefore—because among those states that possess only sustained application (*avitakka-vicāramatta*), there is not even one that is dissociated from sustained application (*vicāra*)—therefore. "Those" refers to the states possessing only sustained application. Even in a single phenomenon... [and so on] ...is established.
As in: “States that are not conditioned by a cause; unconditioned states.
The commentary on the sixth method, the section on association and dissociation, is concluded.
7. Seventh Method: Commentary on the Section on Associated and Dissociated States.

306. Even though there exist associated states such as the three aggregates or parts of the three aggregates within those [states] beginning with the truth of origination, and even though there exist other states dissociated from those associated ones—such as material form and Nibbāna—there is no absence of dissociation [from the primary state].

To demonstrate in detail the meaning stated in brief, it was said, "For not... and so forth. From that, [it follows that] there are other states distinct from the arising of consciousness accompanied by greed.

There is no dissociation whatsoever among the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena within the aggregates and so forth, because they are included within the five aggregates and the rest.
"Those very same mental arisings" means those very mental arisings accompanied by greed (*lobhasahagata-cittuppāda*).

Regarding the phrase "of other phenomena," it should be understood that the word *pi* ("also") has been elided; thus, it means "of other phenomena as well. By the word "thus" (*tathā*), [the following is indicated].
It is not that those very same phenomena constitute one and a half bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu); rather, he brings forward this point: "those and others besides them. One might ask:
"Is it not already established by their being 'other than those' that the dissociation of the others from them is proven? To this he replies with the words "And not," and so forth.
"By aggregates other than those" means: by aggregates other than that arising of consciousness accompanied by greed, the other phenomena associated with greed are dissociated.
They do not exist. Why? Because of the absence of dissociation from the aggregate... [etc. ...due to the absence of dissociation. The meaning of this is:
because there is no dissociation of the parts—the greed-accompanied states—from the aggregate, which is the collection of other states accompanied by greed;
and likewise, because there is no dissociation from the aggregate of those parts that, having been individual components, constitute the aggregate of others. By means of this aggregate...
It shows that there is no dissociation between a part and the whole, nor between one part and another part; rather, it is only between a part and its own constituent parts.

"This is the method" means that this same principle stated regarding the truth of suffering applies to the factors of the path, such as the faculty of pleasure and so forth, because they are partial aspects of the immaterial aggregates. "Without remainder" refers to those thoughts that are not externalized. Thought.
For [it is] not external to the aggregate. Since the method already stated—beginning with “That aggregate, indeed”—is applicable here, he says:
“No reason is seen for its non-inclusion.

This same principle should be observed regarding the answers concerning the other truths, such as the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), because the truth of origination and so forth are included here.
The intended meaning is that it is not included. Since the context concerns associated [states], the phrase "by another" refers to something other than what is associated;
thus he says, "the meaning is: unmixed with what is dissociated. Now, in order to establish that same point through contrast as well, it is said:
"Neither-painful-nor-pleasant... are included. By this characteristic, [it means] "unmixed with what is dissociated."
By the characteristic already stated. "Mind" (*citta*) refers to the question: "Those phenomena which [arise] with mental states.

"Seven together with associated terms" means the seven questions that have come down through phrases explaining phenomena associated with mind, beginning with "those phenomena which [arise] with mental concomitants" (*cetasika*).
It is considered "deficient" because of the non-inclusion of three triads (*tika*); it is with reference to these that [it is said]: "In the *Tika*..."
Thus it is said: "three. That triad of terms should be understood as the last [term] among the triads of feeling and rapture, and the first among the triads of applied thought (*vitakka*).
Since the meanings being elucidated by the extracted term (*uddhaṭapada*) are spoken of as "the extracted term" through the metaphorical application of identity, he says:
"by the extracted term, together with the associated [states]. And by that aforementioned extracted term. Joined with the mind (*mano*).
Because it consists merely of the act of cognizing, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is called "mind" (*mano*); thus he says, "associated exclusively with the mind-element.
The commentary on the terms "associated" and "dissociated" in the seventh method is concluded.
8. Commentary on the terms "dissociated" and "associated" in the eighth method.
317. The four immaterial aggregates are said to be dissociated from the aggregate of material form (*rūpakkhandha*).

There is no association of these with anything else, because there is no other such associate [for them] to exist. Furthermore, it has already been stated that there is no association of a whole with a part.
Material form and Nibbāna are dissociated from the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and the others; of these—
"There is no association with anything whatsoever," he said, [expressing this] as "with the aggregate of form... there is none.

"By that" refers to the statement beginning with "those phenomena dissociated from the aggregate of form. The commentary on the section concerning the associated state dissociated by the eighth method is concluded.
9. Explanation of the Terms *Sampayutta* and *Asampayutta* in the Ninth Method 319.
Having stated, "This is a compound word," [the author] says, "Of whichever aggregate, etc.," in order to show what kind of compound it is;
the meaning is: "of whichever [factor], such as the feeling-aggregate (*vedanā-kkhandha*), etc. The phrase "that which is here called associated" refers to this ninth method.

That category of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) which is said to be "associated" (*sampayutta*). In the phrase "among the internal and external matrix-phenomena," such as the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and so forth, the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).
For that category of phenomena is selected as being itself associated with the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and so forth, which are associated with it.
"Non-yoke" (*ayoga*) means non-association. This will be stated in the tenth method (*nayā*). For therein [it says]: "With the aggregate of form..."

Having stated, "Feeling and the other [aggregates] are dissociated; the aggregate of material form is dissociated from them," he says, "But Nibbāna is included within the category of subtle matter," in response to the objection as to how Nibbāna is explained.

For in this context—where it is said, "The mind-base is dissociated from one base and one element by some"—just as with subtle matter, even though it is not explicitly mentioned by its own specific name, it is nevertheless understood.
Since *nibbāna* is indeed included by the phrase "by some," in such instances it is understood that *nibbāna* belongs to the category of subtle form (*sukhumarūpa*);

likewise, here too, by the phrase "or by those mixed with form," it should be seen that non-association is stated even with those things mixed with *nibbāna*, such as the unclung-to and the non-clinging-to.
[This applies] to those factors that function together with words that include all four aggregates without exception.
Because there is an absence of any other associated [mental state], and because association with the past and future does not exist at all, he said, "Only those that are presently occurring...
[etc. ...the meaning is 'by way of the formless existence (arūpabhava), etc. to show its lack of association. "The others" refers to those which do obtain association; but who are they?
They are the components of the formless realm (arūpa) that are unmixed with matter. Therefore he said, "the aggregates of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and so forth."
The commentary on the term "associated" in the ninth method is finished.
10. The tenth method: the commentary on the term "dissociated" in relation to the dissociated.
353. Among those [factors] which are not included in the Canon as being dissociated by way of dissociation, some are dissociated from the dissociated...

Because there is no other separate phenomenon (dhamma), and because it is impossible for there to be dissociation from the aggregates and so forth, he says "the phenomena of the sense-base of mental objects" (*dhammāyatana-ādi-dhammā*) and so on, in order to show this meaning. Therein,

by the phrase "because they consist of phenomena included within all states of consciousness," he expresses the non-existence of any other dissociated phenomenon distinct from the immaterial aggregates (*arūpa-khandha*), which possess specific qualities such as difference in time and so on.

By the phrase "because of the state of being mixed with the objectless," it refers to all [existence] as well. There are these four great existences (*mahābhava*): sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), percipient existence (*saññībhava*), and five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*).

By the phrase "because of the absence of dissociation" is meant because dissociation is impossible. For those things which are dissociated from the Truth of Suffering and so forth, it is not possible for those very same Truths of Suffering and so forth to be dissociated from them.
In the case of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, dissociation from something is possible.
The commentary on the term "dissociated" in the context of dissociation according to the tenth method is finished.
11. The eleventh method: the commentary on the terms "associated" and "dissociated" in the context of what is included.

409. These are the phenomena belonging to the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). By the phrase "by the remaining ones," it refers to the remaining aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), and consciousness (*viññāṇa*).

By the expression "connected with this," the meaning of the Pāḷi passage—"those phenomena associated with the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*)"—is made clearer by way of demonstrating the connection between these terms; thus, the meaning of the word "with some" (*kehicī*) is [explained].
He said, “Of some,” and so forth, in order to perform [the classification]. The connection is: he spoke in order to show the meaning. Regarding the word “distinguishingly”:

here, the distinguishing characteristic (*visesana*) should be understood as the pointing out that those phenomena—excluding craving—are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), the base of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*), and the element of phenomena (*dhammadhātu*);
for that reason, they are stated to be comprised by the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*) through their inclusion within the aggregates and so forth.
It is said, “by those things that are not associated with itself,” meaning by those things that are subject to the fault of being a self. Therefore it was stated:
“Consciousness should not be said to be either associated with consciousness or dissociated from consciousness.
The qualification “by those things capable of association” is made with reference to two things—subtle matter and Nibbāna—and not to craving and the like.
The commentary on the terms "associated" and "dissociated" as included in the eleventh method is finished.
12. Commentary on the terms "included" and "not included" by way of association in the twelfth method. 417.
In the ninth method, those associated that are distinguished by association were set forth; and in the twelfth method, those [associated] distinguished by association...
Regarding the terms "included" and "unincluded," since both are taken as distinguished by association (*sampayoga*), it is said: "The twelfth... are found.
The commentary on the terms "included" and "unincluded" associated with the twelfth method is concluded.
13. Commentary on the terms "associated" and "dissociated" with the unincluded in the thirteenth method.
448. By "which" is meant by way of the aggregates such as the form-aggregate (rūpakkhandha) and the bases such as the dhamma-base (dhammāyatana).

Also by the threefold inclusion of aggregates, bases, and so forth. Again, by "which" is meant by way of the immaterial becoming (arūpabhava) and so on. These are indeed gross bases because they are not included even within the inclusion of bases and elements (āyatanadhātu).
"Those" refers to the four-constituent becoming (catuvokārabhava) and so forth. "The remaining mentioned" means those left over from the form-aggregate, the dhamma-base, and so on. Even though...

Since association with those things not included by way of non-inclusion is impossible, the aggregates of feeling and so forth do not fit, do not ascend, into the exposition here in the thirteenfold method. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary:
"By means of the aggregate of feeling, material and immaterial phenomena are not included under the categories of aggregates and so forth; and for those, what is called 'association' does not exist."
They are not indeed non-associated [factors], because they exist as a composite state consisting of the five aggregates and so forth, which are free from conceptualization (*avikalpa*).

"Those" refers to the phenomena mentioned by the word "and so forth" in the phrase "the truth of suffering and so forth. They might be non-universal... [etc. ...like phenomena that are without initial application and sustained application (*avitakkavicāra*).
There is no dissociation between them, because a mental state (*cittuppāda*) occurring apart from them is impossible. [This applies] to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*).
Because those not included [in the aggregates] lack both an object and a mixture [of factors], it is not said that there is "existence through dissociation. Thus it is said:

"Material and immaterial phenomena are not included. "Due to the absence of both" means due to the absence of both association and dissociation. All consciousnesses together with their non-objective [factors], as well as the factors associated with them and those two types [associated and dissociated], are to be understood by way of the non-mental, the mental, the mundane, and so forth.
The commentary on the terms "associated" and "dissociated" as included in the thirteenth method is finished.
14. Fourteenth Method: Commentary on the Terms "Included" and "Not Included" by Way of Dissociation 456.
"Because it is merely the intrinsic nature of phenomena": because phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) are merely phenomena, and because they are merely particular states.

"Samuccheda" (eradication) means that by this [means] something is utterly cut off. This is the fourteenth method, which constitutes the final conclusion of the investigation into the categories such as inclusion (*saṅgaha*).
Therefore, he said, "in the final method. A question devoid of the phenomena to be answered is a "vain question" (*moghapucchā*);
even though it is of such a nature, it serves as an indicator of the absence of any phenomenon to be answered. Thus he said, "Because their question is vain, those [phenomena] are not found."
"His questions are vain," thus he is "one of vain questions. This is the eighth method, because there all questions are vain.

"And together with that" means together with that eighth method; in this concluding method—and in the eighth method as well—these [factors] such as the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) and so forth are not found in any way whatsoever.
He states the reason for this: "because even dissociation is absent."
The commentary on the section concerning what is included and not included by way of dissociation from the fourteen modes of conjunction is finished.
The sub-commentary (*anuṭīkā*) on the *Dhātukathāpakaraṇa* is completed.
[Now begins] the sub-commentary on the *Puggalapaññattipakaraṇa*.
1. Commentary on the Matrix (Mātikāvaṇṇanā) 1.

Regarding the statement, "Having taught the *Dhātukathā*, he next spoke the *Puggalapaññatti*," the author explains the reason for this by setting forth its origin, beginning with the words, "In the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*... and so forth. In that regard, although in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*...
An analysis of each successive term (*anupada-vibhāga*) has also been made for phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) and the earth element (*pathavī*), and it is not merely a compendium (*saṅgaha*).

However, that [analysis] was stated for the purpose of demonstrating their inclusion by way of the triplets (*tika*) and pairs (*duka*), such as the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*) and the triplets and pairs of causes (*hetudukādi*). Therefore, it is said: "of the phenomena included by way of the triplets, pairs, and so forth, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. For this very reason, that treatise...

It received the name *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. Granted that even in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, the analysis of the aggregates and so forth is shown by such passages as, "At that time, however, there are four aggregates," yet that is not as preeminent as it is in the *Vibhaṅga* treatise.
Therefore, taking that [latter] as preeminent, he said: "having shown the analysis of the aggregates and so forth in the *Vibhaṅga*."

Because it was known specifically as the *Vibhaṅga*. In the phrase "in the *Dhātukathā*," the locative case denotes the locus (*ādhāra*), as it does in the expression "in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and the *Vibhaṅga*.

For the locus refers to the treatises (*pakaraṇa*) which constitute the collection of those constituent parts—namely, the activities consisting of compendium (*saṅgahaṇa*), analysis (*vibhajana*), classification (*pabheda*), and exposition (*vacana*)—just as one says "the branches on the tree. Alternatively, this is the instrumental case; [it means] "by means of the *Dhātukathā*."
The meaning is "having become the instrument.

And here, while teaching the states to be directly known (*abhiññeyya-dhamma*), the Blessed One, skilled in teaching, first taught the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, showing their classification by way of triads and dyads;
and since analysis is preceded by classification, immediately thereafter—
He taught the *Vibhaṅga* (Analysis) while demonstrating the classification by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth.

Furthermore, he taught the *Dhātukathā* (Discourse on Elements), which demonstrates—by means of the various methods such as inclusion (*saṅgaha*) and non-inclusion (*asaṅgaha*)—those phenomena suitable for the aforementioned classifications and groupings;

for that [work] has the nature of a framework consisting of both internal and external matrices. Indeed, it is not possible to lead the aggregates and so forth, nor the wholesome and so forth, without the method of inclusion and non-inclusion and the rest. Therefore, he said:
“Thus, for those things that have been grouped and analyzed. In order to clarify all of this—the teaching of phenomena (dhamma) by way of their grouping, analysis, and classification;
as well as the conventional designation of a person (puggalavohāra) based on the aforementioned phenomena;
and the classification of that [person] by way of being liberated at times and so forth—the *Puggalapaññatti* has been taught.
This should be understood as the reason for the sequence of teaching of these four treatises (*pakaraṇa*).
"Of them" means of those phenomena (*dhamma*). "By way of intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvato*) means by way of their respective natures, such as "contact," "feeling," and so forth.

"Depending upon" (*upādāya*) means depending upon the aggregates (*khandha*), [as in expressions] such as "person," "being," or "individual. "Description" (*paññāpanaṃ*) refers to that description which is divided according to its specific basis, such as the [conceptual] designation (*paññatti*) of "appropriation" (*upādā*) and so on.

...that designation. As for "by way of classification," it means by way of the divisions such as the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, or those liberated from the conventions (*samaya*) and so forth.

Expanding upon the meaning briefly stated—that by which designation there is a making known both by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and by way of dependence (*upādāya*)—he says: "In that regard, those phenomena... and so forth.

Therein, even in the case of a designation of what lacks intrinsic nature (*asabhāva*), the underlying basis (*mūlabhūta*) of that designation is indeed a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*); however, it is merely [the basis] for them...
Showing that the distinction [between the types of phenomena] arises from their mode of occurrence, their differentiation, and their support, he says: "Those phenomena... [etc. ...arise.
Therein, by the phrase "occurring in a sequence of before and after," he speaks of the designation of a continuum (*santāna-paññatti*), demonstrating its dependence on a continuous flow;

by the phrase "by way of an assemblage of non-substantial entities," he refers to the remaining designations. For there are three designations: the designation of a continuum, [the designation of a collection, and the designation of a concept].

“Designation of a collection” (*samūha-paññatti*) and “designation of a specific state” (*avatthā-visesa-paññatti*). In this context, *pabandha* means continuity (*santāna*), and *samudāya* means a collection (*samūha*).
A specific state refers to such things as arising and so forth, or infancy and so forth.

Since it is established that continuity and collections lack an intrinsic nature (*asabhāva*) when there is no grasping of an intrinsic nature, the phrase “by way of a collection lacking an intrinsic nature” indicates that the mention of “lacking an intrinsic nature” is for the purpose of demonstrating a designation that is distinct from both continuity and collection.
It should be understood that by this, the inclusion [of the aggregates] is stated as a designation for specific states (*avatthāvisesapaññatti*).

"Of those" refers to the phenomena bound to the faculties (*indriyabaddhadhammā*) previously mentioned by the word "which" (*yaṃ*). For this very reason, he said: "and of other external material forms and nibbāna.

"By way of the collection of their own-nature and the differentiation of their own-nature" means by way of the collection of their own-nature such as the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) and so forth.

And [it is so] by way of the specific intrinsic natures (sabhāva) of the eye-base and so forth. There is also a reading: “By way of the distinction between the intrinsic nature of a collection and the intrinsic nature of that which possesses it.
In this context, the “intrinsic nature of a collection” refers to the characteristic itself as a collection, devoid of the distinctions of states within the continuity of the intrinsic nature.

For it is stated that even the designation of the aggregates (khandha-paññatti) is a designation of intrinsic nature (sabhāva-paññatti). “By that” means by the various classifications such as the designation of the bases (āyatana-paññatti) and so forth.

Regarding the designation of intrinsic nature (*sabhāvapaññatti*): "Designation of intrinsic nature has been analyzed" refers to the analysis of the designation of the intrinsic nature of contact and so forth, as in "contact is touching," and so on.
By the word "all" (*sabba*), the particle *pi* includes the designation of wholesomeness and so forth that occurs by way of generality among phenomena possessing intrinsic nature.
A collection of phenomena such as form, proceeding as a continuum and accompanied by specific states, is the basis for the grasping of unity.

"One is designated as a 'being' (satta)," yet that is not a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma); thus he said, "But the designation of a person (puggala-paññatti) is a designation of what lacks intrinsic nature. By "by that" is meant by the designation of a person.

Since the continuity and the collection of phenomena deserve to be described as dependent upon phenomena, therefore [he says]: "Depending upon phenomena that possess intrinsic nature, such as those to be fully understood..."
It is said: "set in motion.

Furthermore, a designation for what exists is called a "designation of intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvapaññatti*), while a designation for what does not exist is called a "designation of non-intrinsic nature" (*asabhāvapaññatti*).
"All designations" refers to all types of designations, such as designations by dependence (*upādāyapaññatti*), designations by function (*kiccapaññatti*), and so forth. If...
All designations (*paññatti*) are shown here; as to how the name "person-designation" (*puggalapaññatti*) arose, he says:
"among the designations of aggregates, etc. "Elsewhere" means in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and other such works. "Those phenomena" refers to those phenomena such as the aggregates.
"By way of being the basis for designation" means by way of being the foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for the act of designating. For the foundation consists of the phenomena that are to be designated.
Of making known. And having done so, the person is included together with the aggregates and so forth. "Those phenomena" (ye dhammā) means those phenomena that are designations (paññatti-dhamma).
"Desirous of making known" (paññāpetukāmo) means desirous of setting them down, desirous of establishing them by way of the distinction of their bases without confusion.

"The delimitation of the designation" (paññatti-paricchedaṃ) refers to the delimitation that constitutes the designation, which is differentiated by the distinction of its bases. In this way, the meaning here should be understood.

"Proclamation of the classification of commonality" (*sāmaññappabhedapaññāpanā*) means the proclamation of meanings that consist of both the general and the specific. The masculine designation (*pulliṅganiddesa*) is used because of its dependence on the word "meanings" (*attha*).
"Therein" (*tattha*) refers to seeing and so forth, which constitute the demonstration of meaning within the context of the proclamation.

"This has such a name" (*idamevaṃnāmakaṃ*) means that this collection of meanings, such as "being afflicted" (*ruppana*), etc., possesses such a name as the common designation (*samañña*) of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*), and so forth.
“Making each respective portion” means bringing about the inclusion of each respective meaning, such as form, feeling, and so forth, within its own distinct classification.
Likewise, because it is precisely the arising of perception, he says: “Laying down is indeed making known.

For “making known” (bodhana) is called “laying down” (nikkhipanā) in the sense that it establishes the meaning to be understood within the continuum of one who is to be enlightened. By the term “establishing” (paññāpanā) and so forth, it is expressed through an abstract noun formation (*bhāvasādhana*).

Having said this, he stated, "But that which... should be understood," in order to prevent the suspicion that another meaning might be intended by the mention of a different means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
"Of those respective phenomena" (*tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ*) means of those phenomena to be made known by each [designation].

[This occurs] because of the fact of being seen by a designation (*nāmapaññatti*) consisting in seeing, and because of the fact of being established by one consisting in establishing. "The cause for that" (*taṃnimittattaṃ*) refers to the cause for that seeing.

And [it shows] its being the instrumental cause for establishing [the term]. For a "cause" (nimitta) is designated by way of its being the agent, as in the expressions "alms provide lodging" and "the truths that produce the state of an Ariya are the Noble Truths" (ariyasaccāni).
"Not occurring in the Canon" means not having been included in the textual recitation, along with specific terms such as "existing" (vijjamāna). Of that which exists...
By saying "of that which exists" (*satoti*) and "of that which is present" (*samānassāti*), he shows this meaning and says, "the meaning is 'of that which has become manifest'.
Likewise (*tathā*): [it refers] to that which does not exist and is not apprehended from the standpoint of the actual and ultimate sense (*saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena*).
In order to make more evident that non-apprehension—which was indicated by the word "likewise" (*tathā*) through the method of contrast (*byatirekavasena*)—he says: "Just as..."
He said, “The wholesome, etc. In that context, “having their intrinsic natures resolved” means having their intrinsic natures analyzed.
“Apprehension” means grasping. “In that mode” means in the mode of form, feeling, and so forth, of that which does not exist.

“In another mode” means in a mode other than that—namely, apart from form, feeling, and so forth—in the mode of the designatum and the act of designating, of that which does exist. [This concludes] the dyad on designation.
This has already been stated [in the text] with the words: "And this doctrine is refuted by the discussion on what is beneficial" (*sevatthika-kathā*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "established merely as worldly convention" (*loka-nirutti-matta-siddhassa*): here, the inclusion of the word "merely" (*matta*) is intended not only to exclude the existence of an actual ontological essence for that conceptual basis (*paññatti-vatthu*), but also to exclude its apprehension as something contrary [to reality].
Demonstrating this, he said: "with a mind free from dogmatic adherence" (*anabhinivesena cittena*).
A fifth truth and so forth—such as another truth or another aggregate—that is distinct from the four truths and the five aggregates;

if someone were to assert that such a thing exists, [the author] says, "It was said... with dogmatic adherence," showing that for one who has grasped what is not as it truly is, that [assertion] would be a mere matter of words.
In both the summary and the detailed exposition, [the person] is mentioned as being possessed of [dogmatic adherence], by way of its predominance.

With reference to their arrival, he says: "In terms of form, [it refers to] the arrival of the three. However, by way of their qualities, the other three designations are indeed included in this treatise within the contexts of the "Upstreamer," "Liberation through Wisdom," and the "Stone-inscription" and so forth.
Without contradicting what was stated thus: "...pe... 'designation of the existent' and 'designation of the non-existent,'" [the following applies].
[This is] by way of non-contradiction. And here, by the phrase "the teachers' doctrines," one's own opinions are to be understood; elsewhere, however, it refers to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

Showing how there is no contradiction, he says "Therefore," and so forth. In that context, regarding the term *paññatti* (concept/designation) as meaning "merely that which is to be made known" because it does not exist [as a substantial entity], he states this alternative analysis of the compound:
"a designation of what is non-existent is a 'non-existent designation' (*avijjamānapaññatti*)."

Regarding "designation of the non-existent" (*avijjamāna-paññatti*): here there are two compounds; namely, "the designation of that which is non-existent" or "the non-existent designation," which is *avijjamāna-paññatti*.
Of these, by the first [analysis], the designation of names (*nāma-paññatti*) is stated; by the second, the others as well, such as the designation of derived matter (*upādā-paññatti*), are included.

"That which possesses its own intrinsic nature" refers to feeling and so forth. "Because of obtaining the name of a corresponding ultimate reality" means because of obtaining the name of a corresponding—that is, suitable—ultimate reality.

The meaning is: because it obtains a name that is ultimate (paramattha) and literal (anvattha); that is to say, because phenomena whose intrinsic natures consist of experiencing and so forth obtain an ultimate name such as "feeling" (vedanā) and so on.
By this, he shows that the word *matta* has the sense of excluding the qualification (*visesanivatti*), and by that, he demonstrates how this specific qualification is excluded.
"To be obtained from another" (*paraṃ labhitabba*) means to be acquired in dependence upon something else, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

"Dependent upon" (*upādāya*) refers to the basis for designation (*paññatti-vatthu*), such as a "being," which is a continuum of a collection devoid of intrinsic nature (*nissabhāva*). "By way of identity" (*ekattena*) means by way of non-difference (*anaññattena*).

"The state of having an unapprehendable intrinsic nature" (*anupalabbha-sabhāvatā*) means the state of having an intrinsic nature that cannot be grasped by knowledge; it is because of this that they are said to be "inexpressible.
A *kirīṭa* (crown) is a specific kind of head-ornament (*moli-visesa*), like those of Vasava and Vasudeva, which has its points curved in the shape of a heap of rice with mice among it.
But since that [term] is indeed also a specific type of crown (*makuṭa*), he said: "A *kirīṭa* is a *makuṭa*.
"The inclusion of all" means the inclusion within [the category of] all six types of designations (*paññatti*) that exist, beginning with the designation by way of comparison (*upanidhā-paññatti*).

"Because it has the quality of being what is to be reckoned" is a statement regarding its characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). For not all [designations] function by way of the reckoning (*saṅkhā*) of a designation by way of comparison, nor do all [of them].

[The first] is predominant in respect of that which is to be reckoned (*saṅkhātabbappadhāna*). However, [the Buddha], showing by way of a partial characteristic that "second," "third," and so forth are designations by comparison (*upanidhāpaññatti*), while "two," "three," and so forth are designations by juxtaposition (*upanikkhittapaññatti*), states "because it is predominant in respect of that which is to be reckoned" (*saṅkhātabbappadhānattā*) with reference to the fact that the latter is predominant in respect of the object to be numbered (*saṅkhyeyyappadhānatā*).
For the word "full" (*pūraṇa*) indicates, by way of illustrating its own meaning, the object that is to be filled.

It illuminates. And because it is "predominant with respect to the reckoned" (*saṅkhāvisaya-padhanova*), the state of being predominant with respect to that which is to be reckoned is stated for the designations beginning with the second [number] up to the tenth;
for as far as the number ten, they are predominant with respect to that which is to be counted. The same applies to the designations such as "two," "three," and so forth.
However, the object to be reckoned may be either existent, non-existent, or both together and separately.
"Missā" (mixed) refers to the six types of designations.

"The others" refers to the designation of the aggregate of clinging, the designation of the continuity produced by that [clinging], and the remaining ones mentioned—the designation of comparison and the designation of proximity.

The designation of clinging, such as the seven types of chariots and so forth, and the designation of comparison, such as long and short and so forth, are non-existent designations (*avijjamāna-paññatti*).

Designations such as "in the hand" (*hatthagata*) and so forth are designations by way of comparison (*upanidhāpaññatti*) and designations by way of combination (*samodhānapaññatti*); these are designations of the non-existent by means of the non-existent.

Likewise, expressions such as "golden-colored, with the voice of Brahmā" possess an internal core of the existent and thus belong to the category of designations of the non-existent by means of the existent;
therefore, it is said: "each respective designation according to its application. By this, it is stated: "the second, the third... and so on.

“They resort to [them],” it is said. The passage beginning with “For that which... and so forth establishes that the aforementioned designations by way of comparison (*upanidhā*) and juxtaposition (*upanikkhitta*) are designations of what is non-existent by means of what is non-existent.
In this context, “that number” refers to the number such as “first,” “one,” and so forth, which is a form to be grasped through the medium of number.
By the word “and” (*ca*), the object of numbering (*saṅkhyeyya*) is included; for that too is to be made known and is thus a designation.
Furthermore, its non-existence in the ultimate sense (paramattha) has already been stated. "Nothing exists" means that nothing exists in the ultimate sense.
By the word "thus" (tathā), this refers back to the state of being non-existent regarding that which does not exist. Therefore he said: "For... [is] not existing.

"In a place" (okāse) means in a location delimited by the Avīci hell up to the Paranimmita-vasavatti heaven; for that is called "desire" (kāma) because it is based upon sensual desire (kāmādhiṭṭhāna).
It is said: by this elision of the latter member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*), he refers to *kāmabhava* as "kāma" in the phrase "in the aggregates produced by karma.
Speech is either sound or volition; because of possessing that [speech], the designation "speaker" (*bhāṇaka*) is applied to the person distinguished by it.

Thus he says: "it follows the side of the designation of the non-existent by means of the existent. For the most part, this occurs through the gateway of perceiving the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).

Since shape is apprehended by means of what is termed "form" (*rūpa*), it is stated—employing a metaphorical identification between the two—that [shape] is "by means of the shape termed the sense-sphere of form" (*rūpāyatana*).
Those belonging to other schools, not knowing how to break this metaphorical identification, claim that the sense-sphere of form has shape as its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
This is because they speak of persons and so forth in such ways as, "a thin person," "a fat person," "a thin staff," or "a fat staff."
The designation [of shape] is the description of the configuration of emaciation and so forth as they are situated within what is reckoned as "form" (*rūpa-saṅkhāta*);

it is not merely the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). Therefore, he says: "Or, when 'shape' is not included in the sense-sphere of form. "By way of the names of individual phenomena" means by way of the respective names of phenomena such as "earth," "contact," and so forth.
This view of the Master also proceeds according to the classification beginning with the designation of function (*kicca-paññatti*).

“Some designations of function (kicca-paññatti) are designations of state (bhūmi-paññatti), designations of the individual (paccatta-paññatti), and designations of the unconditioned (asaṅkhata-paññatti); these are designations of what exists (vijjamāna-paññatti).
Some designations of gender (liṅga-paññatti) are designations of the individual and designations of what does not exist (avijjamāna-paññatti).

Some designations of function are designations of what exists and what does not exist. Some designations of state and shape (saṇṭhāna-paññatti) are [designations] of what exists or what does not exist.”

Because it has been shown that [terms such as] "a discourse on the Dhamma" (dhammakathā) and "the feminine gender" (itthiliṅga) are designations of both the existent and the non-existent, and because the manner of showing how they are designations of the non-existent by means of the non-existent is also demonstrated, he says: "It should be understood as including everything.

Furthermore, in this context, the status of these [designations] as derivative designations (upādāpaññatti) and so forth, and the status of functional designations (kiccapaññatti) and so forth, should be clarified for each according to its appropriate application.

2. "By way of concise classification" means: by way of condensing all the aggregates under the commonality of their nature as aggregates in the phrase "as far as the five aggregates," and by way of dividing the aggregates from that commonality into their specific modes in the phrases "as far as the aggregate of form," and so forth.
"This meaning" refers to this meaning designated as a conceptual construct (paññatti). Or, [it may mean] by way of the commonality of phenomena...

There is a designation, or rather, a specific distinction (*visesa*). Here, this distinction is to be understood in relation to its own generality (*sāmañña*); however, in relation to a further distinction, even that [distinction] becomes a generality.
Thus, as a concise answer to the question, "To what extent is there a designation of aggregates (*khandha*) among the aggregates?", it was stated:
"To the extent of the five aggregates. Regarding that [statement], "among the aggregates..."
Having brought in the phrase "the designation of the aggregates," it should be connected; thus he said, "To the extent that... [etc. ...the designation.
"To the extent that there are the five aggregates, to that extent there is the designation of the aggregates among the aggregates. To the extent that there is the aggregate of form... [etc.

...the aggregate of consciousness, to that extent there is the designation of the aggregates among the aggregates"—in this way, the connection of the text should be made here. For in this way, both in brief and in detail, [it is explained].
And thus the designation of the aggregates (*khandha-paññatti*) has been answered. For, showing that this very meaning was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he said:

"By as much as... beginning with... Therein means: in that statement of the meaning of the answer, or in that reading of the answer and its explanatory statement. "Merely a demonstration of the classification" refers to the classification.

This is merely an illustration. It should be understood that although not explicitly stated, the entire classification of the primary elements (bhūta) and their derivatives (upādā), as well as [the classification] beginning with pleasure (sukha), is intended;
however, that was stated by way of the planes (bhūmi) and the doors (mukha) in the passage beginning, "The aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandha) belongs to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara).
Having thus shown the application of the meaning of the Canon (Pāḷi) according to the method transmitted in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), [the author now proceeds] to show it by another method.
In order to show this, the passage beginning with "Or this" was stated. Therein, "or this" is said with reference to that which is being spoken of.
"In this" means in this exposition of the designation of the aggregates (*khandhapaññatti*). "This" refers to this word. By the phrase "however much...
[is] the classification of the designation of the aggregates," it is shown that there is a division of designations with respect to the classification of the aggregates, both in brief and in detail.
Therefore he said: “He shows [them] by way of the classification of the bases...”. “In another treatise” means in the *Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa*.

For therein the designation of the analysis of the aggregates (*khandha*) is stated with particular excellence. Therefore it is said in the Commentary: “Indeed, by the Fully Enlightened One... [they] were spoken.
And here, in the first method, it is by way of the face-to-face presentation; in the second, it is by way of the basis (*vatthu*) of the designation.
The distinction between these is that their divisions have been shown.

By the phrase "This is the method," he extends the meaning stated regarding the designation of the aggregates (*khandha-paññatti*) to the designations of the sense bases (*āyatana-paññatti*) and so forth.
In that context, the passages "as far as the five aggregates" and "the designation of the aggregates for the aggregates" belong to the scriptural exposition of the designations.

The exposition is given by way of grasping both the beginning and the end. The meaning of the passage, “As far as the twelve bases,” and “the designation of the bases among the bases,” is shown by the phrase, “by whatever means of designation [there are] in brief, the twelve bases.
However, the meaning of the passage beginning with “as far as the eye-base” is shown by the phrase beginning with “analytically, the eye-base. In this regard:
“‘The eye-base... up to ... the mind-object-base’—this is merely an indication of the classification.
By this, everything not explicitly mentioned is also included; thus it was said: ‘Therein, ten bases belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara),’ and so forth.
Alternatively, this is the interpretation of the meaning of the text here: having joined the word ‘yāvatā’ (as far as) with all the terms, [it means] ‘however many twelve bases there are...’”

"However many are the twelve bases (āyatana) and the divisions of the eye-base and so forth that constitute their subdivisions, to that same extent is the division of the manifestation of the bases (āyatanapaññatti).
By this statement, which refers to the division of the physical basis (vatthu) as taught in another treatise, he demonstrates the division of the manifestation of the bases;
in this manner, the same method should be applied to the other manifestations as well.
7. With reference to the phrase "six designations... [etc. ...designation of a person," this passage from the text—"In what way...
[etc. ...in this way there is the designation of the faculties as faculties"—is indeed an exposition (niddesa).

Nevertheless, because it is stated in another section of the treatise by way of the classification of the bases (vatthu), taking into account the various types of designation such as the aggregates (khandha) and so forth, it is merely a summary (uddesa). Thus he says: "The meaning is 'by way of mere summary'."
The Commentary on the Matrix (Mātikāvaṇṇanā) is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Exposition (Niddesavaṇṇanā). 1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Singlefold (Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā).
1. In the sense of burning up contrary states (*paccanīkadhamma*), it is *jhāna*; in the sense of being thoroughly liberated from them, it is *vimokkha*.
Thus, according to the non-figurative sense (*nippariyāya*), the factors of *jhāna* themselves are *vimokkha*: this is the intention of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

However, the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*), considering that—just like the *abhibhāyatana*—the *jhāna* together with its associated states (*sasampayutta*) is the *vimokkha*, stated: "He spoke [thus] by way of intention. These are the *jhāna*-dhammas.
For [the factors] are liberated from their opposites only together with the associated states, not apart from them;

thus, the intention is that there is a joy consisting in an unhesitating engagement with the object by way of delight. Or, just as the designation "jhāna" applies specifically to the jhāna-factors because they stand in a reciprocal causal relationship as conditions for the jhāna, so too the designation "liberation" (vimokkha) applies specifically to those [factors] because of their connection with the function of liberation.
This should be understood by way of metaphorical application to the associated states. First, "the state of being possessed" (*samaṅgibhāva*) is said with reference to acquisition (*paṭilābha*).
For it is stated: "He dwells having touched [it] means he conducts himself having acquired it. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "For that with which... they are called 'acquired'";
thus, here "acquisition" refers specifically to the obtaining of the conditions—such as co-nascence (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and so forth—that are to be accomplished by those [factors].
It should be understood as follows: Just as contact is said to "touch" that object upon which it arises, so too do the associated states [touch it] because they possess that same nature.
Therefore, he says, "for the purpose of touching by means of contact. This is to be connected with the word "opens" (*vivarati*).
By the other phrases—namely, "even access," and so forth—he explains the causes for the attainment of access, preliminary absorption, and subsequent absorption.

"In the sense of a cause" (*kāraṇattha*) refers to the meaning illustrated by the statement: "By means of access... he indeed touches. One should understand that "touching" is a figurative expression for the state of being a cause, in the sense that "one attains the fruit by means of this.

"The first meaning alone" refers specifically to the meaning of possession (*samaṅgibhāva*). By the phrase "those factors" (*tāni aṅgāni*), [it is shown] in their capacity as constituent parts of jhāna.
Only those factors already mentioned are included, not by way of being the "contact-fifth" (the five aggregates) or the "faculty-eighth" (the eight faculties), as it is said:

"The rest... are included. When this is so—that is, when the feeling and the mental joy faculties are to be distinguished from the jhāna factor known as pleasure—then for them there would be the state of being the "toucher" (the subject) and for the other [pleasure] the state of being the "touched" (the object). Therefore he says: "Because pleasure is to be touched."
"By way of the state of being dominated by what is felt" means: by way of the intrinsic nature of feeling, which is defined as the experiencing of an object;
and by way of the state of being followed by associated states, which is defined as a particular kind of pleasure belonging to that very [feeling].

Furthermore, the state of "contemplating" (upanijjhāyana) is a specific form of the aforementioned state of being dominated by what is felt, consisting in the contemplation of a coarse object. For even a phenomenon (dhamma) of undifferentiated intrinsic nature, through the arising of a preceding, distinguished, and specific condition, [becomes so].

In particular, having become differentiated in form, it attains the state of a distinguished fruit. For example, there is a single karma that serves as the cause for the production of the eye and so forth.
Therefore it was said: “The experiencer... because it has been so stated. As for the term “factors” (*aṅgāni*), this plural designation is not used because they are endless;
rather, the plural is used simply because the factors are many. What is established by this? That each one individually...
The construction is thus established. Therefore it was said: "The construction should also be made individually.
If, in the construction "having set aside pleasure," there are the remaining three aggregates, one might ask: should it not be stated that there are the remaining three and four aggregates?
No; because the three are included within the four. Therefore he said: "All constructions... [as] stated."
2. "By means of the liberation at any time" (asamayavimokkha) refers to the liberation of the lower paths.
For that is so called because, unlike mundane liberation, it lacks any specific time that must be prepared for the purpose of experiencing its attainment.

However, the liberation of the supreme path (aggamagga-vimokkha) is not intended here, because of the statement regarding "liberation from certain taints" (āsava). Therefore, he said: "Certain taints have been completely destroyed; one is liberated from certain taints."
He is liberated by the liberation of total eradication from the taints of views. "By means of non-temporal... [etc. ...

"by gain" means by the attainment of that which serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the aforementioned non-temporal liberation. Precisely because of that, he is liberated from certain taints of sensual desire by way of suppression;

this is the meaning. That very person, who has attained the aforementioned partial temporal liberation, is one liberated by occasion (*samayavimutta*). [He is distinguished from] the excellence of non-temporal liberation...

Because it is intended by way of the designation of occasional liberation (*samaya-vimokkha-paññatti*). "He" refers to one who has attained occasional liberation through the supporting condition for non-occasional liberation (*asamaya-vimokkha-upanissaya*).
By means of that preeminent occasional liberation, he is "liberated in such a manner. Here, the word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*):
because he is liberated in such a manner, therefore he is worthy of receiving the designation of "one liberated occasionally. This is for the purpose of full understanding (*pariññā*).

He establishes it by means of a reason. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "But the worldling... was stated in order to make that same point even more evident by way of contrast (*vyatirekamukha*).

Therein, "because of the state of active manifestation" (*samudācārabhāvatō*) means because of the occurrence of active manifestation. "He" refers to the worldling who has attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
If the worldling is not called "one liberated for a time" (*samayavimutta*) due to his nature of returning again, why [is he so called] in the absence of that [nature]?

Because it was not stated that the Arahant is [so] in that way, he said, "But for the Arahant," and so forth. "The state of not being the cause for those" means the state of not being the cause for those liberations, or for that state of being liberated by occasion (samaya-vimutti).
"Everyone" includes the dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka), the one whose vehicle is serenity (samatha-yānika), and even the one who has attained the eight liberations.
The states of being external and internal are established through mutual dependence; they are to be understood according to the speaker's intention.
And he said: "External" means those things existing outside of the supramundane. 3.
Since that which is other than form is not form, in this context the term "form" includes the counterpart-forms such as the kasiṇa-forms;

therefore, by the term "non-form," that which is other than those—namely, the mere objects of the first and third immaterial attainments, being distinct from the non-material aggregates and Nibbāna—is intended.
It should be understood that "taken" means it must be guarded. The very casket of the mind, which is meditation (jhāna), must not be stolen by the thieves of the defilements, who are its adversaries.
Alternatively, it should be understood that under the heading of "concentration" (samādhi), it is actually meditation itself that is being described.

Regarding the phrase "by negligence appropriate to oneself": here, for a non-returner (anāgāmin), this refers to lack of respect, lack of persistence, and failure to act with diligence toward higher wholesome states.
But for one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), [such negligence] occurs through a semblance of negligence of that kind, or through a lack of thoroughness in action of that kind.
This should be understood as being due to the absence of striving in him; for those supreme persons have all striving completely stilled.
"From time to time" (samayena samayaṃ) means at each occasion. For this is both an instrumental and an accusative form used in the sense of a locative. "Because of non-achievement" (anipphattito).
Because it is impossible to attain [the higher paths]. "Assā" means of this commentary statement beginning with "tesañhi.
"Tenā" means by the sutta as it was brought forward. 5.
Expounding that intention for which it was stated that "it should be said 'by means of dhammas'," he says "idha," etc.

In this context, "here" (*idha*) refers to the pair of terms "subject to falling away" (*parihānadhamma*) and "not subject to falling away" (*aparihānadhamma*). "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the pair of terms "subject to agitation" (*kuppadhamma*) and "not subject to agitation" (*akuppadhamma*).
He says, "or merely by a difference in the meaning of the words," because although there is a difference in the verbal expressions, there is indeed a difference in the meanings of those words.
However, regarding the specific meaning to be understood through the gateway of grasping the meaning of the words, there is no difference here.
Because it is by means of these that their status as distinct methods is established.
7–8. *Samāpatticetanā* (volition of attainment) is that volition by which one produces and enters into attainment;
hence he said, "the exertion toward that. Considering that mindfulness (*sati*) is manifested as protection, he said, "guarding... [and so on] ...mindfulness. Hence he said:
“He dwells with a mind guarded by a single guard, which is mindfulness. For it is said of her: “She examines the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states. 11.

One standing on the supreme path, like one standing on the other paths, receives the designation “one who has ceased from fear” because fear has not been severed; thus he said: “And one standing on the path of arahantship... [is] one who has ceased from fear.”

12. "Some" refers to those with weak intelligence who possess rebirth-linking based on three roots; therefore it is said, "they are included by the term 'of weak wisdom' (duppañña). Those whose wisdom (*paññā*) is feeble are "of weak wisdom. 14. It is said, "Where...

[the factors] exist," because for one who possesses indeterminate states (*aniyata-dhamma*), there is the attainment of determinate states through specific conditions. "Due to the absence of that" means due to the absence of a process that is a mixture of both determinate and indeterminate.
16. "To be exhausted" means to be consumed by the path that brings about exhaustion. This refers to the activity of craving (*taṇhā*) and so forth, which acts as a fetter (*palibodha*).

The state of being the "head" (sīsa) should be understood as reaching the summit; however, because Nibbāna is of the nature of the unconditioned (visaṅkhāra), it is the head of all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra).
Therefore he said: "Cessation (nirodha) is the state of seclusion from formations. Some, however, say that "the attainment of cessation is the head of formations";
but that is merely their own opinion, since it is impossible for a mere designation (paññatti) to possess the status of a head, and because formations continue to occur beyond that [attainment].
“Together” (*saha*) means as if in one place. By this, he states the meaning of the word *sama*. For this word *sama* has the sense of “together.
“By the demonstration of accomplishment” means by the demonstration of the completion, the termination, of accomplishment.
“Here” means in this Pāḷi text on the description of persons (*puggalapaññatti*), or in its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). “Of the heads of the manifestation of defilements” means...

[This refers to] those whose heads are turned by the "heads" (i.e., the roots) of the defilements. For when these [defilements] are grasped, the other [rounds] are also already grasped, because they are to be exhausted as defilements and because they share the common characteristic of being exhaustible.
Thus, through the exhaustion of the round of defilements, the Path effects the exhaustion of the other rounds as well.
Indeed, by means of the very Path that cuts off the round, even the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is [exhausted] without remainder.
