Regarding the phrase "it ceases": anticipating the objection as to why the heading for the section on occurrence (*pavatta-sīsa*) is taken separately here, he says, "the heading for occurrence as well," and so forth.

It is stated that the sections on reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa-vāra*), which are accomplished when there is the total exhaustion of defilements (*kilesapariyādāna*) both specifically and generally, must be brought about by that [exhaustion].
For this very reason, he says, "the sections belong to the exhaustion of defilements alone. Now, establishing this point by means of scripture (*āgama*):

He said, “In liberation,” and so forth. The phrase “it occurs with the death-consciousness” is stated because the aforementioned sequence of reviewing the completion of the exhaustion of defilements is delimited by the death-consciousness; therefore, the meaning is that it is delimited by the delimiting death-consciousness.
17. "Should remain" means he should not approach. For "remaining" (ṭhāna) is the cessation of movement (gatinivatti). Therefore it is said, "he should not proceed. 18.
Because attending upon [the teacher] is of great benefit and because one ought to attend upon him. 20.
If one who has not yet attained the two types of knowledge possesses the foremost knowledge, and he subsequently attains those two types of knowledge—

Since he does not lack the two types of knowledge (*vijjā*) that were first attained—as if they were still being attained—it might be argued that his state of possessing the three knowledges (*tevijjatā*) is not in the primary sense (*nippariyāya*).
However, showing that for one who has first attained the two knowledges, this [state] is indeed distinguished, the author says: "By which the task is accomplished," and so forth.

In that context, "supreme knowledge" (*aggavijjā*) should be understood as the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*), or specifically as the knowledge of the supreme path (*agga-magga-ñāṇa*). And that is the "possession of the three knowledges" (*tevijjatā*); such is the construction.
22. “Right there” means precisely at the moment of the full awakening to the Truths.
24. “That” refers to the statement regarding the twofold liberation (ubhatobhāgavimuttatā) of one who has attained the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

“Possessing the characteristics as stated” means being endowed with the characteristics thus described—namely, being liberated in two ways on two occasions—both by way of arising and by way of logical fitness.

"This is the same method" means that just as five "liberated-in-both-ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) were described by way of those who have attained Arahantship after emerging from each of the four formless attainments and from cessation,
so too, it is stated with the understanding that there are five "body-witnesses" (kāyasakkhin) by way of those who have attained the state of a trainee (sekkha).

By the phrase "for the purpose of seeing" (*dassanakāraṇā*), he shows that in the word "having seen" (*disvā*), the suffix *-tvā* has the sense of a cause (*hetu*), as in such examples as "fear arises having seen a lion.
Since the destruction [of the taints] occurs when there is seeing, and not when there is no seeing, he says: "because its destruction depends upon seeing" (*dassanāyattaparikkhayattā*).

"The prior action" (*purimakiriyā*) refers to the action preceding the action of the destruction of the taints (*āsavānaṃ khayakiriyā*). For even though they are simultaneous, it is the causal action [that is designated as such].
It is designated as if it were already established by its prior function. It is so called because of being released from the group of names (nāmakāya).

For it is said that "one who is dependent on name" is one who depends on that by which he is to be released. "Of that" refers to the state of being "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) through liberation from the two groups.
This meaning is stated with reference to Arahants dwelling in the formless world (arūpaloka). Therefore, he says: "For in the Sutta," and so forth.

"By two portions" means by the portions of suppression (*vikkhambhana*) and eradication (*samuccheda*). "Twice" refers to the twice-repetition by way of suppressing and eradicating the defilements (*kilesa*).
"Released from defilements" is stated according to the first and third positions; the other [expression] is according to the second position.

Although the formless jhāna is released from the perception of form and so forth, because it is to be attained by means of transcending them and so on, [it is distinct] from those factors that obstruct its occurrence.
However, showing that his liberation is especially distinguished precisely by the absence of sensual desire and the other hindrances, he said:

"liberated from the mental body known as the hindrances. Furthermore, although the formless jhāna is also liberated from the physical body by way of being secluded from the world of form, that occurs only through the suppression of the desire and lust that are bound to form; therefore, suppression alone is primary.

It is said: “Because of liberation from the form-body through the suppression of craving for form. It is called "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) only in a partial sense, due to the absence of liberation by eradication (samucchedavimutti).

Showing that a designation applied to a whole may also be seen to apply to its parts—just as the expression "the spear-thrower" (sattisaya) refers to the entire group even when used for an individual—he says: “By way of one part of the eight liberations... it is so called.”
26. *Phuṭṭhānaṃ* means "of those touched," that is to say, "of those attained. *Anto* means "like an end"; it refers to a subsequent time relative to the contact (*phassanā*).
For what follows immediately after it is as if it were its conclusion. Furthermore, this word *anta* has time as its domain, but it does not have the meaning of "time" itself.
Therefore he said, "the intention. *Nāmakāyekadesato* means "from a portion of the name-body (*nāmakāya*) known as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). *Ālocito*...
It is "as if manifested" because of the production of a firm resolve for the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*), which is capable of seeing and illuminating through the suppression of obstacles;
however, it is not said to be "liberated," for it is not yet called liberated.
This method, moreover, refers to the procedure set forth in the passage beginning with "Furthermore, of those... by means of that specific distinction—that is, by that particular reason.

This refers to the aforementioned distinction in wisdom between those who have attained through view (*diṭṭhippatta*) and those liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*). The objection was raised because the underlying reason had not been clarified.

Just as in the case of one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) or one liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*), for one who is not liberated in every respect, even though there is a partial liberation, there is no superior wisdom—as there is for one who has attained through view—due to the presence of mere faith alone.
The state of liberation is to be seen. The phrase "resolved through faith" is stated with reference to the predominance of faith by way of its approach;
however, for him, knowledge and vision are indeed direct from the attainment of the path. 31.
"The stream is the name of the Noble Path"—this is said according to the primary sense, with the intention that one who possesses it is a stream-enterer.
The challenger raises the objection, "Why was the word 'also' (api) used? and then reveals his own intention with the words "Is it not," and so forth.
The other [respondent] refutes this with the words "It has not entered," and so forth. One is said to be "endowed" [with the fruit] because supramundane states have an unshakable nature.
"By the others" means by those standing at the second path and so on. "He alone" refers specifically to one standing at the first fruit. "Here" means...

In this explanation of "one who has at most seven more births" (*sattakkhattuparama*): if one were called a "stream-enterer" (*sotāpanna*) simply because they have entered or attained the noble path from the beginning, then those established in the second path and so forth would not possess the status of stream-enterers.

However, in the Sutta, it is said that one is a "stream-enterer" as a possessor of the path because they have entered—that is, they proceed—without ever having abandoned the initial limit of the noble path, the stream. Thus, the one endowed with the path is called a "stream-enterer."
It has been stated. By way of a figurative expression (pariyāya), the other [the non-returner] should also be understood as a stream-enterer because he possesses the nature of not falling away.
Through the reviewing of the defilements that have been abandoned, the truth of suffering is also reviewed, since defilements are included within the two truths;
thus he says, "of the reviewing of the four truths, etc. By the word "etc.," he includes the reviewing of the fruit and the phenomena of the higher path-fruits.
32. *Mahākulam eva* means precisely a noble family, as in such expressions as "one of good family" (*kulīno*) or "son of good family" (*kulaputto*).

33. One who is "devoted to meditation" (*sajjhānako*) is one who has not fallen away from jhāna; having passed away, they go to the Brahma-world. If they still have a latent inclination for the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭajjhāsaya*), they will be reborn higher and higher and eventually attain Nibbāna;

thus it is said, "they are like a Non-returner" (*anāgāmisabhāgo*). Because of this, they are called "one who does not return from that jhāna" (*jhānānāgāmī*). Therefore, it is said, "one whose nature is not to return" (*anāvattidhammo*).

36. In the case of *parayoga*, the word *tā* becomes the final member of that compound and is thus called "in connection with the word *para*"; what is meant is "not having reached," which is expressed by the phrase "having not reached.

37. By "tena" (by that), it is meant by the word "upahacca. Now, one might ask: is not the passing beyond the middle already indicated by the expression "having passed beyond the middle"? This is the intended meaning. 40. "Tanhāvaṭṭasotā" means those bound by the whirlpool of craving.
"Tassa" refers to that stream (*sota*); this genitive case is used here to express a relationship.
Regarding the "one-sided" (ekaṃsikā) [attainment] of one who has an upward stream (*uddhaṃsota*)—meaning those who have gone to the higher realms—he said, "having gone here or there.

"Of him" refers to the one with the upward stream. "Therein" means among the Aviha deities. "With a very swift course" (*lahusālahusagatikā*) means having a very light and quick course, or having a very light and quick course of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
By the phrase "after arising, they pass away," etc., the word "etc. includes such descriptions as "passing away after leaping into the sky," and so forth.

The three similes mentioned include [the first two]; however, it should be understood that the distinction of being "excessive" (*adhimatta*) applies to those who attain *parinibbāna* in the interval (*antarā-parinibbāyin*) and upon arrival (*upahacca-parinibbāyin*), whereas the distinction of being "not excessive" (*anadhimatta*) applies to those who attain *parinibbāna* without exertion (*asaṅkhāra*) and with exertion (*sa-saṅkhāra*), as compared to those who go upstream (*uddhaṃsota*).

The phrase "those very ones" refers specifically to those who attain *parinibbāna* in the interval, upon arrival, and those who go upstream. If this is so, then for those who attain *parinibbāna* without exertion and with exertion...
Anticipating the objection as to why it is stated by means of a simile when it could be expressed by even greater [similes], he says: “Than that greater... for the purpose of showing...
By “that” is meant by the statement, “May it not be for me, and may it not come to be for me. Or, by “that” is meant by the explanation of its meaning as previously stated.
“Of this suffering” refers to this present suffering consisting of consciousness and so forth. The “seeing of its arising” (udayadassana) [is now to be explained].
Knowledge. By the four phrases beginning with “no cassā,” it is said: “that which exists” means that which exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramattha).

Therefore he says, “‘Bhūta’ means possessing its own intrinsic nature (sasabhāva)”; the meaning of “bhūta” is the pentad of aggregates (khandhapañcaka). As it has been said: “Monks, regard this as ‘this has come to be’ (bhūtamidam).
One whose mind is turning away, one whose heart is becoming detached, is one whose inclination has turned back from the stream of craving and the like.
“He is equanimous” means that, like a man who has lost his wealth, he is indifferent, having abandoned both fear and delight.
“Inferior” means low; “superior” means excellent. By saying “in existence” (*bhave*) and then saying “in becoming” (*sambhave*), it is shown that the latter expresses what was not explicitly stated;
thus he says “present,” and so forth. “That which is called ‘become’ (*bhūta*) is said to be just what has come to be.”

That very thing is called "becoming" (*bhava*), as in "it becomes" or "it was. It is a "source of becoming" (*sambhava*) because arising occurs from it; thus, its nutriment is the condition for that becoming.
"By means of the wisdom of the path in due order" means by means of the noble path-wisdom obtained through the sequence of insight (*vipassanā*). "By him" refers to the trainee (*sekha*).
The commentary on the singlefold exposition is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of Pairs (Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā) 63.

"Of anyone" (kassaci) means of anyone at all. "In any way" (kathañci) means by some manner; it is said that this includes even by mere suppression. "Of the grasping directed inward" (ajjhattaggahaṇassa) refers to the grasping that occurs with reference to or concerning oneself (attānaṃ).
83. "Previously grasped" (purimaggahitaṃ) means first grasped by the mind through such thoughts as "I shall do it. "That was done" (taṃ kataṃ) [refers to that which was previously intended].
One who lives off such a benefit—that is, the fruit of merit—stands on the side of those who recognize what has been done for them; thus it is said, "not living off the fruit of merit. 90.
One who is fulfilled through the perfection of virtues is "content" (titta) here in the sense of having obtained as much as needed; hence he says, "free from anxiety because his task is finished.
The commentary on the Exposition of Pairs is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Triads 91.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the distinction from the remaining restraints": this refers to the destruction of restraint other than that which results from physical and verbal transgressions.

Since that [destruction] is being described by way of its doors, it is mental; therefore, he says, "by way of the distinction from mental restraint. Now, [he explains] that according to its modes of classification:
He said, "Or by way of the divisions such as restraint through mindfulness," the meaning of which is: in the occurrence of forgetfulness and so forth.
Since even any conduct that possesses its own intrinsic nature is called "virtue" (*sīla*), the term "virtue" is applied even to what is unwholesome.

94. Regarding the phrase "of those with a common object": the first fruit and so forth are the common (*samāna*) objects for these; thus they are "those with a common object," and it is of them [that this is said].

107. "Having that as its purpose" means having that as its aim; it means one who accomplishes the supramundane. "Because it is a part of its root" means because it is a constituent part by way of being the root of that ultimate teaching (*paramattha-sāsana*).
118. "Haughty" means possessing an arisen, empty pride. 123.

Regarding virtue, there is the non-neglecting of what has been undertaken, the purification of what is impure, and the fulfillment of what is incomplete; thus he said, "in what is to be purified and in what is to be increased. "Depending on higher virtue" means by means of the wisdom arisen with higher virtue as its support (*nissaya*).
124. The intention is to show that it is similar to excrement itself, not that it is similar to a cesspool.

For by means of the excrement alone, the cesspool is also rendered loathsome. Furthermore, this meaning would not need to be stated under the alternative view that "a cesspool is simply a heap of excrement.

130. The Teacher Sarabhaṅga and others, having effected the full understanding (*pariññā*) of the sensual desires of the form realm and so forth, while teaching [others], [demonstrate] mundane full understanding.
He said, "They do not generally succeed," meaning they explain correctly. Alternatively, the construction is:
"And they are not able to explain," referring to their lack of capability.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Triads is finished.
4. Commentary on the Section of Fours (Catukkaniddesavaṇṇanā) 133.
*Parenā* means by another; the meaning is "by one who has been commanded. *Āṇattiyā attanā cā* means "by the command of the commander and by oneself";
the construction is: that which is done by the verbal application (*vacīpayoga*) of that commander, as well as what is done by oneself when commanded.
"By means of an instigation to evil" refers to the evil that has arisen through the act of commanding.

(148) "By means of instruction" means by means of that which functions as the instrument of teaching. "Of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ*) means of those phenomena such as virtue (*sīla*), etc., which are to be understood according to the instruction.
(152) "Immediately following" means it is stated immediately after [the mention of] knowledge having been established. But what is that? He says: "The word."
“Lujjatīti” (it breaks) shows the reason why the word *loka* is used in that sense; thus he says, “connected with a cause.

Regarding “of the combined and the uncombined,” he says, “the meaning is ‘in the combined and the uncombined,’” demonstrating that because of its connection with the word *kusala*, the genitive case has the sense of the locative.

Through the speaking of what is combined, the excellence of the teacher is to be understood; through skill regarding the combined and the uncombined, the excellence of the disciple is to be understood.
He said, "The perfection of the assembly is also a cause for the excellence of inspired eloquence (*paṭibhānasampadā*) in a Dharma-preacher endowed with knowledge," by which he meant:
"the capacity to awaken [others] through the perfection of the disciples.
(157) "By wholesome states" means by the states of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). The fourth [type of person] is mentioned, who neither invites the Saṅgha nor gives gifts.
166. Regarding what was stated as “at the proper time,” namely that which is said in the Pāḷi: “He speaks even that which is dispraise there at the proper time;

he also speaks that which is praise there at the proper time”—in order to show, by way of investigation, what kind of person is meant by the statement in that sentence and discourse that “he speaks at the proper time,” [it says]: “One who knows the proper time...”
The construction is: he states [this] in the *Saṅgaha* (Compendium) in order to show that such passages as “it occurs,” etc., are spoken in the *Pāḷi*. 168.

“Deficiency of previously arisen conditions” means a deficiency of conditions that first arose in that particular existence (*attabhāva*). The construction is: their deficiency is the deficiency of presently occurring conditions. 173.
“Of them” refers to those defilements (*kilesa*) that remain after having been abandoned. There is only the manifestation of liberation, because that manifestation has liberation as its object.
174. *Tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ* is a genitive case used for selection (*niddhāraṇe*).

178. *Nāmakāyo* means a collection of names. *Idameva ca dvayaṃ* refers to these two alone: the fulfillment of the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*) and the non-transgression of the way of life (*sājīva*).
*Tato* means from the transgression of the way of life. The construction is: "the resemblance to turmeric dye and so forth in the discourse."
Therefore he said, "not for a person.
(179) By the word *iti*, he means the word *iti* used in the phrase "a wooden penny" (*dārumāsaka*). By the expression "of such a kind," he includes things such as voting sticks (*salākā*) as well.
(181) "Unscattered happiness" (*avisaṭasukha*) means the happiness of non-distraction (*avikkhepa*).

187. "In regard to the phenomena of the aggregates" (*khandhadhammesu*) means in regard to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhatadhammesu*). "By not obtaining that" (*tadalābhena*) means by not obtaining the path and its fruition (*maggaphala*). "By the goal" (*atthena*) means by the goal consisting of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
The commentary on the exposition of the tetrads is finished.
5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Pentads.

191. "How they should be treated" means: among those five types of persons, how others should treat them appropriately by way of showing the simile and the subject of the simile, through the practice of beneficial instruction; this is the meaning.

The word *ārambha* is intended here as denoting action (*kiriyāvācī*), not as denoting a phenomenon (*dhammavācī*) as in such expressions as "the question regarding the agent of the undertaking" (*ārambhakattussa kasāvapucchā*). Thus he says: "denoting the action of undertaking."
Regarding the phrase "the sound": because it was stated that they "cease," it was said "by way of the function of the Path.
192. "Grasping" is the acceptance [of the truth] as "it is thus. 199. There is no such connection because of their being of different classes (asamānajātika).
The commentary on the Exposition of the Pentads is finished.
6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Hexads 202.
This [set] beginning with the perfect awakening to the truths is included because of the inseparability of the fruit from its cause. Therefore he said:
“Sāma,” etc. The phrase “arisen by oneself without a teacher” is a statement of the qualities existing in the knowledge of omniscience;
it is not an exclusion of other factors incompatible with it, because no such other thing exists.

Therefore, he stated with the words “In that regard,” etc., the point that its being accompanied by a teacher and its arising from another are rejected. In that context, the state of having a teacher—
The state of having another’s instruction as the cause, and arising from another even without instruction—meaning production through reliance [on another]—this is the distinction between these two.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Sixfold Set is finished.
7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevenfold Set.

203. Regarding the phrase "in wholesome states" (*kusalesu dhammesu*), he said "included within wholesome states" (*kusalesu dhammesu antogadhā*) to show that this is the locative case used in the sense of a locus (*ādhāra*), not in the sense of an object (*visaya*).
Now, showing that this locative case has the characteristic of being an object (*visaya-lakkhaṇa*), he said "or in the factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiyadhammesu vā*), and so forth.
The phrase "by way of being helpful to them" (*tadupakāratāya*) refers to the meaning: "when wholesome states are to be accomplished."

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "By means of emerging wisdom" (*ummujjanapaññāya*) means by means of the wisdom that causes emergence, or by means of the wisdom that functions in the manner of emerging.

"Precisely because of that" (*teneva*) means precisely because it is merely an emergence. For just as the arising of knowledge is an emergence from the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*), so too is the arising of faith;
thus he said, "Emergence is indeed what is termed faith. "The turn of the mind" (*cittavāra*) refers to the turn of the continuity of consciousness (*cittappabandha*).
Because those individuals have individually attained standing, insight, crossing over, reaching a firm footing, and the final goal, they are called "many individuals.

Why? Because, by means of that particular existence (attabhāva), they do not grasp for Arahantship. "The state of being the third individual, etc. refers to the state of being an individual who has emerged and is standing, and so forth.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Septads is finished.
10. Commentary on the Exposition of the Decads. 209.
“Stream-enterers and so forth” refers to those endowed with the specific qualities mentioned: stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arahants. Asā…pe… pana.

In this context, however, the word *pana* indicates a specific distinction (*visesattha*). By means of it, one should understand that the phrase "because of the total eradication of the internal fetters" is intended to indicate this specific distinction.
The commentary on the exposition of the decads is concluded.
The sub-commentary on the *Puggalapaññatti* is completed.
Commentary on the commencement of the treatise:
the sub-commentary on the *Kathāvatthu*.
Since the parts are included within the whole, the whole is stated as their basis (*adhiṭṭhānabhāva*), just as one says, "the branches on the tree.
This is shown by the passage beginning with "of the collection of discourses" (*kathāsamudāyassa*). Therein, "discourses" (*kathānam*) refers to three types of discourse:

debate (*vāda*), wrangling (*jappa*), and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*). Among these, that by which the establishment and refutation of a position and its counter-position occur through means of valid knowledge (*pamāṇa*) and reasoning (*takka*) [is debate].

That is the definition. For phenomena that are mutually contradictory and share a single subject matter (*ekādhikaraṇa*) constitute "propositions and counter-propositions" (*pakkha-paṭipakkha*), such as:
"The Tathāgata exists after death" and "The Tathāgata does not exist after death.

However, those that have different subject matters (*nānādhikaraṇa*), even if mutually contradictory, are not called "propositions and counter-propositions," such as: "Form is impermanent" and "Nibbāna is permanent. By means of these [criteria], one should avoid the points of defeat consisting of quibbles (*chala*) and futile rejoinders (*jāti*).
The undertaking of a refutation consists in establishing a position and its opposite; that is *jappa*.
The mention of "undertaking" (*ārambha*) here is for the purpose of showing that there is merely the beginning of an effort, and not the accomplishment of the goal.

However, that by which they strive to refute an opponent's position through the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) and the futile rejoinders (*chala-jāti*) is *vitaṇḍā*. In that case, there is a frustration of speech due to the failure to produce a valid alternative meaning.
Quibble (*chala*) is, for example: “This man has a new blanket; the king is not our witness,” and so forth. Its meaning is:
types of speech that corrupt, which are counterfeits of a reply. The points of defeat (*niggahaṭṭhāna*) will be made clear later.

Thus, among the three types of discourse distinguished as discussion (*vāda*), wrangling (*jappa*), and cavil (*vitanda*), it is here the discussion of a proponent (*vādakathā*) that is intended by the term “discourse. And that indeed is by way of establishing the non-perverted nature of phenomena.
It should be understood that this is not by way of contentious discussion. "By the very act of laying down the matrix" means by the teaching of the summary (uddesa).

"Of what has been laid down" means of what has been taught. For "laying down" (ṭhapana) is so called because the teaching places and deposits the matter to be taught within the mental continuums of those to be trained; it is also called "deposition" (nikkhepa).
The commentary on the commencement of the book is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the introductory narrative (*nidānakathā*):

it has been stated, "...even the very parinibbāna... For even an object whose intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is not distinct [from others] is explained for the purpose of making its specific distinction from other phenomena understood.
They speak by treating it as something else, as in: "Dhammas are so called because they bear their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).

And that [term] refers to the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*). It is stated in the sense of being an instrument (*karaṇa-bhāvena*), with reference to its being the most effective means for achieving the aforementioned tranquility (*upasama*).

"One who speaks of Dhamma" ... [etc. ... weakness is mentioned because, when such wisdom exists, there is an absence of the state of being a partisan for those [views]. "Of the tenets" (*laddhiyā*)...
[This refers] to the tenet: “There is a person in the sense of ultimate reality; an Arahant falls away from Arahantship,” and so forth.
“By means of the Suttantas” means by the *Devatāsaṃyutta* and others. The distinction between the various types of schisms he will explain later himself.
“Having split the root compilation” means having destroyed the original collection (*mūlasaṅgīti*), or having caused a schism in it as it stood.
Then, having done otherwise: "Apart from what is included" means apart from what is included in the Root Recitation (Mūlasaṅgīti). Therefore he said, "a discourse not included.

A text of direct meaning (*nītattha*) is so called because its meaning is to be understood according to the literal expression. A text of indirect meaning (*neyyattha*) is so called because its meaning must be determined by way of the suffering inherent in change (*vipariṇāmadukkhatā*), and so forth.
"By way of three grounds" refers to [the passage]: "The brave and mindful dwell here in the holy life," and so on.
By the three reasons already stated. "It was spoken with reference to something else" means it was spoken with reference to one particular way of living the holy life known as renunciation.

"They established another meaning" means that by way of the entire practice of the holy life, they established another meaning, such as "there is no living of the holy life among the devas," and so forth. And the sutta is another...

Having stated that which was spoken with a specific intention (*sandhāya bhaṇitaṃ*), they set aside what was spoken with another intention; thus one should understand the construction here as: "they set aside its meaning as something else.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "emptiness, etc.," impermanence and so forth are included.
"A certain profound portion" refers to the *Mahāpadesaparivāra* and so on. Some [teachers] expounded the entire Abhidhamma.
They discarded it, just as the Suttantikas did; for they claimed that it was not the word of the Conqueror (Jinavacana).
The statement beginning with "Because the *Kathāvatthu* is subject to dispute" was said with reference to the method set forth earlier in the *Nidāna-aṭṭhakathā*.
However, some consider even the *Puggalapaññatti* to be subject to dispute. Why [is it said] "by way of those [texts] existing prior to the Third Council"?
Has it not been stated that even prior to the Third Council, that [text] existed indeed in the form of a *mātikā*?
Or rather, it should be understood that it was stated thus with reference to the *Niddesa*. "They made them different" (*aññāni*) means they composed other treatises such as those of the Abhidhamma;
the sense is that even those [texts] which were already in circulation, they altered and recited otherwise. Why was "Mañjusiri" mentioned here? For that is not his name.
It was stated [thus] because it is considered that even if it were being grasped by other monks who follow the Three Piṭakas,

it would not be grasped as belonging to the Dispensation (sāsanāvacara) by those who possess thorough knowledge of the Teaching (sāsanikapariñña). "The names of the schools" (nikāyanāma) refers to the names of schools such as the Mahāsaṅghika, etc.,
and the names of groups such as the Dutiya-gutta, etc.

"Among the Saṅkantikas, the division was that of the Suttavādins": among the Saṅkantikas, immediately thereafter, one schism within the school named Suttavādins arose. "Together" (*saha*) means having brought them together into one; the sense is "when being counted.
"With reference to the dispute that arose" means with reference to the dispute that arose at the time of the Third Council.
"Arising thereafter" means those arising in the interval from that point until the disappearance of the True Dharma. And herein, the bringing together of a thousand suttas—
It is for the purpose of refuting the arguments of others and for the purpose of establishing one’s own position.
For even a single portion of a sutta is called a "sutta," since the designation for the whole is seen to apply to its parts, as in the expressions, "the cloth is burnt" or "the ocean has been seen.
Those portions of sutta to be understood here are those that have come down such as, "There is a person practicing for his own welfare," and so forth.
The Commentary on the Nidānakathā is finished.
Mahāvagga 1.
Discourse on the Person (Puggalakathā).
1. The Purely Actual Meaning (Suddhasaccikaṭṭha) 1.1.
Commentary on the Positive-Negative Order (Anulomapaccanīkavaṇṇanā) 1.1.
"Illusion" (Māyā) refers to spells (vijjā) fashioned by means of vows and the like, as well as medicinal herbs prepared in that manner.
Furthermore, showing that here what is intended by "illusion" (māyā) refers to unreal aspects of the knowable produced through illusion, he said:
"Illusion is said to be things such as non-jewels appearing in the form of jewels and so forth. That which is truly real is "the true state" (saccikaṭṭha);
it is the true state in the sense of being the object of non-erroneous knowledge. Therefore, he said: "the actual state" (bhūtaṭṭha). Precisely because of its non-erroneous nature...
The ultimate meaning (*paramattha*) is the supreme goal; it is the nature of phenomena that cannot be pointed out, which has become directly manifest to knowledge.
Therefore, it is called "the highest goal" (*uttamattha*).
By the commonality of the word "exists" (*atthi*), as in such passages as "there is a person practicing for his own benefit," it refers to the common usage of the term "exists."
They say that "quibble" (*chala*) is the obstruction of speech arising from the occurrence of alternative interpretations. "Cutting off the foundation" means corrupting the reason;
the sense is that one makes it a non-reason. For a reason is a "foundation" (*patiṭṭhā*) because it establishes a proposition;

however, showing that reason as being merely a matter of conventional meaning, he says, "If [it is taken] in the sense of ultimate truth," and so forth. But by corrupting it through its application...
This will become clear later on. "Not granting an opportunity" means not allowing the occasion to state a corresponding argument;
or rather, it means cutting off the foundation and overturning the very admission [of the opponent].
For the opponent's admission—that "a person is apprehended"—is indeed untenable when directed toward the proponent, because that which is to be qualified is unestablished.
For this very reason, he said: "Because it is not to be apprehended, your doctrine does not stand," thus turning [the opponent] back. By stating, "And form is apprehended... [etc.]...
he shows," he demonstrates that the reason intended by the opposing debater establishes a contrary meaning.
"It is called 'apprehended'" means that, in terms of its mode of appearance, there is no difference between the mode and that which possesses the mode; this is the intended sense. "Otherwise" means:

*Ākāra*: the distinction between those things that possess aspects (*ākāravanta*). "Of this" refers to the second question stated thus: "From that, the person is apprehended in the sense of ultimate reality and the highest meaning.
"This distinction" means that which is the aforementioned difference in the mode of the intrinsic nature of the objects of the two questions;
this is the distinction between the two questions. [It is] by way of the common characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*) of phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*).
Since even non-distinct things are indeed distinct by virtue of their specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*), another dharma could never be apprehended in the form of something else.

If that were the case, otherness itself would not exist. Therefore, against the opponent who asserts that "even though the person (*puggala*) is not apprehended in the form of its conditions such as materiality (*rūpaṇā*) and so forth, it is nevertheless apprehended in its own sense as the essential nature of the primary elements (*bhūtasabhāva*)," [the author] says: "That which is the true reality (*saccikaṭṭho*)" and so forth.
Showing that there is no occasion for a formal objection (*codanā*), he said: “But as... [etc. ...no refutation (*niggaha*) should be made.
In this context, “refutation” refers to the refutation spoken of as “understand the refutation”; the meaning is the restraining of the opponent by means of charging him with defeat.
Since this [refutation] is caused by a fault in his argument, the *Aṭṭhakathā* explains it by way of the synonyms “fault” (*dosa*) and “transgression” (*aparādha*).
It has been analyzed. Herein, contemptuous disregard is a ground for defeat.

For in this regard there are: loss of the proposition, shifting the proposition, contradicting the proposition, abandoning the proposition, shifting the reason, shifting the meaning, the meaningless, the unintelligible, the irrelevant, the mistimed, the deficient, the redundant, the repetitive, not repeating [the opponent's statement], and the unintelligible.

The proponents of the method of reasoning (*ñāyavādino*) declare that there are twenty-two points of defeat (*niggahaṭṭhāna*): (1) non-rejoinder (*appaṭibhā*), (2) distraction (*vikkhepa*), (3) acquiescence in what is dead (*matānuññā*), (4) indifference toward what ought to be pursued (*anuyuñjitabbassa upekkhanā*), (5) pursuit of what ought not to be pursued (*ananuyuñjitabbassa anuyogo*), (6) the point of defeat consisting in a different meaning (*apasiddhantara*), and (7) fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsā*).

Among these, the admission of a dissimilar example-property constitutes a loss of one's own proposition (*paṭiññāhāni*) regarding the first example; [this occurs] when one negates the very meaning of the proposition admitted.
Pointing out something else [in place of the original] is *paṭiññāntara* (shifting the thesis). Stating a reason that contradicts one's own thesis is *paṭiññāvirodha* (contradiction of the thesis).

Withdrawing what has been asserted in the thesis is *paṭiññāsaññāsa* (retraction of the thesis). When a general statement of a reason has been refuted, stating a specific reason is *hetvantara* (shifting the reason). Stating a point that is irrelevant to the matter under discussion is *atthantara* (shifting the subject).

That which is devoid of meaning, like the mere recitation of a table of contents (*mātikā*), is *niratthaka* (meaningless). Even if stated three times, [it remains so] by the witness and the opponent.

*Aviññātattaṃ* (unintelligibility) is that which is not understood or whose meaning is not known. *Asambandhatthaṃ* (incoherence) is that which lacks connection due to the absence of proper sequence between what precedes and what follows.

*Appattakālaṃ* (untimeliness) is speech in which the order of the parts [of the syllogism] is inverted. *Ūnaṃ* (deficiency) is that which is lacking in its constituent parts. *Adhikaṃ* (redundancy) is that which contains superfluous reasons or examples.

*Punaruttaṃ* (repetition) is the repeated utterance of words or meanings after the restatement (*anuvāda*) has already been made; it also includes the repetition of what is already known to the assembly.

Non-reply is the failure to repeat what has been stated by the three [the proponent, the opponent, or the assembly]. The "unintelligible" is that which has been stated by the proponent and understood by the assembly, but is not understood by the opponent.
"Lack of ingenuity" (*appaṭibhā*) is the failure of the opponent to provide a response when the proponent has finished speaking.
"Evasion" (*vikkhepa*) is the interruption of the discussion by resorting to some other task. [The "admission of one's own fault" is] by acknowledging one’s own defect...
*Matānuññā* (admission of an opinion) is the admission of an opponent’s position as being correct after having attributed faults to it.
*Anuyuñjanā* (cross-examination) is the failure to restrain one who has reached a point of defeat (*niggaha*), or the neglecting of one who ought to be cross-examined.

*Anuyoga* (pursuit) is the restraining of one who has already been defeated, or the restraining of one in a situation where restraint is not required. *Apasiddhanta* (fallacy of a non-tenet) is the introduction of a discussion regarding another tenet in an indefinite manner after having admitted one specific tenet.

The fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsas*)—namely, the unestablished (*asiddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the contradictory (*viruddha*)—mean "counterfeits of a reason. And the statement of these constitutes a ground for defeat (*niggahaṭṭhāna*).
Among these twenty-two grounds for defeat, this one is called "the withdrawal of a proposition" (*paṭiññāsaññāsa*), because it involves the removal of a position through one's own renunciation of it.
For this very reason, it is said: "He shows the defeat by means of disavowal alone."
"Because it is unestablished"—by this, he states that the person (*puggala*) is not apprehended through direct perception (*paccakkha*) or through inference (*anumāna*).
For that [person] is not apprehended through direct perception; if it were apprehended, there would be no dispute at all.
Nor is there such an inference by which they could infer a person. For instance, a proponent of the person within our own teaching (*sāsana*) might say: "The person..."
Because it was said by the Blessed One, "A person is found; there is a person," [the person exists] just like form, feeling, and so forth.
For whatever the Blessed One has stated as "exists" exists in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), such as form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
But whatever does not exist in the ultimate sense has not been stated by the Blessed One as "exists," such as...

The claim that [the term] "nature" and so forth refers to the "nature" of the proponents of nature (pakativādins) and others is incorrect. For here, if the existence of a person (puggala) is intended from the standpoint of conventional usage (vohāra), then the proof is already established;
but if it is intended from the standpoint of ultimate reality (paramattha), the reason (hetu) is unestablished because it has not been stated as such.

Furthermore, it is contradictory (viruddha), because it fails to prove its status as impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, and so forth, since it is seen to be so in the case of form, feeling, and the rest. Thus [it is said].
Because that very state of being causeless is evident.

As for what the various outsiders, the other sectarians, say: "In the ultimate sense, the self (attā) truly exists, because it serves as the basis for the occurrence of what is designated as 'knowledge,' just like form and so forth.
Or else, [they claim] the aggregate of form is a distinct entity separate from the self.

Because it possesses the nature of the aggregates (*khandha*), just like the other aggregates; the intention [of the opponent] is that whatever distinct referent (*padatthantara*) exists here is the "person" (*puggala*).

Furthermore, in this case, the first reason is inconclusive (*anaikantika*) and unproven (*asiddha*). For it is not established—according to our own school—that for something non-existent there can be, in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), the status of being a cause (*nimitta*) for the occurrence of knowledge and designation.
If [the opponent argues] it is from the conventional standpoint (*vohārato*), then that would be proving what is already accepted by us.
The contradiction in meaning [of the first reason] is that a person cannot exist even as a form (rūpa) distinct from the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of form and so forth.

Regarding the latter reason, however, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), because it is accepted that feeling (*vedanā*) and other aggregates arise as ultimate entities (*paramattha*) distinct from the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) as separate referents (*padatthantara*). Furthermore, regarding the apprehension of its specific qualities, for our own school...
There is an absence of an example for the [probandum] because of the lack of a soul-substance (*jīva-pada*) postulated by others. Furthermore, there is a contradiction in meaning:

even if the aggregate of form (*rūpa-khandha*) were accompanied by a soul-substance established by both parties that is distinct from feeling and the other aggregates, it would still not be a "soul" in the same way as the other aggregates are.
As for the inference stated by the followers of Kaṇāda—that [the soul exists] "because of its being the support of pleasure and so forth"—they should be addressed as follows:
—Is there something connected to the self (*ātman*) in relation to pleasure and so forth, such that the self is inferred by virtue of being the support for pleasure and so forth?

If it is [their] arising, then in that case all pleasures and so forth would arise simultaneously, because their cause would be present and independent of anything else. Or, if some other cause, such as the sense-faculties, must be depended upon, then that very [cause]...
Let that be the cause; what is the use of imagining some other unseen capacity?
Furthermore, if they were to say that their functioning is dependent upon a self (*ātman*), even this is not established, because there is no supporting example.

For there exists no such dharma possessing an intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*) apart from form and the rest that could serve as a basis for pleasure and so forth, by means of which [the self] might achieve its own purpose.

They might point to examples [of such usage]. By this same method, it should be understood that because it is untenable for [the self] to be denotable by non-compounded words (*asamāsa-pada*), and so forth, [the opponent's position] must be refuted.

Likewise, by the statement "because another ultimate reality (*saccikaṭṭha*) is unestablished," it should be understood that the inherent atoms (*prakṛti-aṇu*) and other such things imagined by outsiders are also stated to be unestablished. But how are they unestablished?

Because it is not apprehended through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For even for the sage Kapila, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is not established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since the followers of Kapila admit that it is beyond the range of direct perception.

As for their inference: "Primordial nature exists, because we observe a persistence (*anvaya*) among diverse things, just as there is a persistence in a mere collection of parts. This is what they say.
They say this, for by this they admit that the primary status belongs to the existing qualities such as existence (*sattva*) and the rest. Here it is said:
Is the primary status of the "Whole" (*sakala*) and so forth different from its divisions, or is it non-different?

If it were different here, there would be a contradiction with established doctrine (*samaya*), because the entire world would consist of the primary [status], since you admit it to be different elsewhere by way of difference in configuration (*saṇṭhāna*).
If it is argued that this is not a fault, we say no; for even when there is a difference in shape, such as that of a bracelet or a ring, gold is seen to remain undifferentiated.

Indeed, shape is not the cause of the differentiation of the substance, because it is not the material cause (upādāna) of that substance. Whatever is the cause of a thing's differentiation is not its non-material cause;
just as in the cases of a golden jar, a clay jar, a silk cloth, and a cotton cloth, where one is called a "golden jar," another a "clay jar," one a "silk cloth," and another a "cotton cloth."

And the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). For it is not established for the proponents of primordial nature (*prakṛtivādins*) that things such as jars are preceded by multiple causes; nor is it established for the followers of Kapila (*kāpilas*), since they admit some degree of non-difference [between cause and effect]. However, if there were no difference, there would be an absence of an example;
for it is not logical that the very thing to be proven should also serve as the example. Furthermore, the demonstration of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is unestablished.

For it is not logical that the very same thing should be concomitant with itself. Furthermore, the opponent’s demonstration of concomitance by means of a primary factor (*padhāna*) is unproven, because they do not admit that a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) can be a primary factor.

Alternatively, if they define a primary factor as any cause whatsoever—on the grounds that "the fruit is supported here"—this too is unproven, because they do not admit the existence of the fruit within the cause, nor do they admit the distinction intended by the opponent, namely that the probans (*hetu*) possesses an unproven substratum (*nissaya*).

Now, if it is specifically established that the fruit depends on a cause, there is nothing contradictory, because dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is accepted for phenomena according to their respective conditions.

Furthermore, for the proponents of primordial nature (*pakativādin*), "primordial nature" (*pakati*) is the state of equilibrium of the three qualities (*guṇa*) known as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. That—
And they assert: "Sentient beings are not different from *prakṛti* because they possess an unequal nature such as permanence and so forth;

they are not different [from it] because they undergo transformations such as becoming large and so forth. That *prakṛti* of theirs, described in the manner stated, is not established, because it would be non-different from a transformation that possesses a nature contrary to it.
For it is not established when one says: "The horn of a horse is long, and it is non-different from the short horn of a cow."

And what more? Because of the non-existence of the identity of the three. For those who maintain that there is no difference between the three qualities—sattva and the rest—and primordial nature (*prakṛti*), it follows that sattva and the others must also be non-different from primordial nature; yet this is not tenable, as it would mean the identity of the three.
Thus, even in this way, primordial nature is not established. How so? Because it results in manifold faults. For if [primordial nature] were of a distinct essence from its modifications...
If primordial nature (*prakṛti*) were non-different from its unmanifest essence, then while this is the case, numerous defects would accrue to primordial nature, such as:
possessing causes, impermanence, non-pervasiveness, agency, multiplicity, dependence, gender, having parts, and being dependent on others.

It should not be asserted that it is non-different from its modifications by way of genus (*jāti*). If that were so, there would be a contradiction with established doctrine; therefore, [the claim of non-difference] is a mere fabrication.
One must conclude that "nature" (*pakati*) is unestablished.
And since it is unestablished, even "the Great One" (*mahat*) and the rest, which are spoken of as being caused by it, are likewise unestablished.

Just as nature, the Great One, and so forth, so too are the Lord (*issara*), Pajāpati, the Person (*purisa*), time (*kāla*), inherent nature (*sabhāva*), destiny (*niyati*), chance (*yadicchā*), and the like.

Among these, first of all, a Creator (Issara) is not established, because no benefit [conferred by Him] is perceived. For in the birth of beings, the benefit of the parents is seen through their functioning as the seed and the field;
thereafter, the benefit of temperature and nutriment is seen through their roles in growth and support;

and the benefit of the sense faculties is seen through their accomplishment of functions such as seeing. But no such benefit is seen for a Creator. As for the differentiation of beings into inferior and superior classes, this is due to the Creator—[meaning it is His work].
[Objection: That is not so, because it is unproven. It must be established that the specific excellence of assistance mentioned above is produced by a Lord (Issara) and not by karma.
[Response: If you say this is the same for the other case as well, we say no; for the restriction of results is established through karma.
For when there is karma accumulated by an agent, it is proven that whatever therein is unwholesome results in inferiority, and whatever is wholesome results in excellence.
For even by a proponent of a Supreme Lord (Issaravādin), it is impossible to deny karma.
Moreover, many faults arise regarding the existence of this diversity of the world as being created by a Supreme Lord. How so?
If all this diversity of the world were created by a Supreme Lord, it would have to come into being simultaneously with His word, not gradually.
Indeed, it is not logical for effects whose causes are already present to arise sequentially; for if the Lord were dependent on other causes, his power would be diminished.
Furthermore, it is not tenable that the eye and so forth are the causes of visual consciousness and the rest, for a cause is defined as that which "produces.
If the Lord alone were the agent, the causal status of all other causes would be lost. By means of those various specific factors through which the Lord [acts]...
He would have to become pleased with them, and thus he would fall into the state of being an object of their service; likewise, he would become the causal agent for all those who act as causes.
Furthermore, this creation of his might be for his own sake or for the sake of others.

If it were for his own sake, there would be a loss of his sovereignty, because his status as a lord and ruler would cease due to having failed in his duty. Or else, whatever must be done by himself through that which was created by him—
Why does he not do that himself? Furthermore, since this world is called "another" [in relation to him], what is the purpose of his creating hell and so forth, as well as diseases and poisons?
As for his lordship (*īśvaratā*), it must be either self-made, made by another, or causeless.

In that regard, if it were self-made, it would entail the consequence of his being non-lordly prior to that. If it were made by another, [it would entail the consequence of his not being the ultimate cause].
Furthermore, there would be the consequence of non-sovereignty and the state of being surpassed even afterwards. If [the world] were causeless, there would be no sovereignty over anything;
thus, the existence of a Lord (Issara) should be understood as unestablished.
And just as with a Lord, so it is with a Creator (Pajāpati) and a Person (Purisa); here, the difference is merely one of name. By those proponents...
This is what has been conceived: namely, that "Pajāpati is the person.

However, for those who desire the course of the world to be caused by him, the faults and the lack of proof found in the doctrine of Pajāpati and the doctrine of the Person (Purisa) must be understood to apply equally to the doctrine of the Lord (Issara).

Just as these [theories of] the Lord and so forth are untenable, so too is Time (Kāla) unproven, because it lacks defining characteristics. For, in the ultimate sense, among phenomena that actually exist...
A characteristic known as an intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is apprehended. For example, solidity is the characteristic of earth, but it is not so for time;
therefore, time does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*). However, the proponent of time (*kālavādin*) says: "Time has the characteristic of occurrence (*vattanā*).

He should be asked: "What, then, is this occurrence? He replies: "It is the proceeding of hours, moments, and so forth. That too is not [the case], because [time] is distinct from form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates.

Because it is not determined as being a distinct entity. For, if that which has an undetermined intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) were to possess the characteristic of occurrence (*vattanā-lakkhaṇa*) in an ultimate sense, then even things such as a hare’s horn would necessarily possess that characteristic.
As for what the followers of Kaṇāda say: "The marks of time are 'after,' 'another,' 'simultaneously,' 'long,' and 'quick'."
The claim that "time exists because of the presence of its mark" is incorrect, because the possessor of the mark (the marked) is not perceived.
For when marks have an established relationship [with their objects], the cognition of the marked object would occur through the apprehension of the mere mark.

However, no one with an unerring mind has ever previously apprehended a marked object designated as "time" together with such a mark. Therefore, it is not correct to say, "because of the presence of the mark..."
“If you argue that time exists because it serves as the cause for distinctions such as ‘later than another’ and so forth—this is not tenable. Why?

Because those [distinctions] have their causes in being born first and so on. Furthermore, there is no such thing as ‘being born first’ and so forth as a real phenomenon apart from mere conventional designation;
thus, in the ultimate sense, time does not exist at all. Moreover, it would entail the absurdity of many things becoming a single entity.”
Indeed, there are many divisions of time according to worldly convention through the classification of past and so forth.

Since you assert this [time] to be one, and because there is no single entity underlying those many [divisions], time does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*). Likewise, it would follow that a single thing could become multiple.
For this very time which is present today was future yesterday and will be past tomorrow; and what was present yesterday...
Today has passed, and likewise tomorrow will be present and the day after tomorrow will follow.
Since it is not logical for that which possesses a single nature to possess multiple natures, time is unestablished from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*).

However, it should be understood as a mere conventional designation (*vohāramatta*), because it is designated through the mere conceptual construction based on the occurrence of phenomena (*dhamma*) and the worldly consensus regarding the divisions of past and so forth.

Intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), destiny (*niyati*), chance (*yadicchā*), and so forth, are also unestablished. Why? Because they lack defining characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*). For destiny and chance do not arise from an intrinsic nature.
If such a thing as these were to exist, they would have to possess a characteristic known as their intrinsic nature, and there is no establishing cause for them.
However, when these doctrines are subjected to scrutiny, they collapse into the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).
Thus they persist; nor is the variety of the world without a cause, for that would entail the consequence of there being no distinction.

For if existence were causeless, the specific distinction among humans, gods, hell-beings, animals, and so forth—consisting in their respective faculties and other traits—that is observed in their activity, would be non-existent;
yet this is not accepted by the wise. Furthermore, because it is actually seen: for the visual consciousness and the rest are indeed seen [to arise] from the eye and the rest.
The occurrence of sprouts and so forth from seeds and so forth; therefore, this occurrence is also due to a cause.

Likewise, because of its non-existence before and after. For whatever fruit is produced from whichever collection of conditions, its production is not possible prior to or subsequent to that [collection];
and why say more? If occurrence were without a cause, it would be a causeless occurrence.

Or rather, these words might exist either before or after their respective collection of conditions; yet they do not exist [before or after] because they have not obtained their conditions, and they exist only in the middle because they have obtained their conditions.
Thus, since all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) are likewise [dependent], the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*) is not established.

And that being unestablished, just like the absence of a cause for the process of existence, such things as inherent nature (*sabhāva*), destiny (*niyati*), chance (*yadicchā*), and so forth—which are specific modes of causelessness—are also [unestablished].
It should be understood that these [arguments] are indeed unestablished.
Furthermore, when the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) claim, "Atoms are eternal; from them the effects such as dyads are produced, and those are impermanent;
it is by virtue of these that the world is variegated," this too is merely a false conceptualization. For atoms do not...
Indeed, there are no [entities] existing apart from an aggregation of primary elements (*bhūta*). Furthermore, that [aggregation] is impermanent;
and it is not logical for something impermanent to arise as permanent, because it is impossible for it to function as a cause [for permanence] and because it is not observed to do so.

Moreover, if it were to become a cause for anything, it would necessarily be impermanent due to undergoing transformation. And this possibility does not exist, such that [the aggregation] could remain without undergoing transformation.
“Could a cause produce a fruit? If it undergoes change, what opportunity is there for its permanence?

Therefore, it should be understood that the so-called atoms (*paramāṇu*) posited by others are impermanent beings, and furthermore, other things imagined by outsiders to be permanent and so forth are simply unestablished.
Hence it was said: “But because no other ultimate reality is established apart from the classification of phenomena (*dhamma*).”

Here it is asked: "If, in the ultimate sense, a person (puggala) is not found, then why, when the person is thus not found, did the Blessed One proclaim the existence of a person in various places, saying:
'There is a person practicing for his own welfare,' and 'Monks, these four persons exist and are found in the world'?"

By way of the inclinations of those to be trained. For when the Teacher, who is skilled in training those to be disciplined according to their respective inclinations, teaches the Dhamma, he employs the designation "person" (puggala) here and there in accordance with worldly convention;
it is not because of the existence of a person from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramattha).

Furthermore, for eight reasons the Blessed One speaks on the discourse of persons (*puggala*): to illustrate moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*); to illustrate that one is the owner of one’s own karma (*kammassakatā*);

to illustrate individual personal effort (*paccatta-purisakāra*); to illustrate the immediate retribution of deeds (*ānantariya*); to illustrate the sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*); to illustrate past lives (*pubbenivāsa*); to illustrate the purification of offerings (*dakkhiṇā-visuddhi*);
and to show that worldly convention (*lokasammuti*) is not to be abandoned. “Aggregates, elements, and sense-bases...”
For when it is said, "They feel shame and dread of wrongdoing," the great mass of people does not understand;

they fall into confusion or become resistant, thinking, "How can these aggregates, elements, and sense bases be said to feel shame and dread of wrongdoing? But when it is said, "A woman feels shame and dread of wrongdoing;
a man, a kshatriya, or a brahmin [feels shame and dread of wrongdoing]," they understand and do not fall into confusion.
One does not become an adversary; therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person (*puggala*) for the purpose of illustrating moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*).
The same principle applies even when it is said: "The aggregates (*khandhā*) are the owners of their karma; the elements (*dhātuyo*) and the sense bases (*āyatanāni* [are the fields of experience]).

Therefore, he also speaks of the person for the purpose of illustrating the ownership of one's karma. [And it is said: "The great monasteries such as Veḷuvana were caused to be built by means of the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases."

The same principle applies even when it is stated: “The aggregates deprive their mother of life, their father, an arahant, commit the offense of shedding blood, or perform the act of schism in the Saṅgha; [they are] the elements, the sense bases. It also applies when it is stated: “The aggregates feel loving-kindness;
[they are] the elements, the sense bases,” or “The aggregates recollect past lives; [they are] the elements...”

The same principle applies even when it is said, "the sense bases. Therefore, for the purpose of demonstrating individual personal effort, for the purpose of demonstrating immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), for the purpose of demonstrating the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), and for the purpose of demonstrating past lives, the Blessed One speaks in terms of the person (*puggala*).
Even if it were said, "the aggregates receive the gift; the elements [receive it]; the sense bases [receive it]," the great masses of people would not understand and would fall into confusion.
Or he becomes an opponent, thinking: "How can it be that the aggregates, elements, and sense bases receive [the gift]?
But when it is said, "The person receives," he understands; he does not fall into confusion, nor does he become an opponent.
Therefore, for the purpose of illustrating the purification of the offering, the Blessed One speaks of the person. And the Buddhas [respect] worldly convention...
The Blessed Ones do not abandon conventional worldly designations; rather, remaining within worldly parlance, they teach the Dhamma.

Therefore, it should be understood that for these eight reasons the Blessed One speaks of the "person" (puggala)—even though he does not intend to establish the person as a reality—rather than because there exists a person in the ultimate sense (paramattha).

"By way of the differentiation of phenomena (dhamma)" means that since no real entity other than the differentiation of phenomena such as form and so forth has been established, the person must be apprehended precisely by way of the differentiation of phenomena such as form; this is the meaning. By this [it is asked]:
"When the person is being apprehended by you, is it apprehended through the mode of being affected (ruppana), or rather through experiencing, perceiving, volitional formation, or cognizing?"
He shows this by saying "in a certain manner," because there is no phenomenon possessing an intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) in the world apart from those [two].
The positions of affirming or denying the existence of a person (puggala) through general and specific characteristics are the positions of accepting or rejecting [its existence].
Although both of these two positions are found in the forward and reverse methods, the first method is that which proceeds by setting aside the first [position] at the outset.
Showing this distinction between them—that the former is the second—he said: "The allowance...

should be understood. Furthermore, it should be understood that because it conforms to the tenet as it was formulated, the first method is called the "conformable side" (anulomapakkha), and because it is the reverse of that, the other is called the "reverse side" (paṭilomapakkha).
In the phrase *tena vata re*, the word *tena* here is a term for a reason (*kāraṇavacana*). It refers to that reason by which the existence of a person (*puggala*) is established.
This very reason has already been shown above, both from the perspective of those within the teaching (*sāsanika*) and those outside it (*bāhiraka*).

Furthermore, this designation "reason" (*hetu-samaññā*) is applied to what resembles a reason because the ultimate truth (*paramattha*) is intended. Above, regarding the refutation (*niggaha*) with the words "Understand the refutation,"...

Only a mere indication was given; that [indication], being now analyzed by way of a conclusion through the statement beginning with "what you said there," and by showing its falsity, is made manifest, thus it is "established" (āropita) and "set down" (patiṭṭhāpita).
Therefore, it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "Because of being established."
And here, the proposition-member, “the person is apprehended,” is shown in its own form.

By the word “therefore” (tena), the reason-member is shown in a general sense. Since this reason—being a property that exists in the similar class (sapakṣa) and does not exist in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa)—is alone called "possessing the characteristic" (lakkhaṇūpapanna), and no other, therefore, wherever...
Thus it both exists and does not exist; this twofold member of the example is distinguished by its similar and dissimilar natures.
The application (*upanaya*) is as follows: "Just as form and so forth are perceived, so is the person (*puggala*);

and just as a hare's horn is not perceived, so the person is not [perceived]. This very [point] is stated as: "Indeed, the person is to be spoken of as being perceived in the sense of ultimate reality (*saccikaṭṭha-paramattha*)."
This is what is indicated by this text, which is called "causing to fall" (*pāpanā*) in the commentary along with its reasons and examples.

The conclusion (*nigamana*) appears in the text in its own form, which is called "planting" (*ropanā*) in the commentary. Thus, having determined the members of the proof (*sādhanāvayava*) according to the ancient method, they should be applied.

Now, having determined the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dāharana*)—which are characterized by the opposing position through their formal application (*vattanena*)—by means of demonstrating positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the formulation of the proof (*sādhana-payoga*) should be joined. It might be asked: "What is there to be said regarding the 'reason'?

For it is precisely by means of the reason and the example that the proof or the refutation of one's own and the opposing positions occurs, and not by means of a mere thesis (*paṭiññā*), because the latter is something yet to be established and so forth.

Furthermore, that dyad is elucidated by the text beginning with “*tena vata re*. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is presented under the headings of “causing to fall into [an offense]” (*pāpana*) and “attributing [an offense]” (*āropanā*).

However, it should be understood that the presentation of their respective objects and the fact that they are the basis for the discussion are shown by the act of “establishing an admission” (*paṭiññā-ṭhapanā*).
Therefore, he said: “But as for what he will say,” and so forth. For this very reason, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it says: “This is the *anuloma*... [etc. ...one tetrad.”

He will say, "It is to be understood. And likewise he says, "But as there," and so forth. The intention is that only the refutation (*niggaha*) is mentioned separately, not the counter-remedy (*paṭikamma*).
As for being "mentioned separately," it means it is stated as a distinct factor without being mixed with the bringing of faults (*pāpanā*) or the charging of the offense (*āropanā*);
it is not stated as being included within those [other factors] like one of them, nor is it like the setting aside (*ṭhapanā*).

The meaning is "by way of not being subject to calculation. The phrase "but those who... is said with reference to the authors of the *pada* (verses). Regarding the second [point]... [the text continues]:
the intention is that one incurs [the offense] there because the censure is not according to reality, whereas the counter-measure (*paṭikamma*) is according to reality.

Even by one who knows the position of our own school—that from the ultimate standpoint (*paramatthato*) a person (*puggala*) is not admitted, but from the conventional standpoint (*vohārato*) it is admitted—[it is understood as follows].
When the opponent, without making a distinction through the use of quibbling (*chala*), asks, "Is a person not found in the sense of ultimate reality (*paramattha*)?
the proponent replies, "Yes," with reference to ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*), thinking: "This is a proponent of a person (*puggalavādin*);
his view must be rejected. For what is meant is that [the person] is "not found. Then the other [opponent]...

With reference to conventional truth (*sammuti-sacca*), he said, "That which is the true reality," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows: that true reality established by worldly convention is, for that very reason, not to be rejected by anyone;
therefore, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramattha*), that person (*puggala*) is not found.
Again, since the proponent had previously rejected the person on the basis of ultimate truth, [he now addresses it] on the basis of conventional truth.
Thinking, "He asks," and not rejecting that [position], he said, "It should not be stated thus. Therefore he said:
"The intention is that what is intended by oneself as the 'ultimate sense' (saccikaṭṭha) refers to conventional truth (sammutisacca).

This being established, it should not be stated that "if by the opponent... [the debate] should not be commenced," because in the first inquiry, the ultimate sense belongs to ultimate truth (paramatthasacca).

Because it is intended [in that sense]. As for the statement, "Then the proponent... falls into [a contradiction]," this too should not be said, because in the second question, what is intended is the ultimate meaning (*saccikaṭṭha*) of conventional truth (*sammutisacca*).
If it is argued that both are intended, this—if it refers to the first question—is incorrect, because that [first question] concerns only ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*).

Because it occurs by way of that [conventional truth]. Now, with reference to the second question, having first stated its meaning by way of conventional truth (*sammutisacca*), and then stating it again by way of a mixture [of both truths], it was said:
"Or, having taken conventional truth and ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*) together as one, he spoke thus.
Therefore, that too is certainly not to be asserted. "Both truths" refers to conventional and ultimate truth. Among those two, [the discussion concerns] ultimate truth alone.

In the non-figurative sense, it exists as a reality established in the ultimate sense (*saccikaṭṭha-paramattha*), whereas for the other [conventional person], it exists by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Thus it has been said:

"Illusion, a mirage... [etc. ...the ultimate sense. Therefore, even for one who accepts the apprehension [of a person] by way of conventional truth (*sammuti-sacca*), since they do not accept it by way of ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*), the inquiry—"Is the person apprehended as a reality established in the ultimate sense?"—and so forth, is appropriate. [This applies] to both the primary and the secondary [meanings].

By this very statement, "The accomplishment of the task lies in the striving," the objection beginning with "And there is no inquiry into a portion of the ultimate reality" is also refuted, because the state of being a portion of the ultimate reality itself is unestablished. Furthermore, its status as an ultimate truth need not be investigated;
that is, the opponent should not investigate whether this "ultimate reality" (saccikaṭṭha) is an ultimate truth, [saying] "the person is not apprehended."
The intention [of the opponent] is that even for the proponent (sakavādin), it must be accepted as being "in the sense of the ultimate reality of the true state" (*saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena*).
It is also logical that what is conventionally designated as the "true state" (*voharita-saccikaṭṭha*) possesses the "true state" intended by oneself, because that is what is intended by him.
This very point has already been shown below. The fault is exactly as stated in the passage beginning with, "Both truths... and so forth.
He says this with reference to what was stated immediately prior. Furthermore, its state of being non-hatred has already been demonstrated. Now, as for the phrase "atha na," the construction is:

"then it would not be apprehended in the sense of having the nature of a real entity. As for what ought to be said here, that has already been stated in the passage beginning with "yo lokavohārasiddho" (that which is established by worldly convention);
therefore, in this context, [the point is] expressed by the passage beginning with "paramatthato puggalaṃ nānujānāti" (one does not admit a person from the perspective of ultimate reality).
The underlying intention (*adhippāya*) should be discerned.
"This might be granted" means that this non-apprehension (*anupalabbhana*) should be admitted in the second question just as it was in the first.
"Or nothing need be said" means that, because it is to be set aside (*ṭhapanīya*), nothing at all need be stated.
Regarding the question: for he, in order to show the manner in which it is to be set aside, said "Just as," and so forth.
And here, although a person is not apprehended by way of the two truths, he is nevertheless apprehended by way of conventional designation;
thus, the negation should be understood here as being made on account of the state of being apprehended. [The phrase] "both what is permitted and what is negated" refers to this.
"In the first inquiry it was permitted; in the second inquiry it was refused.
"Based on this evasive speech" means based on this evasive statement consisting of the manner of both permitting and refusing with reference to one and the same matter.
The construction is: "You are to be refuted. "By way of what is possible through commonality" means by way of the state of being a point for refutation that is possible through generalization.
By way of the method of conformity (*anulomanaya*), because of the equality between the granting of permission and the refusal;

by way of the method of opposition (*paccanīkanaya*), the fabrication—that is, the contrived arrangement—of that which is impossible because it constitutes a ground for refutation, deserves to be called "quibbling" (*chala*).
