This very point has been stated [in the *Pakaraṇa*]: "Quibbling is the subversion of a statement through the production of an alternative interpretation of its meaning. By that [word], it refers to the aforementioned fabrication.
Because it is stated as "one who speaks with quibbles" (*chalavādo*). It is merely a commonality of terms that is designated as "quibble" (*chala*);
one speaks by means of this, thus it is "one who speaks with quibbles. Therefore it was said: "Because it is the cause for one who speaks with quibbles, it is 'quibble.

Since it is merely a commonality of terms that constitutes the actual meaning, it is said that "it should be investigated" in reliance upon that quibble as the object; what is there to be investigated here? Even if...
The demonstration that the establishment [of a thesis] (*ṭhapanā*) is the root for both the admission and the denial of a false state is because it is the object of those two;
however, this point is clear: it is by means of the bringing forward of faults (*pāpanā*) and the charging with faults (*āropanā*) that it is elucidated, not by the mere establishment.

4–5. "By that" refers to the proponent (*sakavādin*). "By that method" refers to the method by which the proponent, through the four ways of bringing forward and charging with faults, [establishes his position].
The refutation was made by that method and principle. Showing that such a refutation is actually a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) and is not a refutation at all, he said:
“Because of having admitted the state of being non-refuted,” which means because it has been brought about [as such].

“In this very way” means just as the admission of the state of being non-refuted was stated in the passage beginning with “The refutation made by you against me,” and so forth. “Of this” refers to the passage beginning with “Therefore,” and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the positive-negative method as stated in this text. 2.
Commentary on the Negative-positive Method.

7–10. "By another" means by that which constitutes conventional truth (*sammutisacca*). "Of another" refers to one's own proponent (*sakavādin*); for he is indeed "another" in relation to the opponent (*paravādin*).
It is stated that there is "no contradiction" because the scope (*visaya*) of the admission and the denial is different.
For only things that have an identical locus (*abhinnādhikaraṇa*) and an identical scope can be said to be contradictory, not others; this is the intended meaning. To explain this same point:
In order to clarify this, he said, “For indeed... [etc. ...he does not incur [the offense]. If that is so, how did this become a point of defeat (*niggahaṭṭhāna*)?
To this he replied, “But for himself...,” and so forth. By this, he shows that what is called a “different admission” (*paṭiññāntara*) is indeed another distinct point of defeat.
The commentary on the Converse and Direct Order is finished.
The commentary on the meaning of reality as pure is finished.
2. The meaning of reality as the occasion. 1.
Commentary on the direct and inverse order.
11. Since a general statement is established by means of a qualification, he says: “‘In all cases’ means in every body; this is the meaning.
For a general indication rests upon a particular instance; thus, a particular must be applied by one who possesses that particularity.
By this—namely, by the statement of exclusion regarding “in all cases” according to location.
3. The Meaning of Being Present in Time (Kālasaccikaṭṭha) 1. Commentary on the Positive-Negative Order (Anulomapaccanīkavaṇṇanā) 12.
"At the time of being born as a human" means at the time of the present individual existence (attabhāva). For here, "birth" (jāti) is intended to mean "individual existence" (attabhāva).
The past is the time of previous births; the future is the time of subsequent births.

Regarding these three—in all cases, at all times, and in all things—these refer to these three methods. Since the brevity of the text makes it easy to understand, he set that aside and, demonstrating the similarity of the meaning, said:
"Here too... [etc. ...should be applied. Here also, [it is shown that] there is no intrinsic nature whatsoever...

The meaning expressed here is: "A person is apprehended. For there is no such thing as a time of occurrence for something that is apprehended by way of some intrinsic nature (sabhāva) apart from its being either the whole or a part [of a collection].
4. The sense of reality in terms of parts (avayava-saccikattha).
1. Explanation of the Positive-Negative Order (Anulomapaccanīkavaṇṇanā) 13.
In the third method, it should be construed thus: there is no place of occurrence whatsoever that is devoid of even a single dhamma.
This is the actual meaning of "occasion" (okāsa) and so forth.
2. Explanation of the Negative and Positive (Paccanīkānuloma-vaṇṇanā) 14.

Regarding the phrase "of the positive pentad" (*anulomapañcakassa*) and so forth in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), [the word] "furthermore, therein" (*puna tattha*) refers either to the aforementioned commentary passage or to those negative and positive pentads.
It refers to the portion of the text beginning with "in all cases, a person (*puggala*) is not apprehended."
The meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) by the passage beginning with "referring to the body" (*sarīraṃ sandhāyā*).

"The text of the counter-argument, etc. (*paṭikammādipāḷi*) refers to the text of the counter-argument (*paṭikamma*), refutation (*niggaha*), leading forward (*upanayana*), and conclusion (*nigamana*). "In the three modes" (*tīsu mukhesu*) refers to the three modes of debate mentioned by the passage beginning with "in all cases" (*sabbatthā*).
The connection is: "the text of the opponent has been stated. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to the text. Because it has come down in an abbreviated form...
"When not stated with its own form. [The section on] the Pure [Questions]... pe ... it has been stated: "In all cases," etc.; herein, the distinction is simply this:
that there is no reference to the body and so forth by means of the phrase "in all cases" and so on, whereas here there is; otherwise, they are the same.
The commentary on the *Saccikaṭṭha* is finished.
5. Explanation of the Concordance of the Truly Established (Suddhikasaṃsandanavaṇṇanā) 17–27.

To show that there are two possible compounds—namely, *saccikaṭṭhassa saṃsandanaṃ* (the concordance of the truly established) or *saccikaṭṭhe saṃsandanaṃ* (the concordance with the truly established)—he says, “of the truly established,” and so forth.
In that context, “of the person who is truly established” (*saccikaṭṭhassa puggalassa*)...
Of the person (*puggala*), whose intrinsic nature is truly established and which exists as a reality from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramattha*).

"Connecting with form and so forth" means making it equal to form and so forth by way of the commonality of being truly established. In the phrase "truly established" (*saccikaṭṭha*), it means "by reason of being truly established" (*saccikaṭṭha-hetu*), or else having made that the basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*) therein.
And because the particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) according to the rule "conjunction [is used] in the case of equal connection" (*tulyayoge samuccayo*).
In the sense of being real and by way of commonality with what is apprehended, "form" (rūpa) is brought forward here;

thus, its state of being thus brought forward is appropriate, and so the meaning is stated by way of illustration as "according to form. Otherwise, for what purpose would there even be the bringing forward of form here?

The same applies to the remaining phenomena. Furthermore, the inquiry regarding their distinctness (aññatta) herein serves to reinforce the illustration, since that [distinctness] is based upon distinctness itself.

In the *Opammasaṃsandana*, however, the purpose of illustration is grasped; therefore, the intention here in this *Suddhikasaṃsandana* is that it is appropriate to show the meaning solely by way of synthesis.

As for the statement, "Because form and the rest are merely designations based on clinging, it cannot be said that the person is either different from or not different from them"—this is the sequence of the Teaching (*sāsanakkama*). Thus he says: "From form and the rest... [etc.]..."
"‘The occasion’ means: when that [position] is being permitted, and the sutta is not being rejected at that time.
And it should be understood that this meaning is stated with reference to an opponent who follows the teaching (sāsanika).
The reading ‘ājānāhi niggahaṃ’ must have been seen [in the source], for otherwise the ‘five sets of counter-questions’ would have been shown."
The intention is that it is not possible to say, "the tetrad of counter-arguments and so forth are abbreviated.

Since there is no causing another to admit [a position] without an objection, it is said: "for the purpose of causing admission... for the purpose of objection. For his causing [the opponent] to admit is preceded by an objection;
thus he shows that the cause is stated by way of the designation of the effect. "Because of being undeclared" means because of being unanswerable (abyākaraṇīyatā).

Or because it was not declared by the Blessed One. If [it is argued] that "because it is to be set aside, it should be rejected," then in this counter-position, the proponent must reject [the question] on the grounds that it is to be set aside.

"By the other too" means that even by the opponent, the rejection is made in the conforming position based solely on the premise that it is to be set aside; such is the intended meaning here regarding the pure comparison.

The intention is that even when [the opponent] is engaged with the conforming [arguments], the adversary has indeed made a refutation regarding the charge of otherness in respect to form and so forth.
The commentary on the comparison of the pure [formulation] is finished.
6. Commentary on the Comparison of the Simile.

28–36. By the phrase "the inquiry into otherness through the commonality of apprehension," he extracts both [questions]: "the inquiry into otherness through the commonality of apprehension" and "the inquiry through the commonality of apprehension.
Therein, with reference to the latter, he says: "The similarity of the two," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:
just as there is a similarity between the two—matter and feeling—in terms of their actual reality (*saccikaṭṭha*), so too is there a similarity between matter and the person.
It is not logical that their sameness should be the reason for their difference. Rather... [as follows] ...the fact of being apprehendable;
this reconciliation must be investigated. This is the intended meaning here:

if, by way of the commonality of ultimate reality (*saccikaṭṭha-sāmañña*), a commonality of apprehension is desired for both form and the person, then by that very same [reason], their difference must also be admitted. Now, if...

Their distinctness is not intended on the basis of a difference between ultimate reality (*paramattha*) and conventional expression (*vohāra*); for that very reason, even a commonality of apprehension (*upaladdhi-sāmañña*) should not be admitted.
37–45. "Apprehension" (*upaladdhi*) means the apprehension, the existence, of the person (*puggala*). The construction is: "It is understood as 'the pentad of counteraction' (*paṭikamma-pañcaka*).
The commentary on the correlation with the simile is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Concordance of the Fourfold Method (Catukkanayasaṃsandanavaṇṇanā) 46–52.
“Even from the standpoint of a single phenomenon” means even from the standpoint of one phenomenon among the fifty-seven phenomena that are truly real.
By this, he shows the non-admission of the person’s otherness even from all of those [phenomena]. Therefore, it is said in the commentary: “The entire ultimate truth...”
“With reference to [this],” he says. One should not engage [the inquiry] by way of each individual phenomenon such as form (*rūpa*), because a whole does not exist apart from its parts.
However, since the whole and the parts possess distinct intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*), the proponent of the opposing view raises the apprehension:

“Therefore, [the person] would be worthy of censure on account of the whole,” and so forth. This is the opening for that statement, even though [the person is designated] on account of the collection of fifty-seven phenomena.
One does not accept the otherness of the person (*puggala*), because there is no such thing as a "real entity" (*saccikaṭṭha*) existing apart from those [aggregates];

nor does one accept its non-otherness, even in part, for the whole cannot be the same as its parts. Therefore, in order to show that one should not be allowed to say, "What ground for refutation is there for one who rejects that?", it was said:
"And this... and so forth. It is precisely by way of the analysis of the various categories of phenomena (*dhamma*) such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest...
The first alternative proceeds by way of showing the mode of grasping [the person] as being without remainder;
the second, however, proceeds by way of non-distinction through the commonality of the state of ultimate truth. This is the distinction between these two alternatives.
As for "iti," it is a reference to the aforementioned manner; thus he said, "eva" (thus).

“Because of the separation from intrinsic nature” means because it must be separated by way of its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). For a phenomenon that is distinct in its intrinsic nature receives its separation from other phenomena.
Therefore he said: “because it has an intrinsic nature other than form. “Excluding form” means excluding material phenomena.
“In all three” refers to these very [formulations] as they occur: “the person in form,” “apart from form,” and “form in the person.”

In all three applications [of the argument], it is said: "For he does not accept the view of a real body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi)," because this proponent of the person (puggalavādī) is indeed one who adheres to the Teaching (sāsanika).
By the term "possessor of form" (rūpavā), only the state of having something belonging to oneself (sakiñcanatā) is indicated, not dependence on form;
thus it is said: "And here, by the phrase 'other than form,' the meaning that the person possesses form is included."
The commentary on the *Catukkanayasaṃsandanavaṇṇanā* is finished.
The commentary on the *Saṃsandanakathā* is also finished.
8. The commentary on the *Lakkhaṇayutti*.
54. In the discussion on the application of characteristics (*lakkhaṇayuttikathā*), the reading “but understand the refutation as it should be stated by way of the six [points]” is to be accepted.
The commentary on the application of characteristics is finished.
9. Commentary on the Purification of Words (*vacanasodhanavaṇṇanā*).

55–59. "The two terms have a single meaning" means that when there is a single meaning for the two terms. This is a hypothetical statement (*parikappa-vacana*) made for the purpose of demonstrating a fault, [meaning]:
"If this were so, this fault would follow. It should be understood that the final phrase, "this unity is indeed perceived," is an emphatic restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
Because it shows inconsistency—that "in some cases a person exists, while in others a person does not exist"—it was not accepted by the opponent.
Having established that very point of non-acceptance, he says "of the person" (*puggalassa*) and so forth to clarify it.

Therein, "not to be analyzed" means it is not to be analyzed in such a way as "it is apprehended. "To be analyzed" means it is to be analyzed in such a way as "both the person and something other than that are apprehended. By this, the restriction of the final phrase, "the person is indeed apprehended," is shown.
It should be understood that this does not show the point that "only a person is apprehended.

for if it were other, the fuel would not be hot, and if it were non-other, that which is to be burned would itself be the burner.
In the same way, the person does not exist apart from form and the other aggregates.
The intention of the opponents is that it is designated [as fire], yet it is neither other than those [elements] nor non-other, so as to avoid the consequences of eternalism or annihilationism.

unignited wood and such are the "fuel" to be deposited, while ignited, radiant, and hot [fire] is the "burner"; and that consists of the eight material qualities beginning with nutritive essence (*ojā*), by way of their continuity.
What is active is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated.

If, in this way, the person is distinct from form and the other aggregates and is consequently impermanent, then in the ultimate sense, within that very mass of matter designated as wood and the like, the heat is the fire and the three co-nascent elements are the fuel. "The otherness of fire and fuel" means that the person (puggala), like fire, would be established as something other than the fuel—namely, from form (*rūpa*) and so forth—and as impermanent.

"By the path of the fine-material sphere" means by the fine-material-sphere jhāna. For that is called a "path" because it is the means for rebirth in the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*).
As it is said: "He develops the path for rebirth in the fine-material [existence]. "This" refers to this fine-material-sphere jhāna.

Having raised the objection: "How does the statement, 'The path of the fine-material sphere is the cause for reaching the culmination while dwelling here,' etc., accord with the statement, 'The path developed here [is the cause],' etc., which demonstrates that the non-returner path possesses that same nature?"—the passage beginning with "But previously...
was stated in order to show how they do indeed accord. Therein, by the word "previously," [it refers to] "the path developed here," etc.

They say this; here too, however, [the phrase] begins with “by means of the path of the fine-material sphere” and so forth. In that context, “only the non-returner” refers specifically to one who stands in the fruit of non-returning.

A “jhāna non-returner” is so called because, although he has not yet severed the fetters pertaining to the internal [realms], he is of a nature not to return after having arisen in the fine-material existence, owing to his cultivation of the path [leading to] parinibbāna right there.
“The intention” refers to the meaning of the two aforementioned commentarial statements.
The underlying intention (adhippāya) is one that illuminates non-contradiction.
"Here" means in the sensual world (kāmaloka). "There" means in the Brahma-world (brahmaloka). And in this regard, the opponent should be asked:

"Does the Sutta beginning with 'By three things, O monks' have a meaning to be taken according to the literal expression (yathāruta), or is it spoken with a specific underlying intention (sandhāyabhāsita)? Regarding that:
If one were to say that [the Buddha] spoke with intentional meaning while knowing [the truth],

For just as in passages such as "just as if having consulted with the Tāvatiṃsa gods," [the reference] is made starting from Sakka, the king of the gods, among the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).

The mention of "the Thirty-three gods" is because they are well-known and famous; however, one must accept that this was spoken with reference to the intended meaning of the sutta passage, which does not mean that only they are intended.

Likewise, in the phrase "herein is the dwelling in the holy life," it is the going forth in the Dispensation that is intended by this sutta as "herein is the dwelling in the holy life," because of its great benefit through being the basis for blameless happiness, untroubled happiness, the happiness of renunciation, and so forth.
For that [attainment] is difficult to perform and hard to obtain because there is no opportunity for the gods of Uttarakuru.

In that regard, the existence [of the path] among the gods must be made clear even by means of the revolution of the sun and so forth; however, the state of not attaining any distinction is desired by both [the inhabitants of Uttarakuru and the gods].

274. *Odhiso* means "by way of parts" (*bhāgaso*); the meaning is "by a part. Since a "part" (*bhāga*) is a portion (*ekadeso*), it is therefore said "by one portion, by one portion.

That being the case, in order to show that one fully understands and abandons only a portion of each [truth], such as suffering and so forth, the text states:
"The stream-enterer... abandons a portion," and so on. For if there were multiple realizations (nānābhisamaya), then by means of the first path and the others...

Since there could be a partial abandonment of the three fetters and so forth—which are to be abandoned—through the vision of suffering and the other [truths], it would follow that one is a "partial stream-enterer" (ekadesa-sotāpanna) and so on, standing at the stage of the path of stream-entry and so forth; for supramundane wholesome states have their fruit immediately following them.
But this is not tenable. For it is not possible that the very same person, merely by a difference in time, is both a stream-enterer and a non-stream-enterer.
Thus it is possible to understand [this]. Therefore he said: "In one part he is a stream-enterer, in another part he is not a stream-enterer," and so forth.

Furthermore, this proponent of various realizations (nānābhisamayavādī) should be asked: "When path-knowledge penetrates the truths, does it penetrate them by way of its object (ārammaṇa), or rather by way of its function (kicca)?
If he should say "by way of its object," then [the question applies] to that insight-knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa).

Just as it is not logical for there to be an absolute delimitation or eradication of the origin of suffering because [the path] is not dissociated from it, so too is the seeing of the path [not logical].
For it is not tenable that [the path] proceeds by referring to itself; moreover, if one were to postulate another path, it would lead to an infinite regress.
Therefore, three truths [are established] by way of function, while cessation is [established] by way of both function and object.
And it penetrates: thus, for one who penetrates through non-delusion, there is no separate realization for the knowledge of the path.
For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, he who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering," and so forth.
Nor was this said with reference to seeing at a different time. [As it is said: "Friend, he who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering..."

"He sees the cessation of suffering... [and] he sees the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—this is because it was brought forward by the Venerable Gavampati Thera for the purpose of establishing that meaning in an investigation into whether one who possesses the vision of one truth can possess the vision of the other truths, and because the vision of each of the three truths has been applied individually.
Otherwise, there would be no point in seeing again what was already seen previously.
Since [the path] is not a "seeing" [of the truths], it would follow that the seeing of suffering and so forth must be applied to the seeing of the origin and so forth.
For the supramundane path does not function by way of performing what has already been done, as the mundane path does, because its nature is one of total eradication.

And if it were applied in that manner, every act of seeing would be followed by another act of seeing, resulting in an endless succession of seeings. Thus, both from the standpoint of scripture and from logical reasoning, there is no separate realization (abhisamaya).
It must be concluded here that there is no specific abandonment of the individual paths by way of partial relinquishment (*odhiso*).
The commentary on the discussion of partial relinquishment is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of Abandoning (*Jahatikathāvaṇṇanā*).
1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Non-Extraction of the Thread 280.
Although it is stated in the Pāḷi that “one develops the three paths,” one should understand that the development of the path is solely for the purpose of utterly cutting off the defilements.

With this in mind, [the author] said: “Because of the presence of the task: because of the abandoning of what is to be abandoned by the three. In this context, “by the three” refers to the three lower [paths].
The meaning is: "the cutting off" (*samucchedana*) refers to the abandoning of the internal fetters (*ajjhattasaṃyojana*) that are to be abandoned by the three noble paths (*ariyamagga*).

Furthermore, that is the "function" (*kicca*); specifically, it is the function of the path’s clear realization of abandonment regarding the lower-tier fetters (*adhobhāgiyasaṃyojana*). "By that very path" means by the non-returner path (*anāgāmimagga*) itself.
"This does not coincide" means that sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill will (*byāpāda*) are abandoned even prior to the arising of that path.
The description of attainment does not accord with, nor is it consistent with, this statement regarding the presence of the path’s function.
Therefore, by the word "therefore" (tasmā), he refers back to the aforementioned contradiction. "Of those abandoned" means of those suppressed.

For one who, having attained jhāna, cuts off defilements already suppressed by jhāna through the path, is the one intended here. Hence he said: "In the path of seeing... [etc. ...this is the intention."
The commentary on the Discourse on Relinquishing is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on "Everything Exists": 1.
Commentary on the Logic of the Argument.

282. Regarding the statement "all exists" (*sabbaṃ atthi*): since the proponents of other doctrines hold the view that the past and the future possess an existing nature just like the present, therefore "all" refers to everything divided by time into the categories of the past and so forth.

However, the inquiry "even that which does not exist, that too exists" is made from the standpoint of that which is liberated from time; this is for the purpose of demonstrating the excessive logical extension (*atippasaṅga*).
It is the attribution of faults based on the opponent’s own admission, or it is the demonstration of the method regarding the non-existence of the past and the future.

However, as for this existence—the state of being—since it does not occur apart from place, time, mode, and phenomena, the text proceeds with the passage beginning, “Everything exists everywhere,” etc., in order to show an inquiry by first correlating that existence with those very factors. Therein:
Although "in all places" (*sabbattha*) is a general term, it is applied here as a qualification;

furthermore, since "in all [of them]" (*sabbesu*) is stated later to refer to the specific categories of phenomena (*dhamma*), the Commentary explains its meaning by way of the coarse and manifest collection of material phenomena, stating: "In all places means in the entire body. This is merely an illustration.

Or rather, it should be viewed thus: just as the space, time, and so forth, or the seven primary elements (sattappakatipurisā) asserted by the followers of Kaṇāda and Kapila, so too everything asserted by the opponent must necessarily follow as being all-pervasive.
Furthermore, in the phrase "in every body," the locative case indicates pervasion—just as in the expression "oil in sesame seeds"—therefore, everything must be comprised within the body.
It is said: “The feet [are] on the head...
[and so on]... the meaning. The construction is: “At all times, everything exists. Within this very alternative, his contrary doctrine would be illustrated:
“What exists, that indeed exists; what does not exist, that indeed does not exist; there is no arising of the non-existent, and there is no destruction of the existent.”

"…destruction. Thus, in every way, the connection is that "everything exists" (atthi) in all phenomena; this is the meaning of "existence" (attha). By these positions, however, the doctrine is illustrated:
"Everything has its own intrinsic nature (sabbasabhāva); because of the state of being crowded with many beings, there is no arising from what is non-existent.
"Devoid of conjunction" (yogarahita) means devoid of conjunction characterized by any kind of fitness or unfitness. That...
"Of a single nature," however, means that which is devoid of conjunction is, in actual fact, of a single nature; the meaning is "one dhamma.
By this, the claim of the proponents of the gods—that there is indeed a vision of Brahmā—is shown to be an exaggeration. "He asks 'it exists'":
if your doctrine is that "everything exists," then [he asks] whether, according to my aforementioned view, the state of right view exists as an absolute certainty.
It must be accepted by her; therefore, the meaning is that he asks, "Does he exist?
The commentary on the section on grammatical construction is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Correlation of Time.

285. Regarding "the past... having done": here is the summary of the meaning. Without taking up this distinction of matter—namely, that it is "past" or "future"—one should apply [the mind] to matter distinguished specifically by its present state, which is the object of the sphere of speech, because the states of being "unpleasant" and "present matter" share a common locus.
Although there is a distinction between the qualifier and the qualified, it should nevertheless be treated as if it were not to be divided.

For in the Pāḷi, by the words "iti" (thus), the manner in which that meaning is to be expressed through the terms "present" or "form" is shown; therefore, [it is said]: "by the word 'present'... it is stated."

[The Blessed One] said: "It exists. "Description of form" (*rūpapaññatti*) means the description of the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). For that is a derivative description (*tajjāpaññatti*) based upon phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*).
Therefore it was said: "A presently existing description that occurs with respect to what is delimited by intrinsic nature.

"Based upon an aggregate of forms" refers to those material phenomena which, occurring in the mode of manifesting the absence [of a self], serve as the basis for various individual descriptions of a self (*attapaññatti*).
"Dependent upon a collection. For even the act of depending (*upādāna*) is itself "depending" (*upādāna*).

Therefore, because it is dependent upon a collection and thus exists as a designation for what is not [ultimately] real, there is the "inexpressibility of disappearance" (*vigamāvattabbatā*). This means that disappearance—the departure from the state of being a basis—is inexpressible.
For by the disappearance of whiteness, no state [of the cloth] comes to be. However, it is not logical that the nature of form (*rūpa*) should be subject to disappearance and re-appearance.
The exposition. The phrase "the state of being form" means the nature of the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) and its status as the objective domain of eye-consciousness.
For it is not logical that there should be a necessity for its cessation upon the disappearance of its present state.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the connection with time is finished.
Commentary on the Purification of Words (Vacanasodhanavaṇṇanā) 288.
Regarding the phrase "either future or present," the word *vā* here has the sense of indefiniteness, as in "it should be tied to either a khadira tree or a palāsa tree.
Therefore, in the expression "having been, it becomes," the word *hoti* refers to anything whatsoever among the future and the present.
Showing that one obtains a connection by making an effort, he said: "The future... should be seen.
Therein, "being present" means arising in the present, obtaining the state of being present. Therefore he said:
"By way of its acquisition, that very future becomes that present. And "having been that, it becomes" refers to that which was future.
Having [previously] existed, it is said to "exist having existed" because it has attained a present state; he asks: does that too exist again after having existed?

"Because of the non-departure from that state" means because of not proceeding from the state of having existed to the state of existing. "Because of the absence of a present state" means because of the non-existence of presentness.
By the phrase "it deserves to be spoken," he shows that there is no fault in the mere act of speaking it. This is what is meant:

although for that which has already come into being there is no further state of "having been and then becoming" again, nevertheless, because it must be made known again and again, it deserves to be stated in that same way a second time and even thereafter; thus he affirms, "Yes. Regarding the word "dhamma":

Regarding phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*). By way of their negation, they are non-phenomena (*adhamma*) and phenomena lacking intrinsic nature (*abhāvadhamma*). Therefore he said, "like a rabbit's horn.
Regarding the method of negation: in the passage "having been, it becomes;
having been, it becomes," since you previously asserted that "the future, having become, becomes present" on the basis of the view that "that very same future is the present," [this is now refuted].
It was stated, “Having been future or present, it comes to be. When asked, “Does that too come to be having already been?
the opponent made a denial, saying “No indeed,” because of the absence of further becoming after what has already become.
By that method of denial, even though there is no difference in the entity—since that very same form (rūpa) and so forth which was future becomes present—[it is shown that]...
However, since there is indeed a distinction of time in the phrase "future and present," the negation occurs in order to oppose that distinction of time;
thus he says, "by the method of negation, that is, by way of difference in time. For it is by this [method] that both that [previous position] and this negation are established.
As for the phrase "by the method of affirmation," he says this with reference to that which was affirmed immediately following the aforementioned negation.
For just as that declaration was explained and set forth by way of non-difference in meaning, so too is this. Therefore he said, "by way of non-differentiation of meaning" (*atthānānattena*);
the meaning is: by way of the non-differentiation of the referent (*attha*) which serves as the basis for the designation of time, such as the future and so forth.

Just as, despite the non-differentiation of the referents such as material form (*rūpa*) which serve as the bases [for designations], there is no lapse of their three moments, yet there is a lapse of their state of being future or present through association with them.

Thus, showing the meaning that "being spoken of there as 'becoming' and 'having become,' they are designated as prior and posterior actions respectively because they have occurred in prior and posterior [moments]," he states, "He asserts the non-difference of the referent (*atthānānatta*)...
and so forth, and then further supports that very point with the words, "For it is indeed the non-difference of the referent," and so on.
However, as for one who asserts, "The soul is the same as the body" (*taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīraṃ*):

Just as one falls into the non-difference of the soul and the body by asserting that "the soul is the body" or "the body is the soul," so too for one who claims "that which is future is that which is present," the future and the present fall into non-difference; thus,
the states of existence and non-existence mentioned regarding the present and the future would necessarily apply to the future and the present as well.
It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “This being so, that which has not yet come is indeed called ‘it is,’ and that which is present is also indeed called ‘it is.

Regarding the phrase “of the matter already admitted”: this refers to the matter already admitted by [the question], “Is that very same future thing the same as the present one?”—answering, “Yes”—with reference to the non-difference in meaning (*atthānānatta*).
For a matter that is intended to be known is a question. The fault (*dosa*) has been stated regarding the future...
In the former method, the fault consisting in the future becoming present again after having been present is stated.

In the latter method, however, the meaning is that the fault consisting in each of the future and the present attaining the state of "having been" and "being" is stated. Regarding the "rejected question": "Is that very same future [dharma] that present? No.
"In this way it should be said"—thus [it refers to] the question rejected with reference to the diversity of time.
"By that" means by the negation of the existence of the future and the present after having been.

"Challenges" means he challenges [the opponent] by saying that the future is called "having been," the present is called "having been," and both, because they are not different, possess the nature of both. "In this regard" refers to the phrase "having been, it becomes."
Regarding the question, "How is it that there is fault? he challenges. He resolves it with: "Of that very same [person].
How is the challenge formulated, and how is the resolution formulated? The challenge is based on the fact that the permission and the prohibition have different objects;

the resolution is based on their having the same locus, because although the time and the purpose differ, the object is not distinct. For "of that very same" means "of the opponent's [position] itself."
“Taking both together” means taking both—that which is future and that which is present—into one.
“Each one” means each one among those. “Only each one” means not taking both together, but only each one separately;
the meaning is that it is not appropriate in this position [to take them] in that way. “This is the method” is an extended application (*atidesa*) made because [the text] is abbreviated. That...
“Difficult to understand” is explained by the passage beginning with “For that which is future,” and so forth.

The intention is that it must be admitted [as difficult] because the future and the present, respectively, exist after having been non-existent (*abhūtvā bhāva*). The method of commentary proceeding with the words “That which was stated by you,” and so forth, follows the previous method;
for therein, the state of “having been and then becoming” (*bhūtvā bhāva*) was challenged by the passage beginning with “If, for you, that which was future. “Another... [The text continues].

The second method begins with the words “the method,” and so forth. For therein, in each case among the future and so on, it is urged that there is the name “having been” (hutvā hoti) for each one; thus, “for the future...
having been, it simply has the name ‘having been’.
The commentary on the clarification of the statements is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Past, etc. (290).
Why is it asked, "How is it said? It is stated thus because by the word "that" in the second question, this phrase "knowledge of the past" is referred back;
and that is present knowledge which is called "past" because its object is a past dhamma.
Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "When asked again, [he says] 'present knowledge with a past object,' and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of past knowledge and so forth is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the discussion of the Arahants and so forth.
291. Since the contradiction with the Sutta—beginning with the words “an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed”—is evident, he says, “The contradiction with reasoning...

should be seen,” in order to demonstrate this very point. In that context, “non-differentiation” means absence of distinction. By the word “etc. in the phrase “and so forth,” the inclusion of such terms as “one who has finished his task,” “one who has laid down his burden,” and so on, should be understood.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the Arahants and so forth is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion on the Purification of Words: 295.
That object which is denotable by the word "past" (atīta) is also denotable by the word "exists" (atthi); thus, both have the same grammatical core (samānādhikaraṇa).

It was stated [by others] that this is because the words *atīta* (past) and *atthi* (is) have the same meaning; however, this is not so, because it is precisely that which is denoted by the word *atīta* which is also denoted by the word *atthi*.
Therefore he said: "And because the meaning of the word *atthi* is itself a past state. What is established by this? He says: "The past is indeed the past, and what is 'indeed past' is the past.
This is what is meant: if, according to your view, the past exists (*atthi*), then...
And as for the phrase "and now it has passed away" (*ca nvātītaṃ*), [the meaning is that] our past may be past, and likewise, our past may exist and our past may be past.
Just as in the statement "the past exists," one should not take this as a restrictive rule that only the past exists, because the existence of even what is not past is intended [to be included].
For this very reason, he said: "The past may exist; it may indeed have passed away. For by which...
The opponent maintains that the past exists by way of its specific mode; he likewise maintains that the non-past—the future and the present—exists by that same mode.
But by what mode does he maintain this? By the mode of being conditioned (*saṅkhata*).
Therefore it is said: "In that way, the past is indeed past; the non-past is indeed not past. Consequently, the restriction here is that the past truly exists.
It should be understood thus. For while the past is restricted by its existence (*atthibhāva*), existence is not restricted to the past;
however, in the statement "Nirvana does not exist," it is possible that Nirvana alone exists—this restriction also applies there, and therefore that [meaning] alone should be accepted.
For even though Nirvana, by virtue of its ultimate existence, is a subsequent term that is emphasized (*avadhāraṇa*).

It is obtained because of the non-existence of anything else; nevertheless, since nothing else is apprehended in the form of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*), when the meaning of the restrictive particle in the first phrase is taken as "nibbāna alone exists," there is no room for the objection: "Nibbāna might exist, or it might not exist.
However, the restrictive particle in the first phrase [does not apply] to the past and so forth by the opponent...
"Taken" (gahita) means there is no over-extension here; moreover, its non-taking is understood from the text itself.

Thus, in this context, the fault of "contradicting what is desired" (iṭṭhavighātadosāpatti) applies only to the opponent who asserts the existence of the past and so forth, but not to our own proponent who asserts the existence of Nibbāna.
This should be understood as the method of demonstration and establishment.
Here it is asked: "Does this statement, 'the past exists,' etc., intend that the past and the future exist in an ultimate sense (paramatthato), or rather not in an ultimate sense? For what reason?

If, first of all, they exist in an ultimate sense, then because of their existence at all times, it follows that conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) are eternal; and that is not tenable, because it contradicts both scripture (āgama) and logic (yutti)."
Furthermore, if [it were not so] in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), the objection beginning with "everything exists" would be pointless; yet it is not pointless.
For that opponent, by stating "whatever form there is, whether past or future," etc., has asserted the status of the aggregates (*khandhabhāva*) even for the past and the future.
And if the past did not exist, how could the fruit of wholesome or unwholesome karma arise in the future? Regarding this:
Otherwise, how could knowledge of past lives and so forth, as well as knowledge of future states and so forth, function?
Therefore, this [definition] was formulated with reference to that which one asserts exists in the ultimate sense:
namely, that the past and the future truly exist. And this must be accepted unconditionally. Those who say "everything exists"—namely, the past, the future, and the present—are called Sarvāstivādins.
These Sarvāstivādins are of four kinds. Among them, some are proponents of the distinctness of entities (*bhāvānyathātva-vādins*).
For they hold that "just as when a golden vessel is broken and fashioned otherwise, there is a change in its shape alone but not in its color and so forth;
and just as milk, while transforming into the state of curd, relinquishes its taste, potency, and maturation but not its color—so too do phenomena."
They say that those passing from the future period into the present period abandon only their future state, not their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*);
likewise when passing from the present period into the past period. Some, however, are proponents of the difference in characteristics (*lakkhaṇaññattika*);
they maintain that a phenomenon occurring within the three periods is "past" when it is endowed with the characteristic of the past and disjoined from the other characteristics.
"Likewise, the future and the present [are distinct]. Others say: "Just as a man who is attached to one woman is not attached to others.

Still others are proponents of the theory of difference in state (*avatthāññattika*); they maintain: "A phenomenon (*dhamma*) occurring throughout the three time periods is designated as this or that different thing upon reaching each respective state, due to the difference in state, but not due to a difference in intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
It is like a single die [being called by different names depending on its position]."
"It is called 'one' when placed alone; it is called 'hundred' when there are a hundred parts, and 'thousand' when there are a thousand parts—it is of such a nature.

Others hold a different view regarding the threefold nature (aññathāññattika), saying: "A phenomenon occurring throughout the three time periods is designated by a different name according to its respective relation to each [time period].
Just as one and the same woman is called both 'mother' and 'daughter'. Thus these [teachers]...
There are four Sarvāstivādins.
Among them, the first should be included among the followers of Kapila because of his doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*).
For the second as well, a confusion of time occurs, since everything would possess all characteristics. For the fourth as well, there is likewise a confusion; for a single phenomenon...
At the moment of occurrence, all three times coincide. For the preceding and succeeding moments are the past and future respectively, while the middle one is the present.
However, there is no confusion in the third classification, which concerns the difference in state, because time is defined by the functional activity of the phenomenon (*dhamma*).
Indeed, a phenomenon is "present" at the moment it performs its own function; prior to that, it is "future," and after that, it is "past."
In that regard, if the past exists by way of its present intrinsic nature, and the future likewise exists, why is it called "past" or "future"?
Is it not stated that [the distinction] is "due to the demarcation of time by way of the function of a dhamma"?

If this is so, what is the function of the present eye? It is the production of the fruit when all conditions are assembled without exception. This being the case, the same would apply to the future as well.
In that case, there would be a confusion of characteristics, as one would have to say that its existence is due to that [activity]. And here it must be said:
if a phenomenon exists by virtue of its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), what obstacle is there to its performing its function (*kicca*)?

Why does it perform its function only sometimes and not other times? If you say it is because of the presence or absence of the convergence of conditions (*paccaya-samavāya*), [we reply: no, because the function itself lacks such convergence; for it is eternal.
Because the state of existence is intended [as real], for that very reason there would be no determination of time.
For if a phenomenon (dhamma) exists by its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva), why would it sometimes be called "past" and sometimes "future"? There would be no determination of time.
For that phenomenon which has not yet arisen is "future"; that which has arisen but not yet ceased is "present"; and that which has ceased—

Thus it is past. This alone must be said here: if the past and the future exist in the same way that the present exists, then for a phenomenon existing in that manner, how can there be its unarisen state or its ceased state?
For how can it be established that a phenomenon existing with that very same intrinsic nature is "unarisen" or "ceased"? Was it not previously existent, such that...
It is said that it is "unborn" because of its non-existence; yet there is nothing subsequently that exists, of which it could be said that it is "ceased" due to non-existence.
Therefore, the three time periods cannot be established in any way if they do not accept that [a thing] comes into being after not having been, and then perishes after having come into being.
As for what was stated—that "there is no consequence of eternalism because of its connection with the characteristics of the conditioned"—[that too is untenable].

This is merely a matter of words, since there is no occurrence of arising and passing away; yet that phenomenon (dhamma) exists at all times, and it is not eternal—how can such a statement be consistent?
The intrinsic nature (sabhāva) exists at all times, yet the phenomenon is not called eternal.
The Dhamma is not other than its intrinsic nature; oh, what skillfulness regarding the Dhammas!
As for the statement, "Whatever form, whether past or future," and so forth—since it is stated that the past and future possess the status of aggregates (*khandha*), we reply:
the past is that which has previously come to be, and the future is that which will come to be when conditions are present.

Because both [past and future phenomena] do not transcend their intrinsic nature of being subject to change (ruppanādi), they are described as having the status of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and so forth.

Just as past phenomena and future phenomena are so called because they do not transcend the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva), and not because they possess the intrinsic nature of the present. And who says that "it exists in the same way as the present"?
How, then, does it exist? By way of its past and future intrinsic nature. But this [objection] is yours alone.
If it exists at all times, how can it be called past and future?

As for what is stated in the Sutta, "He does not pass away until that evil has been exhausted," this refers to the capacity to produce its fruit which was deposited by that karma within the specific continuum (saṃtāna) in which the karma was performed and accumulated.
This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*), not because past karma possesses a presently existing intrinsic nature (*dharamānasabhāva*).
For if that were the case, how could that which exists by its own nature be called "past"? Thus, this must be accepted as follows:

formations (*saṅkhārā*) come into being having not existed before, and having existed, they pass away; for them, there is no [intrinsic nature] prior to their arising or subsequent to their passing away.
There is indeed such a thing as "stability" (ṭhiti), on account of which it could be said that the past and the future exist. Therefore it was said:
"They have gone beyond storage, they are broken; there is no heap remaining in the future.
Even those things that have arisen and persist are like mustard seeds on the point of an awl."
If the future existed in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), it would be impossible to say that it "comes into being after not having been.
If you argue that it comes into being after not having been at the time of its present occurrence, no; for time is merely the manifestation of phenomena (*dhamma*).

If, on the other hand, you mean that it comes into being without possessing its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), then it is established that the future does not exist in the ultimate sense. And as for what was said regarding [its existence] when it is non-existent...
"How could there be a future fruit for wholesome or unwholesome karma performed in the past?"—here, however, the arising of a fruit from a past karma is not intended;
rather, it is due to the continuity (santāna) because of that [karma] having been performed and because of the specific quality (visesa) deposited therein.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "Because of having performed and accumulated wholesome karma pertaining to the sense-sphere, its result..."
“Eye-consciousness has arisen. But for one who holds that the past and future exist in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), the fruit exists eternally;
what, then, would be the efficacy of karma therein? If it is in the act of producing [the fruit], then it is established that this [fruit] comes into being after not having existed.
As for what was said: “If the past and future do not exist, how could knowledge operate with respect to them?”
In whatever way that object exists, it is remembered in that same way. And how does that object exist? It is said: "It was" and "it will be.
For no one, when recollecting the past, recollects it as "it exists"; rather, they recollect it as "it was.
Just as a present object is experienced, so too is that past object recollected. And just as the present [object] will be [in the future], so too is it recollected.
Thus it is apprehended by the Buddha and others. And if that [object] exists in that very way, it would have to be something presently existing.
But if it does not exist, then it is established that "that which is non-existent becomes an object of knowledge.

For these [factors]—mind and mental concomitants—are called "objective" (*ārammaṇā*) because they possess an object (*ārammaṇa*), whether that object is a presently existing mental designation or one that is non-existent; it is not only that which is presently existing.

Because it proceeds by referring [only] to that which has arisen, therefore the Sabbatthivāda does not maintain that only the present—possessing a currently existing intrinsic nature—is real, while the past and future are not.

However, some say: "The Sabbatthivādins are not so called because they admit the existence of the past and so forth, but rather because they admit the existence of the 'all' (sabbassa) of the sense-bases (āyatana).
According to their opinion, all those belonging to the Teaching (sāsanika) [are Sabbatthivādins].
"All things exist" refers to the Sarvāstivādins.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the purification of terms is finished.
The commentary on the discussion concerning "all exists" is finished.
6. Discussion on Past Aggregates, etc.
1. Exposition of the Discussion on the Non-Establishment by Sutta 297.
"The past, the future, and the present"—this is a conventional expression delimited by the divisions of time regarding phenomena (*dhammas*).
It is designated in dependence upon this or that specific state. For a phenomenon (*dhamma*) is "present" at the moment it performs its own function;
prior to that it is "future," and after that it is "past"—this is precisely what has been stated.
In this regard, although phenomena are unstable due to their impermanence, their aforementioned states are nonetheless fixed; therefore, the designation of time based upon them is likewise fixed.
For the past and so forth are not designated by way of the future and so forth; however, the designations of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so on do not depend on specific temporal distinctions.
For in all three times, the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) remains simply the aggregate of form, and likewise for the remaining aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

This being the case, since the opponent applies this designation "exists"—which is restricted to the present—to the past and the future as well, [it follows that he must admit the existence of the past and future].

He superimposes [the concept]; therefore, he creates a long-term confusion. Because he employs conventional expression by treating what does not exist in the ultimate sense as if it did exist, this discourse beginning with "the past aggregates" was commenced in order to distinguish him from that [error].

Furthermore, because one takes together as a single unit those phenomena—which possess intrinsic natures such as being "malleable" (ruppaṇa) and are divided into categories such as "past"—and [perceives] therein the sense of a "heap" (rāsa), [it is called a "khandha"].

The designation of aggregates (*khandha-paññatti*) is based upon [the five aggregates]; and the designation of bases (*āyatana-paññatti*) and elements (*dhātu-paññatti*) is based upon the meaning of causes and so forth, as well as the sense of emptiness, with respect to the eye, visible forms, and the rest.

Therefore, that [designation] is common to all three periods of time; it does not have the specific time-periods such as the past as its primary referent in the way that the designations "past" and so forth do.

Thus he said: "Because they do not abandon their nature as aggregates and so forth, [the designation applies] to the past and future. Now, these [aggregates and so forth] which are past and so forth...
The opponent, perceiving [the past and future] as having an intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) just like the present, asserts that they "exist";
thus it is said, "for one who maintains the existence of the past and the future. Whatever else needs to be said here follows the same method already explained above.
The sutta beginning, "Monks, there are these three pathways of language," is the *Niruttipatha-sutta*. For in that [sutta], only the present...
The state of existence (atthibhāva) is spoken of [in relation to the present], not that of the past and future. Therefore it was said:

"Because its existence has been excluded. If this is so, how is it that [the Sutta] says, "Bhikkhus, Nibbāna exists"? That was said because it is apprehended at all times, for the purpose of making known the permanent nature of the unconditioned dhamma;
whereas here, however, the state of existence refers to conditioned dhammas by virtue of their possession of the three moments.
In order to establish that there is nothing prior to or subsequent to it, it is said: "Bhikkhus, whatever form... [etc. ...there will be no designation for it.
By this, it is shown that because the conventional designation "it exists" is not grasped, the past and the future do not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
"By this same method" refers to what was stated as "because they do not abandon their status as aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth."
By means of a reason (*hetu*). For here, "method" (*upāya*) refers to the reasoning that establishes through proof (*upapattisādhanayutti*).
The commentary on the discussion establishing by means of the Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion Establishing by Means of the Sutta.

"298. These phenomena (dhammā): these are the phenomena consisting of the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu). 'Bringing forward the suttas' means bringing forward the suttas that follow the path of linguistic derivation (nirutti). 'Of these' refers to those of the past and the future.
The commentary on the discussion establishing the suttas is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the past aggregates and so forth is finished."
7. Discussion on the Existence of Certain Things 1.
Explanation of the Discussion on Certain Things, such as the Past 299.

Those wholesome and unwholesome states that have been performed and accumulated, which have not yet provided an opportunity for the giving of their result, and those which have provided an opportunity—these are what are called "arisen by having made an opportunity."
...are so called. Furthermore, those whose results have been only partially ripened—all these should be understood as "having unripened results.
The opponent maintains their existence with the intention that the capacity for them to yield a result has not departed.

However, regarding those wholesome and unwholesome states whose results have entirely and completely ripened, the opponent maintains their non-existence because that capacity has departed. Therefore he said: "It exists..."

“Some exist, some do not,” and so forth. To show that for the opponent who asserts this, just as he falls into the position that some things do not exist even among those without ripening (*avipāka*), so too he necessarily falls into such positions regarding those with ripened ripening (*vipakkavipāka*) and those with unripened ripening (*avipakkavipāka*), the Pāḷi proceeds with the passage beginning, “some phenomena with unripened ripening,” and so on. Therefore it was said: “Of the three...”
"...should dwell among those who are seated," and so forth. "By way of conventional expression" means by way of the conventional expression of the non-cessation of the fruit;
however, since he stands upon the tenet that the causal function exists as unceased and uninterrupted, he must indeed be challenged.
For the opponent maintains that the continuity of the fruit, which occurs by way of non-interruption, exists as a conventional expression, yet his [conception of] the cause...

The opponent [claims]: "In the ultimate sense, because it is that which accumulates karma, there exists a single dharma called 'accumulation of karma' (*kammūpacaya*), which is dissociated from consciousness (*cittavippayutta*) and is non-perished—just like the states of having attained or not having attained their own nature—and this too is a synonym for that very [karma]. It is with reference to this that he says:
"Karmas do not perish, even after a thousand eons."
“Having obtained the completeness of the requisites, living beings ripen in due time.

And it is with reference to this that he will later say, in the discussion on merit consisting in enjoyment: “He admits the thesis that ‘merit consisting in enjoyment arises dissociated from consciousness.
The commentary to the Discussion of the Existence of Certain Things is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhānakathāvaṇṇanā) 301.

Regarding the phrase "because they are the foundations of mindfulness in the ultimate sense" (*paramatthasatipaṭṭhānattā*): this shows that only supramundane right mindfulness—and even within that, specifically that which constitutes the Path—possesses the status of a foundation of mindfulness in the primary sense (*nippariyāyena*), because it leads to liberation (*niyyānikattā*); whereas other types of mindfulness possess it only in a figurative sense (*pariyāyena*). This refers to the right mindfulness of the Path and its Fruit (*magga-phala-sammāsati*).
Since there is a method for the cultivation of the recollection of the Dhamma, it is said: "of that which consists of the mundane and supramundane foundations of mindfulness.
The intended meaning is: "of that which consists of the collection of mindfulness," and not "of that which is the object of mindfulness.

For if it were the object of mindfulness that was being urged toward the status of a foundation of mindfulness, the Pāli would have begun with "the eye-base is a foundation of mindfulness. Therefore, it was said: [etc.]

"It was stated by way of a question concerning the classification of all phenomena. Furthermore, it should be understood that in this demonstration of the suttas, the first [section] is shown by way of the mundane foundations of mindfulness, the second by way of the mixed, and the third by way of the supramundane.
The commentary on the discussion of the foundations of mindfulness is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Meaning of "Whatever" (Hevatthikathāvaṇṇanā) 304.

Regarding the discussion on the meaning of "whatever," the opponent's doctrine—which asserts that "every phenomenon exists by its own nature and does not exist by the nature of another"—is such that it should not be answered categorically, just as it cannot be answered through analysis or by counter-questioning. Thus, it is not to be answered with a one-sided (ekamsa) reply.
Because there is no distinction [between them], he says "by a subsequent non-statement" (avattabbuttarena) with the intention that it remains solely on the side of the "to-be-set-aside" (ṭhapanīya).

For just as the proposition that "all doctrines have counter-arguments" is to be regarded with equanimity because it is a statement of fact and thus a subsequent non-statement, so too should this be understood.
Therefore he says "by what is to be regarded with equanimity. Alternatively, "non-statement" is the subsequent [term] to "not to be stated" (avattabba); thus it is "subsequent non-statement."

Just as, regarding those who maintain the doctrine of impermanence, it is not necessary to state the further argument that "sound is impermanent because its existence is dependent on conditions"—since that would be proving what is already established—so too should it be understood here. For proving what is already established is as useless as burning what is already burned;
however, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, since a phenomenon (dhamma) possesses whatever intrinsic nature (sabhāva) the opponent [asserts] for it...
Because it exists with that very same intrinsic nature, it is established as "non-existent" only when devoid of the conceptual grasping of temporal distinctions and the like;
therefore, it is said, "because it was established through improper attention (*ayoniso patiṭṭhāpitattā*).
And here, by the opponent who asserts "it exists in this way" or "it does not exist in this way," [the position is undermined] just as [a thing is undermined] by its own and other natures.
The existence of form and so forth has been admitted; likewise, that existence has indeed been admitted even with respect to differences of time, place, and so on. For this very reason it was said:
"The past does not exist by way of the future and present, nor do the future and present exist by way of the past and so forth.
If this were the case, the doctrine of the naked Nigaṇṭhas would be illustrated. For they say: "It may exist, it may not exist, it may..."
They assert [the existence of] all categories [of phenomena], beginning with "it both exists and does not exist.

In this regard, if "non-existence" is intended in terms of the very intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of the entity, or by way of place, time, and continuity, then that is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because it is accepted even by our own proponent.
For whatever the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon may be, it is not perceived as something other than that. If it were perceived otherwise, [it would follow that it is not its true nature].

It might be argued that this [non-existence] would be something else entirely. However, in this context, a general characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*) need not be demonstrated, because a specific characteristic (*salakkhaṇa*) is intended here, and because non-existence lacks such a specific characteristic.
Just as there is no dispute regarding non-existence by way of another state (*parabhāva*), so too is it with respect to other places and times;
for conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) are momentary, and thus they do not migrate to another place or another time.
By this same method, non-existence (*natthitā*) should also be understood as being rejected.

Just as existence and non-existence cannot find a footing in a single phenomenon without a difference in time—because they are mutually contradictory—so too [existence] cannot exist at all times because of its permanence (*niccatā*).
As for what they say: "Just as gold, existing in the form of a bracelet and so forth, undergoes the state of being a necklace and so forth..."
“Permanent and impermanent. For that [gold] is permanent because it does not abandon its nature as gold, and impermanent because it abandons its state as a bracelet and so forth;
thus it is with all phenomena. They should be asked this: “Is the state of being a bracelet that of the bracelet, or rather that of the gold?
If it belongs to the bracelet, it would be independent of the gold, like the state of something else. If, on the other hand, it belongs to the gold, then at all times...

In that case, the state of being gold would be perceived, just as it is in the example. Nor can it be said that the two are identical, because even when the bracelet is destroyed, the gold is not destroyed.

Now, if it is thought that this fault does not apply because of the relationship between the successive states (*pariyāya*) of the gold bracelet and so forth—for instance, just as the underlying substance (*pariyāyin*) remains exactly as it was even when the cessation of the state of being a bracelet is followed by the arising of the state of being a necklace—[then we reply:
... [the underlying substance] remains exactly as it was even when the cessation of the state of being a bracelet is followed by the arising of the state of being a necklace.
Thus, when there is the cessation of the human modality and the arising of the divine modality, the substance of the living being (*jīvadravya*) persists;
therefore, it is both permanent and impermanent, and so too are all substances. This is like answering a question about a mango tree by speaking of a breadfruit tree.

For one who asserts that the very same thing is both permanent and impermanent, acknowledges permanence in one respect and impermanence in another; thus, [the distinction between] the modality and the possessor of the modality—

If non-difference is intended, then in that case the mode (*pariyāya*) would also be permanent because it is not different from the possessor of the mode (*pariyāyin*), just like the nature of the mode itself;
or else, the possessor of the mode would be impermanent because it is not different from the mode, just like the nature of the mode itself.
Or, if their non-difference is something other [than identity], then in that case one does not escape the two faults already stated. Furthermore, what is this so-called "mode"? If—
Regarding shape: let us first consider gold. How can it be a substantial entity (*dravya*) if it lacks a material form?

If you maintain that even this [gold] possesses shape, then, in that case, a single continuum of a sentient being would result in being multiple and having material form, because we observe the same [multiplicity and materiality] even in the case of pustules and the like which possess shape.
Alternatively, if you mean a distinction in its activity (*pavatti*), even so, multiplicity and momentariness would follow.
Therefore, one must first establish the nature of the figurative expression itself.
As for what was said— that "gold exists in the form of bracelets and so forth"— in that case, among the distinguished visible forms, odors, tastes,
and tangibles that are perceived through their association with excellence, is it one [of these], or rather their collection, or something distinct from them?

Or is it another phenomenon (*dhammāntara*) that is gold? In this regard, first of all, each individual factor such as visible form (*rūpa*) is not gold, because the function of gold is not accomplished by them individually;
nor is there another phenomenon apart from those [factors], because such a thing does not exist.

If, on the other hand, it is the collection [of factors] that is gold, then since that is merely a conceptual designation (*paññatti*), neither its permanence nor its impermanence is possible. And just as it is with gold, so it is with the bracelet as well.
"Because it is a mere designation. This illustration establishes for the opponent that even the "substance of the soul" (jīvadravya) is a mere designation;
so how could there be any question of its being permanent or impermanent? Enough of this excessive elaboration.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the existence of a self is concluded.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.
2. Second Chapter: 1. Commentary on the Section on Bringing from Another.

307. Since overestimation (*adhimānikatā*) is impossible for those who have suppressed passion (*vikkhambhita-rāga*)—as opposed to those who have not suppressed it—the intention is that they fall asleep with full awareness (*sampajañña*) as long as they remain overestimators.
Regarding the phrase "of the overestimators," he says, "those who were previously overestimators are intended," because this refers to their former state.
308. That which is called the cause for grasping a doubt is said to "illuminate the other" with the intention: "Come now, indeed!"—thus it is stated, "it is joined in the sense of a cause.
However, regarding the certainty of grasping a doubt, it is stated that it "illuminates the other" with the phrase "come now, indeed!"—thus it is stated, "in the sense of the word itself."
The commentary on the *Parūpahāra* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Differentiation of Speech. 326.
"He" refers to one who has attained the first path. "Therefore" means because "the dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma arose."
Having misunderstood the meaning of the sutta— "Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation"—
insight arises at the moment of the Path through the influence of the contemplation of rise and fall,
such that "suffering" presents itself; therefore, they say, "He utters the word 'suffering' alone."
328. "Wished for" means when it has been accepted by the opponent. "Established" means when it has been fixed upon that meaning through the determination of reasoning;

thus, [the objection] is applicable. However, the claim that "one hears that sound after the moment of its vocal origination" is not applicable to what is "wished for," because the intention is that auditory consciousness has only a present object. But as for that which has been uttered by oneself...
One hears sound oneself; therefore, it should be understood that the *Aṭṭhakathā* states that ear-consciousness is "that by which one hears that sound.

(332) Regarding the phrase "at the moment of the supramundane path," this refers to the moment of the first path belonging to the first jhāna. In the statement "the intention must be explained regarding the citation of the *Abhibhu Sutta*," he shows that there is no connection for citing that [sutta]. Therefore, he says: "Consequently, it is not a proof."
The commentary on the discussion of the differentiation of speech is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Duration of Consciousness: 335.
*Evaṃ* means in the manner stated [in the verse], "A single consciousness lasts for the duration of its life-span. *Aññattha* means other than the immaterial realm (*arūpabhava*).

"In another. By this—namely, by one who asserts, "Only a single consciousness remains in the formless realm, remaining for as long as its lifespan lasts"—the second half of the commentary should also be understood.
The intention is that the statement regarding its remaining for a long time in the first discourse is merely an elucidation of its actual existence.
"Of the former" means of the question, "It remains for as long as its lifespan lasts," which precedes it.
For in that case, to the question "Does it remain for a hundred years?", the consent "Yes" was given;
but in the latter case, regarding the statement "A single human consciousness remains for the duration of its life-span," the rejection "It should not be said so" was made.
The lack of contradiction must be clarified, since the consent was given in that very instance and not in the latter—this is the intended meaning. [The phrase] "a hundred years, etc."...
And by the word "etc. (*ādi*), it should be understood that not only such statements as "two hundred years" are included, but also such statements as "one consciousness lasts for a day.
Regarding the remark, "The question 'It arises moment by moment' was stated as if it were asked by the proponent himself," this must be investigated. [As for the phrase: "It arises moment by moment."

The opponent’s question [is answered] by the proponent according to the meaning of such suttas as "Those subject to arising and passing away," and so forth; thus it is said that the admission belongs to the proponent.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Stability of Consciousness is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of Gradual Realization (Anupubbābhisamaya).
339. He says "or else" and so forth with reference to the claim that "those four knowledges are in fact only a single stream-entry path.
"Of the four knowledges" means of the four knowledges beginning with the knowledge of suffering.

"Because of being a single path" means because they constitute a single path, such as stream-entry and so on; for even though those knowledges occur successively, they perform the respective functions of each path.

The intention is that, by way of its accomplishment (*sādhana*), there is only one path. Therefore he said: “He acknowledges... of the single path. (344) Regarding “seeing,” it means the seeing of the path.

(345) Because of the state of cause and fruit between the phenomena and their bases, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*) and the analytical knowledge of bases (*attha-paṭisambhidā*) may serve as the cause for the fruit of stream-entry.
Because that [analytical knowledge] is absent, the other analytical knowledges are not; thus he says, "The language... should be investigated.

Furthermore, the fact that all the analytical knowledges are causes for the realization of the first fruit should be investigated, since they are obtainable only through the attainment of the path, just like the fruits themselves.
Therefore, according to the method presented here in the *Nikkhepakanda* under the heading "by means of eight knowledges":
It appears as though it were appropriate to say "by means of eight knowledges" by way of the knowledges of suffering and so forth, and the knowledges of the past limit and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of gradual realization is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discussion of Conventional Designation (Vohārakathā).
347. "Regarding the objects and the subjects" refers to form, the eye, and so forth; for these, being included within the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), are exclusively mundane (*lokiya*).

"Of the object alone" means of sound alone. For that [sound] is called "convention" (*vohāra*) in the Canon because it is what is conventionally expressed and because it is the instrument by which conventions are made.
There is no reason here [to exclude others], since even among the subjects, there is no absence of the state of not having taints (*āsava*) and so forth as their object.
