The intention is this: since that sound-base (saddāyatana), which has not yet attained the supramundane state, is exclusively subject to the outflows (sāsavatā), its status as supramundane according to your own view [is untenable].
The term "it might be struck" (paṭihaññeyya) is a hypothetical statement (parikappavacana). And because a hypothetical statement is not a factual reality, he says: "For... there is not.
For water, even if hypothetically imagined to be fire, does not burn or cook. Is it by means of mundane knowledge?

The inconclusiveness of the reason here should be understood as follows: is it mundane because it is something to be known, like the sense-base of form and so forth, or is it supramundane because it is being reviewed, like the path and so forth? Therefore he said: "Because it occurs both in the mundane and the supramundane.
The commentary on the discussion of conventional terminology is finished.
11. Commentary on the Discussion of Cessation (Nirodhakathāvaṇṇanā) 353.
"Of which two": of which two truths of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). "By means of two cessations": by means of the two cessations known as non-reflection (*appaṭisaṅkhā*) and reflection (*paṭisaṅkhā*).
In this context, "reflection upon suffering and so forth" is *paṭisaṅkhā*, a specific excellence of wisdom (*paññā*). By that [wisdom], it is to be described.

Cessation is analytical cessation (*paṭisaṅkhā-nirodha*). The opponents' tenet is that which is called "disjunction from defiled phenomena" (*sāsava-dhamma*), a cessation consisting in the absolute obstruction of the arising of phenomena due to the deficiency of conditions, is called "non-analytical cessation" (*appaṭisaṅkhā-nirodha*) because it cannot be designated as having been produced through analysis.
[They hold] that it is "ceased without analysis," meaning its non-arising due to the deficiency of conditions.
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). Therefore he said: "not having arisen, [they] do not cease. For non-arising is also called cessation;
since in the reverse order of the exposition of characteristics, following the statement "with the arising of this, that arises," it is shown as "with the cessation of this, that ceases.
"Therefore" means because neither the cessation through deliberation (*paṭisaṅkhā-nirodha*) nor momentary cessation (*khaṇika-nirodha*) is intended here.
The commentary on the Discussion of Cessation is finished.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
3. The Third Chapter.
1. Explanation of the Discourse on Powers (Balakathāvaṇṇanā) 354.
"By way of exposition" means by way of the modes explained in the passage beginning with "It is impossible, it is out of the question.
Since that [exposition] is detailed, it is therefore said "in detail. All [obstructions], such as the obstruction of defilements and so forth—each one of these individually—

"In every aspect" means by way of the distinction between the modes of occurrence. For "all" here is a grasping [of things] according to their own nature, whereas "in every aspect" refers to the distinction between the modes of occurrence.
Indeed, when the Blessed One knows phenomena, he knows them without leaving out any of their distinct modes of occurrence.
As it is said: "All phenomena come within the range of the door of knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, in every aspect."
“From a summary” means from one part. And since that one part is not an extensive treatment, he said “in brief. The connection is with the words “as they know.

“Even by a mere summary” means even by a mere summary of the underlying tendencies (*āsaya*) and so forth, which are classified as the knowledge of views as they really are (*diṭṭhigatayathābhūtañāṇa*), etc.
Therefore he said: “with reference to the mere knowledge of the sharpness or dullness of the faculties. “By the Elder” refers to the Elder Anuruddha.

"Even so" means by way of merely knowing the basis (*ṭhāna*) and so forth through a summary description. Since this point is indeed accepted even by the proponent himself (*sakavādī*), he asks: "How could this one be challenged?

(356) "In the remaining [knowledges]" refers to those knowledges other than the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*). "The refutation" refers to the refutation of their being uncommon (*asādhāraṇatā*). Anticipating the objection, "But do not the others also have the quality of being uncommon?", he says: "The basis... [etc. ...the intention."
The commentary on the Discourse on the Story of Bāla is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Noble Truths (Ariyantikathā): 357.
"Of one who asserts [the self] with reference to formations" means: with reference to formations that are empty of a being imagined by [wrong] view.
This refers to one who, having been asked, "Does he attend to emptiness? admits, "Yes.

The intention is: how does the convergence of two types of contact come about for one who, according to the method stated, attends to emptiness regarding formations that constitute both possible and impossible states? "According to the method stated" means [by way of] a being imagined through views...
“By way of the method of the formula ‘the five aggregates are empty. Or else, “by the aforementioned method” means by the method stated thus:
“Attention directed toward what is possible and impossible has formations as its object; attention directed toward emptiness has Nibbāna as its object.
Because it was said, “of one who asserts [this] with reference to formations,” [the question arises]: “How does the convergence of two types of contact come about?”

He said: Even though there is emptiness through the emptiness of beings, it is logical to raise the objection regarding the convergence of two types of contact—the attention to what is possible and impossible for formations being one thing, and the attention to emptiness being another.

However, one must investigate how the status of an Ariyan could be established for one who claims [to understand] formations by means of the knowledge of what is possible and impossible and so forth. Or rather, what is the use of this deliberation on logic?
For the argument of an opponent is like the talk of a madman. This same principle applies in other such instances as well.

"Having superimposed" means having superimposed upon the appropriation of form and so forth a non-existent appearance, such as that of a woman, a man, or the like, or simply the appearance of a sentient being (*satta*).

For here, what is intended by "superimposition" (*abhūtāropana*) is the act of mental aspiration (*paṇidahana*). Therefore, he said, "by way of conceptualization. "That" refers to the aforementioned aspiration. "Even in a single aggregate" (*khandha*).
The commentary on the Discourse on the Noble One is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on Being Liberated. 366.
At the moment of the path, the mind is liberated in one part and unliberated in another part; this refers to the phrase "the liberated and the being liberated."
There is a fault in this tenet (*laddhi*). For it has been said: "partially liberated, partially unliberated.

And in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, this very meaning is shown as follows: "For at that time, his tenet is that [the mind] is being liberated by way of a partial liberation through the liberation consisting in eradication (*samucchedavimutti*).
In the description of the "uncompleted" state, there is the description of the incompleteness of the act of liberating; with reference to this, he said: "liberated..."
"‘Being liberated’ is stated because it refers to the state of being incomplete. "By him" means by the opponent. [The phrase] "...vimuccamānassa...

is stated thus because there is an absence of the state of being liberated for one who is in the process of being liberated; however, the intention is that it was stated in that way by way of a distinction between those who are liberated.
And the fault regarding the description of the incomplete should be brought forward and applied. A single part serves as a qualification of liberation that is not limited.
"By way of being uninterrupted. "By the fruit-consciousness" means by the first fruit-consciousness that has arisen.
The commentary on the discussion of the consciousness being liberated is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Eighth [Person].
368. "They would be abandoned" means they are not currently being abandoned; this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the discussion of the eighth person is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties of the Eighth Person.

371. "The state of being faculties (indriya) belongs only to faith and the other [qualities] when they are supramundane (lokuttara), not when they are mundane (lokiya)"—this was said by way of the opponent's intention, beginning with the words "because the faculties have not yet been obtained.
In this context, "cultivating those that lead to liberation" means producing or increasing them in such a way that they become conduits to liberation.
However, once they have attained the status of faculties, there is no further need for cultivation.
Showing his intention, he said: "But it is not by developing the faculties.
The commentary on the discussion of the faculties of the eighth person is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Divine Eye.
373. It is called a *visaya* (object) because it binds (*visinoti*) specifically, creating a bond for the self of those who possess sense-objects.

It is an *ārammaṇa* (objective support). It is an *ānubhāva* (power/efficacy) because one experiences (*anubhavati*) by means of it; the meaning is "capacity" or "strength. It is a *gocara* (sphere) because it acts as a range of activity. Thus, "the power and sphere within the object" refers to the object... [and so on] ...it moves (*carati*).
By means of these, there arises a distinction (*visesa*) that is distinguished (*yathā visiṭṭhaṃ*) accordingly, through that which has become a condition.

"Strengthened by the state of jhāna" means having its strength established and its power augmented. Here, the "grasping of the object" is shown as the place of occurrence for the exercise of power and the making of the range;
for it is because of being supported by those [jhāna factors] therein that the augmentation of its power becomes manifest. Therefore he said, "In such an object," and so forth.
And this augmentation of power arises from superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) and from specific sublime states (mahaggatadhamma).
There is a specific attainment through the arising of sublime mind-born material forms (*cittajarūpa*). Some say that it is "by depending on which there is a transformation.
The compiler states that the former [the fleshly eye] is merely the fleshly eye itself, because of the aforementioned bestowal of power.
The apprehension of the object has already been established in the Canon; it is not for the purpose of showing a distinction between objects.

It is not for the purpose of showing a distinction in the object (*visaya*). For since the objective sphere (*rūpāyatana*) is the same for both, it states the similarity of the object—that is, its lack of distinction—or rather, it illuminates the distinction within what is similar; such is the construction of the sentence. [The phrase] "supported by the Dhamma" ... [etc. ...
refers to the underlying intention (*adhippāya*); otherwise, the very tenet (*laddhi*) would not exist—this is the sense. "Path" (*magga*) means a means (*upāya*).
The meaning is "cause. For it is only for one who possesses natural vision that the divine eye arises. Why?

Because the production of the knowledge of the divine eye occurs by expanding the light of the *kasiṇa*; and that [expansion] does not exist without the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*) within the *kasiṇa* circle.
Therefore, it is said: "It was stated specifically for the purpose of showing the dependence upon the physical eye (*maṃsacakkhu*). By that [word], "the path" is meant.

By way of speech. "By way of the condition of fine-material-sphere jhāna" means those [material phenomena] arisen through fine-material-sphere jhāna acting as a condition, which are produced by the mind of fine-material-sphere jhāna.
Regarding those produced by jhāna and kamma, there is simply nothing to be said; for such is his (the opponent's) tenet. 374.

By means of that which is the desire and the admission [of the existence] of the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*) from the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). It would follow that there would be three eyes—the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the eye of wisdom—since he speaks of them as being distinct types of eyes; therefore, the meaning is that he does not accept that [distinction].
The commentary on the Discourse on the Divine Eye is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of Passing Away According to Kamma: 377.
Because it serves as the basis for the divine eye, it is said: "In the divine eye, which is the decisive support for the knowledge of passing away according to kamma."
This is because that [knowledge of rebirths according to one’s deeds] lacks the specific function of the divine eye, which is the function of knowing where beings have gone according to their karma.
Therefore, since whatever is not other than this is also not other than that, he said: "By this... it must be so.
In that context, he excludes its being a different thing because the knowledge of rebirth according to one's deeds belongs to the same category as the knowledge of the divine eye.

It prevents [the confusion]. For that knowledge of his is the "knowledge of the surrounding area" (paribhaṇḍañāṇa). The intention is that it does not prevent the divine eye from being a distinct state from the "knowledge of the destination according to karma," because it belongs to its own category.

The opponent maintains that the function of the divine eye is the "knowledge of the destination according to karma," but not that the function of the "knowledge of the destination according to karma" is the divine eye;
therefore, regarding that point, he says: "The knowledge of the destination according to karma itself..."
Having applied the term "divine eye" here, he says "And the word ‘eva’... and so forth, in order to demonstrate it.
The commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of how beings fare according to their karma is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discussion of Restraint (Saṃvara).

379. Since it is stated in the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta, “Bhikkhus, there are yakkhas who for the most part have not refrained from the destruction of life,” the presence or absence of restraint among the Cātumahārājika devas is established without dispute.
However, in order to show that those [devas] such as the Tāvatiṃsa and others are included only where there is a dispute, the phrase “of the Cātumahārājikas” is used to demonstrate this point.
It has been said. "If this were so" means: if there is neither restraint nor non-restraint among the Thirty-three gods, that being the case.
Regarding the phrase "drinking liquor," here too the word "is heard" (*suyyati*) should be supplied and connected to the sentence. How is it heard? For this was stated in the *Kumbha Jātaka*:
"Having drunk which, the ancient gods became negligent..."
"Having passed away from the eternal and blissful Tāvatiṃsa heaven,
O Great King, how could one who knows that this liquor is so utterly useless drink it?"
In this context, "former gods" (*pubbadevā*) refers to the *asuras*. For they were known as "former gods" because they existed prior to the arising of the Thirty-three (*Tāvatiṃsa*).

"Negligent" (*pamattā*) means having fallen into negligence through the drinking of liquor. "The Three Realms" (*tidiva*) refers to the divine abodes that constitute the third world, starting from the human realm and the world of the Four Great Kings;
or it is simply the name of that divine realm. "Eternal" (*sassatiyā*) means merely long-lived.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). The sense is that he has fallen away together with his own asura-illusion, along with the asura-spells.
And it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “When the visiting devaputtas arrived, the residents prepared fragrant drinks.
Sakka gave a signal to his own retinue. Therefore he said: “It should not be said that they lack restraint regarding the drinking of liquor.”

Thus it was said. Furthermore, from the time of the manifestation of the Thirty-Three Gods (Tāvatiṃsa), even the drinking of fermented liquor did not exist there, let alone the taking of life and so forth.

Because there was no need to abstain [from such things], in the heavenly worlds above the realm of the Thirty-Three, there are no restraints (saṃvara) that must be undertaken through the excellence of formal undertaking and abstinence;
however, supramundane (lokuttara) restraints certainly do exist. Likewise, there are no non-restraints (asaṃvara) to be abandoned by them.
For it is not the case that there are no defilements to be abandoned by the path for those whose underlying tendencies have not yet been abandoned.
The commentary on the Discussion of Restraint is finished.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
4. The Fourth Chapter. 1.
Explanation of the Discussion on Whether a Householder Can Be an Arahant.

387. "Because of being associated with desire and lust for household life" means because of being accompanied by desire and lust for the state of a householder and for the state of one who enjoys sensual pleasures.
The commentary on the discussion regarding whether a householder can be an Arahant is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discussion on Possession (Samannāgata-kathā). 393.

"Attainment" (*patti*) means realization (*adhigama*). It should be understood that in the text, "realization" is synonymous with "possession," as possession by the four factors beginning with contact (*phassa*) is what is being indicated.
The commentary on the discussion of possession is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of Possession of Equanimity: 397.
Regarding the phrase "all should be applied": here, if that Arahant [possesses] six kinds of equanimity just as he possesses the four aggregates...

Since this is the case, the six types of equanimity are each accompanied by contact and the other factors; thus, the passage beginning with “endowed with the six [types of] contact, etc. should be construed accordingly.
The commentary on the discussion regarding being endowed with equanimity is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discussion Regarding Whether One is an Awakened One by Means of Awakening (Bodhi).

398. "By way of the state of having attained" means by way of the formation dissociated from consciousness, which was described in the passage beginning with "What is called the state of having attained?
The question is: "Is one awakened by means of awakening? The inquiry is: "When awakening has ceased, vanished, and subsided, does one become unawakened?
In this same manner, other questions and inquiries are to be understood.
The commentary on the discussion of the Buddha’s enlightenment is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Marks (Lakkhaṇakathāvaṇṇanā). 402.
Therefore: because the possession of the marks belongs not only to a Wheel-turning Monarch who is not yet a Bodhisatta, but also to a Bodhisatta.
Since there is no possession [of these marks] anywhere other than in the final existence, this does not establish the point that a Bodhisatta is one who possesses the marks.
Therefore he said: "Even when brought forward, it is just like what was not brought forward.
The commentary on the discussion of the marks is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of Entering the Path of Certainty (Niyāmokkantikathāvaṇṇanā) 403.

“The fulfillment of the perfections” (pāramīpūraṇaṃ) is a characteristic mark of the conduct of enlightenment (bodhicariyā), not a demonstration of the state of the perfections having reached their fullness.
Therefore, it should be understood that by this term, their undertaking, formal adoption, and so forth are also included. Starting from the Great Resolve (mahābhinīhāra)...
For it is said that great beings are "destined" (niyata). As it is said:

"Thus, those men endowed with all factors are destined for enlightenment," and "He will certainly become a Buddha. They do not prophesy because some specific state called "the fixed course" (niyāma) has arisen;
rather, they prophesy on the grounds that, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), he will undoubtedly become a Buddha.
It refutes other doctrines imagined by opponents, but it does not refute the certainty of enlightenment. Therefore he said, "For it is not merely...," and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of entering the path of certainty (*niyāma*) is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discussion of the Abandonment of All Fetters (*saṃyojana*).

413. Although some fetters have already been abandoned by the lower paths, the statement regarding the abandoning of all fetters—made by way of praise in such passages as "with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters"—is intended to signify their abandonment without remainder;
thus it is a figurative expression (pariyāya-vacana). Therefore, he said: "without taking this figurative sense."
The authors of the text state that they hold the view that "it is precisely the highest path (aggamagga) that abandons all fetters," because it abandons them by means of the path of arahantship.
"If this were so" means: if he makes such a claim merely on the basis of its being exhaustive [of the defilements].
The commentary on the discussion of the abandoning of all fetters is finished.
The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is finished.
5. The Fifth Chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Discussion of Liberation.

418. The connection is as follows: "Knowledge of fruition does not exist; the remaining [knowledges]—namely, the knowledge of insight, the knowledge of the path, and the knowledge of reviewing—are not to be called 'liberated.

"In this" refers to these four knowledges. That which is included by the mention of "insight" is excluded because its functions are remote from those of the path and so forth, and because it is the conclusion of insight.
The commentary on the Discussion of Liberation is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of the Asekha 421.

The opponent’s position is that it is called "knowledge of the asekha" because it occurs with reference to those who are asekhas; it is not included within the asekha-dhammas themselves. To refute this, he says: "By this... [etc. ...he shows."
The commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of one beyond training is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of Perversions: 424.
He speaks [of ignorance] as if it were "peace" when it is not peace, just as one uses the conventional expression "peace" for what is not peace. …pe… he speaks.
The commentary on the Discourse on Perversions is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on Certainty (Niyāmakathā).
428–431. "That" refers to that knowledge. "In conformity with the truths" means conducive to the penetration of the truths. Because of the pursuit of what is contrary [to the truths]...
Having counted from the beginning, he said "the fourth," not [counting] from the entry into the fixed course (*niyāma*) of one who is undetermined (*aniyata*);
this is because it is counted starting from the point of unerring application. If that were the case, it would be the fifth state and would possess a distinct status.
The commentary on the discussion of the fixed course (*niyāmakathā*) is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidākathāvaṇṇanā) 432–433.

Regarding the phrase "all knowledge," it was stated, "For even the knowledge of non-noble ones is indeed knowledge," with the intention that this [term] is not qualified by the preceding word "of the noble ones.
Alternatively, he spoke thus taking the text as it stands, which speaks of "all knowledge" without qualification.
"If it is the knowledge of the noble one, then he would reject it," [the opponent] says; therefore [the author] replies, "This refers to the knowledge of the ignoble one.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidākathā) is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of Mental Objects (Cittārammaṇakathā).
436–438. *Vattabbapaṭiññā*: The admission that "knowledge regarding the object of contact is knowledge of the penetration of others' minds" (*cetopariyañāṇa*)—this is the admission as it occurs.
The commentary on the discussion of the mind as an object is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Future.

439–440. Some maintain that there is knowledge regarding both the immediately preceding and the future consciousness. However, in that case, just as with the present momentary [consciousness], such knowledge might arise only occasionally through a corresponding preliminary exercise (*parikamma*). Therefore, it was said: "There is absolutely no knowledge regarding the immediate [successor].
The commentary on the discussion of knowledge of the future is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Present.

441–442. When it is said, "When all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) have been seen as impermanent," it follows by implication that the knowledge which constitutes that vision would also be seen in the same way, because it shares the essential nature of a conditioned phenomenon. It is with reference to such a statement that he says, "a statement that follows by implication.
However, since that knowledge too is "seen as impermanent," [it does not fall into error].
It occurs by way of acknowledging; therefore, it is called "the word of acknowledgment.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of sharp knowledge regarding those [insights] occurring as a continuous succession of contemplations of dissolution.

10. Explanation of the Discussion on Knowledge of the Fruits (Phalañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 443–444. "The higher and lower state of the fruit" refers to the excellence and inferiority of the fruit. "By power" means by the power of knowledge.
The explanation of the discussion on knowledge of the fruits is concluded.
The commentary on the Fifth Chapter is finished.
The Great Fifty is complete.
6. The Sixth Chapter.
1. Explanation of the Discourse on Certainty (Niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā) 445–447. Of this noble person.
The explanation of the discourse on certainty is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādakathāvaṇṇanā) 451. "Established in the sense of being a cause" means that there is no deviation from its status as a cause.

For when a particular phenomenon (dhamma) is the cause of another phenomenon at a given time, there is no alteration of its state at that time; and in actual fact, this is simply its nature as a cause.
“It is simply the state of being a cause,” he said.
The commentary on the Discourse on Dependent Origination is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Attainment of Cessation.

457–459. It negates the status of being a functional phenomenon (*sabhāvadhamma*) because there is no such thing as a functional phenomenon devoid of both those characteristics [of arising and ceasing].
Because of the statement, “Purification (*vodāna*) is also emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*),” he says, “And purification is a synonym for emergence.

If it were established as a functional phenomenon, it might be unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) due to its remoteness from the conditioned; therefore, he says, “because it establishes the status of being a functional phenomenon.”
The commentary on the Discussion of the Attainment of Cessation is finished.
The commentary on the Sixth Chapter is finished.
7. The Seventh Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discourse on What is Included (Saṅgahitakathāvaṇṇanā) 471–472.

"Included" (saṅgahita) means taken together by way of inclusion and so forth. However, because they are like bonds due to their commonality—such as being of a single kind—the text says "connected" (sambandhā).
The commentary on the Discourse on What is Included is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of Association (Sampayuttakathāvaṇṇanā) 473–474.

The state of that which is to be entered and that which enters would be tenable only when there is a distinction between them, not otherwise; thus, by breaking down the simile, he shows the distinctness of the thing illustrated, saying: “The determination of their diversity... [etc. ...shows.
The commentary on the discussion of association is finished.

3. Commentary on the Discussion of Mental Factors (Cetasika-kathāvaṇṇanā) 475–477. Regarding the phrase "contact and so forth" (*phassikādayo*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) here has a delimiting sense.

By this, in the presentation of the arising of consciousness, feeling and the other factors shown therein are included, but not the material phenomena produced by them. Thus it is said: "There is no co-nascence devoid of simultaneous arising and so forth."
The commentary on the Discussion of Mental Factors is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of Giving. 479.
“For the purpose of illustrating the existence of the giving of fruit” means for the purpose of illustrating the actual presence of the giving of fruit. The giving of fruit has been stated.
"It is as if it were [the mind] itself" means that the giving of the fruit by the mind is stated as if it were the primary factor;

otherwise, it would not be possible to speak of "the state of being a gift. For even the state of being a gift has indeed been spoken of in such passages as, "Giving has an undesirable fruit," and so forth.

"For the purpose of preventing that" means for the purpose of preventing the giving of the fruit. "That" refers to the statement beginning with, "Giving has an undesirable fruit," and so forth. By way of medicine and so on...
The state of the gift not being completed should be understood as a figurative expression for the fact that the fruit of the object to be given is not yet completed.
To clarify how the same Sutta applies to both the arguments of our own school and those of the opposing school in response to the objection, it was stated, "But not in one sense alone.

To explain this, it was said, "The gift is simply the object to be given," and so forth. In that context, the particle *eva* (only/simply) functions specifically in the sense of exclusion (*nivattanapakkhe*).
It is not appropriate [to apply this] to the side of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), because for both [the giver and the gift], the state of being a gift is intended. Therefore he said:
"The meaning should be understood as 'mental' (*cetasika*) or else 'the object to be given' (*deyyadhamma*). For this very reason he said: "Of the two gifts," and so forth.

"For the purpose of releasing from the state of confusion" means for the purpose of releasing from the confusion of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) even though the state of being a gift exists in both. Therefore he said: "Of the mental," and so forth.
The commentary on the Discourse on Giving is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on Merit Consisting in Use. 485.
“Of that view” means of the view that there is a convergence of the five consciousnesses. “Of these” refers to the merits consisting in use belonging to the presently occurring mind.

486. This argument fails because there is an absence of actual enjoyment. Merit belongs only to the volition of relinquishment (*cāgacetanā*), not to that which is dissociated from consciousness (*cittavippayutta*).
"In this way" means: by way of the state of merit [arising] when the object to be given has not been enjoyed.

For it is precisely because merit exists even when the object to be given has not been enjoyed that what was given during the stage of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) also becomes [meritorious] when an Arhat enjoys it.

It is certain that for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), there is only merit consisting in giving. The first alternative establishes the position of our own school (*sakavāda*) by way of refuting the opponent's doctrine;
the second, however, establishes the position of our own school directly. This is the distinction between them.
The commentary on the discussion of merit consisting in enjoyment is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discourse on What is Given Here (Itodinnakathāvaṇṇanā) 488–491.
“By that very gift of robes and so forth” means by the gift of robes and so forth offered by the donor without a formal expression of thanksgiving (anumodana).
Therefore he said: “Even without an action performed by oneself. “For this reason” means because they have expressed thanksgiving for those [deeds] therein.
"Because enjoyments arise"—this is the reason. "If they were not to live," and so forth, is a demonstration of the manner in which the opponent establishes their own position.

In that context, "if they were not to live, how could they rejoice, clarify their minds, produce joy, or obtain gladness?"—this refers to certain others who, having seen other *petas* living after performing acts such as rejoicing, [themselves] perform rejoicing and the like.
They perform [meritorious deeds], and therefore they subsist on what is given from here; this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the discussion of "what is given from here" is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Threefold Ripening of Earthly Karma.
492. “By means of faulty contacts” (attavajjehi) means by means of faulty contacts (*phassavajjehi*). For it is not that very [consciousness] which is associated with that [fault];

rather, the word “that” refers specifically to the contact. “Accompanied by advertence” (*sāvajjane*) means together with advertence; the meaning is that it proceeds only after having made advertence its precursor.
“Only that which has become a decisive support for kamma” (*kammūpanissayabhūtameva*) refers to that kamma by which the aforementioned contacts and other factors have been produced.
It is precisely the supporting condition (*upanissaya*) for karma. Regarding the phrase "of suffering," it refers to suffering arising in the future.
The construction is: "it shows that [craving] is the root-craving. The same applies to the term "supporting condition" (*upanissayabhūta*).

Craving, established previously as the cause for the accumulation of karma, is the supporting condition for karma; it functions by inclining one toward states of existence (*bhava*) and so forth once karma has been performed and accumulated.
For this is the decisive support (upanissaya) for the result.
493. The state of final nibbāna, having not exhausted that which has arisen by providing space, is consistent with the exhortation according to one's own system. 494.
By the phrase "when there is karma," he states merely that karma is a condition for the earth and so forth, not its status as a producer. Therefore he said: "It is called 'conducive to that.'"
The commentary on the discussion of the triad of earth, karma, and result is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Triad of Aging, Death, and Result 495.

Regarding the phrase "having a single object" (*ekārammaṇā*): this is stated by way of establishing their lack of an object (*anārammaṇatā*), because the absence of the characteristic of association (*sampayoga-lakkhaṇa*) has been extracted [as the reason]; it is not stated because that [object] itself is the characteristic of association.
496. "Of the indeterminate" means of the resultant-indeterminate (*vipākābyākata*). In the other case, there is simply nothing further to be said.
497. "That" refers to the statement: "The impurity of complexion is indeed aging itself.
The commentary on the discussion concerning aging, death, and the resultant is finished.
10. Explanation of the Discussion on Resultant and That Which Is Subject to Ripening 501.
With the intention that a resultant state, when acting as a condition for another resultant state, constitutes a mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), it is said:
"For which resultant, the [other] resultant is a mutuality condition. [This refers to] the arising of another resultant by virtue of that [condition].
Furthermore, from such statements as "having intended," it can be understood that [kamma] is a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for birth, aging, death, and so forth.
"By the previous admission" means by the admission that "it is both result (*vipāka*) and a state subject to result.
"Of this objection" refers to the objection proceeding in the form: "It is both result and a state subject to result," and so on.
The commentary on the discussion concerning "resultant" and "subject to result" is finished.
The commentary on the seventh chapter is finished.
8. The eighth chapter.
1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Six Bases (Chagatikathāvaṇṇanā) 503–504.

"Color-appearance" (*vaṇṇanibhā*) means that colors alone appear by way of blue and so forth; its meaning is the sense-base of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*). "Shape" (*saṇṭhāna*) refers to long and so forth.
The explanation of the discourse on the six bases is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Intermediate State (Antarābhava) 505.
"Intermediate places" (*antaraṭṭhānāni*) means intervening spaces. This is because [the being] travels by breaking through obstructing places and by way of space.
If that state did not exist between states, then that intermediate state (*antarābhava*) would not exist between the states of sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) and the others.

"If it were not in the interval"—there is no reason for the statement of one's own school (sakavādin), which asserts "there is absolutely no such thing as an intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*), to be refuted; for he does not refute it while keeping the reasons for its refutation in his heart.
Rather, the meaning is that, being unwilling to accept it in that way, he refutes it solely out of dogmatic adherence (*laddhi*).
506. "He does not desire birth" is the connection [of the sentence].

507. "Thus he does not desire that there" means that, unlike in the case of the realms of sense-desire (*kāma-bhava*) and so forth, he does not desire that succession of death and rebirth-linking (*cuti-patisandhi*) in that state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
For he [the being in the intermediate state] [arises] solely from the karma that produces his future existence.
Since he desires the process of existence (*pavatti*), how could there be birth, aging, and death, or the succession of death and rebirth-linking?

This position has been stated by certain proponents of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). As for those who say, "A being reaches rebirth-linking in a short time, namely in only seven days," and those who say, "Having passed away right there, it returns; thus it takes seven times seven days," [this is their view].
Since the succession of death and rebirth-linking is authorized by them, they should be regarded as modern [theorists], because it is stated in the Pāḷi:
"Is it the case that beings are born, age, die, pass away, and reappear in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
One should not say so. And just as this is so, these moderns also maintain his status as one who has gone to hell and so forth; for they speak thus:

“With feet upwards, the hell-being,” and so forth. In this context, in order to show that basis upon which the opponent imagines what is called the *antarābhava* (intermediate state), it is stated in the Commentary:
“Having misinterpreted the Sutta passage ‘one who attains Nibbāna in the interval’ (*antarāparinibbāyī*). For regarding this [passage], [the opponent argues]:
“Without having exceeded the midpoint of the lifespan in various places such as the Aviha heaven, one attains the highest path in the interval...”
The meaning of the sutta passage, “He attains final nibbāna by means of the complete extinction of the defilements;

he is one who attains final nibbāna in the interval,” is this, and not that there exists an intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Therefore, it was said: “Having misinterpreted the sutta passage ‘one who attains final nibbāna in the interval.
As for those who say, “Because of the expression ‘seeking rebirth’ (*sambhavesī*), the intermediate state certainly exists; for he seeks after *sambhava*, which is rebirth (*upapatti*)”—

They say, "seeking rebirth" (*sambhavesī*); yet even those who have truly become [enlightened] and will not be born again—those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*)—are referred to as "become" (*bhūta*) in this context by the phrase "for the stability of beings that have become.
Those who seek rebirth because they are opposed to that state are "seekers of rebirth" (*sambhavesino*);

these are the trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) because the fetter of existence has not been abandoned. Or alternatively, among the four modes of birth (*yoni*), it refers to egg-born and womb-born beings.

As long as they have not broken through the eggshell and the womb-membrane, they are called "seeking existence" (*sambhavesī*); once emerged from the eggshell and the womb-membrane, they are called "become" (*bhūta*).

For moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) and spontaneously born (*opapātika*) beings, they are called "seeking existence" during the first moment of consciousness, and from the second moment of consciousness onwards, they are called "become. Or, by whatever posture they are born, as long as [they remain] in that...
As long as they have not yet reached final knowledge (*aññā*), they are called "seeking existence" (*sambhavesī*); beyond that, they are called "beings" (*bhūta*).

Since the meaning is thus straightforward and follows the canonical text (*pāḷi*), what is the purpose of postulating an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or a personal existence (*attabhāva*) that has not been determined?
[Such a view] should be rejected.

But some say: "The uninterrupted manifestation of phenomena proceeding as a continuum in different locations is observed—just as it is in the non-conscious continuum of rice and so forth, so too must there be manifestation in different locations without interruption in the conscious continuum as well.
And this principle is consistent only if an intermediate state (antarābhava) exists, not otherwise."

They speak of what is logical; for them, logic must be stated regarding how one who possesses psychic power (*iddhi*) and has attained mastery over the mind resolves upon a body that follows the mind, so as to approach here from the Brahma-world in an instant, or to go from here to the Brahma-world.
If the occurrence of phenomena in a completely disconnected location is not accepted anywhere, even if it were the case [for others], for those possessing psychic power—
“The domain of psychic power (*iddhivisaya*) is inconceivable”—this is the same here as well, because of the statement that “the ripening of kamma (*kammavipāka*) is inconceivable.
Therefore, that [claim] is merely their own opinion. For phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) are by nature inconceivable;
they manifest in some cases in a delimited location due to conditions, and in other cases in an undelimited location. Thus, it is through conditions such as the sound from the mouth and so forth...
It is observed that in another location, such as the region of Mount Ādarśa and so forth, reflections, echoes, and the like are produced.
Here it is said: First of all, the reflection is not a valid illustration because it is unproven and because it is dissimilar.

For it is unproven that what is called a "reflection" arises as a distinct material form (*rūpa*) altogether. Even if its existence were proven, it would still not be a valid illustration because of its dissimilarity.
It might be [objected] that in one place there is an absence of two co-existent locations.

For wherever the form of the mirror and the form of the reflection are seen, it is not logical for two forms to exist together in a single location, because of their dependence on their respective bases;
and this [reflection] is unlike [the original], because its connection consists in its being connected to the mirror, whereas the connection of the face [to the reflection] is not such a connection.
The manifestation [of a reflection] in another location is said to occur without interruption directed toward [the original object], not from a non-continuum;

thus, the *tanti* (tradition/scripture) is indeed dissimilar. In that regard, as for what was stated—"It is unproven that what is called a 'reflection' arises as a distinct material form, because two things cannot occupy the same place simultaneously"—this simultaneous occupancy of a single place has been urged [as a reason] despite being a non-continuum, since their supports (*nissaya*) are different.

For there is no such thing as a common location for things that have distinct bases. Just as the light-form of many jewels, lamps, and so forth, while occurring in a single place, appears as if it has a non-distinct location due to its being contiguous and without gaps;
yet, because it has distinct bases, it actually has distinct locations—it is merely perceived as a non-distinct location due to the particularity of its apprehension.
The same should be understood regarding the forms of reflections in a mirror and so forth.

For, through the convergence of such conditions, that reflection arises and passes away there; and this must be accepted as such because it enters the range of the eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
Otherwise, it would be perceived even without light, or it might not be the range of the eye-consciousness at all. Of that...
But that power belongs to the harmony [of conditions], such that there is a vision in that way.

For even by one who says, "The distinction in the efficacy of phenomena is indeed inconceivable," this very point is established, because [the reflection] appears as if its locus were undivided, even though it has a divided basis.
By this alone, the objection that there is no form of a reflection in water and so forth should be understood as refuted.
Once the reflected image is established, its status as an illustration is indeed proven, because it demonstrates that causes and fruits can exist in separate locations.
As for what was said—"It is not an illustration because it is dissimilar"—that is incorrect. Why?
For an illustration is not always identical to the thing being illustrated. [The rebirth-aggregates arise] in a separate location from the death-aggregates...
In order to establish the meaning of "they appear," it is intended here as an illustration that a reflected image, which is the fruit thereof,
is produced in a place separated from the form of the face; by this, the objection regarding the lack of continuity should be understood as refuted.
Or, because the relationship of cause and effect between the reflected image and the face is established, that [objection] is likewise rejected.

For the conventional designation of a "continuum" (santāna) applies to relationships of cause and effect. By the two aforementioned reasons, the reflection arises from both the original object (*bimba*) and the mirror;
however, the aggregates of rebirth do not arise in a disconnected location in this manner. And just as here...
The reflected image has been demonstrated; in the same way, echoes, lamps, seals, and so forth should also be demonstrated.
For just as echoes, lamps, seals, and the like arise from causes such as sound and do not go elsewhere, even so is this mind.
Furthermore, this proponent of intermediate existence (antarābhava) should be asked thus: "If there is no arising of phenomena in a disconnected location..."

The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) has been postulated [as a solution] because it is argued that the arising of body-consciousness and mind-consciousness is "appropriate" in the bodies of Rāhu and others;

however, how can the arising of body-consciousness and mind-consciousness be appropriate in locations separated by many thousands of *yojanas*, such as the places of the feet and the heart? If you argue that this is possible because they belong to a single continuum (*ekasantāna*), then the same applies here as well.

Furthermore, since they are immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), this is not sufficient as a defense against the objection regarding the fivefold plane (*pañcavokāra*), where both material and immaterial phenomena coexist.
Because they are mutually related. First, the arising of a fruit in a location separated from the presently occurring conditions is established;

how much more so, then, in the case of past five-aggregate existences? Wherever there is a condition for the resultant consciousness, there also occurs the basis (*vatthu*) which serves as its support, as well as the co-existent aggregates (*khandha*); thus, having gained its opportunity, [the fruit arises].
When resultant consciousness arises— being produced by kamma and accompanied by the remaining conditions—
the fact that its location is separated [from the previous life] is not capable of acting as an obstruction.

And just as the aggregates at the moment of death (cuti-kkhandha) serve as the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) for the aggregates at the moment of rebirth (upapatti-kkhandha) even across the interval of many thousands of eons, so too is it with an interval of many thousands of yojanas.

Since they serve as the immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*) for those [subsequent aggregates], there is no spatial distance. Thus, immediately after the cessation of the aggregates at death, the rebirth-linking aggregates manifest in the place of rebirth through the convergence of other conditions;

therefore, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) at all. And since that [intermediate state] does not exist, as for what some say regarding the karma that produces a future existence—that it [produces it] from that very [intermediate state]...
They describe its characteristics and causes as follows: "It has the form of its future or past existence; it is the object of the pure divine eye of those born with it;

its faculties are unimpaired; it moves unhindered by anything; and it feeds on odors. Such descriptions should be understood as being like a dispute over whether the son of a barren woman is short or tall.
The commentary on the discussion of the intermediate state (antarābhava) is finished.
3. Explanation of the Discourse on the Strands of Sensual Pleasure (Kāmaguṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 510. "All [these]" refers even to the wholesome and unwholesome aggregates and so forth.

For the intention is that even these may have the sense of "desiring" (kamanaṭṭha) by way of the desire characterized as the wish-to-act (kattukamyatā-chanda) which has them as its object. In the *Dhātukathā*, it says: "Sensual existence (*kāmabhava*)."
Because it is stated: "It is included by five aggregates, eleven bases, and seventeen elements; by how many is it not included?

It is not included by any aggregates, by one base, and by one element," he said: "In the *Dhātukathā*, the state of being the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) is shown as belonging only to the aggregates acquired by clinging (*upādinnakkhandhā*).
The word "five" is a numerical limit, intended to exclude any other number.

The statement “the five strands of sensual pleasure” excludes the existence of those [sensual pleasures] other than these; thus it is said: “Only the five divisions of sensual pleasure are called ‘kāma’.
For that very reason, the term “kāmadhātu” (the sensual element) is not the name for something else, but rather the name for those [five] themselves—this is the meaning.
And this [position] is merely the opinion of the opponent, as stated by the words “with this intention. Thus, it is merely a matter of terminology.
Thus, the meaning is that [the Buddha] spoke merely the words "these five strands of sensual pleasure" without [intending to convey] the actual, unerring meaning of the matter.
The commentary on the discussion of the strands of sensual pleasure is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Form Realm.

515–516. Regarding the phrase "because it is stated as 'the form element'": this is because it is spoken of as "the form element" in the passage, "the sense-sphere element, the form element, and the formless element.

"By means of phenomena possessing form" means by means of those phenomena whose intrinsic nature is to be affected (ruppana). They are "delimited" by such expressions as "these three existences" and so forth;
that is, they are delimited as "these three existences" and "the three elements. In a context where "element" (dhātu) is used, it should be delimited by "existence" (bhava).

For it has been said: "In the context of existence (bhava), it should be delimited by way of the element (dhātu). Therefore, it is precisely the phenomena (dhammas) belonging to the sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere that are spoken of in this way when they are delimited as belonging to their respective planes.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Element of Form (Rūpadhātukathāvaṇṇanā) is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Formless Realm (Arūpadhātukathāvaṇṇanā) 517–518.
"In the preceding discussion" means in the discussion of the form realm (rūpadhātu). "Without distinction" means without making a distinction based on the place of occurrence.
The commentary on the discussion of the formless realm is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Bases in the Realm of Form (Rūpadhātu-āyatana-kathāvaṇṇanā) 519.
"By way of being a location" means by way of being a physical basis (vatthu). "Of such a kind" refers to the form of the nose and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the bases in the realm of form is concluded.
8. Explanation of the Discussion on Form in the Formless (Arūperūpakathāvaṇṇanā) 524–526.

Escape exists only when there is something to escape from, not when there is nothing; therefore, he said: "In the formless existence there is subtle form, and because there is escape from that, it is called 'formless'.
The explanation of the discussion on form in the formless is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Kamma-condition for Matter (Rūpa-kamma-paccaya-kathā-vaṇṇanā) §527–537.
"Pakappayamānā" means fashioning in various ways, and thereby enabling the functions of its own associated states. Hence he said: "Exercising a predominant activity among the associated states.
The commentary on the discussion of the kamma-condition for matter is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discussion of the Life-faculty (Jīvitindriyakathāvaṇṇanā) 540.

"He speaks by taking the end" means that regarding the question, "Is there for immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) life-span (āyu), stability (ṭhiti), subsistence (yapanā), maintenance (yāpanā), movement (iriyanā), persistence (vattanā), and preservation (pālanā)? Is there an immaterial life-faculty (arūpajīvitindriya)? he answers, "There is an immaterial life-faculty."
He speaks by taking this as the limit and the conclusion. It is appropriate to say that one who desires the whole necessarily desires its parts;
for there is no such thing as a "whole" apart from its parts. (541) "That very same" refers to the formless (arūpa), which is indeed dissociated from consciousness (cittavippayutta).
542. *Tadāpi* means even at the time of entering and emerging from that attainment. 544–545.
*So yutto* (that is appropriate) because both the material and immaterial life-faculties (*rūpa-jīvitindriya* and *arūpa-jīvitindriya*) are accepted in their respective systems.
The commentary on the discussion of the life-faculty is finished.
11. Commentary on the Discussion of the Cause of Karma (Kammahetukathāvaṇṇanā) 546.
Regarding the statement, “Because of the karma of taking life,” and so forth: since this discussion of decline has not yet been presented there, he says, “He states ‘the rest...
in order to show the very method that has been presented therein. “A statement of acceptance” means a statement for the purpose of causing acceptance.
He spoke the words beginning with "the side" (*pakkha*) in order to show that this refers to the opponent, or to the acceptance and instilling of various respective convictions.
The commentary on the discussion of the cause of kamma is finished.
The commentary on the eighth chapter is finished.
9. The Ninth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discourse on Seeing the Advantage. 547.
Even though, due to the diversity of minds, the opponent might later [object] regarding what is to be seen from the perspective of its disadvantage and its advantage—
It was admitted [by him] previously by making [the two positions] one; yet he did not abandon that tenet.
Therefore, it should be understood that the crushing of his intention is appropriate. For this very reason, he said: "Because of the admission of impermanence... etc.

"By way of the object" means by way of making it an object, not by way of the accomplishment of a function—this is the intended meaning. This is an inquiry into the discussion of benefits (*ānisaṃsa*).

And the seeing of benefits. The intention is that, just as with penetrative knowledge (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*), it is appropriate for the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā*) to perform its function regarding proceeding and ceasing according to what is suitable, even for the knowledge of conformity (*anubodha-ñāṇa*).
The commentary on the discussion of the seeing of benefits is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Deathless Object (Amatārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 549.

Regarding the phrase "by means of such scriptural passages as these," the word "etc. includes such Sutta passages as: "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is free from taints and the practice leading to the state free from taints.
The commentary on the discussion of the deathless object is concluded.

3. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning Form as Having an Object (Rūpaṃsārammaṇantikathāvaṇṇanā) 552–553. In such passages as “That which is without support is without an object,” the word *ārammaṇa* has the sense of a condition (*paccaya*).
In such passages as “The visible-object base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element and its associated states by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*),” [the same applies].

He said, "The sense of dependence is the sense of clinging," meaning "the sense of condition is the sense of clinging. Thus, while such a distinction exists: therein, the sense of condition (*paccayaṭṭha*) is the state of existing in dependence upon conditions;
the sense of clinging (*olubbhaṭṭha*) is the state of providing support for the weak mind and mental factors by way of being an object of apprehension, like a staff or a rope.
Or, it may be so stated by assuming there is no difference between them due to their commonality as conditions.
The commentary on the discussion regarding whether form has an object is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discussion Regarding Whether the Latent Dispositions (anusaya) Are Without an Object (anārammaṇa). 554–556.
By the phrase "when this exists," the state of not having been ceased by this path is also included; thus he said, "precisely because they have not been abandoned."
"It is said that 'it exists'"; however, he shows by means of this restriction that it is not [excluded] because of its actual existence.

The meaning is: "because of its being actually present, because of its being currently existing, and because of its possessing the three moments. The commentary on the discussion regarding the fact that the underlying tendencies (anusaya) are without an object (anārammaṇa) is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Knowledge is Without an Object (Ñāṇamanārammaṇantakathāvaṇṇanā) 557–558.

Referring to that supreme path-knowledge by the attainment of which the delusion regarding what is to be fully understood and so forth has vanished without remainder for an Arahant, they say, "of path-knowledge.
Because of its state of constant mindfulness (*satokāritā*) toward all that [remains to be known],...

...as well as clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). Therefore, by virtue of that knowledge, he is "one possessed of knowledge" (*ñāṇī*). For that Supreme Person has attained the full development of mindfulness and wisdom.
The commentary on the discussion concerning whether knowledge is without an object is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning Being Overcome by Applied Thought (*vitakkānupatita*).
562. "Even by two" means by two distinctions; the meaning is: without making a distinction between one distinction and another.
The commentary on the discussion concerning discourse accompanied by applied thought (*vitakka*) is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning Sound as the Emanation of Applied Thought (*vitakkavipphāra*).
563. "In every way" (*sabbaso*) means in all modes. Since those modes are to be understood by way of place, location, and time, he says, "in every place or at every time.
Furthermore, because of the statement beginning with "one who is thinking," those places and times are to be understood by way of specific states of consciousness;
thus it is said, "in minds accompanied by applied thought" (*savitakkacittesu*). This refers to the Sutta passage: "Having applied thought, one breaks into speech."
Having understood this incorrectly, he said, "Sound is merely the vibration of thought.
The commentary on the discussion of the sound of the vibration of thought is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of Speech Not According to the Mind.
565. "There is no false speech" means there is no offense; this is the connection [of the text].
The commentary on the discussion of speech that does not correspond to the mind is finished.
11. Commentary on the Discussion of Possession of the Past and Future.
568–570. *Samannāgatapaññatti* means a description by way of possession (*samaṅgibhāva*).
For this very reason it is said: “One who possesses present phenomena is called ‘possessed’ (*samannāgata*)”. *Paṭilābhapaññatti* means a description by way of attainment (*adhigamana*).

This refers to the mode of being that can be predicated of the person spoken of as “possessed”; this is what is called a “description by way of possession”. This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well.
The commentary on the discussion concerning possession of the past and future is finished.
The commentary on the ninth chapter is finished.
10. The tenth chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discussion of Cessation (Nirodhakathāvaṇṇanā) 571–572.
Within our own system, it is maintained that "the subsequent consciousness arises immediately after the cessation of the preceding consciousness.
However, the opponent asserts that "at the very moment the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅgacitta) exists, at that same moment a functional consciousness (kiriyamayacitta) arises."

[The opponent] says: "If this were so, then even the coexistence of preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness would have to be admitted. Therefore, he said: "Together with the moment of dissolution.

And since that would be the case, one would have to assert—according to the method already stated—the coexistence of functional-resultant aggregates with resultant-functional aggregates, of resultant-resultant aggregates with [resultant-resultant] aggregates, and of functional-functional aggregates with [functional-functional] aggregates. Demonstrating this point, he said: "Of the life-continuum consciousness," and so forth.

In this context, the resultant aggregates (*vipākakkhandhā*) are called "to-be-approached-at-rebirth" (*upapattesiyā*) because they are to be sought or desired by way of the state of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
Regarding these, it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "Of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgacitta*) that has attained the designation 'to-be-approached-at-rebirth'.

For its beginning and end consist merely of the consciousness of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhicitta*) and the consciousness of death (*cuticitta*), while its objective support (*tadārammaṇa*) is [the same as that of the rebirth-linking].

"It is called precisely *bhavaṅga*. It is stated that because it falls in the midst of the activity of eye-consciousness and the others, its inclusion by the mention of the "four functional aggregates" (*kiriyā-catukka-khandha*) is appropriate.

For by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "eye-consciousness etc.," one should understand that not only ear-consciousness and the rest are included, but also the receiving (*sampaṭicchana*) and investigating (*santīraṇa*) consciousnesses.
The commentary on the Discussion of Cessation is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of the Path for One Possessing the Five Consciousnesses 576.
Characteristic: The characteristic of the five consciousnesses is their state of having arisen objects, etc., and their nature of being of one undifferentiated kind without falsity.
Granted that mental consciousness (manoviññāṇa) may sometimes be without a physical basis (avatthuka), yet when it does possess a basis, it possesses only a presently arisen basis.
For this reason, in the Pāḷi, regarding the establishment [of the argument], it is stated: "If the five consciousnesses have presently arisen objects.

Since there is also a way of speaking regarding mental consciousness having a presently arisen basis, instead of saying "the five consciousnesses," it says "the six consciousnesses have presently arisen bases."

Having said this, he stated, "The six consciousnesses... [is] what is intended," showing that one cannot say, "Indeed, for one possessing the fivefold sensory consciousness, there is no cultivation of the Path.

(577) "Signless, empty, and wishless" are synonyms for Nibbāna. Since visual consciousness possesses the quality of grasping the signless, it might also have emptiness as its object; therefore, it was said, "The intention is that this very [consciousness] is emptiness."
The commentary on the discussion of the path for one possessing the fivefold sense-consciousness is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Fivefold Sense-Consciousness Being Without Volition (Sābhoga) 584–586.
That [consciousness], however, occurs having been directed [towards the object]. "Grasping the mode of the object" means grasping the desirable or undesirable mode of the object.

"Grasping. This shows that "mental application" (*ābhoga*) is that grasping of the mode of the object by which there is association of a wholesome consciousness with non-greed and so forth, and association of an unwholesome consciousness with greed and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the lack of mental application in the fivefold sense-consciousness is finished.

6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Two Kinds of Virtue (Sīla) §§587–589 "Non-arising cessation" means the cessation of non-production. "Cessation through the non-transgression of virtue" means that the very absence of transgression constitutes the cessation of the violation of virtue. [The Blessed One] was observing the momentary cessation of diverse phenomena.
The commentary on the discussion of the two kinds of virtue is concluded.

"Unpleasant fruit... [and so on]... "Therefore, mental dhamma is giving"—thus the text proceeds. Following that, one should bring forward scriptural passages establishing the mental nature of virtue, such as:
"Is it not to be said that virtue is mental? Yes. Is virtue an unpleasant fruit? and so forth.
By demonstrating this meaning, it shows that non-mental dhammas, such as form (rūpa), [do not produce] future result.
[The text] gives [this]. If that [volition] were itself morality (*sīla*), one would be called "virtuous" even without the undertaking of restraint and without abstinence (*virati*).

However, since it is the volition of undertaking, the abstinence, and the restraint that constitutes morality, therefore the construction should be made as follows: "Morality has a desirable fruit, a pleasant fruit," and so forth.
It is with reference to this meaning that it was said, "by the method already stated," meaning: according to the method already stated.

The meaning is as follows: Since, however, in the Pāḷi there is a discussion stating that "virtue is non-mental," but no separate discussion stating that "generosity is non-mental" has come down, it is therefore said, "that discussion must be sought.
The commentary on the discussion beginning with "Virtue is non-mental" is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Cause of Undertaking (Samādānahetukathāvaṇṇanā) 598–600.

In this discussion of the cause of undertaking, from the point where it begins with “Contact gives [the fruit]” up until the citation of the *Ārāmaropa* and other suttas stating that phenomena characterized by dark and bright counterparts come into manifestation—this much alone constitutes the discussion of enjoyment (*paribhoga*).
He says, "They are similar... [as follows] ...should be seen.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the cause of undertaking [the precepts] is finished.
11. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Limit of Immorality Without Intimation.

603–604. The claim that "non-intimation" (*aviññatti*)—which arises dependent on the great elements (*mahābhūtāni*), occurs even at moments of other types of consciousness, and is associated with wholesome or unwholesome [kamma]—is subsumed under the category of "the accumulation of demerit dissociated from consciousness" (*cittavippayutto apuññūpacayo*).
Therefore, to show that this [non-intimation] is distinct from that, it is stated: "By means of an instruction... [etc. ...this is the intention. In that context, one who is instructed...
When one accomplishes an act such as violence by means of being commanded, then the command should be understood as a constituent factor (*aṅga*) in the taking of life and so forth.
However, the intention of the opponent is that such a command is called "devoid of explicit communication" (*viññatti-rahita*) by virtue of its status as a formal proclamation (*pārivāsika*);
to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "on a single day" was stated.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the end of unmanifested misconduct is finished.
The commentary on the tenth chapter is finished.
The second fiftieth section is completed.
11. The Eleventh Chapter: 4. Explanation of the Discussion on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 614–615.
Those referred to as "Andhakas" are, for the most part, the Pubbaseliyas, Aparaseliyas, Rājagirikas, and Siddhatthikas.

It was stated, "They would indeed be Mahāsāṅghikas," as in the passage beginning "Previously... they would be. In that context, the word "others" is used because the two statements are direct opposites.

For while one who possesses eye-consciousness and so forth among the former [teachers] is called "one possessing knowledge" (*ñāṇī*), it is stated that according to these [Mahāsāṅghikas], that very same person cannot be called "one possessing knowledge. The "removal of lust" (*rāgavigama*) is the total eradication of lust; likewise...

It is the disappearance of ignorance. Just as one whose ignorance is completely cut off is called "possessed of knowledge" (*ñāṇī*), and by contrast one who possesses ignorance is called "ignorant" (*aññāṇī*), so too one whose ignorance is not yet cut off is called "ignorant," while by contrast one is called "possessed of knowledge. Because ignorance has vanished, he attains the designation "possessed of knowledge";
however, the intention is that this is not due to the continuous and constant occurrence of knowledge.
The commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Power of Psychic Success (Iddhibala).
621–624. This was said with reference to that life-span in which death occurs through the exhaustion of karma (*kammakkhaya*). Regarding karma...

Regarding the phrase "by way of the result of ripening" (*vipākavasena*), this refers to death occurring through the exhaustion of the life-span; whereas regarding the phrase "by the counting of years," this refers to cases where death occurs before that.

Therein, because of the statement, "And one does not die so long as that evil karma has not been exhausted," it is said—referring specifically to the hell realms—that for the most part, death in hell occurs through the exhaustion of karma, "or by way of the ripening of karma."

It is said: "By the reckoning of years" refers to humans and the gods of the Four Great Kings and so forth, because it is stated that the lifespan of humans and gods is delimited by such measures as "a hundred years," "a thousand years," or "a hundred thousand years," and because for the most part their death occurs through the exhaustion of that lifespan.
Having supplied the word "it is said," the passage should be construed accordingly.
The commentary on the discussion of the powers of psychic potency is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of Concentration (Samādhi-kathā): 625–626.
"In the sense of placing evenly" means having warded off unevenness, such as dullness (*līna*) and agitation (*uddhacca*), and [thereby] warding off distraction itself.

Or [it is so called] in the sense of being established after having been pierced. When one says, "The continuity of consciousness (cittasantati) is concentration," the mental concomitant nature of that [concentration] is thereby rejected;

thus he said, "without taking it to be another mental factor. To deny the existing distinction of one-pointedness (ekaggatā) when it has acquired a specific excellence through cultivation (bhāvanā) is a quibble (chala);
however, this refers to one-pointedness that has not acquired such a specific excellence.
By "by way of commonality," he means "by mere commonality.
The commentary on the Discussion of Concentration is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Stability of Phenomena (Dhammaṭṭhitatā).

627. "The stability of ignorance" refers to the fixedness in the status of ignorance as the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) for the formations (*saṅkhāra*), which is termed the "lawfulness of phenomena" (*dhamma-niyāmatā*).
This is established as a stable intrinsic nature (*ṭhita-sabhāvatā*), not merely by way of being established as a mere phenomenon.

The meaning is that this "stability," which is defined as the state of being an immediate condition, constitutes its conditionality. "Of that which is devoid of the state of mutual conditionality" means...
This should be understood as a negation of conditions such as co-nascence (*sahajāta*), support (*nissaya*), and so forth, but not of mere mutual conditionality (*aññamañña-paccayatā*).

By the phrase "all such [conditions]," it includes immediate (*samanantara*), contiguous (*anantara*), decisive support (*upanissaya*), presence (*atthi*), disappearance (*vigata*), repetition (*āsevana*), and the rest.

Regarding the phrase "and mutual conditionality," the meaning here should also be understood according to the method already stated. Furthermore, in this context, even for that which has arisen by way of a condition...
It should also be applied by way of formations (*saṅkhāra*) because they function as conditions. Therefore he said: "And the other [is] for that.
The commentary on the Discussion on the Stability of Phenomena (*Dhammaṭṭhitatākathā*) is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discussion on Impermanence (*Aniccatākathā*).

628. By the method of stating that "the impermanence of form and so forth exists when form and so forth exist, and does not exist when they do not," its arising and cessation together with them are expressed.
Among the three characteristics, such as arising, there is the conventional designation (vohāra) "impermanence.

Just as the conventional designation "three-staff" (tidaṇḍa), which occurs in dependence upon three staffs, applies to all of them, so too [does the designation] "subject to birth, aging, and death" [apply].
It is not permanent; it is impermanent. Because its nature consists of birth and so forth, it is designated by the term "impermanence.

Thus, it is said that "the conventional usage of 'impermanence' is possible regarding the characteristics such as arising," [expressed as] "in the three... it occurs. "By way of investigating the divisions" means by way of investigating the distinctions.
In this regard, impermanence is as manifest through aging and dissolution as it is through birth; thus it is stated in the Pāḷi.
It should be understood that the classification of impermanence has been shown by way of aging and death alone.
The commentary on the Discussion of Impermanence is finished.
The commentary on the Eleventh Chapter is finished.
12. The Twelfth Chapter. 1. Explanation of the Discussion on Restraint and Formal Acts (Saṃvarokammantikathāvaṇṇanā) 630–632.
Since the entire mind possesses the nature of the mind-door, he said: "By 'resultant door,' he means the life-continuum consciousness."
The commentary on the discussion of the formal act of restraint (saṃvarokammantikathāvaṇṇanā) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of Formal Acts (kammakathāvaṇṇanā) 633–635.

It is as if those [actions] that have a ripening (savipāka) have already been shown, because the meaning is established by the fact that what remains after what has been stated is understood to have a ripening.
The commentary on the Discussion of Karma is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of the Six Bases (Saḷāyatana-kathā): 638–640.
Because there exists a portion of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) that is karmic result (*vipāka*), it is stated [in the text] "without distinction."
The commentary on the Discourse on the Six Sense Bases is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Seven Times at Most. 641–645.
*Assa* means "of this one who has seven times at most as his limit. Therefore he said: "And in the state of having seven times at most..."

"Do you desire the certainty of rightness (niyāma)? By means of which karma of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma). "In the interval" (antarā) means without having produced [the remaining] seven existences, but precisely within the interval between them.
"Some" (keci) refers to the residents of Abhayagiri. "Others" (apare) refers to the authors of the grammatical treatises (padakāra).

"Of him" (tassa) refers to one who has been defined and declared by the Blessed One’s knowledge as "one who has seven births at most," or "one who goes from family to family" (kolaṃkola), or "one who is a single-seeder" (ekabījī); for such a person, there is the aforementioned limit.
There is no attainment of the higher paths in the interim, because his teaching is not otherwise than true. His realization occurs exactly according to the delimitation [of the path];

this distinction among those very individuals must be understood by way of the relative sharpness or dullness of their faculties (*indriya-paropariyatta*), since there is no one else of such a kind according to the fixed order of existence. For even the dull faculties of some, through specific conditions, attain a state of sharpness.
They might attain [the goal]; therefore, with reference to such a person, it was said: "He is called 'capable,' he is not called 'incapable.
However, because the Blessed One does not describe such a person as being "limited to seven more births" and so forth, he said:
