"But the capability to realize [the truth] in the interval has not been stated. And this method must certainly be accepted.
Showing that otherwise there would be a confusion of persons, he said, "And if," and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion regarding those who have seven births at most is finished.
The commentary on the twelfth chapter is finished.
13. The Thirteenth Chapter. 1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Kappaṭṭha. 654–657.
“The intention is exactly as stated above”: this refers to what was said in the *Iddhibalakathā* (Discourse on the Power of Psychic Potency) regarding the past and the future.

Regarding the statement, "He challenges [the opponent] because it was promised that this [person] might remain for an entire aeon (kappa) without distinction," he says, "The 'below' refers to the discussion on the power of psychic potency (iddhi).
In that context, the passage beginning with "two aeons" is presented by way of challenging the capacity to exceed the limit of one's lifespan;
however, here, if a schismatic of the Saṅgha, instead of remaining merely for a life-span aeon, were to remain for one great aeon (mahākappa), [then the challenge would apply].
Just as with one [kalpa], so too should the objection be raised that he might remain for many kalpas.
The commentary on the *Kappaṭṭha-kathā* is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of the Certainty of the One Destined for Liberation (*Niyata*).

663–664. "Of those who have not reached the fixed course" refers to the states of those persons for whom the states of wrongness and rightness fixed by destiny have not yet arisen. Which, then, are they? They are the states included within the continua of the persons already mentioned.

For these are called "belonging to the three planes" because they are included within the three planes of existence. However, as for the indeterminate states that occur in the continua of those who have reached the fixed course, they are not included here.
Inclusion has been made; for there is no state of being undetermined (aniyatā) by virtue of possessing those [qualities]. Therefore he said: "Even one who possesses them is indeed undetermined.
By the phrase "this is a mere conventional expression" (vohāramatta), he shows that there is no such thing as a dhamma called "determination" (niyāma);
rather, it is simply the capacity to awaken due to the accumulation of requisites that is spoken of in that way. This is stated as the reason for the term "one who is determined" (niyata).
The construction is: "it is said. "Of both" refers to the two statements: "one who is destined enters the fixed course" (*niyāma*).
The commentary on the discussion of the destined one is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of Attachment to the Unpleasant (*asāta-rāga*).
674. “Thus occurring” means occurring in the manner of a longing, thinking, “O, may it be mine! “Otherwise” means in the manner of delight (*nandana*) and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of attachment to the unpleasurable (*asāta-rāga*) is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of Whether Craving for Phenomena (*dhamma-taṇhā*) is Indeterminate (*abyākata*).
676–680. “Having taken” means that this refers merely to the act of grasping; it does not mean that such a craving actually exists.

For there is no craving that is supramundane in its object or indeterminate. “By way of three sections” refers to the sections of craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatanha*), craving for existence (*bhavatanhã*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavatanha*).
These comprise all six types of craving, distinguished as craving for form (*rūpatanha*) and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion concerning whether craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) is indeterminate (*abyākata*) is finished.
The commentary on the Thirteenth Chapter is finished.
14. The Fourteenth Chapter.
1. Explanation of the Discussion on the Linking of the Wholesome and Unwholesome (Kusalākusalapaṭisandahanakathāvaṇṇanā) 686–690.
Here, "linking" (paṭisandhāna) and "joining" (ghaṭana) refer specifically to the state of being an immediate condition (anantarapaccaya). Therefore, it is said: "it produces [the result] immediately.
The explanation of the discussion on the linking of the wholesome and unwholesome is finished.

2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Arising of the Six Bases (Saḷāyatanuppattikathāvaṇṇanā) 691–692. "Some proponents" refers to the followers of Kapila. For they are proponents of manifestation (*abhivyaktivādins*);
they maintain that the effect already exists within the cause in an unmanifest state, and subsequently attains manifestation, [just as] in the case of the seed-state.
Even though sprouts and so forth exist within trees and the like, they do not manifest; rather, it is said that only the seed undergoes manifestation.
The commentary on the discussion of the arising of the six sense bases is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of the Condition of Immediate Proximity (*anantara-paccaya*).
693–697. “Observing immediate succession” means imagining the arising of ear-consciousness immediately after eye-consciousness.

By the very mention of “ear-consciousness,” its dependence on the eye and its having visible form as its object are rejected, while its dependence on the ear and its having sound as its object are affirmed;
thus he says, “That [consciousness] does not have sound as its object in the eye.”
In this context, "sound as an object" should be connected by supplying the words "desires ear-consciousness.
This is known because of the tenet that ear-consciousness arises immediately after eye-consciousness; thus he says, "because it has entered [the stream] by way of immediate succession.
The commentary on the discussion of the condition of immediacy is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of Noble Form (Ariyarūpakathāvaṇṇanā) 698–699.

“Right speech and so forth” refers to right speech and right action. In that context, right speech has the nature of sound, while the other (right action) has the nature of bodily intimation; or, with the intention that both are intimations, his view is that they are form (rūpa).
The commentary on the discussion of noble form is finished.

5. Explanation of the Discussion on the Latent Disposition Being Different (Añño-anusayo-tikathā-vaṇṇanā) 700–701. "At that time" means at the moment of a wholesome or indeterminate consciousness. "So hi" is the reading of the latter [recension].
The explanation of the discussion on the latent disposition being different is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Ending with the State of Being Disjoined from Mind (Pariyuṭṭhāna-cittavippayutta-antika-kathāvaṇṇanā) 702.
"Those" refers to lust and the other [defilements]. "Therefore" means because lust and the others arise even in one who is practicing insight (vipassanā), therefore [this is so].
The commentary on the discussion concerning the ending with the state of being disjoined from mind is finished.

7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Included (Pariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā) 703–705. “By way of the defilements, the bases, and the spheres” means by way of the defilement-desire (kilesakāma), the object-desire (vatthukāma), and the plane (bhūmi).

It underlies [the mind] by way of being accompanied by the fine-material element (rūpadhātu); thus, sensual lust (kāmarāga) is worthy of arising when the conditions are assembled together with the sense-desire element (kāmadhātu), which is comprised of sense-desire thoughts (kāmavitakka).
The meaning is: "the same [is true] even in the realm of form (rūpadhātu). For *anusaya* (latent tendency) is the state of being unfit for arising when the causes such as lust (*rāga*) are obtained.
The commentary on the discussion of the included (*pariyāpanna*) is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Undeclared (*abyākata*).
706–608. "In every way" means both by way of being non-resultant and by way of being eternalism and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the indeterminate is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Unincluded.
709–710. Therefore, they explain the meaning as follows: "The view is not included within the mundane.

If that were so, there would be the over-extension (*atippasaṅga*) of applying such designations as "free from hatred" (*vītadosa*) and so forth. Consequently, explaining the meaning otherwise, he says:

"By the view of form," and so on. Therein, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), he includes the view of the formless (*arūpa-diṭṭhi*) and the rest. This analysis of the meaning is according to the intention of the opponent.
He said: "And if it were included. The meaning of "and that being so" is: given that the view is included within the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu).
"Therefore" means because of the absence of such a designation as "one who has transcended views.
For that view has not departed from him, such that he would not be called "one who has transcended views. "By which" refers to the state of possessing views regarding sense-pleasures.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Unincluded is finished.
The commentary on the Fourteenth Chapter is finished.
15. The Fifteenth Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Discussion of Conditionality (Paccayatākathāvaṇṇanā) §§711–717.

“Established” (*vavatthita*) means unmixed (*asaṃkiṇṇa*). For if a state (*dhamma*) that is a condition by way of one particular mode of conditionality were also to be a condition by way of another mode of conditionality, its conditionality would be called “mixed.
This is because [the simultaneous occurrence of] contradictory and impossible [modes of conditionality] is precluded.
It rejects the coexistence of conditions that are mutually incompatible.
The commentary on the Discussion of Conditions is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of Mutuality Condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*).
718–719. The intention [of the text] is that because it is stated as "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*), ignorance is not stated [here] as a condition for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).

For volitional formations are indeed conditions for ignorance by way of proximity (*anantara*) and so forth as well. The mention of the associated [condition] immediately after the mutual and proximity conditions, rather than after the non-disappearance condition, constitutes a distinction in the sequence;
it refers only to those phenomena that function as a presence-condition (*atthi-paccaya*), which is already included by the inclusion of the word "existent" (*atthi*).
"It is a dependence-condition (nissaya-paccaya). "By way of non-commonality" means by way of not being common to other words. Therefore he says, "For he will say," and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the mutuality-condition (aññamañña-paccaya) is finished.
9. Commentary on the Third Discussion of Perception and Feeling (saññā-vedayita).

732. Even though "the rest" (*sesa*) might refer to something other than what has been mentioned, [the author], showing that here it refers only to what is delimited by the context of the treatise, says:
"The intention of those... and so forth. Then, including even those without perception (*asaññasatta*), he says:

"And also of the non-percipient beings," etc. Therein, the construction is: "the intention is with reference to all beings. The passage beginning with "They move even from the touch of a hand" and so forth...
The connection is with the phrase "the nature of the body.

(733–734) The proponent of an opposing view does not accept the assertion that "one neither passes away nor is reborn by means of the five types of sensory consciousness"; therefore, he says: "The sutta... [etc. ...should be stated.
The commentary on the third discussion of perception and feeling is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discussion Concerning the Non-percipient Beings (Asaññasattupikākathāvaṇṇanā).

735. To show that his position is as follows—that just as an attainment occurring through the fading away of applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, and pleasure is devoid of applied thought and the rest, so too an attainment occurring through the fading away of perception must likewise be devoid of perception—he said:
“She too [is] ‘without perception’... [as before]... she demonstrates this.

(736) Anticipating the objection, “If it is the attainment of the fourth jhāna, how can it be the attainment of non-perception? he says: “It is ‘without perception’ because it is attained by means of the fading away of perception, not because of the total absence of perception.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the non-percipient beings is concluded.
11. Commentary on the Discussion of the Accumulation of Kamma (Kammūpacaya-kathāvaṇṇanā) 738–739. When asked, “Is the accumulation of kamma co-nascent with kamma?
he rejects it with reference to association and co-nascence, but affirms it with reference to dissociation and co-nascence. For even that which is dissociated possesses the quality of co-nascence.
The intention is that it is like [the relationship] of mind-originated matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*).
741. "Of the three" refers to the karma, the accumulation of karma, and the fruition of karma.
The commentary on the discussion of the accumulation of karma is finished.
The commentary on the Fifteenth Chapter is finished.
The Third Fifty is completed.
16. The Sixteenth Chapter.
3. Explanation of the Discourse on the Bestowing of Happiness (Sukhānuppadānakathāvaṇṇanā) 747–748.

“Not for him”: it does not belong to the one to whom it will be bestowed, nor to the one who bestows it. For here, “it” is intended as that which is distinct from both the one who bestows and the one to whom it is bestowed.
The explanation of the discourse on the bestowing of happiness is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Discussion of the Mindfulness Directed Toward Comprehension (Adhigayhamāna-manasikāra-kathāvaṇṇanā) §§749–753.

Regarding the phrase "by way of that state of mind": here, when one who is attending directs the attention to all conditioned phenomena together as one, the very mind by which he attends, because it is included within all conditioned phenomena, at that very moment [becomes] that [state of] mind.

To show that the fault called "identicalness of mind" (taṃcittatā) would follow—on the grounds that [the object] must be attended to by the mind—he said, "that very same thing becomes the object," and so forth. By this, he states the impossibility of that very [object] being attended to by that [mind];
however, by the words "or that," etc., he points out the consequence of falling into the doctrine of self-cognition (sasaṃvedanāvāda). This is the distinction between these two positions.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the grasping of attention is finished.
The commentary on the Sixteenth Chapter is finished.
17. The Seventeenth Chapter. 1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Accumulation of Merit by One Who Is Not an Arahant.

776–779. “Excluding the inoperative (kiriyā) indeterminate consciousness”: this means not including the “inoperative indeterminate consciousness,” but rather including it by virtue of its occurrence through acts such as giving and its status as merit consisting in giving and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the accumulation of merit even for an arahant is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discussion that There is No Untimely Death for an Arahant.

780. “*Aladdhavipākavārānan*” means those for whom there has been no opportunity for the giving of fruition (*vipāka*). “*Byantībhāvan*” means having reached the end; the meaning is their disappearance, that is, the non-fruition. 781.
“*Tato paran*” (beyond that) establishes the meaning through negation (*vyatireka*), not merely through affirmation (*anvaya*).
Thus he says: “He rejects the tenet that ‘it does not proceed until then, but proceeds beyond that. In this context, “beyond that” refers to the karma previously performed.
"Beyond the point of total exhaustion": the intention is that there is no longer killing because the characteristic of killing is absent.
To demonstrate that very absence of characteristics, it is said: "the perception of a living being as a living being," and so forth.
In this context, "not by that" means that he did not die by the assault performed by another; rather, he died through natural death alone—this is difficult to discern.
Whether it be difficult to understand or easy to understand, for those who possess undifferentiated knowledge, killing is [defined] solely by the completion of the constituent parts.
The commentary on the discussion regarding the absence of untimely death for an Arahant is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discussion: "All this is due to kamma."
"784. 'From seedless' means entirely from that which is not seed, and from other seeds. 'That' refers to the object to be given; the meaning is 'a requisite for the sick.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding 'all this as an act. 4.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding What is Bound by the Faculties (Indriya-baddha-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

788. "Even apart from the sense of impermanence" (*vināpi aniccaṭṭhena*) means even setting aside the sense of impermanence, or not excluding it; it does not mean by way of being devoid of the sense of impermanence. For there is nothing bound to the faculties that is devoid of the sense of impermanence.
The commentary on the discussion of what is bound to the faculties is finished. 7.
Commentary on the Discussion of Whether the Saṅgha Purifies Offerings That Should Not Be Specified.
793–794. "By way of non-receiving" means by way of the absence of a recipient.
The commentary on the discussion of whether it should be stated that the Saṅgha purifies the offering is finished.
11. Commentary on the Discussion of the Purification of the Offering.

800–801. "Independent of the recipient" means independent of the specific qualities of the recipient; the sense is that it does not depend on his status as a person worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
Therefore he said: "without the recipient acting as the condition. "This is true" is stated by way of acknowledging the very fact expressed through the praise of the doctrine.
The production of the result for the recipient is the great fruitfulness of the volition of giving.
For it is only the state of being a condition for that [result], not the causality of that [volition]. Therefore he said: "If it were produced by the volition of giving," and so forth.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Purification of the Offering is finished.
The commentary on the Seventeenth Chapter is finished.
18. The Eighteenth Chapter.
1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Human World.
802–803. "Grasping" means wrong grasping.
The commentary on the Discourse on the World of Humans is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Teaching of the Dhamma: 804–806.
Having received the teaching from that created Buddha, it was also taught by the Venerable Ānanda himself.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Teaching of the Dhamma is finished.
6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Transition between Jhānas (813–816):

The state of the mind being dispassionate toward applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), the attention to their disadvantage (*ādīnava*), and the mental aspect directed toward that [disadvantage] constitute the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) of the second jhāna. Therefore, it is said: "Applied and sustained thought should be attended to as disadvantageous; thereafter, one should attain the second jhāna."
The commentary on the Discussion of the Transition between Jhānas is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Intermediate Jhāna (Jhānantarika-kathā): 817–819.

Showing that this is not a jhāna because it lacks applied thought (*vitakka*)—and thus is not the first jhāna—and because it possesses sustained thought (*vicāra*)—and thus is not the second jhāna—it is said: “It is not a jhāna because it neither possesses nor lacks the state of being any one of the [standard] jhānas, such as the first jhāna.”
The commentary on the discussion of the intermediate jhāna is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of "One Sees a Form with the Eye" (826–827).
By the phrase "having seen a form with the eye," there is a lack of approval for the non-inclusion of the admission [of seeing] by means of eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
Sūceta said: “It is indeed with reference to the acknowledgment of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) that he spoke. For this very reason, he said:

“But as for the acknowledgment of mind-consciousness,” and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is: because it is precisely the acknowledgment of mind-consciousness that is intended. “This being so” means:
if one discerns form by means of form, then even though the mind-consciousness is discerning form, it is the discernment of form.
It exists, yet it is not the seeing of form; thus he asked, "But how can the admission of mental consciousness be the seeing of form?
The commentary on the discussion of "seeing form with the eye" is finished.
The commentary on the eighteenth chapter is finished.
19. The Nineteenth Chapter. 1. Explanation of the Discourse on Abandoning the Defilements (Kilesapajahanakathāvaṇṇanā) 828–831.
“But those” refers to the defilements that have been abandoned by means of the Noble Path; however, it should be understood here that these are indeed the defilements to be abandoned by the Path.
If the development of the path were absent, those [defilements] that ought to arise would be called "not yet arisen" because they have not arrived during the three moments;
however, since they will not arise at all, they should be understood as not being described in that way. Therefore it was said: "nor will they exist.
The commentary on the discussion of the abandoning of defilements is finished.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on Emptiness (Suññata-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 832.

In the sense of being subject to lack of mastery (*avasavattana*), those phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) are called "non-self" (*anattā*) because there is no self belonging to them as postulated by others;
this very non-selfhood is what is meant when it is said: "The mode of lacking mastery is non-selfhood. Now, this...
Since, in terms of its actual meaning, it is simply the lack of essence, he said, "In meaning, it is just aging-and-death," in order to show that by means of one part of it.
If this were so, there would be a confusion of characteristics; however, it should be understood that this is merely a statement of their intended purpose.

For it is precisely because non-material phenomena (arūpadhamma) have the mode of being subject to no mastery over themselves that they are included within the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) under the characteristic of non-self.
The commentary on the Discourse on Emptiness is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life. 835–836.
"The state of attainment" refers to the possession [of qualities] mentioned below.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Fruits of Recluseship is finished.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on Suchness (Tathatā) 841–843.
By the phrase "the intrinsic nature of form and so forth," he rejects the view that form and the other aggregates themselves are the intrinsic nature.
Because the opponent maintains that it is not included among form and the other aggregates, he said: "He speaks of *bhāva* as suchness (*tathatā*), not of the application of *bhāva*.
In this context, "*bhāva*" means a mere phenomenon (*dhammamatta*), in the sense of "nature" (*pakati*), as in the expression "subject to birth" (*jātidhamma*) and so forth.
For the opponent's view is that the nature of form and the rest—namely, their quality of being subject to change (*ruppana*) and so on—is likewise unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*). Therefore, it was said:

“Not the conjunction of existence. For that by which existence—the phenomenon possessing its own intrinsic nature—is joined, such that it attains a state of oneness, is the “conjunction of existence,” characterized by deformation and so forth.
Furthermore, that is not other than matter and the rest; for that very reason, it is conditioned. Yet, in the sense of being non-erroneous, it is called “suchness” (*tathatā*).
The commentary on the Discussion of Suchness is finished. 6.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Wholesome (Kusalakathāvaṇṇanā) 844–846. The construction is: “It is wholesome by the mere fact of being blameless. “Because of that” means: because that which is free from blame is blameless, and because it is wholesome by the mere fact of being blameless, therefore Nibbāna is wholesome.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Wholesome is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on Absolute Certainty (Accantaniyāmakathāvaṇṇanā) 847.
As for that which says: "Once submerged, he remains submerged; for him there is no more emergence from existence."
The statement "it does not exist" appears in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, but that is the opinion of the teachers (*ācariyavāda*), not the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself; thus, showing this, he said:

"In that birth... pe... conceiving. Therein, "in that birth" means in whichever birth a person is possessed of obstructions such as the obstruction of karma (*kammāvaraṇa*) and so forth, [he is so] in that birth.
The state of being a mere "crack" (*khāṇuka*) in *saṃsāra*—like Makkhali and others [who were like] seeds for the next year's harvest—is [what is meant].

And it should be viewed as being like that. Furthermore, this should be understood solely as the fruit of wrong view, such as the view of no-cause (ahetuka) and so forth, because there is no such thing as an "absolute certainty" (accanta-niyāma) for anyone.

For just as there is no such thing as a "certainty" (niyāma) for one who is being liberated—apart from the delimitation of existence (bhava-pariccheda) effected by the Path—likewise, for one who is not being liberated, there is no such thing as a "certainty of saṃsāra. For one of such a kind...

However, when wrong view is powerful, the continuity of saṃsāra lasts for a much longer time, delimited by immeasurable eons, and there is rebirth in the states of misery— wherein the designation "seed of saṃsāra" applies.
As for what some say, namely, "There is indeed one who wanders eternally because the category of beings is infinite," that too—
This may have been said with reference to a mental continuum (*santāna*) that is preponderant in demerit (*apuñña*).

For there is no such thing as a "determinacy of saṃsāra" (*saṃsāraniyāma*) that acts as an obstacle to the liberation of beings—like the determinacy of falsehood (*micchattaniyāma*), which is an obstacle to entering the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*) within that very same existence—as it does for those who have killed their mothers and so forth.
However, as long as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the Path and its Fruit is not found, [the cycle continues].
Samsara is undelimited; however, it should be understood that when it is apprehended, it is then delimited.
Just as with right view fixed [in its object], so too, by means of wrong view fixed [in its object], there must be a reaching of the peak through a one-sided grasp within its own domain;
thus, for a person endowed with that, how could mindfulness not be absolutely fixed?
If, regarding that object of adherence, a non-uniform apprehension were to arise, or if another contradictory adherence were to arise, there would be no absolute certainty (accantaniyāma).
Thus, in the Pāḷi, the objection is raised concerning the arising of doubt and the arising of a different certainty.
For just as with persons destined for rightness (sammattaniyata), so too for persons destined for falsehood (micchattaniyata) and those destined for rightness, [doubt] arises respectively.
Dharmas fixed in rightness or fixed in wrongness may never arise [simultaneously], yet there is no contradiction in their belonging to different fixed categories (niyāma).
Therefore, just as with the "immediate" (ānantarika) interval, the views of eternalism and annihilationism—which are of the same nature as wrong view—do not exclude it;

thus, in order to show precisely what is contradictory, only these two views, like doubt, are mentioned in the Pāḷi. In this way, here [is shown] the arising of doubt and the arising of the other fixed categories.

The state of being a cause for turning back from the arising of other [wrong] paths should be understood; however, it might be said that one must "accept this only after investigation," as it is contradictory to say that absolute certainty (accantaniyāma) will turn back.
The commentary on the discussion of absolute certainty is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties (Indriyakathāvaṇṇanā) 853–856.
Just as the supramundane faith and so forth are indeed the faculty of faith and so forth, so too are the mundane ones. Why?

Because even there, the function of a ruler (*indaṭṭha*) exists by way of the characteristic of resolution (*adhimokkhalakkhaṇa*) and so on. In the objects such as that which is to be believed, there is merely the act of believing and so forth.
Indeed, showing this meaning, he said: “The supramundane... [etc. ...should be seen.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Faculties is finished.
The commentary on the nineteenth chapter is finished.
20. The twentieth chapter. 2. Explanation of the Discussion on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 863–865.
Granted that there is indeed a full understanding of suffering even during the prior stage, it is that occurring at the moment of the Path which accomplishes the goal.
Thus, referring to the supreme thorough understanding of suffering (*dukkhapariññā*), he said, "It is only the knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*) that illuminates [it].

However, that restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) should not be seen as excluding other types of knowledge; rather, it should be understood as excluding other types of knowledge from performing the function already accomplished.
Therefore, he said, "Not the state of being that very knowledge," and so forth.
The commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discussion of Hell-Wardens (Nirayapāla-kathā): 866–868.
They are called hell-wardens (*nirayapāla*) because they ward off those in hell, protecting them by way of not permitting their exit from there.
They are called *nirayapāla* (hell-wardens) because they are capable and sufficient for the purpose of guarding hell or for being overwhelmed by the suffering of the denizens of hell.

But are these hell-wardens themselves denizens of hell, or are they not? What of it? If, first of all, they were denizens of hell, then—being produced by karma conducive to rebirth in hell—they too would experience the suffering of hell; and likewise...

If they were not hell-beings, they would be incapable of inflicting the torments upon other hell-beings, and there would be no distinction such that "these are the hell-beings" and "these are the hell-wardens.
Furthermore, if those who inflict the torments were equal to others in appearance, strength, and stature, there would be no fear or terror in the others.
If, on the other hand, they were not hell-beings, how could they possibly exist there? It is said in reply: the hell-wardens are not hell-beings.

They are produced by karma that leads to rebirth in the hell-state. For they are produced by a specific karma other than the karma that leads to birth in hell itself, because they belong to the class of *rakkhasas*. Thus it is said:
"Angry, of cruel deeds, and likewise delighting in evil..."
“They rejoice among those who suffer; they are born as Yama-rakkhasas.
Regarding this, as for what some say—“because they do not experience the suffering of torment, otherwise they would torment one another,” and so forth—this is like scratching a hair on the sky;
it applies only to the hell-guardians themselves being hell-beings.

Because they do not exist. But as for those who might say: "Even if the hell-guardians are not inhabitants of hell, how is it that they do not experience suffering while rolling about on the hellish ground made of iron, which is burning, blazing, and aflame?
It is because of the power of karma. For just as Mahāmoggallāna and others, possessing psychic powers and having attained mastery over the mind, felt compassion for the hell-beings—
Just as those who have reached the plane of hell by the power of psychic potency (*iddhi*) are not afflicted there by the suffering of burning, so too should this be understood.
If it is argued that this is because the scope of psychic potency is inconceivable, then this is likewise because the ripening of karma (*kamma-vipāka*) is inconceivable.
For they were reborn by such a kind of karma that, while remaining entirely unafflicted by the sufferings of hell, [they appear] among the denizens of hell.

They go forth; yet the absence of external objects does not exist merely by that [fact], because the quality of being desirable or undesirable is distributed among the individual gatekeepers according to their respective natures.
For what is desirable to one gatekeeper may be undesirable to another, and what is undesirable to one may be desirable to another. And having established this, as for what some say: "There is no..."

Such statements as "by means of karma, through heat, there is the scorching of others" are thereby refuted. As for what they say—"How can those who are hell-beings (nirayika) come to exist there?"—it is because hell-beings are beings who have reached their [karmic] end.

For it is karma, producing a personal existence (attabhāva) suitable for the torment of a hell-being, that brings about rebirth in the very place of hell, having been directed toward such a desired destination.
And those [beings] have greater strength, height, and girth than the denizens of hell, and their methods are exceedingly terrifying, distressing, and cruel.
By this very fact, it should be understood that even crows, dogs, and other such creatures are described as being born there.
Furthermore, it should not be said that beings in one destiny afflict those in another destiny, because such a thing is observed elsewhere as well.
As for what some say—that the hell-wardens, the hell-dogs, and so forth, lack a sentient nature—that is merely their own opinion, because such is not seen elsewhere.

Indeed, no such occurrence of phenomena has ever been observed that is insentient by nature and yet accomplishes a functional purpose without being employed by presently existing sentient beings. [This is like] those who ward off water from the hungry ghosts (petas).
There is no specific reason why men with clubs and other weapons in their hands would not be non-afflicted [by the defilements].
Furthermore, even harm caused in a dream is irrelevant to the capacity for performing one's purposeful duties, because that purpose is accomplished merely by seeing [the object] and so forth.

For instance, there is no accomplishment of a purpose through the enjoyment of food and such in a dream; however, the argument regarding the "created form" (*nirmāṇarūpa*) here has already been answered, since the sphere of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is inconceivable.

If it is argued that here too [the existence of hell-wardens] is due to the inconceivability of the ripening of kamma, that is not so, because it is unproven. That the ripening of kamma for those in hell consists of hell-wardens is unproven;
rather, by the method already stated, only their status as sentient beings is proven.

For it can be said that the occurrence of phenomena designated as "hell-wardens"—which are reckoned as sentient beings—is intentional and harmful to others, owing to the presence of a purposeful function.

It is like a continuous succession of *ojāhāra* and other types of *rakkhasas*. Furthermore, it cannot be denied that these are produced by prior intention (*abhisandhi*), because they are tormented in various ways according to that very intention; for this reason alone, there is no lack of consistency with cases such as the Saṅghāṭa mountain.

As for those who say, "The guardians of hell (*narakapālas*) are merely specific types of beings (*bhūta*) possessing particular colors, shapes, and so forth, appearing in a terrifying form," [that is not correct].
[The claim that they] "receive a common designation" is unproven. For in the Canon itself, it is established by way of direct statement that "there are hell-guardians in hell.
Furthermore, just as in the Noble Discipline the mere existence of hell-guardians is not proven, so too [it is not proven] for one who maintains that they are mere designations.

Their claim that these [guardians] are merely composed of the primary elements (*bhūta*) is unproven; for there are no such things as "primary elements" belonging to him. If he speaks by taking the ultimate reality (*paramattha*) as his basis, then why does he reject [the existence of] feeling and so forth?
Let this investigation of arguments stand aside for those whose reasoning is unstable and whose delusion and perversion are not abandoned.
Thus, one must reach the conclusion here that the guardians of hell do indeed exist.

Furthermore, it should be understood that even if those [guardians] exist, the claim that there is a restriction of location and so forth— as in the case of hell— even when external objects are absent, is not established.
The commentary on the discussion of the hell-wardens is concluded.
4. Commentary on Idle Talk (Tiracchānakathāvaṇṇanā) 869–871.

“Of him” refers to the son of the gods named Erāvaṇa. Regarding the phrase “of the elephant-nāga,” this is said with reference to his transformation into the form of an elephant during his time of sporting there.
The same principle applies here to the phrase “of the divine vehicle. For indeed, in a place that is a condition for absolute happiness, [one does not engage in such talk].
In heaven, the arising of a personal existence produced by unwholesome kamma and characterized by suffering is appropriate.
Therefore he said, “not for one who has gone among the animals.
The commentary on the talk about animals is finished.
6. Explanation of the Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 876–877.

Herein, showing that the supramundane nature of knowledge having twelve bases is being established in the statement, “Supramundane knowledge has twelve bases,” [the author] first states the first alternative and then again [states] the fact that supramundane knowledge has twelve bases.

He said, "That... [etc. ...is the meaning," in order to show that it is being established. Regarding the term *pariññeyya* (to be fully understood), the word *iti* here has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*) or the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*).
By this, he includes such terms as *pahātabba* (to be abandoned) and so forth. The same method applies here to the term *pariññāta* (fully understood).

Through the expression "*pariññeyyaṃ pariññātan*" (what is to be fully understood has been fully understood) and so on, it is shown that [the fruit] is to be produced by the activity of full comprehension and the rest.

The state of having been produced (*nibbattitatā*) is shown, not the state of being produced (*nibbattiya-mānatā*). To show by what means that [production] occurs, it is said: "But as for the knowledge of the truths," and so forth.
Therein, "knowledge of the truths" (*saccañāṇa*) is the knowledge that awakens to the intrinsic nature of the truths such as suffering;

referring to this, it was said: "This is suffering," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "also at the moment of the path" (*maggakkhaṇepi*), by the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that it occurs before and after that moment as well.
It is to be seen. The intention is that it exists by way of accomplishing tasks such as full understanding, and by way of non-delusion regarding the object.
The commentary on the discussion of knowledge is finished.
The commentary on the twentieth chapter is finished.
The Fourth Fifty is completed. 21. The Twenty-First Chapter:
1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Teaching (Sāsanakathā).

878. *Samudāyā* refers to the collections of words that proceed by way of questions, such as "Has the new dispensation been made? and so forth. *Ekadesānaṃ* refers to its constituent parts. "In all three questions" is stated thus in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇabhāvena*).
The commentary on the Discourse on the Dispensation is finished.
4. Commentary on the Discourse on Psychic Power (*Iddhi*)
883–884. "By way of intention" means by way of the intention of resolving in such and such a manner.
The commentary on the discussion of supernormal power (iddhi) is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Dhamma (Dhammakathā).
887–888. Since the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of matter is the "matter-state" (*rūpaṭṭha*), it is said: "There is no so-called matter-state other than matter.
Furthermore, whatever is other than something is not of that same nature; thus it is said:

"And there is no matter other than the matter-state," meaning that there is no matter [apart from its own state]. By this, he establishes that point through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Therefore, because the matter-state is not other than matter...

There is no form other than the state of being form; therefore, by means of the particle *eva*, it is shown that "form is indeed form, indeed the very nature of form," thereby excluding the nature of feeling and so forth. "By way of intention" means by way of the intention that the state of being form is not something other [than form].

"Otherwise" means: if they were other, then by way of the state of being form, form would necessarily have to be called "determined"; this is how the construction should be understood. It has already been shown.
It exists in meaning because it is established [as such]. For one does not create a distinction through another synonym when the underlying basis (*vatthu*) is undivided.

"Otherness" (*aññatta*) refers to the intrinsic nature of form and the locus of form. Since there is no actual division established by a designation that implies a possessor—as in the expression "the body of a stone statue"—and since this division is merely a conceptual construction (*kappanāmattato*), it is not ultimate reality (*paramattha*);
thus he said, "it proceeds as if having grasped [them]."
"Only difference by way of feeling and so forth" means only otherness from feeling and so forth. "That is its own-nature" means that is the own-nature of matter (*rūpa*).
"For the purpose of making known the difference" means for the purpose of making known the distinction thus: "The own-nature of matter is not [the own-nature] of feeling and so forth.

And "that statement" refers to the statement: "Matter is not fixed in the sense of being matter. "In the manner stated" refers to [the passage beginning]: "Because there is no matter other than that which has the characteristic of matter," and so on.
In the manner stated. The construction is: "If it is with fault (*sadosa*), then why does he admit it?
The reason already stated refers to the logical justification (*yutti*) stated thus: "Form is form alone; it does not have the nature of feeling and so forth.
"Challenged by another" refers to the challenge posed by the opponent (*paravādin*) in such statements as: "It should not be said that 'form is determined in the sense of being form.'"
He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "Having shown that very reason" means having shown that very reasoning already stated by means of the passage beginning with "For here...
He "averts the objection" means he averts the objection stated as: "Then why does he acknowledge [it]?
In order to show what purpose was intended when it was said "other than this," the passage beginning with "Form, etc. was stated.
The commentary on the "Discourse on the Dhamma" is finished.
The commentary on the twenty-first chapter is finished.
22. The Twenty-second Chapter.
2. Commentary on the Discussion of Wholesome Consciousness (Kusalacittakathāvaṇṇanā) 894–895.
"At the moment of the preceding impulsion" means at the moment of the preceding series of impulsions that immediately preceded the consciousness of final Nibbāna.
The commentary on the discussion of wholesome consciousness is finished.
3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Imperturbable (Āneñjakathāvaṇṇanā) 896.

Because it resembles the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) in its having as its object a state associated with a cause that is similar in nature to its own object, the death-consciousness (cuticitta) is called "life-continuum consciousness" (bhavaṅgacitta).
The commentary on the discourse on the imperturbable is finished.
5–7. Commentary on the Story of Tisso-pika (898–900).

He thinks that even the attainment of Arahantship occurs while still in the womb; for Sopāka the novice and others attained Arahantship at the age of seven. The opponent’s intention is that there is also a seven-year-old fetus [who attains it]. [The Buddha] was traveling through the air.
It is like a dream, a dream of the sky. Showing this by way of illustration, he said, "as if it were the higher knowledges (abhiññā) such as traveling through the air.

The construction is: one imagines that there is the realization of the Dhamma through the attainment of the four lower paths, and the attainment of Arhatship through the attainment of the supreme fruit, even within a dream.
The commentary on the Tisso-pika story is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Condition of Repetition (Āsevanapaccaya-kathā). 903–905.
"The seed does not take on the state of the four sweets"—this was stated according to our own school (sakasamaya), whereas in other schools (parasamaya) [it is said otherwise].
Furthermore, material phenomena (rūpadhammā) are intended to be of the same moment as immaterial phenomena (arūpadhammā). For this very reason it was said: "All phenomena (dhammā) are momentary.
Even though they are momentary, a specific kind of development (bhāvanāviseso) is found even in insentient things and in material forms not bound to the sense faculties;
how much more so, then, in those that are sentient? To show this, he said: "Just as a seed does not take on the state of the four sweets..."
It should be understood as an illustration. The intention is that there is no such thing as "repetition" (*āsevana*) because [the momentary state] does not persist due to its brevity.
Nevertheless, repetition is obtained precisely through its momentary duration.

For "perfuming" (*vāsana*) is the repeated engagement in performing what is to be done by means of an application similar to oneself—whether it be wholesome or otherwise—and thus bringing about similarity to oneself.
"Repetition is like a book previously familiarized [with which] one becomes acquainted with the subsequent [part].
The commentary on the discussion of the condition of repetition is finished.
10. Commentary on the Discussion of the Momentary.
906–907. “In material phenomena such as earth, etc. means in material phenomena such as earth, etc., which consist of a collection of many groups (*kalāpa*).
For there, while some previously arisen [phenomena] remain, there is the arising of some others different from them;
and then there is the cessation of some of those that arose earlier. This is because each individual group of material phenomena has a simultaneous arising and cessation. Thus it is established.
The meaning is that there is a continuous occurrence and persistence through a succession characterized by non-simultaneous arising and cessation, as previously described.
Now, as to why this aforementioned occurrence belongs only to the continuity of matter (*rūpasantati*), he says: "For not [of] material phenomena," and so forth. The meaning of this is:
if all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) were of the same moment, then, in that case, the continuity of matter would be just like the continuity of the immaterial (*arūpa*).
There might be an occurrence according to the method of the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and so forth, but that is not the case.
If it were so, there would have to be the arising and ceasing of earth and the other elements in every single moment of consciousness.
The commentary on the discussion of momentariness is concluded.
The commentary on the twenty-second chapter is finished.
23. The twenty-third chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Discussion on the Single Intention.
The word *eka* can also mean "another," as in such passages as "some thus assert" (*ittheke abhivadanti*).
Here, "another" should be understood as meaning "one whose intention is lust. However, because an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) enjoys things with desire according to their own will, it is said:

"It is meant that his intention is other than [that of one free from lust], namely, an intention of lust. But what is this "intention of another"? It is an intention of compassion (*karuṇā*). By that—

It is said: "By means of the intention of compassion, there is a single intention. And this method was stated with reference to an opponent who maintains that for a Bodhisatta who fulfills a woman's desire out of compassion for the sake of protecting her life, there is no destruction of his restraint;
however, with reference to one who maintains that it is the intention of a formal vow, it is said: "There is a single intention."
"Herein," and so forth, has been stated. It should be understood that even the intention to see the face of one's son is included right here.
"In a single state" means in concomitance.
The commentary on the discussion of a single intention is finished.
3–7. Commentary on the Discussion of Wielding Sovereignty at Will (Issariyakāmakārikā-kathāvaṇṇanā) 910–914.
“By sovereignty” means by mental sovereignty, not by mastery over the mind; this is the meaning. “Wielding sovereignty at will” means the accomplishment of whatever is desired.
“For the sake of the cause of wielding sovereignty at will” means for the purpose of producing that state of wielding sovereignty at will; this is the meaning.
"It is performed by means of wrong view" (micchādiṭṭhiyā karīyati) means that any kind of ascetic practice is performed solely through a false adherence.
The commentary on the discussion concerning the performance of desires for power is finished.
8. Commentary on the Discussion on Resemblance (Patirūpakathāvaṇṇanā).

915–916. "Like loving-kindness and so forth" means: just as loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), and gladness (muditā), although having the nature of affection, are not lust because they have the nature of non-attachment and are undefiled, even so there is no state that resembles lust except for loving-kindness and the rest.
The meaning is that the mode of moistening another's mind is simply the mode of occurrence of lust itself. For this very reason, it is said: "It grasps only lust."

"Likewise with regard to hatred (dosa)" means that, just as with envy and the rest, there is no "counterfeit hatred" distinct from hatred itself; therefore, one should understand that the term refers to hatred alone.
For, apart from envy and the like, any mode of being corrupt toward another's mind is simply a manifestation of hatred.
The commentary on the discussion of counterfeits is concluded.
9. Explanation of the Discussion on the Unaccomplished (Aparinipphannakathāvaṇṇanā) 917–918.
“The state beginning with impermanence” means that its nature (pakati) is the phenomenon (dhamma) consisting of the state of being impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, and so forth.
“Only suffering is fully accomplished” refers to the question being asked with reference to the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca).
The meaning "not merely suffering" is understood from the statement "for it is not only the first Truth that is suffering.
If that were so, the opponent would not be able to admit the established existence (*pariniṣpannatā*) of the eye-base and other such phenomena similar to them.
Why? Because even these are included within the Truth of Suffering, and not within the other Truths.

For that which is produced from the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*) is, in the primary sense (*nippariyāyato*), the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*); the other [the external world] is suffering by way of the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*).
Demonstrating this meaning, he said, "Indeed, not only... and so forth.

Therein, by the phrase "not included among the clung-to" (*anupādinnāni*), he states the absence of inclusion of the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so on within the truth of the origin. By the term "supramundane" (*lokuttarāni*), he refers to their exclusion from the truths of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*magga*).
If such a logical inconsistency were to be stated here, what is there to be said?
For this is the inherent nature of the opponent’s doctrine, namely, that it lacks internal consistency between what precedes and what follows. Indeed, it has been rejected by the wise;

and we have already demonstrated this very point in various places. This refers to the claim: "Form (*rūpa*) is not fully established (*aparinipphanna*); only suffering (*dukkha*) is fully established."
As for what was said by you, that indeed should not be said. Why? Because of the suffering-nature of form (*rūpa*).
For form is impermanent and is the basis for suffering. Therefore it is said: "What is impermanent, that is suffering," and "In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
The commentary on the discussion of the non-actualized is finished.
The commentary on the twenty-third chapter is finished.
The sub-commentary on the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa* is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Beginning of the Text for the *Yamakapakaraṇa-anuṭīkā*. "In brief" means by way of a mere enumeration;
this refers to what was called "the laying down of the matrix" (*mātikāṭhapana*). "Among phenomena" means among phenomena such as the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth.

And regarding wholesome and other phenomena: when phenomena are grasped without error, the teaching proceeding by way of the Root Pairs (Mūlayamaka) and so forth brings about various kinds of skill in those to be trained and accomplishes the task of full understanding; it does not do so when there is erroneous grasping.
Thus he said: "The erroneous grasping... was undertaken. By this, [it is shown] that immediately after the teaching of the *Kathāvatthu* manual, the teaching of the *Yamaka* manual [was undertaken].
He states the reason: therein, "misapprehension" refers to wrong grasping, such as the grasping of a person (*puggala*).

Regarding the bases such as phenomena (*dhamma*), persons, and locations: [it is] with respect to phenomena by way of such statements as, "Whatever wholesome phenomena there are, all those have wholesome roots," and so forth;

with respect to the person by way of such statements as, "In whom the aggregate of form arises, in him the aggregate of feeling arises," and so forth; and with respect to location by way of such statements as, "Wherever the aggregate of form arises..."
[This refers to] those [discourses] that proceed by depending on and taking as their object a location, such as "the aggregate of feeling arises," and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of the person, space, arising, cessation, both together, full understanding, and so on, should be understood. Regarding "of certainty and doubt":

certainty (*sanniṭṭhāna*) is the making of a definitive decision regarding the meaning asked about, by means of methods such as providing a response according to the sequence of the text, showing the form [of the answer], rejecting, or prohibiting; doubt (*saṃsayo*) is the state of wavering due to the absence of that [certainty].

Regarding those [terms] "certainty" (*sanniṭṭhāna*) and "doubt" (*saṃsayānaṃ*): although here, for those who receive the Dhamma, certainty is preceded by doubt and thus doubt should be mentioned first,
this [sequence] is intended to show that for the Blessed One, who is teaching, certainty comes first and doubt follows.

The sequence of the words has been established. For the Lord of Dhamma—who stands having made all that is to be fully understood as directly evident before him like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand—has no doubt regarding anything whatsoever.

Nevertheless, wishing to provide an answer, he poses a question by way of a doubter, demonstrating the doubt residing in the inclination of those to be trained; thus, through this method of answering a question, there is neither finality nor doubt.
The meaning "they are obtained" is thus shown; however, here certainty and doubt should be understood specifically by way of the dhammas whose doubts have been resolved.
Therefore, it was said in the Commentary: "Because there is no doubt as to whether wholesome states are indeed wholesome or not," and so forth.
For that very reason, the term "certainty" is mentioned first in the phrases "of certainties and doubts" and "by way of certainties and doubts."
This is the *Yamakapakaraṇa*. Regarding its time of teaching (*desanāsamaya*) and so forth which ought to be stated:

the time of teaching is immediately after the teaching of the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa*; the place of teaching is the Tāvatiṃsa heaven itself; and the manner of teaching—by way of the pairs (*yamaka*) such as the roots of the wholesome and unwholesome—is explained by the verses beginning with "In brief indeed," etc., which clarify the analysis through their indicative marks (*nimitta*).
This constitutes the promise of the commentary together with its sign.
Showing this meaning, he said: “By way of teaching at the appropriate time and place,” and so forth. For this is the sign (nimitta) here in the commentary:
namely, that the sequence of arising and the carrying of the burden have come about because of the wise performance of the duties of the wise.
In that context, the connection is: “having shown what has arisen.”
“Tattha” means in that [context] of showing the time and so forth. “Yama” means restraining or ceasing;
thus he said, “When there is birth, death occurs,” and so on, up to “the domain.

In this regard, just as birth is the domain of Yama in the sense that “when there is birth, death occurs,” so too the aggregates of clinging are the domain of Yama in the sense that “when the aggregates of clinging exist, death occurs.”
The word "domain" (*visaya*) should be supplied [to the end of the compound]. For they are subject to death.
Indeed, it is only when death has arrived that the messengers of Yama inflict various punishments upon a person who has committed evil deeds, not before death has arrived;

thus, death is said to be the domain of Yama. "The place where his command prevails" is a synonym for the meaning of the word *visaya*. "Or a region" refers to the regions of the three realms, such as the realm of sensual desire (*kāmadhātu*), and so forth.
He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). For the King of Death is the lord of the three realms.

The five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariya*), the proclamation of another teacher, and together with that, the five enmities (*verā*) and the six states of incapacity (*abhabbaṭṭhāna*). "Turning back" (*āvattā*) means turning to the right (*padakkhiṇāvattā*). "Fine hairs" (*tanuruhā*) means body hairs (*lomā*).
The commentary on the beginning of the book is finished.
1. Explanation of the Section on Enumeration (Uddesavāra-vaṇṇanā) regarding the Root Pairs (Mūlayamaka).

"Of the collection of pairs" means of the collection of pairs beginning with the Root Pairs (mūlayamaka), such as those found in this treatise (*pakaraṇa*). For the Root Pairs and so forth [are so designated] in consideration of the treatise.
Although it is a constituent part, it is called a "pair-group" (yamakasamūha) in view of its constant constituent parts. Therefore he said:
"And of that entire collection, [namely] the whole treatise.

Regarding the phrase "of the distinctions of wholesome and unwholesome roots": this refers to those things comprised by the terms of doubt mentioned in the second question, which are reckoned as wholesome.

The construction is as follows: because it has been stated that there is a state of "meaning-yamaka" (atthayamaka) regarding the specific qualities designated as wholesome roots (*kusalamūla*), which were spoken of in the first inquiry.

For just as the wholesome phenomena (*kusaladhamma*) spoken of in the first inquiry by way of possessing specific qualities are spoken of in the second inquiry by way of being those specific qualities themselves, so too [are those spoken of] in the first inquiry by way of being specific qualities.
The wholesome root-dhammas are stated in the second inquiry by way of their state of being possessed of a distinction (*visesavantabhāva*).
For the distinctions and the states of possessing distinctions among dhammas arise according to the speaker’s desire for expression.

The intended meaning is that the wholesome roots and the wholesome [states] are possessed of a distinction from the specific wholesome roots and wholesome [states] included within the words of doubt. And here, by way of the distinction required by that which possesses the distinction...
The first alternative interpretation has been stated; however, the second is by way of the distinction between the qualifier and the qualified.
This is their difference. Therefore he said, "Of those desired to be known," and so forth.
Therein, "of those desired to be known" means of those that have become the objects of the question. "Of the distinctions" means of the distinctions among wholesome states and wholesome roots.
"Of those dependent on what possesses distinction" means of those who are dependent on what is called wholesome by way of wholesome roots and wholesome states.

"That which possesses distinction" refers to the wholesome roots and wholesome states. "Of those dependent on distinction" means of those who are dependent on the distinctions between wholesome states and wholesome roots.
"In this" refers to this *Mūlayamaka*. "The state of being primary" is said because, in the first alternative, the question itself is characterized by doubt regarding what is primary.
The preeminence of the specific qualities (*visesa*) is to be understood. For they are "possessing specific qualities" (*visesavanta*) in relation to those who are still subject to doubt.
In the second alternative, however, since what are called "specific qualities" depend upon those possessing them, the preeminence of those possessing the specific qualities should be seen therein.
But the preeminence of two things together is not tenable; for it is only when there is something non-preeminent that there can be such a thing as "preeminence."
Therefore he said: “With each question, only one single meaning is included. And this must be accepted as such;

otherwise, the status of being the primary subject here would not be tenable given the distinctions to be determined and specified. It is not a word denoting a phenomenon (*dhamma*); that is, it does not denote a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
For even a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature is called “meaning” (*attha*) in such passages as “one of profound wisdom who sees the subtle meaning,” and so forth.
In such passages as “Knowledge of cause and fruit is the analytical knowledge of meaning” (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), the word *attha* should be understood as denoting cause and fruit.

By the word “etc. (*ādi*), its denotation of benefit and so forth—as found in such passages as “the realization of the goal” (*atthābhisamaya*)—is included. “By that very fact” means precisely because it denotes the meaning of the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
Regarding the phrase "all three terms," the word *pi* (also/even) here has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), and that conjunction occurs in the sense of equal coordination (*tulyayoga*).

Since there might be a suspicion that the term "name" (*nāma*) alone comprehensively includes the wholesome and so forth without exception, he says, "all three... the state of being comprehensive," in order to dispel that suspicion.
In that context, the word *matta* in the expression "the mere state of being comprehensive" (*saṅgāhakattamatta*) has the sense of excluding further qualifications (*visesanivatti*). By this—
In order to show the specific distinction [between the two], it is said: "It is not a comprehensive inclusion of everything without remainder.

For that which is called "matter" (rūpa) is not included by the term "name" (nāma). One must understand the restriction to be: "only the wholesome and so forth are name," and not "only name is wholesome and so forth.
And with reference to this very restriction, he says: "it was stated merely with the intention of including the wholesome and so forth. Even if...
The term "name" (*nāma*) does not include all wholesome states and so forth without exception; rather, it includes those that are wholesome and so on, and it was taken for that very purpose.
Thus, showing that the inclusion of names within the triad of the wholesome (*kusalattika*) has been stated, he said: “Wholesome... [etc. ...stated.
The commentary on the section on the enumeration is finished.
Commentary on the Section of Expositions (Niddesavāravaṇṇanā) 52. Regarding the second set of pairs (Dutiyayamaka):

in the "Single-Root Pairs" (Ekamūlayamaka), just as the inquiry was commenced with the words "Whatever states are wholesome," so too here, in this "Mutual-Root Pairs" (Aññamaññamūlayamaka), the inquiry must likewise be commenced with the words "Whatever states are wholesome."
It may be so. Why? Because of the non-occurrence of the previous *yamaka*... [etc. ...
This was stated because the second *yamaka* likewise does not occur; however, the third *yamaka* does occur in that very same way. "Some" refers to the authors of the *pada*;

for they have formulated the subsequent questions by means of a reversal of the preceding questions in the first and second *yamakas*, such that the preceding question [is contained within] the subsequent question.
Setting aside the reverse order, it is not so in the *Aññamaññayamaka*. For there, both questions are dissimilar to one another.

If, even in that case, both questions had to be similar, then the first question would have to begin with "Whatever states are wholesome," or the latter question would have to begin with "All those states [arise] through the wholesome root."

It could have been stated as "having a single root. However, instead of saying that, and rather than making the preceding and following questions identical—as is done in the first and second triplets—the difference between them in the third triplet arises because [the latter] does not begin with "whatever states are wholesome. Therefore, this point is intended:
there must be a positive (anuloma) question corresponding to the negative (paṭiloma) question; thus, [it says] "whatever... [and so on].
They say it is stated [in the text] as “without having asked whether they are wholesome.
“By way of the meaning” means by way of the meanings of those things that are possible and whose doubts have been resolved.
“Appropriate to that” means suitable in both sense and phrasing to that preceding question; for the latter depends upon the former.
It must be so. "Therefore" means for that reason. Because even when doubt has been resolved regarding the direct order (*anuloma*), doubt still arises regarding the reverse order (*paṭiloma*);
if it did not arise, there would be no purpose at all for the questions in the reverse order. Therefore, the preceding question does not correspond to the subsequent question;
rather, as stated, the subsequent question corresponds to the preceding question, and by virtue of that correspondence—
Because two terms are connected by way of meaning and so forth, they are called "meaning-yamakas" (atthādi-yamaka).

Furthermore, the direct and inverse order (*anuloma-paṭiloma*) should be understood here according to the sequence of the teaching, since after stating "the wholesome are wholesome roots," it is stated that "the wholesome roots are wholesome.

This same method applies to the remaining yamakas as well. [The term] "distinguished and distinguished possessor" is used because of the grasping of the distinction and the possessor of the distinction.
Or rather, the direct and reverse order should be understood here.

For in the first question, having taken those phenomena that possess distinction as the basis for certainty and showing them by saying, "Whatever wholesome states there are," the second question—"Are they all rooted in wholesomeness?"—is asked in order to show that which is the basis for doubt regarding the specific distinction among them. In the second question...

However, by way of the reverse of that, in order to demonstrate the specific distinction by which those [states] possess such distinctions—having reached a definitive conclusion on that point—the Teacher said, "Or whatever wholesome roots," and then asked, "Are all those states wholesome? in order to show those possessing the distinctions as the basis for doubt.
For the definitive conclusions and doubts of beings are based on indeterminate objects due to the multiplicity of their underlying inclinations (*ajjhāsaya*).
“By this phrasing as well” means by this sentence: “Whatever [beings] have a single root with the root of wholesomeness.
He explains that very intention with which it was stated that “it is not possible to say so,” beginning with the words “For it is not...”.

Therein, “by that very [reason]” is because the meaning of the phrasing for wholesomeness is distinct from the meaning of the phrasing for having a single root with the root of wholesomeness. “The answer” refers to the response.
Analysis (*vibhajana*). "Otherwise" means when the question is posed using wholesome roots (*kusalamūla*) as the single root-term.
"Those statements" refers to the statement regarding the wholesome and the statement regarding the wholesome roots as the single root.

Its indication of the indeterminate (*abyākata*) should be understood by way of matter (*rūpa*) originated from wholesome consciousness (*kusalacitta-samuṭṭhāna*). "In this case" means: "Because that very same meaning is possible through this term as well."
Regarding this statement: "Whatever wholesome [states]... [omission] ...arise," by this he shows the absence of deviation due to the single-rootedness of wholesome states with the wholesome roots.

For that very reason he says, "Indeed, there are none... [omission]. For by this phrase "because they arise," which refers to the meaning of the expressed words, the intended meaning is clarified through the statement of the non-existence of arising for that which is not expressed in words.

For just as the meaning of "having a single root" [applied] to the wholesome root deviates from the meaning of the term "wholesome," the meaning of the term "wholesome" does not deviate from that [meaning of having a single root].
How is the objection formulated, and how is the resolution given? The objection is formulated thus:

"Because they have a single root with the wholesome root, they are exclusively wholesome. The resolution, however, is: "It is because they have a single root with the wholesome root that they are wholesome."
It should be understood as "occurrence. Regarding the phrase "without asking," as in the second dyad, it means without asking, "Which ones are wholesome?
"By wholesome roots" means by wholesome roots (*kusalamūla*). "They" refers to those that have a single root by virtue of the wholesome root.
In the phrase "arise together," the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" or the sense of "manner. By this, [it is implied] "the wholesome roots have a single root..."
This indicates the remainder of the text beginning with “and also mutual roots. It was stated [previously] that “the answer should be given in the same manner as explained below.
In this context, “below” refers to the answers to the questions in direct order (*anulomapucchāvissajjane*).

“In the manner explained” refers to the method stated in the passage beginning with “those roots which arise together. “That too” refers to the passage beginning with “by a wholesome root (*kusalamūlena*).”
The word of the *Aṭṭhakathā* also [states this]. "In that way" (*tathā*) means: "In that manner;

the answer should be given just as in the case of a direct question (*anulomapucchā*)," such is the meaning. To show the reason why it was said, "It is not possible to state [it]," he said, "Or those who...
and so forth. In that context, the answer must be simply "Yes" (*āmantā*).
Just as in the question, "Are all those states wholesome?", even when asked, "Do all those states have the same root as the wholesome root?", only an answer by way of a counter-question is obtained;
there is no answer that demonstrates their identity in form, as in the case of a direct (anuloma) question, because there is nothing further to be analyzed and shown.
For those states which have the same root as the wholesome root are not [identical to] those states...

Those which have mutual roots by virtue of a wholesome root necessarily have mutual roots. Furthermore, those which have mutual roots by virtue of a wholesome root necessarily have a single root by virtue of that wholesome root.
Therefore he said: “For... [there would be] no distinction to be made.
In this context, “by which” means by way of the absence of a single root among those with mutual roots; “wherein” means in whichever arising of consciousness associated with knowledge.
The intention is that [the roots] have mutual roots and have a single root.

For when it is stated that each one among two [roots] has the other as its mutual root, it follows that they also have a single root for each, since the word "one" (eka) has the same meaning [in both cases]. Therefore he said: "But where...
[they] do not have a single root. This is incorrect; for in both cases, each one has the other as its single root.
"It is indeed possible. Therefore, he said: "For the purpose of preventing this apprehension," and so forth.

By elucidating the meaning of the statement, "Those states which have mutual roots through a wholesome root have a single root by way of that wholesome root," the word "Yes" (āmantā) here indicates that wherever two roots arise, the fact that each one has the other as its single root is already made manifest.
He said: "By the very answer 'Yes,' that [possibility] is excluded. Regarding the phrase "because they are determined," one might ask:
"Let it be granted that three roots arising from a single source are determined to have a mutual single root; but how is this so for two?
To this he replied, "Because they have mutual roots," and so forth. By the restrictive particle *eva* ("only") in the phrase "only a common root," the intended exclusion is indicated.
To show this, it is said: "not having a common root with one another. By this, he shows the following meaning:

the mention of a single root is intended merely to state that those things which have mutual roots possess a common root; it is not for the purpose of demonstrating a common root qualified by their specific conditionality as mutual roots.
"Of two roots" means of two things that have a single root and arise together. As to how they have a common root...
To demonstrate that, it was said: “Among those...,” and so forth. “By others rooted in them” means by other co-nascent states (sahajātadhamma) than the two roots [of the wholesome].
Now, in order to show the intention for which the question was asked in reverse form as simply “Are they wholesome?

and not as “Are they rooted in the same root as the wholesome root?,” he said: “But when there is mutual rootedness... should be understood as having been asked. For it is not by the wholesome root...
In the section on mutual roots (*aññamaññamūla*), it has already been stated that there is nothing that possesses only a single root.
The intention here is that he speaks only of what is connected with roots, not of what is disconnected from roots; otherwise, there would be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

"By that very [fact]" means because it is being spoken of precisely as being connected with roots. "In both cases" refers to both locations: "mutual roots" and "single root. [The phrase] "by a wholesome root" (*kusalamūlena*)...

It is said that the meaning is "associated with a wholesome root. If both statements express only association with roots, then why was the mention of "a single root" made only in the forward inquiry (*anulomapucchā*) and not in the reverse inquiry (*paṭilomapucchā*)?
It should be understood that it is to be taken in both places, or else it is not to be taken at all. For in this way, through these partial teachings on the root and the single-root *yāmaka*...
Having taken into account the objection that the teaching on the *aññamañña* (reciprocal) *yamaka* might be of the same flavor [as other types], he says "In that regard" (*tattha*), and so forth.

Therein, "in that regard" (*tattha*) means in that *aññamañña-yamaka*. Although these two phrases—“having a single root” (*ekamūla*) and “having reciprocal roots” (*aññamaññamūla*)—express only the state of being connected with a root according to the method already stated, nevertheless, there is indeed a distinction in their meaning as general and specific characteristics.

To demonstrate this, it was said: “In the commonality of root-yoga,” and so forth. The term “single-rootedness” (ekamūlattā) refers to the state of having a common root among those things that possess roots;

this expression of a single root speaks only of the general presence of a root in them without distinction, not of a specific quality found among roots as the word “root” might imply in relation to one another.
Furthermore, a determination regarding a generality does not dispel doubt concerning a particularity; thus he said: “In the commonality of root-yoga…” and so on.
By the phrase "it occurs," [the author] indicates that the determination regarding the particular (visesa) occurs precisely while dispelling doubt regarding the general (sāmañña).
Thus he says: "But as for the particularity of the root-yoga... it becomes determined. The word "therefore" (tasmā) refers back to that very same reason already stated;
for, because of the inseparable connection (avinābhāva) with the determination of the particular, the general is thereby determined, or else there is no doubt regarding it.
The meaning [is as follows]. Therefore he said: “Without having asked ‘of what single root’.
It does not indicate the state of being wholesome because it indicates other categories besides that; therefore he said: “because of the presence of doubt regarding the state of being wholesome.
The phrase “mutually rooted” intends merely the statement of mutual roots. Regarding the context of the wholesome...
By the phrase "because they follow along," he states the reason for including the term "wholesome" (*kusala*) in the statement, "All those phenomena are wholesome.
