For it has been shown that there is no purpose in grasping them as having a single root; furthermore, this teaching is presented by way of the wholesome. 53–61.

"The meaning is stated precisely when the method of the roots is explained" means that the meaning is stated precisely when the wholesome and other phenomena are explained by way of their roots. For the wholesome and other [phenomena]...
In this context, "meaning" (*attha*) refers to phenomena (*dhamma*) that constitute the subject matter of the textual tradition (*pāḷi*).

This is stated in order to clarify [the term] by way of its being a root of the wholesome (*kusalamūla*), by means of qualifying the root, and by indicating its connection with roots. The compound construction is: "roots that have become roots of the wholesome" (*kusalamūlabhūtā mūlā kusalamūlamūlā*).
For the word "root" (*mūla*) is common to both those things to be excluded and those to be included; thus, there are indeed unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena that are also roots.

The root-phenomena are distinguished by their state as wholesome roots (*kusalamūla*). By the inclusion of the term "root," the connection with the roots of those things that possess roots is illuminated.
To clarify this through the commonality of the root, the qualification of the root, and the illumination of the connection with the root, it is said: "having a single root as their root.
Furthermore, to clarify this through the mutual state of being a root, the qualification of the root, and the illumination of the connection with the root—

The construction is: “‘Rooted in each other’—thus the method of ‘root and sub-root’ (mūlamūla-naya) is stated. In all three dyads, this very distinction already mentioned should be understood as another synonym (pariyāyantara).
“To illustrate the connection with roots” means the intention is to illustrate precisely the connection with roots by making it primary and preeminent.
For instance, in the external-object compound *kusalamūlakāni*—meaning "those which have wholesome roots"—the connection with the word *mūla* (root) is stated as being predominant.

It is not so in the case of a possessive compound where the meaning of the final member is predominant, such as when it is stated simply as *kusalamūlā*—"roots reckoned as wholesome"—or with an attribute as *kusalamūlamūlā*.
Therefore he said: "to illustrate the meaning of another word... and so forth.
"Of the kind already stated" means: in the method of the root-and-rooted (*mūlamūla-naya*), by way of qualifying the root as "by virtue of being a wholesome root," and so forth;

and in the method of the rooted (*mūlaka-naya*), by way of the letter *ka* at the end of a compound whose referent is distinct, and so forth—it is precisely of the kind already stated. The sequence of statements should be combined by joining the methods of the root-and-rooted together.
(74–85) "By those not obtaining the state of having a single root" means: that which does not have a single root with an indeterminate root is not to be described in such a manner.
Because it cannot be obtained together with the eighteen types of rootless consciousness-arising, rootless matter-originated [matter], and Nibbāna—which are obtained individually.

For just as the aforementioned consciousness-arisings and so forth receive the designation "rootless" (ahetuka) due to being devoid of root-conditions (hetu-paccaya), materiality originated by those with roots does not. Therefore he said: "having excluded the designation 'rootless'. And here, "all..."
Because it has been stated that "matter is neither with cause nor without cause," although matter produced by a cause is indeed without [a further] cause, [it is said]:
"An indeterminate state is a condition for an indeterminate state by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*);
roots that are resultant-indeterminate or functional-indeterminate are a condition by way of the root-condition for their associated aggregates and for mind-produced matter."
However, because of the statement "condition" (*paccayo*), it is said that by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), there is no designation as "rootless" for matter produced with roots.
Some, however, say: "Having made it 'not included' (*abbōhārika*) means having made it not included by the designation 'with roots';
otherwise, one could not say, 'It is rootless, indeterminate, and has the same root as the indeterminate root.'"

Regarding this, what ought to be said has already been stated, because the status of being "with cause" (sahetuka) is established by way of the absence of the conventional designation "rootless" (ahetuka).

Furthermore, because of the presence of both root-cause (hetu) and condition (paccaya), the designation "with cause" certainly applies to it. Therefore he said: "Or rather, as in the 'With-Cause' dyad...
[it is] made non-designatable. Here, "here" means in this dyad based on a single root. "By way of the connection with or lack of connection to root-cause and condition."

The meaning is: by way of the presence or absence of the root-cause condition (*hetupaccaya*), and by way of the existence or non-existence of that root-cause condition. It receives the designation "with root-cause" (*sahetuka*) because of the existence of the root-cause that serves as its condition.
However, others say: "By this statement, 'matter originated by mind with root-cause is itself rootless and indeterminate'..."
Even though it is included [in the category of the indeterminate], because it possesses a root, one cannot say that "it does not have the same root as the indeterminate root.
And although it possesses a root, because it is not causally conditioned (*sahetuka*) in the primary sense, one cannot say that "it has the same root as the indeterminate root.
Therefore, the indeterminate that is without cause (*ahetuka*) does not have the same root as the indeterminate root, whereas the indeterminate that is with cause...

As for the statement, "It is said that because it is not restricted to either of the two positions—that 'the indeterminate is one-rooted with the indeterminate root'—it is treated as being outside the classification (abbohārika)," that is merely their own opinion;
for in the Commentary, the fact that it has a single root is definitively established by the statement: "Matter originated from the indeterminate-with-cause is one-rooted with the indeterminate root.
Therefore, it is according to the method already stated [that it should be understood].
And here the meaning should be understood as follows.

86–97. Since the apprehension and determination of immaterial phenomena (arūpadhammā) occurs through the specific distinction termed "measuring" and "being measured"—namely, by way of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—it is said:
“Because of the determination of the names (nāmānaṃ). By this, he expresses their preeminence (adhikabhāva).
"Because it is not delimited by the context even while being understood. If this is so, why was the term "nāma" (name) included in the alternative reading, "A name without cause, a name with cause"?
He says: "For the sake of making it very clear. The intention is: what more need be said when it has been stated in such a way as to make it fully manifest?
The commentary on the Section of Explanations (Niddesavāra) is finished.
The commentary on the Root Pairs (Mūlayamaka) is finished.
2. The Pairs on the Aggregates (Khandhayamaka).
1. The Section on Designations (Paṇṇattivāra). Commentary on the Section of Enumeration (Uddesavāravaṇṇanā):
2–3. Regarding the *Khandhayamaka*... [omission] ...the statement "and full understanding (pariññā) should be stated" is a demonstration of what ought to be stated by way of its primary importance.

For the Abhidhamma is indeed the discourse on what is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*); and since that [discourse] extends only as far as full understanding (*pariññā*), there can be no full understanding through comprehension (*pariññā*) without the full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*).

And such investigation occurs pre-eminently by way of the analysis of time, persons, and worlds, through the discernment of the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the aggregates both individually and collectively—this being intended for the sake of providing complete assistance to others.

Showing this meaning by the words "not otherwise," the Teacher, who is skilled in teaching, extracts the primary point that must be stated: "In the six divisions of time... [and so on]... full understanding (pariññā) must be explained.

Therein, just as there is no full understanding of abandoning (pahānapariññā) without the full understanding of scrutinization (tīraṇapariññā), so too there is no full understanding of scrutinization without the full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā).
And since that [latter] is rooted in knowledge consisting in what has been heard (sutamaya-ñāṇa), the Teacher—being skilled in teaching—[proceeds].

Desiring to reveal the various modes of full understanding regarding the aggregates (khandhas) by means of demonstrating the analysis of the whole, its parts, and their referents through both positive and negative concomitance, [the author] begins the teaching with the words "five aggregates" and so forth. Showing this, he says "those aggregates," etc.
"By five phrases" means by five collective phrases.

"Therein" (*tattha*) means among those terms for the whole (*samudāya*) and its parts (*avayava*). "Dhamma" refers to the knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhamma*) such as being subject to transformation (*ruppana*), and so forth.
"Of the term for the whole" refers to the term for the whole such as the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), and so forth.

Although from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*) there is no so-called "whole" existing apart from its parts, nevertheless, just as a part is not the whole, so too the whole is not the part; thus, even though [the distinction exists],...

Since there is a distinction between the whole and its parts, one might suspect that because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) of the two words, there is actually non-difference in their meaning—that is, the two words would have the same referent.
Therefore, he says: "In this point of doubt. In such cases as "The eye-base is included in the reckoning of the aggregate of form;
the consciousness-aggregate is the corresponding mind-consciousness-element," etc., a single part constitutes the referent of the whole.
However, in such passages as, "Whatever form... this is called the aggregate of form" (*rūpakkhandho*), it is said to be "entire"; thus he says, "the meaning is 'form and so forth...

Here, because the constituent parts—which function as the qualifier and the qualified—share a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇatā*), they are stated to have the meaning of a collective term (*samudāyapadatthatā*);
for that very reason, even collective terms possess the meaning of their constituent parts. Indeed, [there is no contradiction] between the qualifier and the qualified.
An absolute distinction or non-distinction is not intended; rather, there is both distinction and non-distinction.
Therefore, the first method is stated by way of showing non-distinction, and the second method by way of showing distinction.

For that meaning of a "heap" (rāsa), characterized by "being affected by change" (ruppana) and so forth, is analyzed through the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the constituent terms such as "form" (rūpa) and the word "aggregate" (khandha).
This very meaning—namely, the sense of "being affected" (ruppana) and so forth—is intended here as a collective mass (rāsibhāva).
Just as the meaning of a collective term exists even when it is expressed by its constituent parts, so too the meaning of a constituent part exists when it is expressed by collective terms. Thus:
"Is the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) both form and the aggregate of form? Is the aggregate of form form?"
Showing that the purification of the terms has been performed by means of [the words] beginning with “Āmantā,” he says: “By the words ‘rūpa’ and so forth, which are constituent parts...

the section on the purification of terms is stated. In this context, because a certain constituent term may function elsewhere [to denote something else], there might be uncertainty regarding the fact that the meaning of the constituent part is the meaning of the whole;
however, since that is not the case for the whole term, [it follows that] the meaning of the whole is indeed the meaning of the constituent parts.
It is said, "to show [the meaning]," because the absence of deviation (*vyabhicārābhāva*) has been demonstrated by the canonical text: "Is the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) 'form' (*rūpa*)?
Yes. Regarding the phrase "the aggregate of form" and so forth, it is stated, "of the primary word *khandha*," because the meaning of *khandha* must be qualified therein.

And because the meanings of the subordinate terms (*upapada*) such as "feeling" (*vedanā*) and so on are possible, [the term is used] in cases such as "the aggregate of feeling" (*vedanākkhandha*). [The phrase "stated by the word for a part of form"] refers to...
The state of being the "form aggregate" (rūpakkhandha) belongs to the meaning of "aggregate" (khandha) when it is expressed as a qualifying term by means of the member-word "form" (rūpa).

Therefore it was said: "Is the form aggregate 'form'? Yes. Therein—that is, in that word "form aggregate"—because it must be qualified by its predominant [constituent], does the state of being "deformed" (ruppana), which is expressed by the member-word of the aggregate, possess the nature of the feeling aggregate and so forth?

The construction is: “it occurs. The intention [of the objection] is: since the status of being denoted by a word for a constituent part is the same, why is that meaning which is understood through the non-predominant term not also understood through the predominant one?
“A phenomenon stated by a word for a constituent part of the aggregates” expresses the sense of a collection (*rāsa*).
Therein, “anyone” refers to the sense of being affected by change (*ruppana*). “By some collective term” means by the term *rūpakkhandha*, and not by terms such as *vedanākkhandha* and so forth.
Therefore he said, "not all by all. This same method applies to the aggregate of feeling and the others.

By way of clarifying the terms for the parts and the wholes—such as the aggregate of form and so forth—the "Wheel of Terms" (padacakkavāra) is based on the clarification of terms through the four aggregates that occur therein.

And by the phrase "showing it in this way," he refers to the specific meaning (atthavisesa) presented in the manner shown by the terms for the parts, such as form and so forth, and by the terms for the wholes, such as the aggregate of form and so forth.
One speaks of it as "that. The state of being a qualifier (*visesanabhāva*) exists because, by way of differentiation, it generally functions as a delimiting factor;

the state of being the qualified (*visesitabbabhāva*) exists because, through its connection with non-difference, it cannot be delimited from other differences; and the state of having a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇabhāva*) exists because those [states of] difference and non-difference both depend upon a single entity.
"By that" means by the relationship of qualifier and qualified as previously stated.
"In this" means in this case of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Or, "by that" refers to the state of coreferentiality; "in this" refers to the term *rūpakkhandha*.

Just as in the compound *nīluppalapada* (blue lotus), the blue—which serves as the qualifier of the lotus—is specifically distinguished and not just anything, so too here, the form (*rūpa*) which serves as the qualifier of the aggregate (*khandha*) is also specifically distinguished.

Showing that it "might be," he said: "Is it from the aggregates...? Likewise, by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) in the phrase "that which is matter is also an aggregate," it follows that whatever is matter is an aggregate, and whatever is an aggregate is matter;
thus he said: "All [of these]... must be qualified. And indeed, a qualification must be of a nature that has been definitively determined.
Because it functions as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), and not in an undetermined form, he asks, “But what is that?
and so forth; the intention is that it is not [the object] of the "lovely form" (*piyarūpa*) or the "pleasant form" (*sātarūpa*), since only that [specific form] has been grasped.

For that [form] was not grasped as a qualification of the aggregates (*khandha*); rather, the answer is given regarding that very thing—this is the construction. The statement “there is no form other than the aggregates” means that the meaning of “form” (*rūpa*) is “being affected” (*ruppana*).

This was stated having made [this point], for that [form] does not exist apart from the aggregates (*khandha*). "By that very reason" means precisely because of the non-existence of form as something separate from the aggregates, as previously described.

Since the word *rūpa* is found used in such passages as "showing a lovely form, a pleasant form," even when it does not refer to that specific meaning [of the aggregates], it is stated with the qualification "by that word *rūpa*.
This refers to the distinction between the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya*), which is being discussed.
“Dhamma-born. “By the pure” means by the absolute; the meaning is that it is even without the word *rūpa*.
This is stated with reference to its being delimited by the context (*pakaraṇa*) and so forth, or else to its grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

For the term *khandha* which is coreferential with the word *rūpa* expresses its meaning just like the aforementioned word *rūpa*. Therefore he said: “The aggregates are the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).”
Even though the aforementioned form is indeed an aggregate (*khandha*), an aggregate is not necessarily form alone; therefore, he says: “Nor are all... [etc. ...to be distinguished.
“By that very fact” means precisely by the existence of an aggregate whose intrinsic nature is non-material (*arūpa*). “Those” refers to the aggregates.
“They are to be analyzed” means that having extracted the phrase “the aggregate of form is an aggregate,” one should state: “The aggregate of form is both an aggregate and... [etc.]”
They should be shown by way of analysis as follows: "The aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and the remaining aggregates are not the aggregate of form," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "there is doubt concerning the qualification of the aggregates by 'form'...":

here, is there feeling other than the aggregates from which [the term] feeling is excluded to serve as a qualification of the aggregates? And are all the aggregates [included] within that which serves as the qualification of the aggregates?
The construction should be understood as: "they are to be distinguished by feeling. "Some" refers to those of various kinds, such as experiencing and so forth.
"By some qualification" means by a qualification such as feeling and so forth.
And here, the designation of form and so on, and the designation of the aggregates, occur in such ways as: "form is an aggregate," or "the aggregates are the aggregate of form," and so forth.
Because it occurs with respect to meanings such as "being affected" (ruppana) both individually and collectively— sometimes occurring with respect to that which constitutes a part,
and sometimes with respect to that which constitutes a whole— when its mode of occurrence has been thus determined,

the aggregates of form and so forth are said to be "clarified" both in terms of their verbal expression and their meaning, since doubts regarding them have been dispelled; therefore, "the aggregate of form is indeed form..."

By the first section, proceeding in the manner beginning with, “The aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and [the term] ‘aggregate of form’—is it form?”—it is shown that just as the meaning of the parts is expressed by means of the words for the parts such as “form,” so too is the meaning of the whole expressed by means of the words for the whole.

However, by the second section, proceeding in the manner beginning with, “Form is the aggregate of form; the aggregates are the aggregate of feeling,” etc., [the distinction between the two is shown].

Just as with words denoting specific [parts], even by means of a general term for the components such as "form" (*rūpa*), it is shown that only that particular component of the aggregate (*khandha*) which is distinguished by its respective [quality] expresses the meaning of the whole, and not every [component] does so.

Since there is no such thing as a "form" intended in this sense apart from the aggregates, although the aggregate itself is indeed form, it is not every [aggregate] that is form; rather, [only that specific one is].
A single portion of that [aggregate] is thus, and so too are feeling and the others;
this meaning is shown by the third section proceeding in the manner of “matter is an aggregate, aggregates are matter,” and so forth.

However, by the fourth section proceeding in the manner of “matter is an aggregate, aggregates are the feeling-aggregate,” and so forth, once it is determined that “matter is an aggregate,” this [matter] is indeed called an aggregate.

It is not only form (rūpa) that is so, but feeling (vedanā) and the rest as well; thus, in the exposition of the status of feeling and the other aggregates as "aggregates," this meaning is shown: that not all aggregates possess the specific qualities of feeling and so forth, but only certain ones are designated as such by those respective specific characteristics.
By demonstrating this, this scripture, through the means of purifying the aforementioned designation of the aggregates, [clarifies their true nature].
It leads to the determination of identity; and showing that this is for the purpose of determining their arising and so forth, he said:
"Thus, for those who... it should be understood.
The usage of a term for a whole is seen even when referring to a part, as in "the cloth is burnt" or "the ocean is seen"; thus he said: "because of being a constituent part of the wheel..."
"‘Wheels’ refers to what have been stated as pairs. "Having bound together" means having bound them by way of being pairs, or else by way of being the root of the pairs.

The state of being a root is the state of connection; and that state of connection—the similarity of the root words and so forth to the hub and other parts of a wheel—should be understood [in this way].
Because there is nothing new to be said, the teaching here is not connected solely by way of being a circle (maṇḍala).
He said: "Because it is not connected by way of a circular arrangement.

Although there is nothing new in the section based on the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*), in the sections based on the aggregates of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and so forth, since the teaching proceeds by way of perception (*saññā*) and the rest, it might appear as if it were presented in a new sequence through a circular arrangement;
however, the text does not proceed in that manner. Therefore he said: "By the connection with the aggregate of feeling... [etc.]... and so on.
The lower clarification is indeed the non-connection of the latter with the former. By taking "merely the attainment of the pure aggregates" means:

in the phrase "the aggregates are form," one takes by way of enumeration only the mere state of being an aggregate—obtained through the word "aggregate"—which is unmixed with form and the other [aggregates].
Even though in the enumeration there is a qualification of the aggregates as "form," etc., [it is still taken in its general sense].
In the phrase "the aggregates are form" (*khandhā rūpaṃ*), only pure form and so forth are grasped;
nevertheless, because there is no universal (*sāmañña*) devoid of particulars, one does not remain there in the state of mere pure form and so forth.

The expression "reckoned as the state of being a particular of the aggregates" is used to show the purpose of the particular—namely, the characteristic of being afflicted (*ruppana*) and so forth—as it has been explained according to the way the aggregates were attained as particulars. It is exclusively...
Not taking that [term], one should connect it with the word *khandha*... [etc. ...the construction is: "It is called the 'Pure Khandha Section' because of its analysis.
The commentary on the Section of Enumeration is finished.
1. The Section of Designation (*Paṇṇattivāra*).
Commentary on the Section of Exposition (Niddesavāravaṇṇanā) 26.
"Thus it was said": this means it was stated by way of classifying the phenomena that arise at the doors, together with the objects of those doors.

It has the nature of the pleasant and is born of the pleasant; as in such passages as, "In what way, friend, is it through form? and so forth, it is used in the sense of having the nature of the pleasant.
"Form is not form in the sense of being subject to deformation," it is said: "That which is a lovely form... [etc. ...form, but not the aggregate of form.

Even though that which is included in the aggregate of form—such as the eye and so forth—is indeed a "lovely form" by way of its mere state of being dear according to one's desire for expression, it does not enter into the category of the "aggregate of form" in the sense of being subject to deformation;
thus he said: "It is called 'that which is a lovely state... [etc. ...but not the aggregate of form.'"
Regarding the statement, “But where there is a distinction (*visesa*),” the intention is that the word *visesa* does not carry over; thus he says, “it is a remainder of the statement (*vacana-sesa*).

For there is no need to supply by ellipsis (*ajjhāharaṇa*) what is already obtained through the governing context (*adhikāra*). Alternatively, this should be understood as a partial citation of the phrase “perception of views” (*diṭṭhi-saññā*).
Its distinctiveness, however, is evident from the very promise: “We shall describe the distinction. “The remainder... [etc.]
The same principle applies here to the phrase "volitional formations" (*saṅkhārā*). Because one knows and adheres by way of fetters (*saṃyojana*), perception (*saññā*) is called "view" (*diṭṭhi*);
thus he says, "perception is indeed view. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and view," he includes the remaining "proliferation" (*papañca*).
For it was said in the *Papañcasūdani* regarding the expression "the conceptualization of proliferated perception": "Or rather, proliferation itself is stated under the name of perception."
28. Regarding the positive formulation, "The aggregates are the feeling-aggregate," an answer is obtained by showing their identity;
however, it is not the same for the negative formulation, "They are neither aggregates nor the feeling-aggregate.

Here, however, the answer is given by way of a counter-question. Explaining that meaning: "In the absence of the occurrence of the word 'aggregate,' [is there the occurrence of the word 'feeling-aggregate']?"
And he said, "and non-existence. By this, he shows that this negative particle (*na*-kāra) serves to negate existence.

And here, the inclusion of the word "sound" (*sadda*) is made either because designation (*paññatti*) is based on sound, or with reference to its similarity to sound; for this is a clarification of designation.
Therefore, he said, "it performs merely the clarification of designation. By this, [there is] another dhamma to be excluded...
It shows non-existence. For this reason it was said: "The mere presence of other phenomena is not the criterion here.
And by the words "Having done so," etc., he supports the aforementioned meaning with an alternative reading. Granted that in some cases, although the aggregates exist, the feeling aggregate does not;
yet because feeling lacks the intrinsic nature of an aggregate, it is said: "Is it not the case that the aggregates are not the feeling aggregate? Yes, they are."
It should be understood as having been stated thus. Therefore, it says in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “designated as Nibbāna,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “other than form,” here, just like the phenomena consisting of the primary elements and derived matter, even the pleasant intrinsic nature is included by virtue of the commonality of being denotable by the term “form”;
thus he says, “the supramundane feelings and so forth are to be understood. The phrase “merely the non-occurrence” refers to the non-occurrence of the application of the word “aggregate” (*khandha*).
He speaks with reference merely to the purification of the designation, [thinking] that there is an absence because of the absence of the occurrence of the terms "form" and "sound";
and thus he says, "And having done so," etc. By this he shows:
since every other real phenomenon (sabhāvadhamma) besides the eye is included by the inclusion of the sense-base (āyatana), there is nothing whatsoever apart from those two; it is merely...
For the purpose of clarifying the designation, in order to show that very non-existence, it was said: "Setting aside both the eye and the base, the remainder is neither the eye nor the base.
Likewise here too, for that same purpose, in order to show the non-existence of anything distinct from both, it is said:
"Setting aside both form and the aggregates, the remainder is neither form nor the aggregates."

Thus it is said. This is the fiftieth [section]. For regarding the statement, “Having set aside the eye and the base,” one can indeed say that there is nothing to be grasped by the inclusion of the remainder, because there exists no dhamma with an intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma) apart from the bases (āyatana).
Therefore he says, “If it were so. However, regarding the statement, “Having set aside matter and the aggregates,” it is not possible to say the same.
Because of the existence of a phenomenon possessing its own intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) apart from the aggregates.
If, however, it were stated that such a category of phenomena included within the aggregates does not exist, then this [statement] would be appropriate.

For in that case, as in the passage beginning "But in the Commentary," only the apprehension of a conceptual designation (paññatti) is cited. Furthermore, there would be no basis for craving (taṇhāvatthu) by virtue of the inclusion of the remainder.
"Being taken" (*gayhamāna*) is connected [to the subject] by bringing it forward. The construction is "it may be a *khandha*.
The commentary on the section of the exposition (*niddesavāra*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (*pavattivāra*).

50–205. Regarding the pairs (*yamaka*) that involve distinctions of unmixed time, [the author] says, "Because there might be a difference in meaning due to the different times of the words," and then adds, "because there is no difference in meaning in the sections concerning unmixed distinctions of time. Now, he explains that very point with the passage beginning, "Of the former...
and so forth. "By that" means by the absence of a difference in meaning. "In this" refers either to this reading of the section on occurrence (*pavatti-vāra*), or to this [text].
In the commentary on the section on active occurrence (*pavattivāra*), the intention is that only six [factors] are mentioned, not nine. Therefore, he says, "by the past," and so forth.
However, he says "these three" with reference to those shown separately by himself immediately following.

"As they have been shown" means that in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), the past and so forth—along with the present—are to be demonstrated by way of analysis, whereas in the Canon (*pāḷi*) they appear directly as they are. "Not..."
The phrase "found separately" clarifies the meaning already stated by making it more evident through the words "in this and that place," and so forth.

Therein, "by means of reverse questions" refers to those questions proceeding in reverse order from what was stated in the first clause, such as: "Or, for whom the aggregate of feeling had arisen, does the aggregate of form arise for him? "By that very same [reason]"...
It is precisely because they cannot be arranged according to this method. Regarding the phrase "and in the cases of mixed temporal divisions":
the meaning is that it is not only in the cases of unmixed temporal divisions, but also in the cases of mixed temporal divisions.
He said, "The unmixed... were stated," showing that the previous non-arrangement was not merely due to the difficulty of arrangement, but also for the sake of easy comprehension.
"By which reason" means by that reason known as the attainment of the arising and the cessation of the aggregates comprised within two single words.

The names "prior question" and "subsequent question" are stated according to their respective order. By the word "and" (ca), one should connect the passage after determining that the name "prior-and-subsequent question" is also stated.
In that context, however, the phrase "comprised within two single words" [is used].
This should be understood by taking it as a whole. He explains that very point with the words beginning, "For one whose... and so forth. Therein, "yassa" means "of which question.
And here, "question" (pañho) should be understood as speech proceeding by way of inquiry. For this very reason he says:
"because of the inclusion of the meaning to be answered after having fulfilled [the inquiry]. That is the answer, shown by its own form.
"Taṃvissajjanaṃ" means that [verse] is the answer; or, "taṃvissajjano" refers to one for whom that aforementioned answer exists, and thus it is "of that one who possesses the answer.

"By the first section" means by the first term of the enumeration (*uddesa*). Therefore, here "samānatthatā" (identity of meaning) refers to the similarity of meaning with the term of the answer, not merely with the first word.
"By a single word" means by a single *yamaka* (chiming) word, whether primary or secondary, and not by the first word alone.
The meaning is as follows. "By the mere commonality of the obtainability of arising or cessation" means by the mere fact of being equal in terms of the availability of either arising or cessation.

The phrase "a word of definitive conclusion... is appropriate" is stated because, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), the preceding question was presented as "Where the aggregate of form does not arise," and so forth. Even though there, [in that context], it was answered with "it arises."

It has been stated that "the arising of the aggregate of feeling is found"; however, the intention is that the prior question is appropriate by way of that non-arising of the aggregate of form—which is included within the category of definitive terms and stands as permitted by the Canon.
For in this way, there is a similarity of meaning with the preceding section.

Regarding the statement, “For one in whom the aggregate of form had not arisen, has the aggregate of feeling not arisen?”—here, by way of negating the prior non-arising of the aggregate of form, the other is negated;
thus, the negation as previously stated is expressed primarily with respect to the aggregate of form itself.
This same method applies to other such instances as well; therefore, he says: “It is for the purpose of providing a definitive conclusion.”

“Rejection is the act of rejecting. However, in the passage, “When the aggregate of form arises for someone, does the aggregate of feeling cease for that person?”—having established the characteristic of arising for the aggregate of form—the cessation of the aggregate of feeling is what is being asked about;
thus, it is that very [cessation] which is denied with “No. This same method applies to other similar instances as well.
It is said: "Negation is the warding off of the object of doubt. By the phrase "devoid of the letter 'na'," he states that the negation has itself been negated.
If this is so, one might ask: what is the distinction between the negations found in the text and the answers? To this he says: "In that regard, their arising," and so forth.
"By way of inserting a portion of them" means by way of inserting a portion of those four questions and five answers.
By way of insertion. Therefore, it was said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"In the first instance, for one whose question is complete, by showing the form [of the answer] in the preceding section," and so forth.

To show that which receives insertion here among the questions and answers in twenty-seven instances, it was stated: "Only the complete question," and so forth. From the demonstration of the establishment of the text, etc.

Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of the Analysis of Questions (*pucchāvibhaṅga*), the bases of the answers (*vissajjanāṭhāna*), and the method of application (*yojanānaya*) for a single question is to be understood.
Having extracted the passage from the Canon beginning with "Of those in the Pure Abodes" (*suddhāvāsānaṃ*), this [section] is commenced for the purpose of demonstrating its meaning.
This is the answer to the following: "For whom, where the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) had not arisen, for that person there, had the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) not arisen?"

It is said: “For those Pure Abode (Suddhāvāsa) beings, there is [no rebirth] there. In this context, “there is no second rebirth on a single plane” means that for a single noble person (ariyapuggala) within one plane, there is no taking of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) for a second time.
There is no need to speak of a third occasion and so forth. To show how this meaning is made known, [it says]: “From rebirth-linking...”
For it is said: “From that time onwards... [and so on]... they have proceeded. By this, he shows that this teaching proceeds by way of the temporal present (*addhā-paccuppanna*).

In response to the objection—“If the continuity of kamma-born matter, delimited by its taking up and laying down, is taken as a single unit, and the arising and ceasing are spoken of with reference to that, then how are the non-kamma-born states, such as the wholesome and so forth, treated?”—the reply is: “They too are included here as being dependent upon that.”
Showing that it is indeed so, he said: “For in that... [etc. ...is shown. “By that very same” means by the continuity of the kamma-born [existence] itself.
“Therefore” means because the resultant continuity produced by a single kamma is grasped as a unity. “Of that” refers to the continuity of the kamma-born [existence].
Regarding the five Pure Abodes, according to the aforementioned scripture, there is no rebirth on a second level within each individual plane.

Since it is stated without qualification that “there is none among the Suddhāvāsas,” one might raise the objection: “If it is absent in the entire Suddhāvāsa realm, why is it not understood by that [statement]?
Having thus raised the objection, the author says “But why? and so forth, in order to resolve it himself.
In this context, when there is no ripening of the faculties belonging to a lower plane within the Suddhāvāsa realms, there is no arising of those belonging to a higher plane.

It can be refuted because of the statement regarding those who go upstream (*uddhaṃsota*). For one whose stream of craving and the stream of the round of existence (*vaṭṭasota*) have turned upward is called "one who goes upstream.

Therefore it was said: "Because of the existence of the textual tradition concerning those who go upstream. "Should be reconciled" means they should be interpreted in such a way that they do not contradict one another;
and it has been commented upon accordingly.

"By this determination" means by the certainty based on the arising of the material form that will manifest in the marked space. "Distinguished" refers to those possessing such a state of material form that is destined to arise.
"Even non-percipient beings" means not only those of the five-aggregate realm, but also non-percipient beings;
the intention is that only those very non-percipient beings are included in the first category. "Therefore, those excluded by this determination" means by that aforementioned determination.

The meaning is that those who are devoid [of form] should not be described in that way. Now, he demonstrates this with the words “from there,” and so forth. “From there” means from the non-percipient realm (*asaññābhava*).

Regarding the term “those in their final existence” (*pacchimabhavika*), the phrase beginning with “Is it the five-aggregate realm, etc.? was stated in order to show the nature of that final existence directly.
Just as the aggregate of form does not arise for those in the formless realm (*arūpa*) within the formless existence—even for those in their final existence—so too...
In this context, because the aggregate of feeling of those in their final existence is also included, he said, "because it is comprised within this determination.
Therefore he said, "Of them... [etc.]... he said. Therein, "of them" means of those in their final existence. "Therein" means in the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*).
And "the non-arising of the other" refers to the fact that the other aggregate of feeling does not arise there. This applies even to those who possess rebirth-linking (*sappaṭisandhika*).

It should be understood that the term "final nibbāna" (parinibbāna) applied to the breaking up of the aggregates (khandhabheda) of the Suddhāvāsa deities is stated because of their commonality in the pacification of defilements (kilesūpasama), owing to their abandonment of gross faults.
The phrase "of all of them" means of all the Suddhāvāsa deities residing in their respective planes. By the words "But as...
and so forth, he makes this very meaning more evident. The expression "infinite world-systems" (anantā lokadhātuyo) refers precisely to the absence of any spatial limit.

This was stated in order to show [this]. Because they are impossible in terms of spatial location (*okāsa*) due to having a common substratum (*samānādhāra*) and being simultaneous (*samānakāla*) in terms of the person (*puggala*), yet possible in terms of spatial location, it is said:
"there is a state of being mixed (*saṃkiṇṇatā*). The commentary on the section on the process of existence (*pavattivāra*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra-vaṇṇanā) 206–208. "Of that too" means of the section on persons and bases as well. "In the base, of the person alone" means:

in whatever base has been taken, it refers specifically to the person who is distinguished by that base; this is the meaning. Furthermore, just as [the analysis] is obtained in the section on persons...

The objection, "If the attribution of a person (puggalokāsavāra) is possible, then the attribution of a location (okāsavāra) should also be possible," is addressed by the statement, "And the attribution of a location as well.
"Therefore" means: because even when a location is being spoken of, it would be spoken of only as a qualification of the person and not independently; therefore.

"Otherwise" means: taking the continuity of kamma-born matter, which is delimited by its acquisition and relinquishment, as a single unity, just as in the section on the process of existence (pavattivāra).

Regarding the statement on full understanding by way of arising and cessation: by means of demonstrating the absence of a meaning included within the definitive phrase “one who fully understands the aggregate of form,” it is stated “because of the absence of the full understanding of the aggregate of form” in order to show the non-existence of the other [phases] as well.

And since the answer “Yes” has been given, the meaning is that here, during the course of existence, the three periods of time are obtained only by way of the moment of consciousness. [And] “the one possessing the highest path...”

The connection of the two phrases "arahantañca" with the two phrases "do not fully understand the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and have not fully understood the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha)" is respectively as follows.
Furthermore, the phrase "the remaining individuals, excluding [these]" should be applied to each [of the preceding categories]. By the statement "there is none... [omitted] ...
in the supreme path," it is shown that through the very knowledge of the path to Arahantship, the goal of full understanding (pariññāmattha) has been attained.
This shows that the task of full comprehension (*pariññākicca*) is preeminent, and because of its absence, the others are not;
for this reason, only that [task] is described as being like a thunderbolt, while the remaining ones are compared to lightning. "By that" means by the statement just mentioned.
"All other persons than him" means all persons other than the one who possesses the supreme path (*aggamaggasamaṅgī*). However, those who wish to avoid the aforementioned fault...
“They say [this] with reference to ordinary worldlings and so forth.
The commentary on the section on full understanding is finished.
The commentary on the Twin Exposition on the Aggregates is finished.
3. Āyatanayamaka 1.
Paṇṇattivāra Commentary on the Section of Enumeration (Uddesavāravaṇṇanā)

1–9. *Vuttanayena* means by the method stated as follows: "The meaning of the collective terms is either a portion expressed by the constituent terms or the whole [meaning], whereas the meaning expressed by the constituent terms is exclusively [the meaning of] those constituent terms themselves," and so forth.

By this, he shows that the meaning should be understood accordingly in all the sections on the rules (*paṇṇattivāra*), etc., through the demonstration of the method for explaining the meaning as it has been stated.
The commentary on the section of the summary (uddesavāra) is finished.
Commentary on the section of the exposition (niddesavāra), verses 10–17:
Blowing (vāyana) is the occurrence [of air] pervading its own domain; this is found, for example, in the sense-base of odors (gandhāyatana).

The same applies to virtue (*sīla*) and the other [perfections]. Thus, it is stated in the *Pāḷi* as “the fragrance of virtue” (*sīlagandha*), etc., taking the phrase to mean that virtue itself is the fragrance. Therefore, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

“The fragrance of virtue... these are the names. However, because in that context there is a pervading of its own object, or a state of being diffused, or a state of being manifest, it is therefore said:
“in the sense of spreading forth, or in the sense of being manifest. Of oneself...

The term *vatthu* means either indicating or weaving. Since the words *kāya* and *dhamma* appear even in collective designations (samūha-paññatti) such as “the hosts of devas have assembled” (*devakāyā samāgatā*) and “phenomena as conceptual designations” (*paṇṇattidhammā*), he specifies [the meaning] as “possessing its own intrinsic nature” (*sasabhāva*). By the word *kāya*... [omission] ...there is none;

this refers to the fact that in the phrase “neither phenomenon nor base” (*na dhammo nāyatanaṃ*), the word *dhamma* denotes all phenomena possessing their own intrinsic nature (*sabbasabhāvadhamma*), which is the specific quality to be excluded.

It should be understood that this was stated with a specific intention (*sandhāya*), and not as a statement intended to denote the specific category of phenomena (*dhamma*) known as the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*).
The commentary on the section of the Exposition (*Niddesavāra*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (*Pavattivāra*).
18–21. In this section on occurrence (*pavattivāra*). “By obtaining a mere question” means that it is a futile question (*moghapucchā*).
“Each one” refers to each individual [question], such as: “For whom the eye-base arises, for him does the sound-base arise?
and so forth. “Five” refers to the five [questions], such as: “For whom the sound-base arises, for him does the odor-base arise? and so forth. By obtaining a mere question...

Permitting the inclusion [of certain items], he said, "They should be excluded by way of distribution. With the words "For he will say," etc., he supports the aforementioned point with the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Since the term "similar distribution" is a general statement that must be applied to a specific qualification, he shows that qualification as follows:
Having stated, "It was said with reference specifically to the section on persons (puggalavāra)," he says, "But in the section on locations (okāsavāra)...
it is answered," showing that because the answer to that [previous case] was not all-encompassing due to its similarity [to other cases], it is therefore answered wherever there is a similar case.
In that context, "that" refers to the second [case]. "Even in the section on persons" means: even in the section on persons where the answer is similar.
"Dismissed," let alone "warded off from opportunity"—this is the intended meaning. "Produced by karma in which desire has been detached":

that by which desire has become detached through the power of meditation (*bhāvanā*) is "that in which desire is detached" (*virattakāma*); it refers to fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) karma, and [the phrase means] produced from that.

"Rebirth-linking itself is the seed" is *paṭisandhibīja*; [it refers to] that. By the phrase "because of having such a nature," [it is shown that these states] are, without exception, caused by karma rooted in craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*).
This indicates the nose and so forth. And by saying "the odors and so on do not exist," he speaks with reference to the total non-existence of those as well.
Regarding that, what ought to be said has already been stated above.
The word "truth" (sacca) should be understood according to what was previously mentioned; having accepted the point stated by the challenger, [he says] again:
In order to show the intention by which those pairs have identical answers, it was said, "But just as... and so forth.

Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: therein, among those based on the eye-base, the pairs concerning the tongue-base and the body-base have identical answers according to the method [shown] by the pair concerning the nose-base, namely, "for those who are reborn with eyes but without a nose," and so on.
Likewise, here, among those [questions] rooted in the nose-base dyad, the tongue-base and body-base dyads have similar answers according to the method beginning with:
"Does the tongue-base arise for one in whom the nose-base arises? Yes," and so forth.
Thus, this is stated because both of these [dyads] have mutually similar answers when taken separately, not when taken together.
Because of their mutual similarity in response. Therefore he said: "Therefore, in each respective case, the reason for the similarity in response is its not being included in the *pāḷi*.
And this being so, he asked, "What is the purpose of including the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) at the beginning? and replied, "By way of illustration," and so forth.
In that context, "by way of illustration" means by way of those things that serve as illustrations, namely, the mutual similarity in response.
The intention is that [the answer] is by way of being an illustration, but not because it is a response identical in every respect to those things to be illustrated.
To show the majority [of cases], the phrase "for the most part" was stated; then, in order to demonstrate that majority, the words beginning with "for among them" were spoken.
By the word "thus," there is the acknowledgment that the aforementioned statement itself constitutes the response through the reply "Yes, sir."
"Is to be done" draws out this meaning. "Sā" (that) refers to the second question. "By the *ghānāyatana-yamaka*" means by the *ghānāyatana* pair among those rooted in the *cakkhāyatana*.
"The rest of them" (*taṃsesāni*) means the remaining [questions] together with that *kāyāyatana-yamaka* rooted in the *ghānāyatana*.
Regarding the phrase "not included because their answers are similar," here only the word "not included" (*anāruḷhāni*) is connected with the word "likewise" (*tathā*).
It is drawn out [in the commentary] not to show that it is "because of a similar answer," but rather—having stated "so...
by way of conventional designation" (samaññena)—it is now stated "of the nose, tongue, and body bases, however...

and so forth, in order to show the absence therein of that "similarity of answer" which was spoken of as being "by way of similarity of cause" (kāraṇasāmaññena). In that context, "of those occurring among those who do not dwell in a womb" means:
Here too, the phrase "due to coexistence" (sahacāritāya) should be brought forward and connected; likewise, [the phrase] "occurring among those in the womb" (gabbhaseyyakesu).
The other two pairs based on the nose-base (ghānāyatana)—namely, the two pairs based on the tongue-base and the body-base—are not answered;
for when the pairs based on the nose-base have been answered, the other two sets based on the tongue-base and the body-base [are understood].

It should be understood that they are not answered because there is no distinction and no specific distinction. In this regard, in the *Kāyāyatana-yamaka*, the absence of distinction (*appavisesa*) is to be understood by way of the second question, while the lack of distinction (*avisesa*) is to be understood by way of the other [questions].

As for the phrase "together with the base of visible forms and the base of mental objects," this is stated with reference to the base of mental objects rooted in the base of visible forms; thus he says: "The intention is... [etc.]... regarding the base of visible forms.
For this very reason, he said: "In those rooted in the base of visible forms," and so forth.

"Of the pairs" means of the pairs consisting of the bases of odors, tastes, and tangibles that are rooted in the base of visible forms. "Of the second questions" means of the second questions of those very same pairs as previously stated.

"By the method already stated" refers to the method stated beginning with "those with form" and "those without consciousness. "Of the first questions" refers to the first questions of those very same pairs.
Regarding the phrase "by those below": although this is a general statement, he says "smell, taste... [etc.

...the meaning" with reference to those cases where a similar response is possible. A "response" (*vissajjana*) is the statement of specific distinctions that can be found among the phenomena listed, in accordance with the enumeration (*uddesa*);
however, it is also permissible not to mention that which cannot be found there in its entirety, possessing qualities that correspond to the enumeration.

Since, in terms of meaning, the answer itself constitutes the response, he said: "By the very fact that [the answer] is not obtained through non-response—that is, by showing its unavailability—it is considered answered.
Showing that one who is deficient in both eyes and ears can be found just as one who is deficient in either the eyes or the ears, he said: "Even one born blind... [etc.]...
should be understood," including [the deficiency] by means of the word *pi* (also/even) in the Aṭṭhakathā. Only those with complete sense bases are *opapātika* (spontaneously born).
Regarding the phrase "spoken with intentional meaning" (*sandhāya vuttaṃ*), the word *eva* here is used in the sense of "impossible" (*aṭṭhāna*).

To show its proper application, he says, "the meaning is 'it has indeed been spoken'. Then, showing that by this [statement] the inclusion of those with incomplete sense bases is established—since one with complete sense bases is not restricted to that [specific case] alone—he says, "By this, it is not precluded that the statement was made even with reference to those who are blind from birth or deaf."
22–254. Why is it said, "Because that person has not been touched [by the question]"?
For even by the statement, "He asks about the world of form-possessing Brahmas," it is precisely the *okāsa* (the spatial location) that is touched upon.

Having raised the objection, "If you say 'Yes' (*āmantā*), for what reason was it admitted?"—with the intention of explaining the underlying reason—the author, wishing to show that reason, says "Is it not so... and so forth, [referring to] the state of being an embryo-dweller (*gabbhaseyyaka*).
"He will attain final Nibbāna after going" is said with reference to one in their final existence (*pacchimabhavika*). "Of that state" means of the state of the final existence.
"Of what is to be" means of what is yet to come. "Because it must be admitted" means because it must be admitted that "it will arise.
Now, as for the question "Why?", this is the summary of the meaning here: if [it is argued] that "for whom the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) will arise..."
In response to the question, "Will the eye-base arise? one should answer in accordance with the method stated therein.

But then, for what reason is it answered "Yes" to the reverse question, "Or rather, for whom the visible-object-base will not arise, for him will the eye-base not arise," when this [latter] appears to be mutually contradictory?

By the words "nanu" (surely) and so forth, the challenger clarifies that very contradiction. The meaning is: "It will not arise" does not mean "it will not arise at all," but rather "it will arise [at some point].
"In that existence" (*tasmiṃ bhave*) and so forth is the response to that.

Therein, "in that existence" means in whichever existence it was stated that "the visible-object base will not arise," because it is currently occurring; that is, in that existence, by way of its future state.

The intention is that [the term] "inexpressible" (*avacanato*) refers to its being inexpressible by way of a future state of existence, and its being in process by way of a state of having already begun to arise.

For this very reason, he says, "In another existence," and so forth. The connection is with the words "but it is not said. By means of the alternative reading beginning with "And having done thus," he supports the point as it has been stated.

In whichever personal existence (*attabhāva*) there must be certain sense bases (*āyatana*), for a being or a continuum in whom those respective bases are bound to arise by virtue of the karma that produces them:
"Will the eye base arise for one in whom the visible-object base will arise?
"Yes. "Or, will the eye base not arise for one in whom the visible-object base will not arise? [Yes.]
“Will it not arise?”—to this, the response given to these two questions is well-established because the acquisition of the sense bases (*āyatana-paṭilābha*) constitutes birth.
Here, by the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in the phrase “those in their final existence and so forth,” those who attain final nibbāna after having arisen in the formless realm (*arūpa*) are included.
This too is a response. Because it is to be rejoiced in, [the answer is] “Yes.”
Because it is to be admitted.
As for the statement, "for those who are being reborn in the sense-sphere realm (kāmāvacara) without a nose," that is the connection [to be made].
That karma which produces the nose-base (ghānāyatana) is such that its result will be cut off even prior to the arising of the nose-base.
It has been stated. But how is it known that such a type of karma exists? To this he said, "For whom, where," and so forth.
Furthermore, in response to the objection, "How is it known that here the term 'one without a nose' (aghānaka) refers specifically to one who dwells in the womb?
he stated, "Indeed not," and so on; and in order to establish that point, he said, "In the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*," and so forth. Even the fact of its not being mentioned...

For indeed, in the Abhidhamma, which is the teaching according to the Dhamma, there is only negation (*paṭikkhepa*). "Here" means in this *Āyatanayamaka*. "In the cases as they have been shown" refers to the types of formulations shown such as:

"Or for whom the ear-base will not arise, for him the eye-base does not arise," and "For whom, in whatever [place], the nose-base does not cease, for him the visible-form-base will not cease in that [place]."
Regarding the questions: the construction is, "It is said that [the answer] is 'Yes'; then why is it not understood? The intended meaning is:
"In these questions, why is no answer given by way of a reply? This refers to the meaning grasped through a definitive determination (*sanniṭṭhāna*), such as:
"Or for whom the ear-base will not arise," or "For whom the nose-base will not cease at a certain place."
And because of the non-occurrence of a response that constitutes doubt regarding a portion [of the matter]—
due to the possibility of a doubtful meaning in one part of the meaning already grasped by such a term of certainty (*sanniṭṭhāna*)—
and because of the non-giving of a reply such as “Yes” (*āmantā*), which would serve as an antithesis to the meaning of certainty, [the opponent] does not break the meaning [of the proposition].
Because they must be spoken as a single unit and not separately. Therefore he said: "There is no answering with a reply regarding matters that must be broken [into parts].

"If there were" means: even if there were a matter to be stated after breaking it up, if there were an answering with a reply, it would not be a complete answer, because there would be no opportunity for it and because it would have to be broken up—this is the meaning.
For instance, [regarding] "those attaining final nibbāna in the five-aggregate realm..."
“For those who are final-existence beings in the formless realm, and for those who, having been reborn in the formless realm, will attain final nibbāna— when they are passing away,
neither the ear-base nor the eye-base arises for them”; and likewise,
“for those attaining final nibbāna in the fine-material realm and for those in the formless realm, there the nose-base does not cease, nor does the visible-form base.”
The phrase "it will not cease" is a supplementary reading occurring there by way of distinction.

Now, as for the question "Why?"—if the response to the inquiry concerns that which is not to be broken rather than that which is to be broken, then, such being the case, by means of this response to the inquiry:
"Or, for whomsoever the faculty of mental joy arises, does the eye-faculty arise for him? Yes," [the point is established].
"Why is it not understood that there is no rebirth-linking with mental joy (*somanassa*) for those born from a womb?
Should it not be accepted that there is no answer to a question that ought to be answered?"—to show that this is not so, because the meaning is understood from another passage of the Canon, he says:
"In the realm of sense-desire," and so forth.
“Is that consciousness which arises and does not yet cease destined to cease and not destined to arise?

“Yes. Just as the cessation of that very consciousness was stated to exist in its future state at the moment of its arising, so too the cessation of that very kamma-born continuity must be described as existing in its future state at the moment of its arising. Therefore, this—
It shows this: "If even for a single moment of consciousness, its cessation at the moment of arising is spoken of as being in the future state, how much more so for an entire mental continuum?
This applies everywhere throughout the entire section on the future. That cessation was described as being in the future state specifically with reference to those who are about to be reborn;
why, then, is cessation not described here with reference to those who have already been reborn?
He said: “But as for those that have arisen,” and so forth. “Of that very same” means of that very continuum born of karma (*kammaja-santāna*) as it has proceeded.
“Therefore” means because cessation is said to commence from the moment of arising onwards;

therefore, even though there is a difference [in the state of the dhamma], and even though there is a cause for not perceiving a difference in time, the two answers are indeed appropriate by way of not perceiving a future time and by way of cessation itself.
"It is indeed appropriate. Because it is impossible to speak of cessation in relation to others, the term "of the Arahant" is used.
If cessation is said to begin immediately after rebirth, then why is there a mention of cessation at the moment of death?
Addressing this objection, he says: "But because it is the finality of that [existence], there is a mention of cessation at death. Regarding the phrase "because it is the finality of that":
Because that continuum reaches its termination. The passage beginning with “pavatteti” (it proceeds) clarifies the meaning already stated. In this context, “tassa” (of that) refers to the continuum.

The passage beginning with “vakkhati” (he will speak) is a statement of the reason for taking only the cessation at death—without including the cessation during the course of existence—as the point of reference.
“Tena” means by that alternative reading as previously described. “Ettha” means in this [context].

Regarding the passage beginning with “for whom the eye-base will cease,” which occurs in the *Āyatanayamaka*: if it were intended that even for what has ceased during the course of existence (pavatta), its cessation occurs only through death, then how could one speak of “those possessing eyes” and so forth? To this he says:

“In the cases of ‘possessing eyes’ and so on, the meaning is understood as ‘those who have acquired the eye,’ etc. “Those” refers to those in their final existence in the formless realm (*arūpa*). The construction is: “and the expression ‘not possessing eyes’ is incomplete (sāvasesa).”
The commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra) is finished.
The commentary on the Twin Verses on the Bases (Āyatanayamaka) is finished.
4. The Twin Verses on the Elements (Dhātuyamaka).
1–19. Regarding the phrase "connected with the sound element":
this was stated with reference to those pairs of sound that are rooted in the eye element and so forth, as well as all those rooted in the sound element itself.

For these do not occur by way of death and rebirth-linking (cuti-paṭisandhi) like those connected with the eye-consciousness element and so forth; for this very reason, in the *Āyatana-yamaka* as well, in the section on the course of existence (pavatti-vāra), [only] those connected with the sound element [are mentioned].
And the non-availability of the *yamakas* (pairs) should also be understood.
The commentary on the *Dhātu-yamaka* is finished.
5. The *Saccayamaka* (Pairs on the Truths).
1. Explanation of the Section on Designation (Paṇṇattivāra-vaṇṇanā) 10–26.

"That" refers to the word *dukkha*. "In another sense" means in the contexts of the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*), and the suffering of pain (*dukkhadukkha*).
"Independent of anything else" means not dependent on other terms such as "formations" and so forth. "By that" means by virtue of employing the term *dukkha* independently of anything else.

When that suffering-as-suffering (dukkhadukkha) has become the object [of the term], this word "suffering" (dukkha) is the first instance of the word "suffering" in the phrase "Suffering is the truth of suffering.

And that is suffering-as-suffering. Regarding the phrase "Suffering is the truth of suffering," one should not accept this as an exclusive restriction (avadhāraṇa)—meaning "suffering is only the truth of suffering"—but rather it should be accepted as "suffering is indeed the truth of suffering," as he said.
“Exclusively the truth of suffering alone. Among the origins (samudaya) mentioned in the *Saccavibhaṅga*, there is none among the states that are fruits;

thus, among the origins explained in five ways in the *Saccavibhaṅga*, not even one exists among those having the nature of a fruit—the meaning being that there is no state having the nature of a fruit.

Furthermore, the reading “there is no state that is a fruit” (*phaladhammo natthi*) is also found. And the word “path” (*magga*) refers to the factors of the fruit—that is, the factors of the common fruit (*sāmaññaphala*).

The intention is that the word *magga* (path), as it occurs in such passages as “the path-factor, included in the path” (*maggaṅgaṃ maggapariyāpannaṃ*) regarding right view and so forth, applies to the fruit of the path by way of metaphorical designation based on its cause.
Therefore he said, “not because of the presence of the function of the path,” and so on. “Therefore” means:

because in the teaching of the truths, only those phenomena whose intrinsic nature consists of originating and so forth are spoken of by way of the terms “origin” (*samudaya*) and so on, and not those whose intrinsic nature consists of non-originating and so forth.

Therefore. And here, since the phenomena belonging to the three planes are included within the truths of suffering and its origin as appropriate, he extracted only the phenomena that are fruits, setting aside those phenomena that possess intrinsic nature but do not possess the intrinsic nature of a truth. But are not the phenomena associated with the Path also of a nature that is not a truth?
Should they not also have been extracted? No; because they belong to the category of the Path. [This is indicated by the phrase] "among the phenomena that are fruits."
Here, by the inclusion of the term "dhammas," it should be understood that those [states] are included just like the states associated with the fruit (*phala*).
By the phrase "by the purification of the words... they are included here," he indicates that states which do not possess the true nature of reality are excluded from this treatise.

"Of them" refers to suffering and so forth. "The distinction resulting from their connection with specific qualifications" means being distinguished by that connection with the specific qualifications of suffering and so on.

Since the fact that suffering and the other truths are to be fully understood and so forth is established precisely by their being qualifiers of the truth, he said, "Because they are exclusively truths.
And as it is here—meaning, just as in this Truth-Yamaka, in the section on pure truths, suffering and the others are taken only as qualifiers of the truth—so too in the Khandha-Yamaka and elsewhere;
thus, the meaning is that this method is not shown only in the section on pure truths.

In the section on the purification of terms (*padasodhanavāra*) and in the section on the wheel of their roots (*tamūlacakkavāra*), because only collective terms such as "matter is the aggregate of matter" (*rūpaṃ rūpakkhandho*) and so forth are stated, there is nothing further to be said; therefore, it is said, "in the sections on the pure aggregates and so forth.

Likewise, even here, this method is shown only in the pure section. If, in the sections on the pure aggregates and so forth, [the terms] that serve as the qualifiers for the aggregates and so forth...

One might raise the objection: "Since there must be a grasping of form and so forth, why is the meaning shown by way of other forms and so forth as well, rather than through the specific distinction of the aggregates (khandhas) and so on?
Addressing this, he says: "But in the Commentary... and so forth. Only the former meaning is appropriate;
for the reading is stronger because it is more logical.
The commentary on the Section on Designation (*Paṇṇattivāra*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Section on Process (*Pavattivāra*). 27–164.
From "the full understanding of suffering" up to "for the purpose of surmounting suffering": although it occurs with reference to specific instances, it brings about that very purpose.
He said, "Because of being noble... having said so," showing that there might be some suspicion that [the state] could arise.

However, some here state the reason as "because of being established in the final existence" (*antimabhava*); that is not tenable, because birth involves the investigation of suffering (*dukkha-vicāra*), and furthermore, not all inhabitants of the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) are in their final existence, since they are described as "those who flow upwards" (*uddhaṃsota*).
"[For whom the truth of suffering arises]"—[this refers to those in the lower realms].

The state of arising. Showing that, without distinction, the phenomena included within the truth of suffering and the person possessing them are spoken of solely by way of their relationship [to that state], he says, "All those being reborn," and so forth.

Since this meaning has been grasped in a definitive form, and because there must be a demonstration of the divisions of a meaning once it has been definitively grasped, he says: "Among those very... and so on.
He said, “Only those who have been reborn. In that context, the connection is: “some among those very ones are being shown.

“Possessors of rebirth in a single category” means possessors of rebirth in the category of suffering. “Among them” refers to those selected by way of determination. “Possessors of the arising of the path and fruit” means possessors of the arising of the path and fruit;
or this is the reading itself.
With the words "And here," etc., he shows the summarized meaning of the passage beginning with "of all.
Therein, the phrase "of the arising of the truth of suffering mixed with the arising of the truth of origin" uses the genitive case in a sense of disregard (anādara).

This is because, in some instances, even within the truth of suffering that is mixed with the arising of the truth of origin, there is the observation of the arising of the truth of suffering devoid of that [origin], namely, devoid of the arising of the truth of origin.
The construction is: "it is said. However, some read, "of that which is mixed with the truth of origination" (*samudayasacca-avomissa*);
for them, the phrase "devoid of that" (*taṃrahita*) should be understood as an explanation of the meaning of the preceding term.

The construction is: "of that which is accompanied by it" (*taṃsahita*) is said by way of showing the arising of the truth of suffering accompanied by the arising of the truth of origination. "Of those" refers to non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*) during their course of existence (*pavatti*).
The meaning is that the arising of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is not included in either of the two portions mentioned by the phrases "in the course of existence" (*pavatte*) and so forth.
However, it is indeed shown that its arising in rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is included by the first portion.
Likewise, "and its cessation" means that just as the arising of the truth of suffering in the rebirth-linking of non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*) is [included] by the first portion...

The meaning is that while it is included [in the category of suffering], in its actual occurrence (*pavatti*) it is not included in two portions; likewise, the cessation of those [two] is also not included.

For indeed, the text in the section on cessation (*nirodhavāra*) proceeds with the words: "In all those passing away, and in the moment of dissolution of a consciousness dissociated from craving during the course of existence (*pavatta*)," and so forth. "This is the same method" refers to what was stated beginning with "And here... and so on.
The method of exposition for the *Samudaya-saccayamaka* (the Pairs on the Truth of Origination) has been stated in the text;

the same method applies to the *Magga-saccayamaka* (the Pairs on the Truth of the Path) as well, and thus the meaning should be understood there in exactly the same way. For indeed, the text proceeds there with the passage beginning, “of all those being reborn,” and so forth.
And when this is so—meaning, when there is the grasping of an occasion by way of moments—the sense is that it does not admit the aforementioned meaning.
He affirms. Regarding the answer to this: in the answer to this pair of crisscrossed terms (*yamakapada*). “At the moment of the arising of the supreme path;
at the moment of the arising of the consciousness of those who are Arahants; at the moment of the arising of that consciousness immediately after which they will attain the supreme path;
and for those beings reborn in the sphere of non-percipient beings—at these points, the truth of suffering exists for them.”
Because the first section states, "it arises, but origination-truth (*samudayasacca*) will not arise there for them," there is no contradiction;
thus, the words "in the latter section" and so forth were spoken. In that context, "therefore" (*tasmā*) means:

because the moment of the arising of the rebirth-consciousness is not the locus of the future origination that is presently arising, but rather the sphere such as the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), therefore [it is said]. This concludes the section on persons and spheres.

Because this is a section concerning the bases (*okāsa*) of persons, therefore, in the phrase "of them there" (*tesaṃ tatthā*), the meaning of the word "there" (*tattha*) should be understood by way of the basis. If, in the section concerning the bases of persons,
the meaning is to be taken solely by way of the bases such as the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth,
and not by way of the moment (*khaṇa*), then why— without referring to the basis in the passage beginning with "of all those being reborn"— is it said "there"?
He says, "In that regard... pe... it is just so," with reference to the process of interrogation. Therein, "in that regard" (*tattha*) refers to the section on locations (*okāsa*).

"For the purpose of showing a distinction of persons" means for the purpose of showing the distinction designated as "persons. "Where those [persons]" means in whichever location, such as the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), those persons reside.

"Some" refers to the Elder Dhammasiri. For he states the reason that, in the passage "at the moment of the dissolution of consciousness during its occurrence, the truth of suffering does not arise," it is specifically the materiality born of consciousness (cittaja-rūpa) that is intended, because it exists bound to consciousness.
Others say that since the word "unformed" (arūpa) here also relates back to the preceding [phrase], it qualifies "occurrence" by way of the unformed existence (arūpabhava).

"This meaning has been stated; therefore, in such passages as 'Does the truth of suffering arise for one in whom the truth of origination ceases?'—the answer being 'No'—the meaning should be understood in this same way," they say.

The statement that "the person is apprehended without regard to the mind" is said because the mind is not intended [as the primary subject] there. However, where there is an intention to show the arising of the truth of origination...
In that very context, it must also be understood that there is a desire for its non-arising;
