and since a person is not apprehended apart from the mind, it can be known that in the phrase "for whom the truth of origination does not arise," the mind—which is the support for the truth of origination—is indeed included by way of its actual meaning.
Furthermore, even among those things bound to the faculties, not every arising of material form is invariably dependent upon the arising of consciousness.

It might be argued that this can be said because the arising of matter is seen there even without the arising of consciousness; therefore, one must reach the conclusion here that only matter born of consciousness arises at the moment of consciousness's arising, while the other [matter] arises during all three moments.
One might object: "In the first section, there is nothing that has not been analyzed, so this point should have been clarified."
But in the second instance, this is merely an analysis; this contingency does not apply here, nor does it apply in the first instance either. Why?
Because this is the nature of the *yamaka* (the paired method), namely, that its application is according to whatever happens to be available.
Regarding the phrase "when the second consciousness is occurring," they say: "The first is the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), the second is the consciousness. This refers to the craving for existence.
Others maintain that even the adverting consciousness (āvajjana) can be called "the second" because it is dissimilar to the occurrence of resultant consciousness;
therefore, it should be said that from that point onward, the truth of origination (samudayasacca) had not previously arisen for him there.
However, what is intended here as "the second consciousness" is the first consciousness co-nascent with craving for existence (bhavanikanti); that which occurred prior to this is [the first].
Because all [these states] are of the same genus by virtue of being indeterminate (*abyākata*), they are treated as "one";
from that point on, the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*) will never arise again for him there. Therefore, he said: "At the very minimum," and so forth.

"In that" refers to the second consciousness. "By having the same destination as that" means by having the same destination as that aforementioned second consciousness, and for one who possesses it...

Or, the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) had arisen, but it cannot be said that the truth of the origin (samudayasacca) [had arisen], because they share the same destiny (*samānagatika*) in terms of their status as such.
And "having done so" means precisely because that shared destiny has been shown by that [statement].

"As previously stated" means that all consciousnesses prior to the second unwholesome consciousness are not included, because of the absence of the other state. This very meaning is stated by way of another reading:
The words beginning with "yathā" (just as) were spoken in order to establish [this point]. "Tet" refers to those belonging to the four-aggregate realm (*catuvokāra*).
"Vajjetabbā" (to be excluded) means they are to be set aside by the qualifying term "of the others.

Just as the aforementioned Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*)—which are five-aggregate beings (*pañcavokāra*)—exist as previously described in the manner of possessing the second moment of consciousness, so too do the four-aggregate beings exist.
The construction is: "Those mentioned previously do not exist.

Regarding the phrase "for whom and where," since the person (puggala) and the location (okāsa) are expected to stand in the relationship of the contained and the container, he said: "The person and the location are taken as mutually delimited.
In the passage "those born in the sense-sphere realm...," here, for one who has fully realized [the truth] in the sense-sphere realm, the form-sphere realm...
"Those reborn" refers to those who have realized the truths in the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) and are reborn in the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*).
By the word "or" (*vā*), it should also be connected to the case of those who have realized the truths in the sense realm (*kāmāvacara*) and are reborn in the formless realm.

"Therein" (*tattha*) means in the place of rebirth. "Realization" (*abhisamaya*) refers to the realization of the higher paths; until one becomes reborn [in a higher plane], those persons reborn there [in the lower plane] remain here.
When this [category] beginning with "those who have fully realized" is stated, [the persons and locations] are not included in the second section because persons and locations are mutually delimited.
If that is so, one might ask: "Are they not included in this *Yamaka*? To this he says: "But those... and so forth.
Therein, regarding what was said—"they are of the same destination and thus are not shown separately"—in order to make that more evident, he says: "those who have not fully realized," and so forth.

It has been stated. Its meaning is as follows: by the first phrase, "those who have not yet fully realized," all those who have not yet realized [the truths] within the *sampatti-bhava* (births of attainment) where the arising of the Path is possible—including those in the Suddhāvāsa realms—are included.

Among these two types of Suddhāvāsas, it should be understood that they are "those who have not yet realized" at the specific time when they are so designated therein; for them, that is the time at which they must be understood in that manner.
It was stated, "when the second consciousness of the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa) is occurring," for the purpose of specification.

By this means—that is, by this statement—the term "purification-consciousness" (vodānacitta) refers to the consciousness that serves as the immediate antecedent condition (anantarapaccaya) for path-consciousnesses;

however, in this context, it refers to the consciousness of the supreme path (aggamagga-citta). "From that" means from the aforementioned purification-consciousness, [referring to] one who possesses the preceding consciousness.

[This applies] to one possessing a consciousness associated with conformity-knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), as well as to those possessing the remaining insight-consciousness leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāmini-vipassanā-citta*).
Therefore he said: "As long as one possesses a consciousness associated with even the most subtle craving, [the suffering-truth and so forth] are shown for that long.

The moments of dissolution and arising of rebirth-linking and death-consciousness are [identical to] the moments of dissolution and arising of consciousness in the course of existence (*pavatta*). Regarding the suffering-truth and so forth:
The phrase beginning with “in the course of the [present] consciousness” (pavatte cittassa) is stated because [the factors] share the same destiny regarding arising and so forth.
In that context, the construction should be understood as follows: the inclusion of the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa) must also be seen to apply to the death-consciousness (cuticitta).

Regarding the phrase “in both sections,” this refers to the preceding and succeeding sections occurring by way of the non-rejection and rejection, respectively, of the future cessation of the truth of origination (samudayasacca).
“Not specified” means that although there was no rejection of what was stated, it was not stated by way of specification.

The meaning is that for even a single person who possesses such a path and fruit at the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa), because the prior portion alone is not included and because the two portions cannot coexist, [the term is not used]. Now, in order to explain this very point: “For whom... [the text continues].
The phrase beginning with “the truth of suffering” has been stated. This genitive case ending is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*) for certain individuals.
When it was said, “of the path and the fruit,” showing the paths and fruits mentioned, he said, “of three fruits and two paths.
These should be understood as the three lower fruits and the two middle paths, respectively, without interruption.

"Without having produced" means: without performing that constant application which must be done by one who, having made [the mind] unmixed with opposing states, produces the path together with insight; this is the meaning. Therefore he said: "Having [produced it] from time to time...
etc. Since it was stated without distinction as "in the immaterial [realm], at the moment of the dissolution of both the path and the fruit," how is this distinction [to be understood]?

He says, "It is obtained," with the words "even by a term expressing generality" and so forth. By this, he demonstrates that it is a world-established principle that prefixes enter into their application according to the scope of exceptions.
The commentary on the section on occurrence (pavattivāra) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra) 165–170.
“In this very [work]” means in this *Saccayamaka* itself. Regarding the phrase “for the purpose of showing that there is nothing to be fully understood”:

here, the negative particle *a-* does not denote the absence of anything to be fully understood, nor does it denote the opposite of what is to be fully understood; rather, it denotes something other than that.
Just as it is necessary to see even those things such as what is to be abandoned that are found among the truths according to their respective fitness, this section is intent upon seeing;
yet, showing that for certain specific qualities—even though they are found among some truths—this section is not intent upon seeing them, he says: "and for the purpose of realizing... seeing."

He said: "It is indeed appropriate to say that regarding the origin (samudaya), only the full understanding through abandoning (pahānapariññā) is mentioned, and not the full understanding through scrutinization (tīraṇapariññā), because the nature of the origin is such that it must be scrutinized.
But why was it said that regarding suffering (dukkha), only the full understanding through scrutinization is mentioned, and not the full understanding through abandoning?
Is it not the case that suffering is simply not to be abandoned? [This refers to] certain things mentioned in the Vibhaṅga of the Truth of the Origin...

Since the categories of the origin [of suffering] are included within the truth of suffering, this should be understood as a statement of facts, having been taken up precisely so as not to confuse the truth of suffering with the truth of its origin.
"In both cases" means as stated regarding suffering and its origin. Why? Because they are common to both.
Thus, the aforementioned task of full understanding (*pariññākicca*), which is divided by the distinction between what is common and what is uncommon, [is to be undertaken] in the preliminary stage.

To show that even though [the factors] are obtained at different times, they are obtained at one and the same moment during the time of the path because of the single function of a single knowledge, it was said:
"For the knowledge of the path... and so forth.
The commentary on the section on full understanding is finished.
The commentary on the *Saccayamaka* is finished.
6. The *Saṅkhārayamaka*. 1.
Commentary on the Section on Designations (*Paṇṇattivāra*).

1. Although mindfulness (*sati*) is also analyzed as a root of the wholesome (*kusalamūla*) and so forth, he said, "previously unanalyzed like the aggregates (*khandha*) and so on," showing that the analysis of the aggregates and such is more preeminent than that.

Alternatively, the word "and so on" (*ādi*) here has the sense of "manner" (as in "the roots of being and so on"), and thus it should be understood as including the roots of the wholesome and the rest.
[It was] because they were not understood by those listening. Or, it has the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

Here, "elided" (lutta) means that which is indicated [by elision] because it is not explicitly expressed. Although the relationship of cause and fruit is intended for the bodily formations even in both alternatives, he says, "of the body...
in the sense of the agent," showing that there is indeed a distinction in meaning when the form of the genitive case is not manifested.
"That, moreover" refers to the sense of the agent.
2–7. "By way of each single term in its pure state" means by way of each single term that is unmixed with the others in pairs of terms such as "body" and "formation.
"Because of the absence of meaning" means because of the absence of the intended meaning. Otherwise, meanings such as the "body born of karma" (karajakāya) and so forth do indeed exist.
For this very reason, he said: "Because of the purification of the terms... [and so on] ...because of the inexpressibility. Now, regarding that very absence of meaning:
Showing it by way of contrast (*vyatireka*), he says “Just as,” and so forth.
But why, when the status of being a compound word is the same in both cases, is the meaning found there but not found here? Because their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) are different.

For in that case, the terms such as “the aggregate of form” (*rūpakkhandha*) have a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*); thus, a single meaning based on two words is obtained. But here, the terms such as “bodily formations” (*kāyasaṅkhāra*)...
Regarding the phrase "having different bases," such a meaning is not obtained; therefore he says, "because of the absence of the intended meaning.

When he says "without illuminating separately," he speaks by way of a supposition: that even though the term *kāyasaṅkhāra* is spoken together with [the other terms] beginning with "bodily formation" (*kāyasaṅkhāro*), it does not illuminate its own respective meanings individually, but rather illuminates a single meaning. By this, [he refers to] the terms *kāyasaṅkhāra*.
It indicates grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*). Why was it said, “The term *kāyasaṅkhāra* occurs in the sense of bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*)”?
It should rather have been said, “The term *saṅkhāra* occurs in the sense of formation (*saṅkhāra*) alone.

For if that were the case, then—just as the term *khandha* occurring in the sense of aggregate (*khandha*) is qualified by the terms *rūpa* or *kāya*—this [term *kāyasaṅkhāra*] would likewise require qualification.

The statement would be appropriate; however, since the terms *kāyasaṅkhāra* and *sadda* share a common grammatical substratum (*samānādhikaraṇatta*), it is not only the word *saṅkhāra* that functions in the sense of "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāratthe*), but the word *kāya* as well. To show this meaning, it should have been said:
"The term *kāyasaṅkhāra*, while functioning in the sense of bodily formation," the intention being that it is [the word *kāya*] which shares the same substratum with the word *kāya*.
However, since there is indeed a need to qualify *saṅkhāra* by means of a different grammatical case (*byadhikaraṇena*), [the author says] "of this section.

"Of this section" refers to the section on pure *saṅkhāras*. If it were stated merely as "shown by the purification of the words," then, due to the commonality of being "shown therein," one might include the pure body (*kāya*) and so forth as well; therefore, for the purpose of preventing that, [he specifies...]
He said, “only those intended [by the author]. Because they are not included by the terms “body” and so forth means because they are not included by the bare terms “body” and so forth.

“But here,” however, refers to the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Although it was stated with reference to the section on pure formations (*saṅkhāra*), he did not grant that this refers solely to the section on pure formations;
rather, he said, “but here in the *Saṅkhārayamaka*,” meaning it pertains to the entire scope of the *Saṅkhārayamaka*. This constitutes the abandonment of the intended meaning.
The non-grasping of the intended meaning, such as inhalation and exhalation, and the grasping of unintended meanings,

such as the formations of the volitional body and so forth, [constitute the fault]. If, because of the absence of a basis for the meaning, the pure formations— the wheel-turnings rooted in the idea that "the body is a formation" and so on— should not be taken here,
then why was the teaching not undertaken solely by way of the mode of occurrence (*pavatti-vāra*), but instead taught otherwise?

He said, "By means of the section on the purification of words, the root-cycle, and so forth," because there arises a doubt due to the commonality of the terms *kāyasaṅkhāra* and the rest being expressible by the word *saṅkhāra*, and because they stand in a state of different grammatical relations (*byadhikaraṇa*). For that very reason he said, "...shown by [terms] that do not have a common substratum... and so forth.
The commentary on the Section on Designations (*Paṇṇattivāra*) is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra) 19.

Regarding "the state of being the locus for both formations and persons": the state of being the locus for persons in relation to jhāna should be understood through their being the basis-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) for associated states, and through formations being that which is to be entered into by persons. As for the plane (*bhūmi*), however, at the same moment as [it is the locus] for persons...

When there is space for [the first jhāna], then by that same principle, there is also space for the mental formations (*saṅkhāra*). In the passage beginning with “in the second jhāna, in the third jhāna,” *jhāna* is taken as a distinct state of space;
and in the passage beginning with “in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*),” the *bhūmi* (plane) is likewise taken as a distinct state of space.

The word “iti” has the sense of a reason (*hetu*); the meaning is: because *jhāna* is also taken as a state of space, therefore [this is so]. And in the section on persons (*puggalavāra*), persons are included by way of their spatial location.
And in the section on persons (*puggalavāra*), when the bodily formations and so forth are apprehended by way of being the space for the person and the space [of the meditation],
then there is an apprehension by way of those two spaces; that is to say, by way of the two spaces known as the plane (*bhūmi*) and the meditation (*jhāna*)—
namely, where that person is and the meditation which is found in that person— the bodily formations and so forth are apprehended accordingly.
“Grasping is speaking. Therefore—because it is precisely this—therefore. “By way of the spheres consisting of the second and third jhānas”:

they are grasped by way of the spheres known as the second and third jhānas. How? Persons grasped in the manner of “at the moment of the arising of inhalation and exhalation without applied thought and sustained thought” are shown specifically. By what? It should be construed as: “by that very moment of the arising of inhalation and exhalation devoid of applied and sustained thought.”
It was stated that "in the first section, the person is shown by way of the meditation-sphere (*jhāna-okāsa*)," and thus it says, "furthermore...
he shows. The connection is: "he shows the person by way of the plane-sphere (*bhūmi-okāsa*). "Of two kinds" means of those two types distinguished by way of meditation and plane.
"Of them" refers to the persons. And [it says]: "of those who have attained the first meditation, belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*)."

This is a statement common to both that which is to be excluded and that which is to be included; and its delimiter is stated as "at the moment of the arising of inhalation and exhalation" (*assāsapassāsānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe*).
By means of that qualification, the word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even those of the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacarānam-pi*) has the sense of inclusion.
By it, it is shown that [the first jhāna] belongs not only to those who have attained the first jhāna in the fine-material and immaterial spheres, but also to others.

The phrase "even those belonging to the sense sphere" (*kāmāvacarānam-pi*) summarizes the very same point already stated. To the question "Of what kind of beings belonging to the sense sphere?", he says:

"of those in the womb, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those submerged in water or rendered unconscious are included; however, those who have attained the fourth jhāna with death as the fourth [limit], or those who have attained the cessation attainment (*nirodhasamāpanna*), are not.

For these, like those who do not belong to the sense sphere, are excluded by the very fact that they lack the arising of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), just as those possessing existence in the fine-material or immaterial realms are.

"Because of its exclusivity" means because the absence of inhalation and exhalation is exclusive [to those states]. "Shown" means that the fine-material and immaterial-sphere states are stated by way of being illustrations;
the intention is not that other states devoid of them are non-existent. The construction is: "The occasion of the first jhāna is distinguished by the absence of inhalation and exhalation.
Here, the first [instance] refers to the inclusion of those belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres who possess the first jhāna, while the second...

"Of those such as those in the womb, as previously described. "By this method" means by this way or means, namely, the method for classifying individuals according to the stages of meditation (*jhāna*) and the planes of existence (*bhūmi*), which was stated in the passage beginning with "of formations and of individuals.
"In all cases, in all questions. "But when this meaning exists" refers to the meaning already stated, having distinguished the meditation according to the plane of rebirth.
If this meaning were accepted, then in other instances as well, the jhāna would have to be specified by its place of arising;
and showing that such a consequence is undesirable, he says, "In the fourth jhāna," and so forth. To the question, "But what is that undesirable consequence?
he replies, "Because it would result in the non-inclusion of the very fact that the planes [of existence] serve as the locus [for the jhānas]. For wherever jhāna is mentioned, [it must be qualified].

In each instance, that [base] must be specified by its plane of arising (*uppattibhūmi*). If it were so, only the occasion of jhāna (*jhānokāsa*) would be grasped, and not the occasion of the plane (*bhūmiokāsa*), because the latter is subordinate.

Furthermore, in the passage “in the fourth jhāna, in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), in the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*)”, when the fourth jhāna is being specified by the planes of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, only a portion of that [plane] is grasped by way of the occasion.
It may be that not all fourth jhānas [are included]. Therefore he said: "Because of the failure to include all fourth jhānas by way of their respective bases.
Regarding the phrase *jhānabhūmokāsānaṃ*: this refers to the bases for the planes of jhāna, that is, the bases for the planes of the jhāna-bases.
Now, when the bases for the planes of jhāna are applied without confusion, is it not the case that bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) is not present in every base of the first jhāna?
"And there is verbal formation; likewise in all the sense-sphere realms"—referring to the arising of this objection, he said "Even though...
and so forth, in order to state the rebuttal. "Therein" means in the plane of the first jhāna and in the sense-sphere plane.
"The arising of that pair" means the arising of that pair of bodily and verbal formations. Because of the non-confusion of the two planes...

And because this benefit is obtained upon inclusion, he said: “Separately... it need not be stated. Therein, “by way of the mere factors” means by way of the mere jhāna-factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth.
What is to be stated there has already been explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

He said, “Even though free from applied thought, sustained thought (*vicāra*) is indeed verbal formation,” thus: “Without applied thought... it proceeds. This refers to the second jhāna, which has reached its peak.

In the fourfold method, he speaks of the second jhāna. For that [second jhāna], because it is preeminent in its abandonment of the single factor of applied thought (vitakka) through the disappearance of all factors that cause agitation, it receives the designation "the summit.
The phrase "like the non-percipient beings" (asaññasattā viya) should be understood as a dissimilar illustration.
37. All consciousness that has occurred prior to the adverting [of the mind] is of one destiny with the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta).
Having stated this, it was said, "from the first. Therefore he said, "from that which is without applied thought and sustained thought," and so forth.

"For the purpose of showing the beginning of the mental formation" means for the purpose of showing the beginning of the mental formation in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa). The same applies here to the phrase "for the purpose of showing the beginning of the verbal formation.
The commentary on the Section on Occurrence (pavattivāra) is concluded.
The commentary on the *Saṅkhāra-yamaka* is finished.
7. The *Anusaya-yamaka*:
Commentary on the Section of Enumeration Distinguished by Delimitation.
1. “With the arising of ignorance there is the arising of form; with the arising of craving there is the arising of form; with the arising of kamma there is the arising of form.
Greed is the source for the arising of kamma”—since the state of being a condition for wholesome roots, wholesome states, and so forth, has been stated in such passages, he says:
“by the Root Yamaka that illustrates conditions. “He [perceives]: ‘Form is impermanent, form is impermanent.’”

"He understands it as it really is. Because the contemplation of impermanence and so forth have been taught by way of the many aggregates and so on, beginning with "The eye is impermanent, forms are impermanent," it is said:
"Because of the predominance of investigation into the aggregates and so forth. Since there is no function of abandoning beyond the total eradication of the defilements, he says:
"Full understanding as abandonment culminates in the abandoning of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). Even though [the defilements] exist through the underlying tendencies...
The full understanding of abandonment (*pahānapariññā*) does not occur either through association (*sampayoga*) or through the object (*ārammaṇa*);

however, since there is no undertaking of that [abandonment] when the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are absent, it is said: "in order to clarify the full understanding of abandonment by means of the underlying tendencies. "Of those obtained by way of the state of underlying tendencies" means existing by way of the state of underlying tendencies; the sense is "possessing the nature of underlying tendencies. "In three ways" means:
[It is] by way of the three modes beginning with delimitation (*pariccheda*). Regarding the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), he says, "Among them, thus...

because they are difficult to comprehend," showing that if they were not explained according to their enumeration, essential nature, activity, and location, and if their teaching regarding their objects were presented merely by way of persons, locations, and so forth for those who have not understood them, it would not be easy to understand.

Here, the extraction of the word *purimesu* (in the former) is intended with reference to the section on "those possessing underlying tendencies" (*sānusaya-vāra*) and so on, based on the principle that a preceding term may imply both an injunction and a prohibition for what follows immediately.

He said, "Among these, the meaning is 'in the preceding [sections] such as the Chapter on Latent Dispositions (anusaya-vāra),' etc., in order to show that the establishment of the text (*pāḷi-vavatthāna*) was already completed in the Chapter on Latent Dispositions, and thus there is no need to look further.

For, among the three preceding sections beginning with the Chapter on Latent Dispositions, the teaching proceeds from the perspective of 'from where' and 'there,' which occurs in the Chapter on Occasions (*okāsa-vāra*), but not in the Chapter on Latent Dispositions and the others.
This is because there is no difference in meaning; for instance, in the phrase 'of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*)...'"

Because there is no distinction in meaning between the phrase found in the Pāḷi beginning with “cutassā,” and the phrase found in the Aṭṭhakathā and other texts in the form of a *yamaka* (parallel) construction beginning with “kāmadhātuṃ vā pana upapajjantassā.
What is meant by the question, “How can this be a *yamaka*-teaching in the absence of a second term? is as follows:
If this is not a *yamaka*-teaching, then why has it been included here? To this he replies: “In the first section...”

"‘Hī’ and so forth. Therein, "showing the delimitation of the basis for the underlying tendencies" (*anusaya-ṭṭhāna-pariccheda-dassana*) means showing the delimitation by way of being the basis for the underlying tendencies.
Thus, one asks: "How is this *Anusaya-yamaka* [the Pairs on Underlying Tendencies] so called, given the existence of the teaching of the *Yamaka*?

To this he says: "'The teaching of the *Yamaka*... it should be understood as a name. By way of meaning" means by way of the reverse-order meaning. For it is also by way of the reversal of what was stated by the first term.

There is a "pair-teaching" (*yamakadesanā*) in such cases as, “Form is the form-aggregate; the form-aggregate is form,” and so forth; however, in those instances there is a distinction in meaning, whereas here there is none.
Therefore, showing that the teaching was not formulated in that way, he said:
“But it was not stated because of the absence of a distinction in meaning. “By way of its being obtainable” means by way of its being obtainable through the question.
By the statement "it shows that they are capable of arising," it is shown in the non-figurative sense (*nippariyāya*) that the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are future;
for since they are to be abandoned by the path, they are not called past or present, as those have already arisen.
However, when phenomena in their future state are called underlying tendencies, they are described as being of that very same nature even when they are past or present.

For there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena due to a difference in time; therefore, the past and present states of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are obtained only figuratively (*pariyāyato*).
Thus, it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), "it is also past," and so forth. "Of such a kind" means of the kind of underlying tendency;

the meaning is simply that they are capable of arising when the necessary conditions are met. That which is of such a kind arises by means of the word "arises" (*uppajjati*) in the section on arising.
The intention is that [the term] is included for the purpose of indicating the uninterrupted state of being ready to arise.

Therefore he said, "not as in the case of the *khandha-yamaka* and so forth, [but rather] as 'presentness' (*uppajjamānatā*)," which means its state of being present. With the words "by that very same [fact]" and so on, he makes the aforementioned point more evident.
In that context, "without difference" (*ninnānākaraṇo*) means without distinction. It is precisely because there is no difference between arising and the underlying tendency (*anusaya*).
For it is said in the Vibhaṅga: “It is here that this craving, when arising, arises; here that it, when settling, settles.
For what is intended by “settling” (nivisana) here is “underlying tendency” (anusayana).
Now, wishing to show the manner in which the designation “underlying tendency” applies to the past and the present, [the author] also [mentions] the future:
Showing them together as one, he said: "But the appropriate cause... is spoken of.
By this, he shows that the fitness for rebirth in a former destiny should be understood in terms of both the past and the present.
Fitness for rebirth is to be understood as the state where the defilements have not been eradicated by the Path. And that [fitness] certainly exists even in the past and the present.

By another method as well, he demonstrates their state of being latent dispositions (*anusaya*) through a figurative expression (*pariyāya*). For this very reason, he says, "But of the path," and so forth.

"Of such [things]" means of those things which are capable of arising when there is no cultivation of the path; the intention is that it is only the phenomenon (*dhamma*) itself that arises, not the mode of the phenomenon (*dhammākāra*).
For it is not said that the modes of phenomena, such as impermanence and so on, arise. If...
However, those [factors] would be possessors of arising and so forth; they would simply be phenomena (dhammas). Therefore it was said:
"It is not tenable to say that 'the un-abandoned mode arises.
Thus, showing that the objector objects by taking only the sense of being "un-abandoned" while failing to grasp the sense of "becoming firmly established," he says:
He says: "If it is argued that 'one falls into [the state of] existence and underlying tendencies'... Indeed, once the reaching of a firm footing is grasped, there is no room for such an objection.
Therefore, he says "one does not fall into [it]," and so forth. This point is found not only in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) but also within the text itself;
thus, showing that it must be understood exactly in this way, he states: "The firm footing... is appropriate," and then asks: "But what is that reaching of a firm footing?"
Turning back the suspicion of others, he said: "And it is called 'established'... [etc]... so it is said.

In this context, "not shared by others" means that—just as the nature of being a defilement belongs to the bases of defilement and so forth—their own unique individual essence (sabhhāva) is not found elsewhere than in sensual lust and the rest;
for this reason, they are called the seed of existence and the root of existence. And because of their reaching a state of firm establishment...
Their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is not shared with anything else; therefore, it is said that they are "latent tendencies" (*anusaya*). Demonstrating this, he stated:
"The meaning of 'become firmly rooted' is 'possessing a latent tendency' (*anusayasamaṅgī*).

This is shown in the section on latent tendencies (*anusayavāra*), beginning with: "In one for whom the latent tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) lies latent, does the latent tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) also lie latent? Yes. And so forth.
The meaning has already been stated in such passages as: "Does the underlying tendency to sensual lust arise for one in whom the underlying tendency to aversion arises?

"Yes. Since the manner of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) is thus captured by the word "arises" (*uppajjati*) in the section on arising, regarding what was said—that "the section on arising is analyzed as being non-different from the section on underlying tendencies"—one should now investigate that point.
He begins with the words, “Because the sections on the arising of latent tendencies (anusaya) share the same course,” and so forth.
The statement “it arises” might be [intended] as follows: in the section on arising, the expression “it arises” would indicate the aspect of being unabandoned.
And that being the case, just as in the phrase “from the arising of this,” the meaning “of this which has not ceased” is also understood, so too [is it understood] in the case of “it arises.”

When this was said, the meaning expressed is "it does not arise. Showing the objection that this means the state of being capable of arising—which is the un-abandoned mode—does not possess the nature of actually arising, he says:
"If it is argued that it cannot be said that the statement 'it arises' has not been stated [in the previous context].

By the phrase "because both of those have been stated through the specific distinction of the word-meaning," even though there is no difference in the phenomena (*dhamma*), [the two meanings are established].
He shows that there is a teaching on different sections by way of various bases (*padatthāna*), as in the sections on co-nascent associated states (*sahajātasaṃsaṭṭha*).
The passage beginning with "having obtained a corresponding cause" is commenced in order to clarify that very distinction in the meaning of the words.
"Suitable for arising" means fit for arising; the sense is "possessing the nature of arising. It is because of this that latent dispositions (*anusaya*) are said to be "capable of arising."
This must be accepted unconditionally, because of such statements as: "Does the underlying tendency to aversion arise in one for whom the underlying tendency to sensual lust arises?
"Yes. If it were stated merely that "they are called 'underlying tendencies' (anusaya) because they underlie," the following meaning would follow:
do these [tendencies] exist at all times as something not yet fully manifested in the sense of being underlying tendencies? Thus, this interpretation would be reached.
In order to refute that [notion], it is said: "They arise having obtained a corresponding cause. By the phrase beginning with "of the word *anusaya*," etc., he expresses this meaning:
that the statement regarding their connection to arising—namely, that the state of being firmly established through the fitness for arising is the meaning of *anusaya*—is indeed correctly stated.
Thus, there is a determination of the meaning of the word *anusaya* which produces two distinct modes of teaching.
He shows that this too is well-stated by means of this measure of the *tanti*.

Demonstrating that this also refers to the threefold *tanti* mentioned in the passage beginning with "In the Abhidhamma first," he says: "For by the three *tantis* as well, the state of being associated with consciousness is illustrated.
The commentary on the section of the summary (*uddesavāra*) delimited by the sections (*pariccheda*) is finished.
Commentary on the Section on the Basis of Arising (Uppattiṭṭhānavāra-vaṇṇanā):
"Thus, when this is so" means: when there is a need to qualify the feelings and when the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu) is the qualifier.

The fact that the sense-sphere element is the locus for the underlying tendencies (anusaya) has not been stated because it is subordinate; for among what is primary and what is subordinate, activity is seen to reside in the primary.
The intention is that it must be practiced by way of being a qualifier (*visesanabhāvena*). Anticipating that someone might say, "Let it be so;

what is the harm?", he says, "But in the case of two," and so forth. "In two" is the locative case used for selection (*niddhāraṇe bhummam*); the same applies here to the phrase "in three elements" (*tīsu dhātūsu*).
"Therefore" means because the locus of underlying tendencies (*anusayaṭṭhāna*) is threefold according to the division of elements and so on, and therein, of the material and immaterial elements...

Since it has been stated that the latent tendency (anusaya) of attachment to existence (bhavarāga) has its locus there, it must necessarily be said that the latent tendency of sensual desire (kāmarāga) has its locus in the realm of sense-desire (kāmadhātu);
therefore, [the locative case] in "in the three realms (dhātu) and in the three feelings (vedanā)" is used in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa),
while [the locative case] in "in two feelings in the realm of sense-desire" is used in the sense of a substratum (ādhāra).

“In two only” means in the two [feelings], namely pleasure and equanimity. “In all two” means in whichever two [feelings] they may be. “By that” means by the very determination of the specific distinction obtained through the force of the statement: “Sensual lust underlies two feelings.

The spheres for the underlying tendency to lust for existence are the form and formless realms, as well as the corresponding feelings. For it is not the case that only the underlying tendency to sensual lust underlies two feelings.

The restriction is intended [to apply to the first two], but it is intended that [the latent tendency] exists in only two feelings. For this very reason, he said: “It underlies only two, not three. And what is the non-occasion for the latent tendencies?
It is the unconditioned (apariyāpanna) within the personal existence (sakkāya); that is, all supramundane (lokuttara) phenomena.
By the word “and” (ca), he includes the occasion for the latent tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya). Therefore, it was stated: “And just as,” and so forth.
"Other" refers to the two types of feeling that serve as the basis for the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*).
"In others" means in those dissociated from the other two types of feeling. "Pleasant forms and agreeable forms" refers to things of a beloved and sweet nature.
This qualification is made because the state of being desirable in regard to forms and so forth is not fixed across all sense-doors or for all persons.
“By way of craving for pleasant and peaceful happiness” means by way of longing and yearning for pleasant happiness (*sāta-sukha*) and peaceful happiness (*santa-sukha*).

Therein, pleasant happiness is bodily, while peaceful happiness is mental. Alternatively, pleasant happiness is bodily happiness, and peaceful happiness is the happiness of equanimity (*upekkhā-sukha*).
Thus it has been said: “But equanimity, because of its peacefulness, is described as ‘happiness. It is limited (*paritta*).
Or [it is] gross pleasure, which is pleasant satisfaction, and subtle pleasure, which is peaceful bliss.

And here, the mention of "limited" is intended because of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*). "Elsewhere" means other than the feelings (*vedanā*). "It" refers to the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
It lies down having followed after the feelings; thus it occurs only with reference to the feelings, just as the act of nursing by a nurse occurs with reference to her children.
The occurrence known as lying down is indeed the longing for sensual desire (*kāmarāga*). Therefore, it is said: "He desires only pleasure.

Just as in his case, so too for the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) and the others, their lying down within painful feelings and so forth should be understood as the performance of their respective functions according to the stated method.
Hence it was said: "And thus the underlying tendency to aversion," and so on. By the expression "lying down in the three feelings..."
By the statement regarding the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) as they correspond to the three feelings. "In those apprehended as being desirable and so forth" means:

the construction is that [this refers] to those apprehended as being desirable and so forth by way of the nature of the object (*ārammaṇa-pakati*), and to those apprehended as being desirable and so forth even when they are undesirable and so forth, by way of a distorted perception (*viparīta-saññā*).
For the apprehension as being desirable and so forth is not itself a distorted perception.
"Among those" (*tattha*) means among desirable objects and so forth. "In this" (*ettha*) means in the underlying tendency (*anusaya*). The construction should be understood as follows:

"of the sense-sphere existence and so forth, which have become the basis for the relish of sensual pleasure (*kāmassāda*) and so on," which refers to the grasping of the sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial existences that serve as the bases for the relish of sensual pleasure and the relish of existence (*bhavassāda*).

"Among those" (*tattha*) [refers] to the three feelings and the three elements; here the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). "The warding off of suffering" (*dukkhapaṭighāta*) [occurs] in suffering...
Discontent (*anabhirati*). "In this or that" (*yattha tattha*) means in painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*), in the undesirable forms (*aniṭṭharūpa*) and so forth associated with it, or wherever else.

The sublime (*mahaggata*) aggregates subject to clinging (*upādinnakkhandha*) are the states of form and formless existence (*rūpārūpabhava*); the aggregates not subject to clinging (*anupādinnakkhandha*) are the phenomena belonging to the fine-material and immaterial spheres (*rūpārūpāvacaradhamma*).
"Therein" (*tattha*) should be understood as lust for existence (*bhavarāga*) toward the aforementioned sublime phenomena. Therefore it was said: "In the realm of form... (*rūpadhātuyā*).

“In the formless realm, the underlying tendency to sensual lust does not underlie here. Regarding the phrase “the underlying tendency to views, etc.,” by the word “etc.,” the inclusion of the underlying tendencies to doubt and ignorance should be understood.
It is well said that no location for the underlying tendencies to views and so forth, apart from the three elements and the three feelings, has been stated;

thus, in response to the question regarding the locus of the arising of the underlying tendency to views and so forth, it was simply stated: “in all phenomena included within the personality-belief (sakkāya).”

Because it has already been answered. However, in order to show that there exists a locus for the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) and so forth—a locus where sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) does not underlie, yet which is distinct from painful feeling and the form and formless realms—the passage beginning with “But is it not the case that... is commenced.

Therein, “from that locus of its underlying tendency” means from the locus of the underlying tendency of that sensual lust. The others are comprised of the joy and equanimity based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*).

This is the summary of the meaning here: just as the underlying tendency to aversion does not underlie grief based on renunciation, so too the underlying tendency to sensual lust does not underlie joy or equanimity based on renunciation.
Thus, it can be said that "wherever the underlying tendency to sensual lust does not underlie, there the underlying tendency to views does not underlie";
therefore, having extracted that [point], it was not stated [in the text]. "Let them be" refers to the existence of those feelings.
Having acknowledged [the objection] and refuted it, he says, "But not... that was not stated," showing the reason for his silence.
"The locus of their underlying tendencies" means the place where those underlying tendencies, such as the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya), reside.

"Therefore" means because, although there is a locus for the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) other than the locus for the underlying tendencies to views and so forth, that [other locus] is nonetheless distinct from the three elements and the three feelings.
Because there is no state of two feelings; therefore. That pair of feelings was not stated separately;

the meaning is that they are not extracted individually. "Therefore" means: since the point that "where sensual lust and so forth do not underlie, there views and doubt do not underlie" has been stated without distinction by this response of "Yes," [it follows that] "where sensual lust and so forth..."
The meaning that "views and doubt underlie it" is also obtained without distinction;
therefore, by way of non-distinction, suffering is shown to be the locus where resistance underlies. Thus he said: "It should be understood without distinction... etc.
Therein, "without distinction" means without making a differentiation between what is based on the household life and what is based on renunciation. This is by way of the whole.
“Having taken” means having taken it as suffering precisely by way of the collection of the aforementioned components.

The word *tathā* (thus) draws in the sense of “having taken it by way of the aggregate without distinction,” because even in the phrase “in two feelings,” a division such as that based on the household life and so forth is not intended.
If this is so, then how is one to reconcile this with the Sutta passage: “By means of that [feeling], he abandons aversion; therein the underlying tendency to aversion does not lie latent”?
With reference to the objection, he said "Furthermore," and so forth. "Therein" means in that state of mental grief (*domanassa*), or in the resistance (*paṭigha*) associated with it.
He shows that this sutta is of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*)—beginning with "mental grief based on renunciation"—and is not of direct meaning (*nītattha*).
To the question, "Why is it not stated here in the same way as the sutta was cited? he replies, "Because it is a place where the arising of resistance is absent," and so forth.

Thus, he says that there is no contradiction between the readings of the Suttas and the Abhidhamma because this is a teaching by way of the direct method (*nippariyāya-desanā*), whereas that [Sutta teaching] is a teaching by way of the indirect method (*pariyāya-desanā*).

And "having done so" means precisely because it is a teaching by way of the indirect method. By "underlying tendency of lust" (*rāgānusaya*), the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) is intended;
for it has been stated [elsewhere] with reference to its eradication by the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*). Therefore, it is not [the same as the underlying tendency of existence].

Regarding the statement that "exalted states (*mahaggatadhammā*) are a basis for underlying tendencies (*anusaya*)," it was said [in the *Paṭṭhāna*] that, without referring to the first jhāna, "it cannot be said that worldly [states]...
do not underlie. This is because they are "without a basis" (*avatthubhāvato*), meaning they are by their very nature places where [underlying tendencies] do not arise.
"Here" refers to this *Anusayayamaka*. "In the manner stated" refers to such passages as: "having produced grief based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*)."
By the method already stated. "Because it is the opposite of those" means because the Path exists as the antidote to those [defilements] such as aversion (paṭigha).
To show that it is not only because of the existence of the Path, but also because of the existence of powerful insight (vipassanā), he said: "And because of the eradication of that... and so forth.
Now, regarding that which is stated here and there as the "basis for underlying tendencies" (*anusayanaṭṭhāna*), there are two alternatives:
it may be so by way of the object to be grasped, or by way of the specific mode of grasping. With reference to the first of these, he says:

"When the basis for underlying tendencies, namely the object, exists. This is said with reference to the meaning when the form and other objects are taken as the "basis for underlying tendencies" of the underlying tendencies.
It was said, “it is not possible to state [this],” and to demonstrate that, he said, “For it is painful,” and so forth.

“If it were to exist” means if the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) were to exist. “Of this too” means that even for greed associated with the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*), the locus of sensual lust would have to be stated as “among all phenomena included within the aggregates of existence” (*sabbasakkāyapariyāpannesu dhammesu*);
yet it has not been stated. “But if, however,” and so forth, presents the second alternative.
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). Regarding the phrase "by way of inclination (*ajjhāsayavasena*) because of being inclined toward that":

even in the absence of making [the defilements] an object, wherever lust for sensual pleasures (*kāmarāga*) and so forth are inclined by way of inclination, that is their place of underlying tendency (*anusaya*). Therefore it was said: "having followed along, it lies.
Furthermore, the word "said" (*vutta*) connects to what follows. The passage beginning with "as" (*yathā*) is an examination by way of an illustration of the meaning already stated.
The intention is that it functions solely by way of striking against suffering, not by way of making it its object.
It is stated that suffering itself is the locus for its underlying tendency because the underlying disposition (ajjhāsaya) inclines toward it;

thus, suffering alone is stated to be the locus for the underlying tendency of that aversion, and not the apprehended forms and so forth, nor pleasant feeling—this is the intention. "In this way" means as follows.

Even though aversion has other objects as its focal point, it is stated that suffering alone is the locus for its latent tendency because of its inclination toward suffering due to one’s underlying disposition;

thus it is said regarding suffering and so forth... "Suffering must be overcome by means of suffering" and "there is no giving," etc.—by way of such false adherence arising toward the suffering of bodily exhaustion and toward the power of generosity and so forth.

Even greed that has another object and is associated with the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) occurs solely by way of attachment to pleasure, through the inclination [of the mind] thinking, "In this way, there will be happiness.

Therefore, in the Pāli, only the two types of pleasant feeling—the pleasant and the intensely pleasant—are stated to be the locus for the underlying tendency of this greed, and not suffering and so forth as previously mentioned; hence, [the underlying tendency to] existence-attachment... pe...
It is not contradictory. The phrase "in one and the same" and so forth is stated for the purpose of further elaborating upon the second alternative itself.

In that context, the inclination toward pleasure (*sukhajjhāsaya*) regarding lust (*rāga*) should be understood by way of the person possessing it, or else by way of its being a state of leaning toward that [lust], just as the eye has an uneven inclination (*visamajjhāsaya*).
This same method applies to the others as well. Regarding those two—lust and aversion (*paṭigha*)—their status as having different underlying tendencies (*nānānusayaṭṭhāna*)...
The meaning is: "it exists even with respect to a single object.

And by doing so—meaning that although there is no difference in the objects to be grasped, the locus of the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) is differentiated by the specific mode of grasping—it would otherwise contradict what was stated [in the text]:
"Where... [etc. ...not? For, by way of the difference in the objects to be grasped, [there is a distinction] between lust (*rāga*) and aversion (*paṭigha*).
If one were to take the classification [of defilements] according to their underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), one might think they should reside in mere resultants (*vipāka*);
however, that is not logical, nor do all the doors of the person determine what is desirable or undesirable.

Even if, according to the method already stated, the state of sensual lust-underlying-tendency (*kāmarāgānusaya*) can occur in the aforementioned greed, it nevertheless arises in the case of pleasant equanimity and in relation to desirable objects.
The latent tendency of aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) does not exist because hatred, which arises together with mental distress, lacks strength;
likewise, the aforementioned greed does not exist as the latent tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*). To show this point, the passage beginning with “In the commentary, however,” was stated.
In the phrase “not the latent tendency of aversion,” the particle *na* has the sense of negation and no other meaning; however, its occurrence in the other case [is established].

Showing that this is not the case, he says, “But as for this...,” and so forth. Therein, by way of demonstrating that the negative particle (*na*) does not have another meaning, he establishes its sense of non-existence with the words, “For there is no suspicion that mental distress (*domanassa*) has the nature of a latent tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*).
Regarding the phrase “the teaching might become confused,” he shows the confusion of the teaching with: “Even for the lust for existence (*bhavarāga*)... [etc.]”

It is said: “it would be so. The meaning of this is as follows: just as the arising of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) through the act of making the two feelings of the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*) its object has been stated—namely, “sensual lust underlies (*anuseti*) the two feelings of the sense-sphere”—if it were likewise stated that “lust for existence (*bhavarāga*) underlies the two feelings of the sense-sphere,” then for lust for existence also... [and so on] ...it would be so. Therefore...

Furthermore, the teaching on the lust for existence (*bhavarāga*) would become confused with the lust for sensual pleasure (*kāmarāga*), and the distinction between the lust for sensual pleasure and the lust for existence must be shown.
Since that distinction cannot be shown by way of co-nascent latent tendencies (*sahajātānusaya*), it must be shown by way of making [the object] an objective support (*ārammaṇakaraṇa*).
Therefore it was said: "Therefore, by way of the objective support... [etc.]... this is the intention. In that context, "by way of the distinction of the objective support" means:

"By way of the specific object designated as the form and formless realms. "For the purpose of showing the distinction" means for the purpose of showing the distinction between attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*) and attachment to sensual pleasures (*kāmarāga*).

"Thus the teaching was given" means that the teaching was given by employing the locative case with respect to the object, as in: "Herein, the underlying tendency to attachment to existence lies latent in the form realm and the formless realm. Therefore he said: "Because there is no distinction in the co-nascent feeling."
The commentary on the section on the bases of arising is finished.
Great Section 1:
Commentary on the Section on Latent Dispositions (*anusaya*).

3. "By way of the non-cessation of their occurrence" means by way of the non-cessation of the latent tendencies' (anusaya) occurrence; the meaning is "by way of their continuity. But how can there be an occurrence of latent tendencies during a moment of wholesome or indeterminate consciousness? To this he says: "By the path itself... as before. 20.
Since the "station" of mind and mental factors is called the arising of consciousness, he says: "In a single arising of consciousness.

"Of those various individuals" refers to individuals such as worldlings (puthujjana) and so forth. "By nature" means by their own intrinsic essence (sabhāva). They are established by their own intrinsic essence.

For unpleasant feeling is not a place for the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) to lie latent. In the same way, this should be stated accordingly for the remaining [feelings] as well. For he will say:
"It is said with reference to the fact that, by their very nature, painful feelings and so forth are not places for the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and so forth to lie latent.

"By abandoning" means by the total eradication of each respective underlying tendency. "Of the three types of persons" refers to the worldling (*puthujjana*), the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), and the once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*).
“Of two persons” refers to non-returners (anāgāmin) and arahants. “In this” means in this section on the world-sphere of persons (puggalokāsa-vāra).
“In the former method” refers to the previous mode of answering beginning with “of three persons. “Occasion” means a place of arising;
however, here it should be understood as painful feeling (dukkhavedanā). “In the latter method” refers to the subsequent mode of answering beginning with “of two persons.”
Lack of opportunity means the state of not being a locus for underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
The commentary on the section on underlying tendencies is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Section on Those Possessing Underlying Tendencies.
66–131. Regarding the statement, “One who possesses latent tendencies (sānusaya), abandons, and fully understands,” it refers to a person (*puggala*).

In such passages as, “Possessing latent tendencies for sensual lust, one abandons sensual lust, and fully understands sensual lust,” the person is spoken of by virtue of being endowed with latent tendencies and by virtue of being the agent of the action of abandoning and full comprehension;
it does not refer to a phenomenon (*dhamma*). Or, “by way of a specific state of existence” means solely by way of a specific state of existence.

"Or. "In the others" refers to the underlying tendencies such as aversion (*paṭighānusaya*). "Or by a distinction in the underlying tendency toward existence" means either by a distinction in the underlying tendencies specific to the realms of existence, such as the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the state of having underlying tendencies, the state of being without underlying tendencies, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes here the abandonment and non-abandonment [of defilements], as well as full understanding and non-full understanding. But is it not the case that in certain types of existence there is no abandonment of some underlying tendencies? No, that is not caused by the underlying tendencies; rather, [it is due to other factors].
There is no contradiction here because of the deficiency of conditions and the lack of opportunity. Regarding the phrase "in two feelings," one should connect it thus:
in the feelings of pleasure and equanimity, one is "without underlying tendency" toward the underlying tendency of sensual lust in relation to painful feeling.

This too is not [a fault], because it is spoken with reference to a person (*puggala*). Therefore he said: "For there is no... [etc. ...of underlying tendencies for a person. Even if [it were] for a person...
He says "But of the underlying tendency... and so forth, showing that while there is the occasion for an underlying tendency, its cause is the state of having such a tendency and so on.
By the word "and so on" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of those without underlying tendencies and so on," non-abandonment and non-full-understanding are included.
In the section on full-understanding (*pariññā*), it is stated that "the ablative case [expresses] transcendence."

"From the standpoint of being a basis for underlying tendencies" means by way of being a basis for underlying tendencies. The same method applies here to the phrase "from the standpoint of not being a basis for underlying tendencies.

It should be construed as follows: it is for the purpose of showing the state of being a cause (*nimitta*) in the section on "possessing underlying tendencies," and for the purpose of showing the state of being a source of grasping (*apādāna*) in the sections on "abandoning" and "full understanding.
Regarding the word "abandons" (*pajahati*), [it refers] to the fine-material element and the immaterial element...
One should apply this by citing the scriptural passage: "Then one abandons the underlying tendency to conceit. However, regarding the phrase "does not abandon," it says:

"In regard to painful feeling, one does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust from that [feeling]. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in such cases as these," the section on full understanding (*pariññāvāra*) is also included.
The meaning is that they are explained by means of the locative case itself, which carries the sense of a cause.

"By the answer to the fourth question" means by the answer to this question: "Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) necessarily possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya)? For therein, by the passage beginning "In the fine-material element (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial element (arūpadhātu)," the bases for the underlying tendencies are shown according to their specific forms.
"In that sense" means that the purpose (attha) of that [passage] is the demonstration of those bases for the underlying tendencies.

“Of this” means “of that meaning,” [referring to] “in that meaning. Having clarified the point that the word “from which” expresses the locus of the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) by stating, “This section is commenced for the purpose of showing the place of origin of the underlying tendency,” and so forth—it appears as if there has been a scribal error, since the word “arisen” (*uppanna*) is used to denote both the present and the arisen.
However, as in the section on “arising” (*uppajjana*),...
Because the word *uppajjati* (arises) indicates connection with arising, those things capable of arising are so called;

likewise here too, there is no contradiction in speaking of those things capable of arising. As for what he will say—"for that which is not included [in the realms] is not a place where underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are capable of arising"—that too is not a fault.
For wherever the underlying tendencies are capable of arising, taking all such places together as one, it is said "everywhere" (*sabbattha*).
"Vuttaṃ" (it is said). "Tatheva dissati" means it appears as if it were written by mistake.
"Yato uppannena bhavitabbaṃ" means that from the place where the underlying tendency (anusaya) resides, one must be arisen with the underlying tendency for the desire-aggregate (kāmagārānusaya);
therefore, the ablative case is used in the word "yato" to indicate the place of arising for that underlying tendency for sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya). Regarding the word "tathā" here:

The word "tathā" (thus) indicates that just as in the phrase "by that which has arisen," the arising of a latent tendency is stated to be from the place where it arises, so too in the phrase "by that which is arising," that very same thing is being stated; thus he says, "by that which has fallen upon all phenomena...
and so forth. In that context, when it is said "that which is arising," the meaning understood is that it is not something that does not arise.
And this being so, by that [statement] non-arising is determined, and the state of having already arisen is also made manifest. Therefore he said:

“In all phenomena... pe ... he removes. Because of the phrase “from whatever” occurring in the question, “He who is without underlying tendency toward sensual lust from whatever [source] is also without underlying tendency toward conceit from that same source,” in the answer the word “everywhere” (*sabbattha*) is used in the ablative sense alone.
Showing that it can indeed be so construed, he says: “In all places... it is not impossible. Grammarians maintain that the word *sabbattha* occurs in other senses than the locative;
for this reason, it is called the “base for all” (*sabbatthapādaka*). However, in this context, it should be understood as having the sense of the ablative (*nissakka*).
The commentary on the section on "With Underlying Tendencies" is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section on Abandoning (Pajahanavāra).
132–197. "Because of the existence of non-abandoning" means because of the existence of non-abandonment, or of that which is not being abandoned. "Therefore" means because...
One who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust does not abandon the underlying tendency to conceit without remainder;
and one who abandons the underlying tendency to conceit without remainder does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust, precisely because it has already been abandoned.
Therefore, it should be understood that when it is asked, "Does one who abandons the underlying tendency to conceit also abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust? the answer is "No."
If this is so, how is it [explained] in the first inquiry? He says: "But because... [as] stated.
Therein, "merely the act of abandoning" means merely the occurrence of the activity of abandoning, not the abandonment without remainder; this is the intended meaning.

"Excluding those" means excluding the eighth-person (aṭṭhamaka) and others who abandon the underlying tendencies of views, doubt, and so forth, without remainder. "The remaining" refers to [those factors] other than those which abandon each respective underlying tendency without remainder.

[They are] the remaining ones. Among them, even those for whom some underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have been abandoned are said to "not abandon" [them] precisely because of the presence of that which has not yet been abandoned.

And the construction is as follows: they are said to be "devoid," meaning "deprived," of abandonment in its manifest form—that is, in the manner in which it exists through the functional activity of the Path (*magga*).

"Of some" refers to stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), those possessing the path of once-returners (*sakadāgāmi-magga-samaṅgi*), and once-returners themselves. Again, "of some" refers to non-returners (*anāgāmi*) possessing the supreme path (*aggamagga-samaṅgi*) and arahants.

"Both" refers to the two underlying tendencies (*anusaya*): sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and doubt (*vicikicchā*). "The rest" refers to the persons mentioned as "the rest," namely those already described.

"Of these" refers to the two aforementioned types of underlying tendencies. "For one who has not abandoned both" means for one who has not abandoned the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and doubt.
"It is not the cause" means that for those whose underlying tendency to doubt has been abandoned, there is the state of its abandonment;
and for those in whom both [the underlying tendencies] as previously described have been abandoned, it is not the cause for their non-abandonment. Therefore he said:
"Because they have been abandoned, it cannot be said that 'they do not abandon. However, no reason was stated therein by which [it would follow] through a statement of reason...

There might be the occurrence of the faults already mentioned; however, it was stated that "they do not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust" (kāmarāgānusaya) merely for the purpose of showing that those persons were included by way of their definitive determination (sanniṭṭhāna). Even so, the reason for the doubt of one who asks this must be stated.
And that being the case, [the answer would be]: "The remaining persons do not abandon it because that underlying tendency has already been abandoned by them."
Addressing the objection that a reason must indeed be stated, he says, “It should not be so stated,” and so forth.

Therein, “it should not be stated” means that a reason should not be stated according to the method already explained, because the very nature of being a reason is absent. It has been said that “there is no reason for not abandoning both”;
however, in order to show how it *should* be stated, he says: “He who [does not abandon] the underlying tendency to sensual lust... [etc. ...because it ought to be stated.”

He said: This shows that one should not state the reason by way of both what has been abandoned and what has not been abandoned, but rather it should be stated solely by way of those things already abandoned.
Regarding the phrase "included by the term in the sense of doubt": it means included by the word whose meaning is doubt.
However, as for what is included by the term in the sense of certainty, because it is in the process of being abandoned, it cannot be said that "one does not abandon it."
The commentary on the Chapter on Abandoning is finished.
5. Commentary on the Chapter on What Has Been Abandoned (Pahīnavāra): §§264–274.

The teaching has been commenced solely from the standpoint of one who stands in the fruit, not from the standpoint of one who stands in the path, much less from the standpoint of an ordinary person (puthujjana).

Why? Because at the moment of the fruit (*phala-kkhaṇa*), the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are said to be abandoned, whereas at the moment of the path (*magga-kkhaṇa*), they are in the process of being abandoned.

For this very reason, it says: "It illustrates that those possessing the path are not included [in the category of those who have abandoned them]. Indeed, in the reverse order, the teaching is also taken according to the worldling (*puthujjana*):
"For one in whom the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) is unabandoned, is the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) unabandoned? Yes. And so forth.

"Of those consisting of a single moment of consciousness that are absolute counteragents to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*)" means of those consisting of a single moment of consciousness that have become absolute counteragents to the underlying tendencies. "Of those possessing the Path" refers to those standing at the stage of the Path.

And here, by the inclusion of the quality of being an absolute counteragent to the underlying tendencies, one rejects their capacity for arising; for they are not capable of arising again after the occurrence of their absolute counteragent.
[The terms] exist. By the mention of "possessing the path" (*maggasamaṅgitā*), he rejects the idea that they have already attained the state of an Arhat.

For at the moment of the path, they are not said to have "already attained" the state of an Arhat; rather, they are "being attained. By the mention of "occurring in a single moment of consciousness" (*ekacittakkhaṇikatā*), he rejects the activity of a [temporal] continuum (*santāna*).
Therefore, he says, "No one," and so forth. In that context, "they" refers to those possessing the path. It is not only in the case of what has been abandoned...
Then, showing that this applies to others as well, he said:
"The underlying tendencies... [omitted] ...are grasped. (275–296) Since it is precisely where an underlying tendency is liable to arise that one brings about its state of being non-arising, he said:
"They have been brought to the state of non-arising in their own respective locations. For it has been stated thus: "The eye in the world..."
Having stated, "The form that is dear, the form that is pleasant—herein this craving, when arising, arises; herein, when settling, settles," it was further said:
"The eye in the world is a form that is dear, a form that is pleasant; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned;
herein, when ceasing, ceases. Therefore, because it is precisely the state of being the locus for that—the state of being the locus for the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth.

Because the statements regarding the abandoned and unabandoned state of the underlying tendencies (anusaya) are explained, it is said that in the absence of opportunity, the indeterminacy of both [abandonment and non-abandonment] is stated.
This is because the very place where the two underlying tendencies of sensual lust (kāmarāga) and aversion (paṭigha) arise is itself the occasion for their abandonment;
thus, this is an "absence of opportunity" (anokāsa) for them relative to one another. In that absence of opportunity, there is an indeterminacy regarding the abandonment or non-abandonment of both.

It has been stated. For, since the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) has not been abandoned in the sphere where the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) exists, it cannot be said that "it is abandoned there";
yet, because it does not exist [there], it cannot be said that "it is un-abandoned there. Therefore, it is stated that both are inexpressible in a sphere where the other is absent.
"In a common sphere with that" means in a sphere common to that sensual lust. "In a shared location" means...

When this has been said, [it is understood that] within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), [the underlying tendencies] are called "abandoned" in relation to pleasure and equanimity; they are not abandoned simultaneously, because the underlying tendencies of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and conceit (*māna*) are to be eliminated by the third and fourth paths respectively.
The commentary on the section on abandonment is concluded.
7. Explanation of the Section on Elements (Dhātuvāra-vaṇṇanā) 332–340.
Showing that here "following" and "lying down" refer to the state of being present and arising when not yet abandoned, he said: "In which... [the meaning is]...
Here too, the word "connected" (yuttā) refers back to the very same meaning stated previously; for it has been said: "When the cause is obtained..."

"...it shows that they are *arahats* by way of their arising. Regarding the "six negating words": these are words spoken by way of negating the death and rebirth of the three elements (*dhātu*) as distinct [from one another]; for that very reason, they are not exclusions (*niddhāraṇā*) of the elements.

For he speaks with the intention that here, "negation" (*paṭisedha*) refers to the negation of sentient beings (*satta*). However, in other senses, there is no fault in the negative particle (*na-kāra*).
"This element" means this specific element. "Rooted in that" means rooted in the prohibitions. For it is so:

when the first construction is applied as "one who has passed away from the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu) and is being reborn in the sense-sphere element," etc., the specific element is already grasped by the mention of the sense-sphere element and so forth in the description of the rebirth itself;
thus, its meaning is understood even without the explicit inclusion of the term "sense-sphere element" and so on. Therefore he said:
“...the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*) ... is not discerned. “To be analyzed” means to be divided. Since a twofold division is intended here, he says:
“The meaning is that it should be made twofold. Questions and answers are “questions-and-answers.
Just as it must be stated that “there are no analyses of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*),” because their non-existence is not understood when they have not been mentioned, so too...
Therefore, this [question]—"How many latent dispositions (anusaya) are there?"—should also be stated as referring to that [classification]. For an answer depends upon the question.
The commentary on the Section on Elements (Dhātuvāra) is finished.
The commentary on the Latent Dispositions Yāmaka (Anusayayamaka) is finished.
8. Cittayamaka: Commentary on the Section of Enumeration (Uddesavāra), 1–62.
Regarding the phrase "with lust, etc. (*sarāgādi*): here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), [it is intended to include] the passage: "In whom a mind with lust arises, but does not cease," and so forth.
It includes everything from the section beginning with "whose mind is not liberated" up to that point.

Furthermore, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "wholesome and so forth," it includes everything from the section beginning with "whose wholesome mind arises and does not cease" up to the section ending with "whose mind accompanied by lust arises and does not cease. Therefore, [the phrase] is "by means of the wholesome and so forth, such as those with lust (*sarāga*)."
