The mixed sections consist of those [terms] not liberated from passion and so forth, and those not subject to conflict (araṇa) such as the wholesome (kusala) and so forth.

The "pure" ones are the absolute, unmixed [sections] with the aforementioned [terms] such as those with passion and the wholesome. "Three by three" means three major sections each, according to persons (puggala) and phenomena (dhamma).

However, this does not include matter originated by kamma and so forth. The phrase "some say" refers to the Elder Dhammasiri.

He says, "It has been stated. And that statement of theirs is not as it was uttered by them; the meaning is that this proposition is inconsistent.

"Those" refers to the indeterminate (abyākata) states, which possess arising and cessation. [This applies] when they are non-existent...
And [this applies] to the moments of arising and cessation, as in the case of Nibbāna.
Regarding persons apprehended by way of determination (*sanniṭṭhāna*): among them, some possess the moment of arising of unwholesome or indeterminate consciousness;

In that context, even for a consciousness that has already arisen: by the phrase "by way of the culmination of the future state of the wholesome," it is indicated that everything possesses identical characteristics (*samānalakkhaṇa*) through its status as the immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*) following the supreme path (*aggamagga*), which constitutes the culmination of the future state of wholesome phenomena.

By what means? Precisely by that same state of having identical characteristics. "This is the method" means that just as the non-arising of the wholesome [is the cause] for the future state of the wholesome...

Since it is obtained even from what precedes the stated limit because it constitutes the conclusion, this method is shown [in the text] as follows: "That aforementioned limit is merely a characteristic.

"As in the Analysis of the Pairs on the Faculties" means that just as in the *Indriya-vibhaṅga* the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is enumerated immediately after the male-faculty (*purisindriya*) and not after the mind-faculty (*manindriya*), so it is in this *Indriya-yamaka*. In that context, just as the term "life-faculty" (*jīvitindriya*) is a general designation for both the material life-faculty and the immaterial life-faculty, so too is [the term] *upādinnassa* [a general designation].
Regarding the phrase "and of that which is not clung-to," he said: "It is the protector of both those born of karma and those not born of karma.
Alternatively, the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is not only the cause for the momentary persistence of co-nascent phenomena, but is also the cause for the non-interruption of their continuity.

This was stated without distinction; and [it is] the sustainer of those things born of karma that occur during death and rebirth-linking.

"Iti" means therefore. "Rooted in that" means rooted in the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "By way of death, rebirth-linking, and occurrence" means by way of death and rebirth-linking, and by way of occurrence.

It should be stated. As for the fact that the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) was taken last of all among those rooted in the eye-faculty and so forth, in that case—
The reason has already been stated in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

By this, he establishes through reasoning that the material life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) shares the same status as the eye-faculty and the others. [This is also established] from scripture (āgama).

"Shown by the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*)" means that by this [phrase], he shows that "at the moment of arising of the rebirth-consciousness" is merely an illustration.

Therein, "just as" refers to how, by way of a single part, [the state] obtainable at the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*) of many such consciousnesses [is used to represent] the very first one...

likewise here too, that which is obtained during two moments is demonstrated by means of the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*), which is one part of those two—thus the purpose of the demonstration should be understood.

"Of these" refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) and so forth. "Elsewhere" means in the course of existence (*pavatta*). "Here" means in the division of future time. It is not the case that it does not occur.
Because, just as in the moment of rebirth (*upapatti-khaṇa*), the period following that—namely, the moment of occurrence (*pavatti-khaṇa*)—is also of the nature of the future time.
Therefore, because arising as intended is possible even elsewhere than in rebirth;

and showing that this meaning is also seen in another passage, he says, "And having done so," etc. He establishes that very point with the words beginning "For not... and so forth. In that context, *api*...
Regarding "of one with a final... pe ... rebirth-linking": by the word *api* (also/even), he shows: "How much more so for one in his final existence who has a rebirth-linking accompanied by joy.
Since for one in his final existence it cannot even be said that "the faculty of joy will cease after death," he says, "prior to death.
For here, in the first series of questions, [the terms] "the sense of certainty" (*sanniṭṭhānattha*) and so forth [are used].
This is the summary of the meaning: here, in the dyads such as "for whom the eye-faculty will arise," the meaning contained within the affirmative statements refers to those initial questions.
The "basis for the meaning to be asked" means that one such as myself serves as the basis for the meaning to be inquired about, beginning with "for him the joy-faculty will arise."
An object similar to me possesses the faculty of arising at the moment of rebirth, being accompanied by the faculty of the state of arising;
or it possesses both faculties of arising, being accompanied by the faculty of the state of arising during both rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
Even when turning back, the basis for the matter to be asked is indicated by the phrase "or for whom," and so forth, referring to that which is to be asked after turning back.

"Support for one who has doubt"—with this intention, in the second questions such as "Or for whom the faculty of mental joy will arise," it determines the meaning that is indeed comprised by the word of certainty, for the sake of certainty itself.
It does so in those very same first questions mentioned previously. [The question] to be asked is: "For him..."
In such passages as "the faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya) will arise," arising—which is grasped in its own form merely by way of its future state—is what is designated as "arising.

Likewise, in such passages as "his faculty of mental joy will cease," cessation—which is grasped in its own form merely by way of its future state—is what is designated as "cessation. This does not restrict the meaning of the doubt. Thus.
In the manner stated, there is a restriction regarding a matter of certainty, not regarding a matter of doubt; therefore it was said: “Or else, for whom...
[etc. ... yes. This is the method: this same method that was explained in the section on arising (*uppādavāra*) applies also to the section on cessation (*nirodhavāra*).
For likewise: “Or else, for whom the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) will cease, for him the faculty of the eye (*cakkhundriya*)...”
"Will it cease? "Yes," it is said.
"Because it is not stated thus" means because the arising and cessation of the future [phenomena] are not stated in their own form (*sarūpena*).
For they are not stated there in their own form; rather, they are stated by way of negation as "it will not arise. "Therein" refers to the forward order (*anuloma*).
It should not be applied in this way in reverse order. He explains that very non-applicability with the words beginning "For just as... The construction is as follows:

just as it is impossible to apply [the sequence] by asserting that arising and cessation occur after having transcended arising and cessation, so too it is impossible to apply [the sequence] by asserting that arising and cessation occur without having reached arising and cessation.
And while both of these [possibilities] are possible in direct order, they are not so in reverse order.

Therefore he said: “It is not thus... [as before] ...it does not occur. Therein, he states the reason: “Because the occurrence of the non-existence of what has not arisen... [as before] ...is untenable.

“Of the non-existence of what has not arisen” means of the non-existence of what has not arisen; the intention is that it refers to the non-existence of the arising and the cessation of what has not arisen. Therefore he said:
“And the absence of the arising and cessation of what has not arisen is asked about in the reverse order,” and thus: “Yes, it is so.”

And it is said: "the answer was not stated"—this is the connection. Regarding the phrase "of this unreal non-existence devoid of distinction," it means that while some non-existence, such as the non-existence of form (*rūpābhāva*) or the non-existence of feeling (*vedanābhāva*), is accompanied by a distinction, this is not so for an unreal non-existence devoid of distinction.
"Because of the absence of connection with another time" means because of the absence of connection with a specific time.
"Of whatever kind" means of those elements (*bhūta*) that are not present but are capable of arising when conditions are met; the meaning is "of those [elements] in the future.

"Of that which is to be asked by way of the absence of arising and cessation" means of that which is to be asked thus: "It will not arise, it will not cease," by way of the absence of both arising and cessation.
Of the meaning. "Supported" means having a support; it is determined by a definitive conclusion (*sanniṭṭhāna*) and is included within the category of words of definitive conclusion.

Those for which the aforementioned meaning is the support are "supported by that. This is by way of negating the non-arising and non-ceasing of precisely such future occurrences and cessations—namely, the arising and cessation designated as birth and death—and [it applies] to life and so forth as well.
[The same applies] to the life-faculty, the non-faculties, and so forth. The terms "non-arising" and "non-ceasing" are questioned by means of the phrase containing doubt:
"For whom the faculty of mental joy will not arise, for that person will the faculty of mental joy not cease?
It is stated, "Yes," because there is nothing further to be said after analyzing [the question]. Therefore, he said: "It was not stated... [etc. ...the answer."
The construction is: "Those who will have a rebirth-linking with equanimity in the fine-material world (rūpaloka) are included.
"By way of having a characteristic identical to that" means by way of having a characteristic identical to that state of having a rebirth-linking with equanimity.
That [reading] was written down erroneously, because there is no such statement in the *Dhammayamaka*. Whatever needs to be said regarding that has already been stated in the *Cittayamaka*: "No..."
For there is the conventional expression "it arose" regarding what is present at the moment, as in the phrase "there is," and so forth.
The commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra).

"By means of the worldly indeterminate [states]" (lokiya-abyākatehi) means by means of those indeterminate states that are distinct from the fruits, the dhammas, and Nibbāna. "Dependent upon those" (tāni upādāya) means dependent upon those worldly indeterminate states.

For the mental faculty and so forth, which share the same destiny as those [states], their status as something to be fully understood (pariññeyyatā) is stated in such passages as, "Does he fully understand the aggregate of feeling? "Yes," and so on, just as it is for the aggregate of feeling and the others. For whatever is to be fully understood...

This is stated by the passage beginning with "one thoroughly understands that very [object]," and so forth. Even though the meaning has been established as non-erroneous, the objector raises an objection by seizing upon a possible pretext found in the phrase "because of being mixed," saying: "If, because of being mixed with what is to be fully understood... and so on. The meaning of this is:

just as here the state of being "to be fully understood" is stated for things that are mixed with those to be fully understood, so too should that state be predicated of them in other instances as well.
Likewise, there is the necessity of developing those things that are mixed [in their nature]. Therefore he said, "Why [is it] in the *Dhammayamaka*? and so forth.

Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome, there is an adherence to development and abandonment; by means of this, it is stated: "He abandons that unwholesome state and develops the wholesome," and so on.

It is not the case that they are indeterminate (abyākata); for, just as in one instance [it is shown] how the wholesome and so forth arise from the door of contact, so too is there a method for their arising from the door of consciousness.

Thus he shows that there is no way of explaining the "to-be-thoroughly-understood" nature (*pariññeyyatā*) for the indeterminate (*abyākata*) states and so forth, as there is for the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and the rest.

"Not grasped by way of being wholesome or unwholesome" means not grasped by way of the nature of origination (*samudayasabhāva*). "Even though they are wholesome or unwholesome" means even though they possess the state of being wholesome or unwholesome.

They exist even without the states of being "to-be-developed" (*bhāvetabba*) or "to-be-abandoned" (*pahātabba*), namely those which do not belong to the side of the Truths of the Path (*magga-sacca*) or Origination (*samudaya-sacca*).
Just as in the expression “form is impermanent,” the particle *eva* functions solely to exclude its opposite— meaning that form is indeed impermanent and not permanent—
without precluding its other qualities such as suffering or non-self; likewise, in the phrase “it must indeed be abandoned,” the word *eva* excludes only its opposite,
namely that which is not to be abandoned, and does not preclude other specific distinctions from it.

Showing this, he said, "By this, only that which is to be abandoned," and so forth. The very state of being something to be developed is grasped for that faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*), because it is understood as the attainment of the highest excellence. Why was it said, "What was to be written later has been written out of order"?

For the passage beginning with "two persons" was extracted from the direct order (*anuloma*), while [the section] beginning with "he does not fully understand the eye-faculty" and so forth [belongs to the reverse order].

However, in the reverse order (*paṭiloma*). The statement "they do not abandon the faculty of mental distress" (*domanassindriyaṃ na pajahanti*) is an explanatory gloss for the Pāḷi phrase "nor do they abandon the faculty of mental distress.

As for what was said—that "this was stated having moved beyond the basis of the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriyamūlaka*) to the basis of the faculty of mental distress"—that was said with reference to what has come down in the reverse order.
This is not appropriate; for the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā do not skip over a word that appeared first and provide an explanation of the meaning of a similar word that appeared later.
Indeed, in the Aṭṭhakathā, the explanation of the meaning was undertaken and concluded strictly according to the sequence of the words;
therefore, it should be understood that it was written in regular order, not in reverse order.
Because [the section] beginning with “two persons” has been extracted from the *anuloma* (direct order) that was presented there.

“In this” means in this section on full understanding (*pariññāvāra*). “Six persons” refers to the six persons starting from the worldling (*puthujjana*) up to those standing on the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimaggaṭṭha*).
It is taken without breaking [the sequence], because in that context no distinction of function between those capable and incapable has been included.

However, showing that where there is the common application of the term "worldling" (puthujjana), it refers to those capable [of attaining the path], and where it refers to those incapable, it refers specifically to those [incapable ones] by distinguishing them, he said:
"Those worldlings who will attain the path, and those worldlings who will not attain the path," and so forth. "Arahā" means a noble one (ariya); this very [term]...
Or this is the reading. "One who possesses the first path and fruit" means one who possesses the preceding path and fruit. "The other" refers to the Arahat.

"Having thus understood the classification of persons": here the worldling is taken as "incapable," here the capable person, here the noble ones (ariya), and those who possess the fruit of the first path up to those who possess the fruit of the supreme path—thus, as it has been stated.

"Having understood the classification of persons. In this context, "in each respective instance" refers to those various passages in the text where these aforementioned persons—namely, the two types of worldlings and the eight noble ones—are presented according to their divisions and non-divisions.
"By way of determination" means by way of a definitive statement or by way of certainty itself. "Having extracted" means having brought forth [from the general].
"The answer should be applied" means that the connection should be clarified by demonstrating the meaning as stated,
in accordance with the text proceeding by way of the answer.
The commentary on the section on full understanding is finished.
The commentary on the *Indriya-yamaka* is finished.
The sub-commentary (*anuṭīkā*) on the *Yamaka-pakaraṇa* is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Introduction to the *Paṭṭhānapakaraṇa-anuṭīkā*:
"By means of the strands of sensual pleasure, etc.
refers to the strands of sensual pleasure, jhāna, direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), mastery over mind, and so forth. "Sporting" means by way of experiencing playful delights.
They delight. "In these" means in the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) and so forth. "Dwell" means they proceed by means of changing postures and other such activities.
"Enemies" refers to adversaries, both external and internal. "Sovereignty" is lordship in various places. "Position" refers to positions such as chief minister, general, or crown prince;

by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), retinue, domain, and the like are included. "Attained through the power of the application of merit" means acquired through the influence of merit consisting of giving and the rest.

And [it is] by means of the power of yoga, consisting of the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), which has been attained. By "radiance" (*juti*) is meant both the radiance of the body and the radiance of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

And here, just as the word *deva* has the meanings of play, desire for victory, conventional usage, radiance, and movement, so too it possesses the meanings of power (*satti*), praise (*abhitthava*), and veneration (*kamana*), because verbal roots have multiple meanings; thus, in the accomplishment of whatever is desired...
Or it is said, "They are able," and so forth.

This statement regarding the Blessed One’s sharing of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and other qualities with his disciples is made merely in respect to their general classification as supernormal powers (*iddhividha*);
however, showing that by their very nature all Buddha-qualities are indeed unique and not shared with others, [the text says]: "In the unsurpassed play of higher knowledge..."
He said, “By means of the supreme divine, brahma, and noble abidings. The construction is as follows:

[the former] by way of what is termed giving—namely, sovereignty of mind, the seven treasures, and so forth—and [the latter] by way of what is termed grasping—namely, right practice, confident faith, and honor.
And here, "grasping" refers to the delighting in the right practice and confident faith found within those [abidings], as well as in the honor being offered by them.

Rejoicing and acceptance are to be understood [as included]. Furthermore, it should be seen that the formulation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-paññatti*) is also subsumed by the very words of the instruction that accord with the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhamma-sabhāva*), because that instruction conforms to the nature of the transgression.

"The range of knowledge" (*ñāṇagati*) is the comprehension of the knowable (*ñeyya*) which is to be traversed by means of knowledge. Regarding the phrase "by being endowed with": this refers to [the state] in such passages as "sporting with direct knowledge" (*abhiññākīḷā*).
Each [term] should be applied individually, as in the phrase "together with the world including the devas" within the section beginning with "because it is to be gone to.

"Those devas" refers to the conventional devas (sammutideva) and so forth. "By those qualities" refers to qualities such as the higher knowledges (abhiññā). The statement "the deva is more worthy of worship" is said because the word *ati* here functions as a synonym for "worthy of worship" (*pūjanīya*).
"More excellent" (*atirekatara*) means "more superior" (*adhikatara*). "Of the devas by birth" (*upapattidevānaṃ*) is stated because of their predominance.
It has been said. For even pure deities exist there; or rather, it was stated thus by taking only the mere state of being a deity born there as applicable to them.
Regarding the opposites—namely, immorality, negligence, and distraction—or the failure in virtue, covetousness, ill-will, and the remaining hindrances.
Showing both meanings by connecting the two ways of interpreting "the seventh among seers" (*isīnaṃ sattamo*, *isīsu sattamo*), he says: "By way of the realization of the Four Truths... and so forth.
...so he said. Or, they are called *isi* (sages) in the sense of seeking virtues such as morality within their own and others' continuums; thus, the Buddhas and other noble ones (*ariya*) are *isi*.
Furthermore, the meaning here should be understood as "the seventh among the *isi*" (*isisattama*), for he is both an *isi* and the seventh.
Regarding the phrase "the cessation of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpanirodha*), in order to show that name-and-form which is to be ceased, [the Buddha] says: "From which consciousness turns back."
He said: "For it is name-and-form included within the round of existence that must be ceased. When that has been ceased, name-and-form is indeed ceased in its entirety.

As it is said: 'By means of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, through the cessation of volitional consciousness, whatever name and form would arise in the beginningless round of existence—excluding the seven [remaining] existences—these cease right here...'"
“When an Arahant attains final Nibbāna by the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining, with the cessation of the final consciousness,
wisdom, mindfulness, name, and form— these all cease, subside, come to an end, and become tranquil.
This teaching is adorned with an exceedingly profound method because it most excellently elucidates the nature of conditions.
The mode of conditions is profound by its very nature. As it is said: "This Dhamma realized by me is profound," and so forth;
and, "Ānanda, this dependent origination is profound and appears profound," and so forth.
Furthermore, this teaching on the *Paṭṭhāna* (the Book of Analysis) with its infinite methods is exceedingly profound.
The commentary on the beginning of the work is finished.

Commentary on the Enumeration of Conditions (*Paccayuddesavaṇṇanā*): “*Samānane*” means in the sense of bringing together, collecting, or making equal; such is the intention of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). In this regard, they will explain later on: “There are two conformities: conformity with the Dhamma and conformity with the conditions,” and so forth.
The meaning of the name *paṭṭhāna* is the meaning of this term "paṭṭhāna.

Since, however, it is conventionally established for the whole by way of its parts, it is said that "the meaning of the names *tikapaṭṭhāna* and so forth is the meaning of the names *tikapaṭṭhāna* and so forth in their respective parts," in order first to show how it is established in those parts.
Alternatively, the meaning of the name *paṭṭhāna* must be determined for the parts themselves.

Because this treatise consists of a mere collection [of words], it was stated—"The *Paṭṭhāna*... its meaning is not [a single thing]"—in order to show that there is no such thing as a "collection" that exists as a distinct entity.
For this very reason, he said: "The convergence of this treatise... and here the synthesis must be explained.
Through the understanding of the meaning of the collection of words, for one who has understood the general meaning of the *Paṭṭhāna* in detail...
Showing that the discourse on the *Paṭṭhāna* (Conditional Relations) is easy to grasp when it is being explained, he said: "For thus... [etc.
...it is so. Therein, "in those" refers to those aforementioned modes of combination of names and meanings.
"Common to all" means common to all the individual components, such as the *Tika-paṭṭhāna*, and to their collective whole. "In its meaning, it involves various states" means...
It is stated that by the very inclusion of the word "modes" (*pakāra*), the manifold nature of those modes is already included. For "patthāna" means a "place" (*ṭhāna*) by way of modes;
it is a manifold condition. Since this [condition] exists here in the sense of being analyzed, it is called *paṭṭhāna*, meaning both the treatise (*pakaraṇa*) and its constituent parts.
And in this sense, it should be understood that the establishment of its manifold nature is shown even from the perspective of the word itself.

In this context, he says, "Even for one... should be understood," showing that both "conditionality in various ways" (*nānappakārā paccayatā*) and "the conditionality of various things" (*nānappakārānaṃ paccayatā*)—that is, "various kinds of conditionality"—are taken together as a single unit either by way of a general description (*sāmaññaniddesa*) or by the method of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*).

[The phrase] "because it has the nature of multiple phenomena" (*anekadhammabhāvato*) means: that which has many phenomena is "multiple-phenomena" (*anekadhamma*); because of that state, [it is so called].

It should be applied. "The state of being a condition of various kinds" (*nānappakārapaccayatā*) refers to the nature of being a condition of various kinds, which is what is called "the meaning of conditions of various kinds" (*nānappakārapaccayaṭṭha*) in the Aṭṭhakathā.
Granted that there is indeed an analysis of the phenomena that serve as conditions in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and other texts, he says, "By this...
he shows," demonstrating that the nature of being a condition is not analyzed there with such primary focus as it is in the *Paṭṭhāna*.

He said: To show that this treatise and its constituent parts possess a preeminent distinction, and to demonstrate the basis for the aforementioned progression of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), he states, "The words 'herein' (*ettha*) are to be supplied.

"Because it is the locus of the path" means because it is the state of being the place of occurrence. "By others who possess movement" refers to those whose knowledge is unimpeded throughout the three times.
Regarding that omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*):
among the teachings taught by way of threefold classification, there is the conventional expression "triads" (*tika*). Thus he said, "Of triads means of those teachings spoken by way of triads.
For they are called "triads" (*tika*) because they have three measures (*parimāṇa*). "Completely" (*samanta*) means from all sides, in every respect; this is what is meant.
He said: "By all modes, beginning with the direct order (anuloma). "Gatāni" means those that have occurred.

"The twenty-four foundations (paṭṭhāna) on all sides" means the twenty-four foundations taken collectively from every aspect, beginning with the direct order. "From all sections beginning with the direct order" means from the four sections beginning with the direct order.
"The sixfold state beginning with the triads" means the sixfold state resulting from the series of dyads (duka) beginning with the triads (tika).

"Ten" refers to the aforementioned method of exposition. "From all the sections beginning with 'conformity to the Dhamma'" (dhammānuloma) should be understood as including the pairs beginning with the "opposing" (paccanīka), the groups beginning with the "co-nascent" (sahajāta), the conditions beginning with the "opposite" (paccanīya), and the roots beginning with the "object" (ārammaṇa).

He says, "they proceed by means of methods that are not deficient," because no other mode besides those already mentioned is possible. These, then, are the aforementioned *Samantapāsādikā* (Compendiums). And this is the commentary on the meaning.
Showing that [this] accords with everything else according to the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he said: "Therefore he said... by way of...

"By way of cause" means by way of a phenomenon whose intrinsic nature is that of a cause. Although a phenomenon whose intrinsic nature is a cause may also function as an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and so forth, it is stated "and of that which has become a predominance-condition (*adhipatipaccaya*), etc. specifically in order to show its particular distinction. "Being a cause, it is a condition."
When this was said, it was determined that the nature of the cause (*hetu*) of the phenomenon (*dhamma*) was being defined, not its specific condition (*paccaya-viśeṣa*);

thus, its status as a predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) and so forth was not excluded. Therefore, he said: "By this too, the same fault follows. "By this" means by the inclusion of the state of being a cause.

"Here" refers to the phrase "root-cause condition" (*hetu-paccaya*). "The inclusion of the phenomenon" means the inclusion of phenomena such as non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth. "A specific capacity" refers to its own...
Power (*bala*) is the state of being a causal capacity, which is also called "taste" (*rasa*).

Although this [power] is not other than the phenomenon (*dhamma*) itself because it is not shared with anything else, it is spoken of as if it were something else because it is obtained only through the conjunction of other conditions. "Of that" refers to the efficacy designated as the state of being a cause (*hetubhāva*).
In the phrase "having become a cause," here too the word *hetu* denotes the state of being a cause, not a phenomenon that possesses the intrinsic nature of a cause.
He says: "It is stated that 'having been a cause, it is also a condition.
And by the words "And having done so," etc., he supports the aforementioned meaning with the canonical text (pāḷi).

If this is so, why is there a statement in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) regarding the conditionality of the phenomenon (dhamma) alone? To this he says: "But in the Commentary," etc. And for this very reason here...
We too have stated: "Even though it is not other than the phenomenon itself, we treat it as if it were other.

If, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), the efficacy of the phenomenon (*dhammasatti*) has been demonstrated in such passages as "for whatever phenomenon is a supporting factor in the sense of being a root," then why is it that here the efficacy of the phenomenon alone is demonstrated by way of its state as a cause (*hetubhāva*)? This is the objection.
Having taken this into account, it was said: "Or here too... [etc. ...he shows.
However, showing that it is not possible to deny the manifestation of the penetration of the Dhamma (*dhammasatti*) in this context, he said "For not...
and so forth. It is called "meaning" (*attha*) because meaning exists for it; it is stated as "a word expressing meaning. Thus, it is said that "meaning" refers to a word that conveys meaning.
Therefore he said: "And that is a term common to both arising and persistence. For the word "that" refers back to the expression "it proceeds" (*vattati*).
Alternatively, the meaning of the root *eti* is "it goes"; thus, the meaning of the word "goes" is the action of proceeding (*vattana*) in this context.
And "that" refers to that very proceeding. In this sense, it is called a "common term."
Here, the word "vacana" (speech) should be understood as a synonym for "meaning" (*atthapariyāya*), based on the fact that it is "spoken.
One might suspect that whatever serves as a condition for arising also serves as a condition for persistence; therefore, to dispel that suspicion, it is said:
"For some... [the] causes and so forth. And here, just as there is a condition for the arising of those things that ought to arise, only when that condition exists...

Arising and passing away; likewise, even for those things that persist, their persistence should be understood as occurring solely by way of the condition of presence (*ṭhitipaccaya*), just as co-nascent phenomena [persist] by way of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
As for those who deny the persistence of immaterial phenomena, what must be said about them has already been stated above.

Just as the word *hetu* has the sense of a "basis" when used in the locative sense (*adhikaraṇasādhana*), so too it is appropriate for it to have the sense of "arising" when used in the instrumental sense (*karaṇasādhana*).
Demonstrating this, he said, "It goes," and so forth. From such statements as, "Greed is the source for the origination of kamma," the fact that causes are the source of kamma should be understood.
"By this" means by the statement that the state of being wholesome (*kusala*) is established by something other than the causal condition (*hetu-paccaya*). "Some teachers" [hold this view].

"By its own nature" means that just as a lamp, which illuminates other forms, has no need for another agent to illuminate those forms because it possesses the inherent nature of illuminating by itself, so too [the wholesome roots] have no need for another [factor] to establish the state of being wholesome and so forth for others, since they possess that very nature.
He shows that there is no need for a factor to establish its own status as wholesome and so forth, because it is wholesome by its very nature.

With the words beginning "But since," he shows this meaning: that the wholesomeness of non-greed and the rest is not established by their own nature alone, because they possess a dual nature, just like the contact and other factors associated with them. However, that wholesomeness and so forth is dependent upon something else.

"No phenomenon does not exist": among the sixfold phenomena of the conditioned and unconditioned—classified as form and so forth—not a single phenomenon fails to be an object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
This state of being an object-condition has already been explained below in the commentary on the Analysis of the Elements (*Dhātu-vibhaṅga*).

"Dependent upon the prior formative volition" means that which was established previously in the manner described by the phrase "one who possesses desire," etc., namely, the mental formative volition.
Regarding "the decisive support" (*upanissaya*): in the phrase "in the mind" (*citte*), this designation should be understood as referring to the mind by way of its predominance.
For it is not the mind alone that is so conditioned; rather, the mental states associated with it are likewise conditioned. "Accomplishing" (*sādhayamānā*) means exercising control.

Here, "exercising control" refers to conforming to that particular mode [of desire, etc.]. For when desire and the other factors are inferior, middling, or superior, the associated states likewise become so.
They proceed in such a manner. Therefore he said: "Because they follow along with that state of being inferior and so forth.

"By that" means either by bringing them under one's own control, or by proceeding under their control. By those [states], desire and the rest become dominant conditions (*adhipatipaccaya*), because they proceed as the counterparts of things dependent upon oneself.
An object worthy of esteem is a sublime state (*mahaggata-dhamma*), an alluring state, and so forth.
"Succession of immediate arising" means the state of arising immediately after this or that particular consciousness.

"Of that which has been distinguished by its respective cooperative conditions" means having attained a specific quality characterized by the capacity to produce that [consciousness] through various cooperative causes such as the object and so forth.

"By that very same [capacity]" refers to that very capacity for flowering when the scar is removed, which was present during the application of the scar but had found its opportunity once the scar was gone.

It is said that "there is a distinction in meaning even by way of prefixes," which refers to the difference [in meaning] from the mere verbal form (*saddatthamatta*). "From the meaning of the expression" (*vacanīyatthato*) means from the meaning of the state (*bhāvatthato*).
For the meaning of the state is also called "expressible" (*vacanīyo*) because it is to be understood in accordance with the grasping of the expression.
"Because there is no interval between cessation and arising" (*nirodhuppādantarābhāvato*) means because there is no intervening factor between the preceding cessation and the subsequent arising.
"Capability for arising without interval": by this, he precludes the doctrine that cessation arises at the same time as the cessations themselves.
For if there were simultaneity, there could be no suspicion of an intervening gap, since there would be no spatial configuration (*saṇṭhāna*).

The construction is: "having brought it, as it were, into a state of identity with itself, because of the absence of distinctions such as 'this is below,' 'above,' or 'across. Indeed, through the absence of spatial configuration, which is characterized by non-obstructiveness (*appaṭighabhāva*), [it is so described].
The absence of division; by that, it establishes a state of being immediately contiguous as if there were unity. However, because there is no simultaneous existence, it is produced immediately after.

It is called an "aspect" (*ākāra*) because it is made manifest by knowledge through its differentiation; it is the distinction in the occurrence of phenomena. [This refers to] the attainment of the fruit of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The construction is: "by way of the immediate succession of cessation and arising. "Previous death" means the death prior to the arising of the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*).
If there is no interval of time, how is it that this statement—"having entered the attainment of cessation for seven days and having passed five hundred eons"—is spoken?
To this he says: "For of them... would not be said," etc. [Objection: Is there not, however, a continuity of material form (*rūpa-santāna*) between those two?
He says “it indeed proceeds” with reference to the inquiry: “And yet... because of having different continua.
To the objection that if this were so, they ought to have mutual assistance just as they have distinct and separate continua, it is said:

“Material and immaterial... do not exist [in that way]. By this he shows: although material and immaterial phenomena occur in a single person, they do not specifically possess the state of being mutually assisting one another.
They proceed, yet because they possess dissimilar intrinsic natures and thus arise as distinct continua, they do not act as obstructions;
for, according to the principle of continuity, they are not mutually included within one another, which is why it is said that "they are dissociated from one another and unblended.
Furthermore, that which is called a "benefactor" certainly exists even between those whose continua are entirely separate.
One should understand that the non-difference of the mental continuum does not exist merely on that account; rather, their lack of intervention must be understood even more strongly.

Just as the uninterruptedness of thought-moments (*cittuppāda*) of the same class is clearly manifest through their state of immediate succession (*anantarabhāva*), it is not so for those of different classes.

With this intention, it was said: "just as [the intervention] of one impulsion (*javana*) immediately following another impulsion, or of one life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) immediately following another life-continuum."
Regarding the phrase "and here the state of condition": here, the word *ca* (and) has a distributive sense (*byatireka*).

It illuminates that specific distinction by which the moment of arising is [distinguished] here. By the word *ādi* (etc. in the expression "of the immediate condition, etc.," it includes the contiguity condition (*samanantara-paccaya*).
The delimitation of the prior and subsequent limits consists of the existence of what precedes and follows, or the arising and ceasing based thereon; [this applies] to those things thus grasped.
The meaning is: "included within the three moments. Therefore he said: "not receiving the designation 'it arises'.
For that which possesses the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) is called "it arises. Thus it has been stated: "In the moment of arising, it is 'arising,' not yet 'arisen';

in the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*), it is 'arisen,' not 'arising'. "That" refers to the state of being a condition such as the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*). "Indeterminate" means...
"Devoid of delimitation by way of time" means that there is an absence of delimitation by way of the past and the future.
"Precisely for that reason" means because phenomena are grasped as being delimited precisely by way of time.
"By way of its being manifest as a condition for arising"—this is an indication of its status as an illustration. For it is established...
This is the illustration. "Of those arisen by way of conditions" means produced by conditions; the intention is that they have become one's own fruit.

"By way of co-arising" means by way of arising together. For the state of being an assistance to phenomena that arise together with oneself, by virtue of their state of co-arising, is "co-nascence conditionality" (*sahajāta-paccayatā*).
By this, it should be understood that they also assist them at the moment of their persistence. For in this way...
The illustration, “like a lamp for illumination,” is also very appropriate. For a lamp is indeed a condition for the persistence of illumination.

By the phrase “precisely by way of mutualness,” he shows the absence of confusion regarding the characteristics [of the conditions]: it is not merely the state of being a helper to that which assists oneself through such relations as co-nascence and so forth that constitutes the condition of mutuality;
rather, it is specifically by way of the state of being a condition of mutuality. Thus, there is no mixing of defining characteristics.
This shows that the mutual condition (aññamañña-paccaya) does not function in the absence of conditions such as co-nascence (sahajāta). Therefore, it says: "not by way of co-nascence and so forth.
Even though the mutual condition does not exist without conditions such as co-nascence, conditions such as co-nascence can exist even without it;
thus, the mutual condition functions in a manner distinct from the presence of co-nascence and the other conditions.
Having stated, "Co-nascent [phenomena], etc.… do not exist," he said, "And pre-nascent [phenomena], etc.… do not exist," in order to make that same point more evident.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "co-nascent, etc.," it should be understood that dependence, presence, non-disappearance, and so forth are included.
For it is by being established upon the earth element alone that the remaining elements perform their respective functions, just like the derived material forms (*upādārūpa*).
It is said: “The earth element [acts] as the basis for the remaining elements. Here, “in the manner of a basis” means in the manner of a support (*ādhāra*).

And this manner of support should be understood here as their being especially dependent upon it for their existence; for that reason, the primary elements (*bhūta*) are called “that which has no assignable location.
By taking it thus, the fact that the eye and so forth also act as benefactors in the manner of a basis is well-established.

For, apart from the specific quality of being dependent upon them as previously stated, no other mode of support for immaterial phenomena— which have no location— can be found in the eye and so forth.
Although it is true that whatever phenomena arise in dependence upon any given phenomenon, all of them possess the state of being dependent upon that [basis],
yet by virtue of a specific causal relationship, [the support] occurs in accordance with the keenness or dullness of the eye and so forth.
Visual consciousness and the others proceed precisely by way of conforming to that [base];

thus, this specific distinction of theirs is stated on account of their dependence upon it. For in this way, even though there is a commonality in their status as conditions, the distinction between the object-condition (*ālambana-paccaya*) and the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) is established.
This very point has already been clarified in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*. As for the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, they [arise] from their respective supports...
Regarding the phrase "of the aggregates, etc.," the word "benefactors" (*upakārakā*) must be supplied and connected [to it].

When one says that "any cause whatsoever is a support" (*nissaya*), this does not necessarily conform to the definition already stated. By this, he shows that the meaning of "condition" (*paccaya*) here is the meaning of "support. The term "therein" (*tattha*) is in the locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*).
Therefore, it is said: "he specifies. He illuminates the state of being well-made; of what? Of the "condition" mentioned as "its own," which is further qualified by the word *pakata*.
By what means and by whom is it done? It is established that this is by means of its own causes. "In such a way" (tathā) refers to the state of being capable of producing the fruit.

Alternatively, "in such a way" refers both to the manner of production (*nipphādana*) and the manner of attending (*upasevana*). Therein, production is the generation of the fruit through the convergence of causes and conditions;
since that is easily understood, [the author] does not address it here, but instead clarifies only the manner of attending, saying: "Attended... (*upasevito*).
He said, “or. In that context, "causing to adhere" should be understood by way of enjoyment (*paribhoga*). Therefore he said, "the cultivation of enjoyment" (*upabhogūpasevana*).
"By way of cognizing, etc. means by way of cognizing, perceiving, experiencing, and so forth. "By that" means by virtue of the state of having been cultivated as previously described.
The intention is that [this term] is stated for future things as well... let alone for past and present ones.

For even in the case of the present, it is found to exist as a natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) based on such statements as: "By relying upon the present climate, food, and lodging, they arouse jhāna.

Just as those phenomena which serve as postnascent conditions (*pacchājātapaccaya*) for other phenomena are also, in every respect, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions (*vippayutta-atthi-avigatapaccaya*) for them.
Likewise, those phenomena that serve as the prenascence condition for other phenomena also serve as their support and object conditions.
Thus, in order to show that there is no confusion between the modes of these two types of conditions, it is said: "distinguished by the mode of dissociation, etc.;
distinguished by the modes of support and object, etc. For just as the modes of postnascence and prenascence [are distinct].

They are mutually distinct; likewise, the modes such as posterior-arising dissociation and so forth, as well as the modes such as prior-arising support and so forth, are each of a nature differentiated from the others.

By the phrase "by those occurring through the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*)," he indicates that the factors associated with volition also function accordingly toward their own conditionally arisen effects. "Precisely for that reason" means precisely because they provide assistance by way of the nutriment of volition.
By the phrase "of that which is to be done by application," he refers to that which is of a different class and cannot be produced by such application.
It causes [the mind] to turn back. It is stated as "repeated performance" because the sense of repetition (*āsevana*) is evident through its occurrence many times.

However, the occurrence of a single conditioning state (*paccayadhamma*) is only once. "Similar to itself" means similar to itself by way of being an object for immaterial states (*arūpadhamma*), and by way of being white, black, and so forth. This is a qualification of the conditioned phenomenon (*paccayuppanna*);
whereas "producing a nature similar to itself" is [the qualification of the conditioning state].

However, the qualification "state of being a condition" (paccayabhāva) excludes only those things that are of a different genus (*bhinnajātiya*) due to having a dissimilar intrinsic nature (*visadisasabhāva*), and not things belonging to a different plane (*bhūmantara*) and so forth.
For it is not the case that limited (*paritta*) states do not serve as the repetition-condition (*āsevanapaccaya*) for sublime (*mahaggata*) and immeasurable (*appamāṇa*) states.
"Impregnation" (*vāsana*) means causing to take up a scent; here, however, "impregnation" is used in the sense of being like a scent, meaning "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
"In the case of books and so forth" means in the case of books, crafts, and the like. This locative case is used here in the sense of "in relation to," not in the sense of "selection from among.
Therefore, the previously established acts of study and so on, which have books, crafts, and the like as their objects, are referred to as "the preceding, preceding [acts] in books and so forth.
However, since it is the mode of repetition (*āsevanākāra*) that is intended here by way of illustration, he says: "The intention is that they are like the preceding, preceding repetitions."
Or rather, this is the locative case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

For it is the repeated practice directed toward the objects such as the "fetter" (*gantha*) that is called the "fetter," etc., just as the jhāna whose object is form is called "form" in such passages as "possessing form, he sees forms.
Volition, which accomplishes the function for both itself and its associated states, is characterized by way of being the mental activity of consciousness.
He said: "Volition is the application of the mind. "By that" means by that volition.
"Distinguished by the arising of an active process" means having attained a distinction through the arising of the activity of volition, which is termed the application of the mind.
For in whichever continuum wholesome or unwholesome volition arises, it ceases there having produced a corresponding distinction according to its strength; therefore, right there...
When the remaining conditions come together, the resultant and kamma-produced material phenomena, which are its fruits, will arise. Therefore he said: "The remaining conditions... not otherwise.
"Of these" means of the resultant and kamma-produced material phenomena. "By that" means by way of being a mental volitional activity (cittakiriyabhāva). What is there to be said?
Volition is beneficial to those [material phenomena] that are yet to arise even if they are not co-nascent; it is also beneficial to those that are co-nascent.
The meaning is that there is simply nothing to be said.
Regarding the phrase "by way of effortless tranquility" (*nirussāhasantabhāvena*): *ussāha* is effort; one who has no such effort is *nirussāha*;
that very state of being tranquil is *nirussāhasantabhāva*, [and it is] by means of that. Furthermore, "effort" (*ussāha*) is a mode of occurrence of a mental state consisting of activity.
It should be understood that this is what is called "activity" (*vyāpāra*), not "exertion" (*vīryotsāha*).

This [activity] is found with particular intensity in the occurrence of functional consciousness (*kiriya-citta*) among those whose underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have not been eradicated, but it is not so for those whose tendencies have been eradicated.

For that very reason, those [latter] are of a peaceful nature and are devoid of the activity of producing karmic results; nevertheless, because they are occurrences of functional consciousness, they possess exertion.
To further qualify that, it is said: "by way of being tranquil and devoid of exertion.

By this—namely, by the inclusion of the state of being tranquil and devoid of exertion—it shows the state of having dissimilar results (*visadisavipākabhāva*) among the immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) that have reached the state of fruition (*vipakkabhāva*) of that aforementioned tranquility devoid of mere exertion, [characterized] by the state of having an object (*sārammaṇa*), being immaterial, being mental, and being associated with contact (*phassa*), and so forth.
Because it is obtained in this very way. "It" refers to the state of being a result (*vipāka*). Because results cannot be accomplished through effort (*payoga*), [it is said]:

"What is not achieved even for one who has desire? and so forth; for just as wholesome and unwholesome states are produced through the effort of mental volition (*cittābhisaṅkhāra*), results are not to be produced by such effort.
"By effort" means by that which serves as the fundamental cause for the arising of the fruit of karma.
By means of the previous application. This refers to what was stated: "Depending on the perfection of the application, [kamma] ripens," and so forth.
"Otherwise" means without the application. "In the remaining conditions" refers to the auxiliary causes for the production of the result of kamma.

By using the restrictive particle (*eva*), he demonstrates the same point already stated—that whether the application exists or not, it is solely by the fact of having been performed (*kaṭattā*) that kamma produces its result. Regarding the results:
It makes its lack of effort manifest. The intention is that it is not a state of calm like the tranquility found within the mental continuums of meditative attainments (*jhānasamāpatti*).

Furthermore, showing that this tranquility of the resultant states (*vipāka*) is not merely inferential but is established through direct perception, he says, "Precisely because of its state of tranquility," and so forth.
Therein, by the mention of "striking against" (*abhinipāta*), he indicates the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañcaviññāṇa*) by way of their function.
For this very reason it was said: “One does not acknowledge any state through the five types of consciousness other than their mere occurrence.
“Possessing that condition” means possessing the condition of kamma-result (vipāka); the meaning is: those things which are to be assisted by the condition of kamma-result.
[This refers to] non-resultant material phenomena. “Occurring in conformity with the result” expresses the state of being a condition for that which has a tranquil intrinsic nature.
The state of being a support (*upatthambhakatta*) is the providing of reinforcement for those things produced by conditions (*paccayuppanna*) that have arisen from their respective conditions;
however, this is not restricted to the nutriments (*āhāra*), because it occurs in other ways as well.

Having in mind the objection, "If that is so, why is only that [nutriment] included there?", he says: "Even though... by way of being a support. By this, [he distinguishes between] the primary and the secondary.
This shows that the exposition is presented according to the primary [factor], following the proper method.

Although it is stated here without distinction as "by way of being the support for both the material and the immaterial," a general description must be determined as a specific condition according to what is appropriate;
for this very point is made clear by the demonstration of their primary state as supports.
Showing this very point, he said: “For it is by way of being a support,” and so forth.

Contact, mental volition, and consciousness are conditions for the co-nascent states by virtue of their arising together with them; thus he said: “Even though they are producers, [this is so] because the immaterial nutriments [act as conditions].
They possess the quality of being a support because they function as conditions for those states even after their own arising. Even in the absence of...
Because matter that is being supported by its generative function is produced by other respective conditions, he said:

"of the material food that supports matter arising from the four [causes]. To the extent that material and immaterial nutriment are conditions for the arising of their own fruit, to that same extent they are also conditions for its maintenance; thus, it possesses the quality of being a support.
Productivity does not deviate from its nature; therefore, how could nutriment that does not provide support possess productivity?
Thus he said: "But when it is absent... there is none; thus the quality of providing support is primary.
Since nutriment, even while being productive, may also act as a supporter, whereas that which does not provide support is never productive, therefore—
“Exertion” means the state of being a support. Now, showing that the productive nature of the nutriments also occurs by way of supporting, he said, “Even while producing,” and so forth.
“By way of non-interruption” means by way of the continuity of the stream.

If the meaning of “predominance” (*adhipati*) is the conditionality of the faculties (*indriya*), then, this being the case, [one must consider] the faculty-condition as distinct from the predominance-condition.

Having taken into account the question, "What is the difference?", he spoke the passage beginning with "not as in the case of the states that are predominant conditions" (*na adhipatipaccayadhammānaṃ viya*) in order to show that difference to them.
In this context, "obstructing its own occurrence as a predominant condition" refers to other states that are predominant conditions which prevent it from occurring.
"By prevailing over [them]" means by way of its occurrence having been established through prior volitional formations (*purimābhisaṅkhāra*).
"By prevailing through the state of being a bearer. "The state of being heavy" means the state of being the eldest. Herein, this is the summarized meaning:

that state of being the eldest by which desire and the rest prevail, having overcome those factors of equal conjunction that obstruct their own occurrence—just as they would overcome other factors—that is intended here as the meaning of "predominance" (adhipati) in the context of the faculty-condition.
Then, as to the question "What is the sequence?", he says "Then indeed" (*atha kho*), and so forth.

The connection is that among the functions such as seeing, which serve as the signs, the eyes and other [faculties] are to be followed by their respective conditions, such as eye-consciousness and the rest.

Regarding "living" (*jīvane*), it refers to the sustaining [of life] by the co-nascent phenomena together with the life-faculty; and regarding "being happy," etc., it refers to those who are happy, suffering, joyful, sorrowful, or equanimous.

The construction is: "the pleasure and so forth are to be followed by the co-nascent states. By "in their respective functions," one refers back to the functions already mentioned, such as seeing and so forth.
"Those for which the eye and so forth are conditions" means those [states] such as eye-consciousness and so forth, which have the eye and so forth as their conditions.
"Of the eye and so forth" refers to the eye, life, pleasure, faith, and so forth.
"In those functions" means in the functions of seeing and so forth. The meaning of "sovereignty" (*adhipati*) is the lordship of the eye and the other [faculties];

the meaning is that this constitutes the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*). "By following after them" means by following after those eyes and so forth, which are the conditions for the visual consciousness and the rest.
"In that regard" refers to the function of seeing and so forth. And the term "occurrence" (*pavatti*) serves to make manifest that sense of sovereignty. By the follower...

For the meaning of predominance (*adhipati-ṭṭha*) as that which is to be followed is evident in the case of the eye and so forth by way of their specific functions, but it is not so for the two [sexual] natures (*bhāva*).
Showing that for those two it exists merely by way of being such a cause, he said: "But as for the female and male faculties... and so on.
"By conditions" means by conditions such as karma and the like. "From that" means from the state of being the condition for grasping as female and so forth.
“*In a continuum accompanied by that*” means in a continuum accompanied by the femininity-faculty (*itthindriya*) and so forth.

The statement, “The pleasure-faculty and pain-faculty are also included by the mention of the eye and so forth,” was said specifically with reference to the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*); however, by way of the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) and others, they are indeed conditions for material phenomena as well.

“*Consisting of the contemplation of characteristics and objects*” refers to the contemplation of characteristics such as impermanence (*aniccatā*), etc., and of objects such as the earth-kasina (*pathavī-kasiṇa*), etc.
"And by way of close contemplation" refers to those [mental states] that proceed by way of close contemplation.

"Of applied thought and so forth" means of applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), feeling (vedanā), and one-pointedness of mind (citt’ekaggatā). "Having approached and contemplated" means having closely examined;

in its actual meaning, this is simply the clear observation with the eye of jhāna regarding the object of jhāna-contemplation, which is itself reflection. Thus it is said: "It is both beholding and reflecting. For this very reason, he says: "By way of applied thought and so forth."
It is common only to applied thought (*vitakka*) and the others, by virtue of which they alone are called "jhāna factors.

Although the term "the pair of pleasant and painful feelings" is a general expression, because the sense of "contemplating closely" (*upanijjhāyana*) is predominant [in the context of jhāna], it makes known that those [feelings] lack the nature of close contemplation;
thus he says, "the pair of the pleasure faculty and the pain faculty. For that is what is intended here, not the faculties of mental joy (*somanassa*) and mental grief (*domanassa*).

Therefore it was said: "the intention. The factors not belonging to the jhāna—equanimity and one-pointedness of mind—should be understood as being accompanied by the fivefold sense-consciousness, because the factors of jhāna have applied thought (*vitakka*) as their final member. "If this is so": if, by the very mention of the jhāna-factors, the exclusion of those factors not belonging to the jhāna has been effected, then that being the case;
[it is] exclusively, not non-exclusively, like equanimity. For equanimity is non-exclusive.

[Regarding] the state of not being a factor of jhāna (*ajhānaṅgatta*): If the faculties of pleasure and pain were exclusively not factors of jhāna, then how could there be a possibility [of their being so]?

To this he says: "Because they are indicated in the place of jhāna-factors. Alternatively, if the two types of feeling were exclusively non-factors of jhāna, how could there be the conventional designation (*vohāra*) of them as jhāna-factors?
To this he says: "Because they are indicated in the place of jhāna-factors. [The phrase] "even though... etc., is for the purpose of showing...
The construction is: "except for the pair of faculties of pleasure and pain.
If this is so, why are such equanimity and one-pointedness of mind not included along with the two aforementioned types of feeling? To this he says: "Equanimity...

there is," meaning that while they exist, their status as a condition for jhāna does not apply to those accompanied by the fivefold sensory consciousness, but it does apply to others; this is the intended meaning. [The word] "grahaṇaṃ" (inclusion).
The construction is to be understood by bringing in the phrase "of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.
Regarding the expression "from whatever [state]," whether from an unhappy destination or a happy destination, from defilement or purification, it has the sense of "emerging";
this [emerging] occurs either rightly or wrongly according to the sequence. Thus he says: "the meaning is 'rightly or wrongly. In the case of rootless consciousnesses...

Regarding the phrase "they are not obtained," one should understand the restriction here as follows: they are not obtained *only* in the rootless consciousnesses (*ahetuka-citta*), and not that they are not obtained in rootless consciousnesses *at all*.
Therefore, since the non-obtainment in the rootless consciousnesses is certain under the former restriction, it is excluded from their opposites (the other types of consciousness).
Thus he said: "for the purpose of showing the absence of non-obtainment in the root-possessing consciousnesses (*sahetuka-citta*)."
...is said. However, in the second [case], since rootless consciousnesses (ahetukacitta) are fixed in their non-attainment, there must be non-attainment of them without exception.
If that were so, even the presence of the condition for jhāna within any of those rootless consciousnesses would be precluded.

Therefore it was said: "not in rootless consciousnesses," and so forth. In that context, the phrase "for the purpose of showing the absence of attainment" refers specifically to the absence of attainment.
The meaning is that it was not stated for the purpose of showing [that]. By this, the non-attainment of certain things is not excluded. For this very reason, he said:

"In some cases, the attainment of something by someone is not prohibited. When the meaning is understood in this way—that is, when the meaning is being cognized according to the method stated by means of the restriction of the first word—it would be understood as only this much:
that in some causeless consciousnesses, there are certain states of consciousness possessing the conditions of jhāna and the path.
Since it is stated without qualification, one might understand merely that the acquisition of any condition whatsoever is not precluded.

To the question, "What, then, is to be done hereafter? he says: "It is not accompanied by applied thought... [etc.]... performed. Even if it has not been performed, it should nevertheless be understood as having been performed in effect.
The explanation of the meaning by way of emphasizing the final phrase begins with "or for the purpose of showing the absence of acquisition in rootless consciousnesses," and so forth.

"Therefore" means that when this restriction is made—namely, that [these] are not found in rootless consciousnesses—the aforementioned meaning becomes possible; therefore. And in order to show that this meaning also accords with another reading, he says: "By which..."
"By non-attainment," and so forth, was said. "That non-attainment" refers to the non-attainment explained in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*.
"This" refers to this non-attainment mentioned here in the commentary on the *Paṭṭhāna* as "they are not found in rootless consciousnesses.
To show what kind of non-attainment it is, he says, "For just as," and so forth. In that context, "in those with roots" means in consciousnesses accompanied by roots.
"Having gathered together" means having made them non-dispersed. "Making them reach a state of unity" means bringing them to a single state.
In this treatise, however, only the condition of jhāna is stated, because the teaching is primarily concerned with the elucidation of the modes of conditions as they actually occur.
"Evenly" means without unevenness, correctly, or together. "By means of modes" means by such modes as having a single basis, and so forth. "By way of being joined" means...
Because of their association (*saṃsaṭṭhatā*). Now, since that association is, by its very nature, as if many hundreds were attaining oneness, it is said:
"the state of being a benefactor, as if by attaining a state of unity.
And this state of being a benefactor is to be demonstrated by those many [factors] acting together with a single purpose (*ekatta-kāritā*).
"Of those that are conjoined" (*yuttānam*) means of those that are associated, being mutually connected through the aforementioned manner of association.

Furthermore, this state of being conjoined should not be understood as a condition (*paccaya*) among the conditioning factors (*paccayadhamma*) and the conditioned factors (*paccayuppannadhamma*), as is the case with the "association-condition" (*sampayutta-paccaya*).

This is because, in that [mental] context, both [factors] possess an identical nature due to their immaterial (*arūpa*) character; whereas here, because they possess both material and immaterial natures, [the relationship differs].
This is the distinction: "by way of dissociation" means by way of being unassociated. Therefore it is said, "by way of attaining diversity.
Here, this qualification of dissociation—namely, that dissociation which consists in the attainment of diversity—is not a mere absence, as in the case of [terms] such as "dissociated from knowledge";
rather, this state of being a benefactor exists even without association.

It should be demonstrated by its persistence together [with its effect], its performance of function, and so forth. The passage beginning with "For it is not... is an explanation of the meaning stated as "of those that are associated," namely:
"only when such a conjunction exists is there the state of being a dissociation-condition. Therefore he says: "For it is not... and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:
just as the [heart-]base is [a condition] for the aggregates; or co-nascent wholesome aggregates are for mind-originated matter; or post-nascent...

Because of such statements as, “Wholesome aggregates are a condition for this pre-arisen body by way of dissociation-condition,” there exists dissociation-conditionality for those things that are conjoined [with the body] by way of basis, co-nascence, and post-nascence; however, it is not so for those that are not conjoined. … [The same applies to] basis, co-nascence, etc.
… [there is no dissociation-condition]. If this is so, why is a dissociation-condition not stated for material phenomena by way of material phenomena?
He said, "But as for the material phenomena," and so forth. There is no dissociation at all because there is no possibility of association.

For while there might be a suspicion of association between immaterial phenomena and material ones, or between material phenomena and those [immaterial ones], since the characteristic of association does not exist, their dissociation is stated.
Therefore he said: "Association with four; dissociation with four."

When it is said, "There is a bad deed done by me," the existence (*atthitā*) specified as the state of having been performed indicates only the completed state of the action, not its state of being currently accomplished;

thus he says, "The state of existence has the characteristic of having been produced. However, in terms of actual meaning (*atthato*), this existence here should be understood as the fact that the fruit of the action has not yet been produced. As for the phrase, "There is a person" (*atthi puggalo*):
Since that designation must be apprehended, or rather, since the continuity of its appropriation is indeed obtainable, it is said:

"The characteristic of being found is the state of existence (*atthibhāva*). Although the state of existence of a conditioned phenomenon (*paccayadhamma*) consists in its being found from the moment of its arising until its dissolution, nevertheless, just as [it is characterized] from the moment of its arising, so too in the moment of its duration...

The activity [of the cause] is preeminent; thus it is said regarding that which has arisen through conditions: "Even though it possesses the quality of being a producer, its helpfulness consists in its state of being a support through its very existence.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the basis, the object, the co-nascent, etc.," one includes the pre-nascent, post-nascent, and others.
By stating "common" (*sādhāraṇa*), it clarifies the nature of helpfulness as being through existence alone, and not through the status of a support (*nissaya*) or other such relations.
The statement that there is no coexistence of contact and the other [mental factors] does not refer to those included within a single arising of consciousness;
rather, it is said—"when one collection of contact and so forth exists, a second does not exist"—in order to show that they are included within different arisings of consciousness.
This very point is understood precisely through the negation of coexistence by the phrase "there is no coexistence."

This, however, was stated by way of those who do not understand, having opened it up for them. "By that" means by way of the absence of coexistence among the many [factors] such as contact and so forth.

He says "even though" and so on, referring to the objection: "If being a condition by way of non-existence (*natthipaccayatā*) were merely the state of non-existence, it might also apply by way of what is not immediate or what is past.
"Those" refers to the preceding moments of consciousness. "As if giving" means...
Why was it said [that the condition does not give an opportunity]? Does it not indeed give an opportunity? For it has been stated: “It is helpfulness by way of giving an opportunity for occurrence.
True, this is so; however, the word *viya* (as if) is employed to show that, as it were, the conditioning phenomena go to non-existence through such an intention.

Although there is a commonality between non-existence (*natthitā*) and disappearance (*vigama*) in that the conditioned phenomenon is not perceived even when the condition is present, [they are distinguished] in the case of the non-existence and disappearance conditions.
In order to clarify the specific purpose being attained, the phrase beginning with “And here” (*ettha ca*) was stated.
By the mere absence of having been (*abhāvamattena*), meaning by the mere non-existence after having existed;

by this, he expresses the state of being a supportive condition for the subsequent dharma immediately following cessation, just as it is described as “the granting of space. By the phrase “through the departure of its own-nature” (*sabhāvavigamena*), [he shows] that even beyond cessation, because of its state of having departed...

It is said: "The state of having attained cessation. Since the non-existence and disappearance conditions (*natthi-vigata-paccaya*) are stated by way of the non-existence and disappearance of certain conditioned phenomena (*paccaya-dhamma*), when their distinction is shown, the distinction between the non-existence and disappearance conditions is thereby shown. Thus it is said:
"Non-existence is emptiness immediately following cessation; disappearance is the state of having attained cessation. In that context, "immediately following cessation" (*nirodhānantara*)...
The intention is that [the cessation] does not occur simultaneously with the cessation [of the conditioned state]. By the word "tathā" (so), he concludes this point:

just as, despite there being no difference in the conditioned phenomena themselves, a distinction between the causal states of "absence" (*natthi*) and "disappearance" (*vigata*) has been determined, so too is there a distinction between the causal states of "presence" (*atthi*) and "non-disappearance" (*avigata*).

For just as the distinction between "absence" and "disappearance" is characterized by their respective attainment of cessation immediately after the cessation [of the cause], so it is for the conditioned phenomenon.
"By means of the non-approach to cessation while [the factors] are still present, there is the state of being 'not-disappeared'.

But how will this distinction in the nature of conditions—existing within the non-distinction of phenomena—be correctly elucidated when it stands in a form that is difficult to discern? To this he says, "For of phenomena," and so forth.
For the sake of their realization—that is, for the purpose of attaining those specific distinctions among conditions.
Because not even one of the four aggregates is included [in the category of non-conditioned phenomena], the construction is made by changing the case ending from "by way of immediate, etc.
(*anantarādīhi*) to "because of the absence of being included" (*asaṅgahitattābhāvato*). "Other" refers to subtle matter. For that does not function as a pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*).
But has not even material matter been mentioned as having the status of a pre-arising condition in the *Kusalattika*? To this he says, "But as for material matter," and so forth. [This is] elsewhere.

"Even though it has come [in this context]" means that although it does not appear in the triad of the wholesome (*kusalattika*), since it does appear in the triad of the visible (*sanidassanattika*) and others, it is not possible to deny the status of the prior-arising condition (*purejātapaccaya*) for material form; such is the meaning.
The commentary on the enumeration of conditions is finished.
Exposition of Conditions 1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Root Condition (Hetupaccaya). 1.

The state of being a condition by way of the root condition is what is indicated by the term "root condition" (*hetupaccaya*); the meaning is not that it refers to a phenomenon that possesses the root condition.
This is a condition by way of being a cause (*hetubhāvena*).
