And here, as for the state of being a condition that was stated in the first alternative by means of the "cause-condition" (*hetupaccaya*), and that which was stated in the second alternative as a condition by way of being a cause—since these two, in terms of their actual meaning, are simply the state of being a cause-condition for the aforementioned conditioning factors (*paccayadhamma*) toward the aforementioned conditioned phenomena (*paccayuppanna*)—therefore it is said: "In both ways, by way of being a cause."

"It is shown that 'being an assistance' is what is taught as the root-cause condition (hetupaccaya). And just as it is here, so too regarding the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) and the others, one should understand the meaning as follows:
'The state of being a condition by way of an object, or a condition through the state of being an object, is the object-condition,' and so forth.
Thus, showing this, he said, "This method applies to the remaining conditions as well. It is simply the intrinsic nature (dhammasabhāva) [of the dhamma], not...
There is no such thing as a "dharma-power" distinct from the dharma itself. By "beneficial dharma," he means the condition (paccaya-dhamma). "Beneficiality" refers to the state of being a condition.
"Specified individually" means specified by way of the individual [nominative case]; the meaning is that it is specified by the first grammatical case (paṭhamā-vibhatti).
"Tenā" (by this) refers to the first word "hetu," which is presented as a personal pronoun (*paccatta*) and serves as a designation for the state of being a condition (*paccaya-dhamma*).

"Etassa" (of this) expresses the meaning denoted by the word "hetu. For although that [condition] is divided into many categories—sixfold, ninefold, and twelvefold—it is spoken of in the singular number by unifying it as one through the commonality of its nature as a cause (*hetubhāva-sāmañña*). "Dutiyo hetusaddo" (the second word "hetu")...

Having brought [the following] into connection: because of the addition of the phrase "of those associated with the root," it is stated: "Being a condition for those associated with the root, it is a condition only for those associated with the root, not for those dissociated from the root.
Such is this passage. For it is not the case that the root-condition does not exist at all for phenomena dissociated from the root. [This refers to] the word *sampayutta* (associated).

It is said, "Because of the dependence of the word *sampayutta* on its relation," because when "associated" (*sampayutta*) is stated, one must necessarily look for another related term to answer the question, "Associated with what?
Therefore he says, "Another... is understood. This is not an absolute rule;
this refers to the meaning previously stated in the passage beginning, "In the absence of a second word 'cause' (*hetu*)," and so forth. This is not an absolute [rule].
The meaning is that it is not the case that a word seeking another [qualification] must always be a qualifier of something else; this is not possible in every instance.
By the phrase "indicated as a primary referent" (*paccattaniddiṭṭho*), he states that the first word *hetu* does not depend on the word *sampayutta*.
Therefore it was said: "It is occupied only with the sense of 'condition' (*paccayo*) here through the suffix *-ya*. "Unqualified" (*avisittā*) means not specified.

Thus, just as the associated states are not specifically distinguished when the word "cause" (*hetu*) is occupied elsewhere because it is intent upon another function, so too, when the word "associated" (*sampayutta*) is used without the qualification of the word "cause," there might be a non-specific inclusion of all associated states, since that term is occupied only with its own primary meaning.
Therefore, it was said: "by the word 'associated,'" and so forth. [This refers to] that which is not associated with nutriment or the faculties.
"By way of non-existence" means by way of the non-existence of a state of consciousness that is not associated with the nutriments and the faculties.

For there is no arising of consciousness devoid of contact, volition, consciousness, feeling, and life-faculty. Therefore he said: "That which is to be excluded... [etc. ...that has not been done. "To be excluded" refers to that which is dissociated from the cause.
"Even so" means even when it is understood by the second word "cause," the undesirable consequence does not follow. Even though the causes are many, this is a general designation.
Nevertheless, the intention is that [the term] is specified as a qualification for the sake of a general indication. Therefore it was said:

"Because it is stated... individually... By the phrase "even without a second word 'cause' (hetu), the state of being associated with a cause is established," he points back to what was previously stated:
"This is not an absolute rule. However, the expression "not of the causes" refers to the cause's status as a condition (*paccaya*).
This was said with reference to one who might suspect that because [the cause] has already been grasped, its being grasped as a "conditionally arisen state" would not be logical.
For this very reason, he said: "In this way too, there might be grasping. The word "so" refers to the second term *hetu*.

Others, however, analyze the compound *hetusampayuttakānaṃ* here as a dual compound meaning "of both the causes and the associated states. They are independent in their nature as mere bases, and so forth.
The states of cause, jhāna, and path perform the function of being conditions for other states solely by way of their establishment, contemplation, and outlet, without depending on any other states.
"Sāpekkhā eva" means precisely "dependent on others. "Āharitabbaisitabbā" refers to those states that are to be assisted by the conditions of nutriment, faculties, and so forth.
"Tasmā" means because those [states] upon which it depends assist their own conditionally arisen states solely by way of being conditions.
They remain having delimited [them]; therefore he said: "Even without them... it is not made. They delimit, that is, they distinguish.
"That" refers to the second mention of nutriment and faculty. "Therein" means in the exposition of the conditions for nutriment and faculties.
And not only there, but here too—in the exposition of the root-condition—by the second mention of the root, [the conditions] for those things arisen through conditions [are shown].
Furthermore, there is no need for a further qualification. Why? Because the other causes—both those associated with it and others—are not excluded by the cause that has itself become the condition.

He states that the word *taṃ* (that) functions as a correlative reference to the very term already mentioned, since the exposition is dependent upon the preceding statement. When [the meaning] has become manifest...
The meaning occurs in this way; and the state of being manifest (pākaṭībhāvo) is to be understood from its being expressed by a word that does not depend on anything else.
It is "not to be depended upon" because it is occupied with another meaning. "Another" (añño) means other than the causal word (hetusaddo).
There is no indicator of what is to be demonstrated mentioned [here] which could receive a correlative reference (paṭiniddesa) by means of the word *taṃ*.
If this is so, how is it to be understood in the phrase “of those originated by that”? To this he says:

“But by this [phrase] ‘of those associated with the cause,’ etc. In this context, although the word *hetu* (cause) itself denotes those associated with the cause, the particle *pana* (but/however) clarifies a distinction from the word *hetu*, namely, the making manifest of those things to be demonstrated that are obtainable within the term *hetusampayuttaka*. Thus: “Of those associated with the cause.”
He states that this compound word has the meaning of the latter member as its primary referent with the phrase, "by means of the expression 'arisen from conditions'.
And because it expresses only a portion of the intended meaning, since it serves as a qualifier of phenomena, he says, "by means of [the term] 'incomplete'.
A qualifier, moreover, is dependent upon that which is to be qualified; thus he says, "dependent on another expression, namely 'arisen from conditions'. This is because it has already been so stated.
Since there is no [explanation] without a specific reference, it is said, "by what was stated previously.
Regarding the phrase "to be demonstrated by the word 'that' (*taṃ*)," he asks, "What indeed is to be demonstrated by the word 'that' in the expression *taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ*?
[The answer is: "Those which are both roots... [etc. ...associated with roots."
The connection is that by means of the word *ca* (and), the terms "cause" (*hetu*) and "associated" (*sampayutta*) are made manifest as those things to be demonstrated.
"In another way" (*aññathā*) means in a manner other than the mode stated by the phrase "by which causes," etc.; showing that other mode, he says:
"Those causes... [omission] ...when there is a connection. "Here" (*idha*) refers, by a locative indication, to the connection just mentioned immediately prior.
He clings. "By that very [word]" means by the first word *hetu* itself.

"To be demonstrated by the word *tam*" means that just as they are clearly indicated by the word *tam* in the phrase "arising from that" (*taṃsamuṭṭhānānaṃ*), so too in the previous objection regarding the phrase "associated with that" (*taṃsampayuttakānaṃ*), they ought to be clearly indicated in the same way by that very word *tam*. And this being the case, of that which is to be demonstrated... [etc.]

It would not be logical. Or, by setting aside the twofold inclusion of "cause" (*hetu*), he challenges the status of that which is to be designated by the word "that" (*taṃ*)—without considering the twofold inclusion of cause made here in the phrase "causes [are the conditions] for those associated with causes," and instead saying "for those associated with them"—and he resolves it by stating, "because that which is to be demonstrated is not yet manifest," and so forth.
For this [phrase], "Causes are conditions... [End of excerpt]

This was stated because it was considered a discussion of the root-condition (hetu-paccaya). That was not stated means that the statement regarding mind-originated [matter] was not stated. "Of that" refers to the conascence-condition (sahajāta-paccaya).

It might be argued that the state of being a condition for matter produced by past karma (kaṭattā-rūpa) would not have been stated; however, it has indeed been stated: "One resultant indeterminate aggregate [is a condition] for three aggregates..."

"By way of being a condition for the matter produced by karma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) through the conascence-condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*), the three aggregates are a condition for one aggregate and for the matter produced by karma," and so forth;
therefore, it is impossible to deny that mind and mental factors possess the state of being a condition for matter produced by karma.
"Therein" refers to the exposition of the conascence-condition. For therein it says: "Mind and mental factors [are conditions] for mind-originated..."
In the passage, “matter is a condition for matter by way of co-nascence condition,” only mind-produced matter (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*) is specified.
“Here too” means even in this exposition of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*). “It ought to be so” means that it ought to have been stated as “of mind-produced [matter].
If this is so, why was it not stated in that way? To this he says: “But ‘of mind-produced,’ etc.”

It is specified by way of its not being the originator of all mind and mental factors. By the word "by means of" (vacanena) is meant the statement describing the conascence condition as it has been shown.
For in that description of conditions, only the state of being a condition for mind and mental factors is stated there, not their state of being the originator;
this is the intended meaning.

And it shows their dependence on causes and so forth; for to the same extent that they have a mode of existence dependent on the mind, to that same extent they also have a mode of existence dependent on the states associated with that mind.

"This becomes its object" refers to that which, by way of wholesome or unwholesome volition, is the intentioning at the mind-door through volition, and at the other doors through the application of body and speech;
and it refers to the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) of sensual lust and the rest within the continuum.
This is the object, this is the condition for the persistence and establishment of kamma-consciousness (*kamma-viññāṇa*).

When it has reached the stage of establishment—meaning when the kamma-consciousness, having been impelled by kamma, has attained the state of being capable of drawing forth rebirth—it "grows" (*viruḷheti*).
The meaning is that from that very kamma-consciousness, once the seed of rebirth-consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) has grown, it continues to grow. Alternatively, *patiṭṭhā*...

"Consciousness comes to be": when the condition that serves as the object for the persistence and occurrence of *kamma-viññāṇa*—which is comprised of the formative forces of defilements—is denied, there comes to be the establishment of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) in the future;
and when that rebirth-linking consciousness has been established, is being established, or has grown by way of the production of renewed existence, it grows by way of its state as a seed.
“The descent of name-and-form occurs”—this is how the meaning should be understood here. Therefore he said:
“The conditionality of consciousness for the name-and-form of rebirth-linking has been stated.

Regarding the phrase “when it has already been established”: this refers to the earth that was established even prior to the production of the field’s development. It is simply the acquisition of its own being.

And here, showing that it is a "foundation" (patiṭṭhāna) [of the rebirth-linking consciousness] and not the persistence of those material phenomena whose individual existence has already been acquired, he said:
"The foundation of kamma is the arising from what has been done; thus it is meant.

Regarding "the remaining material phenomena," this refers to the remaining material phenomena such as the earth element and so forth at the moment of rebirth-linking, and during the course of existence (pavatta), it includes all material phenomena of the three continua.
Or it shows mere co-existence. For even through co-existence, there is some slight distinction. "In some cases" refers to distinctions such as nature, time, and existence.
Indeed, in the third type of nature, during the first aeon, there is no group of faculties; likewise, in the fine-material realm (rūpabhava), there is no group of the body.
By the word "etcetera," it includes the groups of the nose and tongue in that same realm, and for the blind and others in the sense-desire realm (kāmabhava).

The aggregates beginning with the eye are grouped together. "Because of the non-existence of anything anywhere" means because of the non-existence of anything at all in the sphere of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
"Of these" refers to the kamma-born materiality (*kaṭattārūpa*) and so forth during the course of existence. For a cause is not a condition for kamma-born materiality during the course of existence;

moreover, there is simply no possibility of [kamma-born matter] being produced from temperature or nutriment. Therefore it was said: "There would be the undesirable consequence of [it being] a condition."
[The opponent says: "It does not exist. [The author replies: But it cannot be so, because such a case has not been raised in the section on the opposites of conditions (*paccayapaccanīya*).

The phrase "this" refers to the statement "because of the warding off of the status of being a condition for the materiality produced by kamma (*kaṭattārūpa*) and so forth during the course of existence," which is the answer to the teaching "the roots [are conditions] for co-nascent states.
However, to show that such an objection is entirely out of place, [the author] says "But the Blessed One... and so forth.
It has been said: "Whatever Dhamma has been taught by the Blessed One in a certain way, that should be understood exactly in that way.
The commentary on the exposition of the root-conditions (*hetu-paccaya*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).

2. Regarding the phrase "at the very moment of arising" (*uppajjanakkhaṇeyeva*): here, "arising" (*uppajjana*) refers to the occurrence, the going forth, or the proceeding that begins from the moment of origination and continues until after the moment of dissolution. "The moment of that" is the "moment of arising"; thus the meaning should be understood.
For this being so, by the word "arising," all states of existing activity are included, just as they are by the word "arisen."

[They] exist; it is not a mere arising. "By that" means by way of being the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for visible forms and so forth precisely at the moment when eye-consciousness and the rest are occurring.
"Not being taken as an object" means not being taken as an object in every respect.
For otherwise, when the aforementioned visible forms and so forth lack the status of being an object-condition, they would simply be "not being taken as an objects. "All forms" [refers to...]
"All visible objects" means all those visible objects (*rūpāyatana*) as many as have come into the range of vision and are situated in a suitable place;
"all of them" is the meaning. "They do not exist together" means they do not constitute a single combined object (*ārammaṇa*).

For even when many things have come into the range of vision simultaneously, whatever there was a prior mental application (*pubbābhoga*) toward, that alone becomes the object, not everything. This is by way of a collection [of colors] such as blue and so forth.
This was stated with reference to the aggregate [of visible objects], not with reference to each individual base of form such as blue and so forth.
For it is only the bases of form combined that are the object of eye-consciousness, not individually and separately; this method has been demonstrated in the commentary to the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*.
As for what is also stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, namely, "each of those [colors] becomes an object-condition individually," that too—
This was said with reference to exactly what has been stated above. Otherwise, the sense-sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana) would not be the objective domain of the mind-faculty (manindriya).
The same principle applies to sound and the other [objects]. For this very reason, he said: "So too are sound and the rest.

In order to clarify by means of the canonical text (pāḷi) the meaning already stated—that they do not exist simultaneously—he said: "For the word 'they go' (yanti) distinguishes [them as] visible forms and so forth."
The first meaning begins with “These which...,” while the latter begins with “They do not exist as one.
Why, then, was it said: “Or rather, the meaning should be taken here also by way of having all things as its object (sabbārammaṇatā), etc.”?

For the quality of having all things as its object for the mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa) does not precede this reading, “Whatever phenomenon (dhamma) it takes as its object,” in the same way that it does precede the canonical text, “Whatever [object] it takes as its basis” (yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha).
It has not been stated [there]. For it is said: "All phenomena are a condition, by way of object-condition, for mind-consciousness-element and for the phenomena associated with it.
Indeed, one should not explain another passage by taking up a meaning that has been presented in its own form immediately before in the text.
For in that context, by way of restriction, six objects are mentioned, beginning with "having visible form as its object," and so forth.
Having stated this, [the opponent argues: "The statement ‘whatever [object] one takes as a basis’ is indeed appropriate as a demonstration of having all things as its object (sabbārammaṇatā).

But here, after first stating that it has all things as its object, how could it be appropriate to say again ‘whatever phenomenon one takes as a basis,’ as if demonstrating that it has all things as its object?
Furthermore, the absence of sequence is already established by the non-specific expression ‘all phenomena’ (sabbe dhammā) itself, precisely because of the sequential order of the objects."

Because they are not taken up [in sequence]. For it should be understood that here the objects are not taken up in successive order as they are for the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu), nor is the absence of such a restriction explained in this case as it was there.
Therefore, the meaning here must be understood according to the method stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.

“Proceeding” means the act of proceeding. For it has been said that the flowing of a river and the standing of a mountain refer to the very activity of proceeding in such a way—namely, without cessation and without interruption. Therefore he said: “They flow without ceasing and without interruption.
“Thus” means: just as the present-tense verb “they flow” was stated, so too the phrase “whatever phenomena arise” expresses arising by way of including everything.

Because they have been grasped from the perspective of the excellence of the object, the term "arise" is stated as a present-tense expression; this is the meaning. Therefore, it was said in the Commentary:
“by way of including all times,” and so forth. And thus it was stated: “the intention regarding the past, future... [etc.]”; the meaning is:
of the past, future, and present states of consciousness and mental factors. “By way of a collection” means by way of being gathered together into a heap by means of consciousness.

The word *adhippāyo* (intention) indicates this meaning: that even without the usage of the present tense, it is possible to construe the sense of the present in the phrase "whatever phenomena arise" (*ye ye dhammā uppajjanti*). Therefore he says, "But these... and so forth.
Although some conditioning phenomena (*paccaya-dhamma*) may be past or future, the conditioned phenomenon (*paccayuppanna-dhamma*) is necessarily present; thus he says, "of the past and future..."
"They do not exist. For either at the moment of arising or at the moment of persistence, that which has arisen by way of conditions must itself be a condition.
Therefore—because the past and future do not exist in the ultimate sense (paramattha)—therefore.

"In them" means in those things arisen by way of conditions. "Having this or that as their condition" (taṃtaṃpaccayā): these have this or that object, such as visible form, as their condition; thus they are "having this or that as their condition. This meaning is shown because they possess a common nature (samānasabhāva).

For there is no difference in intrinsic nature (sabhāva) due to a difference in meaning. Nor is the state of possessing respective conditions demonstrated [in the case of the past and future], because that [possession of conditions] does not exist in them in an absolute sense; since only those things possessing conditions are "dependently arisen," and they are exclusively present.

In order to show the basis for this linguistic distinction—namely, that "whatever phenomenon [is perceived], that very phenomenon [is the object]"—the passage beginning with "And here" (*ettha ca*) is commenced.
For material and immaterial phenomena, even when occurring as groups (*kalāpa*), sometimes serve as objects for consciousness and mental factors individually, and sometimes collectively;
there is no fixed rule in this regard. However, it is simply the prior attention (*ābhoga*) that...
This is the reason for including the word "together" (*saha*). To illustrate this, it may be said that the Blessed One made a distinction in his phrasing;

for when even those phenomena included within a single aggregate are grasped together, the collection as a whole is not grasped because there is no mental application toward it, but rather only the phenomena in their combined state.
Thus, even the inclusion of the word "together" follows the same logic as the separate inclusion [of the word].
Therefore, having stated "whichever" (*yaṃ yaṃ*) in order to indicate the existence of separate inclusion,
and then stating "those those" (*te te*) in order to show that even when there is separate inclusion, all of them together constitute a single object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*),
he says "for the four aggregates," etc., demonstrating this meaning. Therein, "among feeling and so forth" means among the four aggregates beginning with feeling, without breaking them apart.
By way of grasping; but having distinguished them, [it is] by way of grasping among contact and the rest.
"And that which consists of form, etc."—this is stated by way of an object common to subsequent consciousnesses; "and those many contacts, etc."—this is by way of an uncommon object.
"All those"—all those objective phenomena (ārammaṇadhammā), including both the common and uncommon varieties. "Taking each one individually" (ekekameva ārabbha).
Regarding the phrase "they arise," that which ought to be said here has already been stated above.
And the phenomena having visible form as their object are manifold due to the distinction of blue and so forth. "Likewise" means manifold.

By this, it includes the sound of drums and the like, the scent of roots and the like, the taste of roots and the like, the tangible of hardness and the like, and feeling and the like. For by the word "manifold," it refers specifically to those things comprised within various groups.

This states that visible forms and so forth serve as objects for the sense-consciousnesses. For what has been stated in general must be demonstrated by being analyzed according to its specific requirements.

"Of the wholesome and its result" means of the wholesome and of its resultant [consciousness]. As for the phrase "Nibbāna was not previously dwelt in," this refers to the passage beginning with "one who has seen Nibbāna."
This was said with the very meaning about to be explained kept in mind.

For the discernment of Nibbāna by means of the knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*) may belong either to one who has not yet seen the Truths (*adiṭṭhasacca*) or to one who has already seen them. In that regard, first of all, it is impossible for one who has not seen the Truths to discern it, because they have not penetrated it;
as for the other, it is even more evident that it is already discerned—thus, it is discerned by that [knowledge].

The intended meaning is that it is so called. And here, by the phrase "nor has that been stated," he demonstrates through scripture (*āgama*) the absence of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*) having Nibbāna as its object;
then, by the phrase "for not Nibbāna" and so forth, he demonstrates it through reasoning (*yutti*).

In that context, why was it said: "not previously dwelt in, because of being unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*)"? [It is because] even that which has been cultivated through the cultivation of its objective sphere (*gocarāsevanā*),...

"Having dwelt" means because of the desire [to do so]. For it is only one who has already seen the Truth (sacca) who clarifies Nibbāna by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, not one who has not seen the Truth.

However, since that knowledge clarifies not only the aggregates but also things connected to the aggregates, it can be understood that when the aggregates—which have Nibbāna as their object—are clarified, Nibbāna itself is also clarified.
By this, the objection regarding the absence of purpose should be regarded as refuted.

"In the same way, this should also be applied to the knowledge of the future. Just as the fact that the knowledge of recollecting past lives has Nibbāna as its object was demonstrated, so too should it be applied appropriately to the knowledge of the future.
In that context, however, the application should be understood by means of the passage beginning with "At the time of discerning what is bound up with the aggregates," and so forth.
Therefore, it is said "as appropriate. This applies to some who have attained direct higher knowledge (abhiññā) in the fine-material sphere, let alone others.
The commentary on the exposition of the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Dominance-condition (adhipati-paccaya):
Because it carries the burden through association with the burden, it is called "the burden" (dhura). Thus he says: "The burden means the grasping of the burden. Regarding desire (chanda)...
Because its state of being praiseworthy is established by its quality of being a precursor, it is called "the eldest" (*jeṭṭhaka*) in the *Aṭṭhakathā*;
explaining that very meaning, he says "the best" (*seṭṭha*). For it is stated thus in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*: "Having made desire the precursor, it is exerted.
[The phrase] "of the preceding desire" refers to what was stated in the preceding term, "having desire as its dominant factor" (*chandādhipati*), by way of a grammatical analysis (*niddesa*).
By a form identical to the word *chanda*, that is, by a similar mode of expression.
"By what is indicated immediately after that" means by what is stated by way of a subsequent indication following that preceding word *chanda*.

And for that very reason, because it shares the same meaning as that [preceding word], it is connected with it; thus, in the phrase "associated with *chanda*," it is by the word *chanda* itself, excluding the word *adhipati*.
The meaning is as follows: "Of that which has become a condition" means of that which has become a predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*).

"The state of being a qualifier for the associated [states]" means that very state of being a qualifier—designated as the predominance condition—for those phenomena associated with itself. By the phrase "this is the method," it refers to [the passage] beginning with:
"In such cases as 'predominance of energy' [meaning] 'for those associated with energy,' the preceding energy, by its identical form... and so forth.
It refers by extension to the words that ought to be stated.
"The occurrence of the wholesome and the indeterminate" means the mode of occurrence of wholesome and indeterminate predominants (*adhipati*).
"An object not yet obtained" means one that is to be obtained, is obtainable, or can be acquired; however, in the second sense, it means that which deserves to be obtained.
It should be understood. "Disregarded" (*avaññāta*) means, even more so, "not disregarded" (*anavaññāta*).
Wholesome functional states that have reached absorption (*appanā*) are indeed of great power and possess a dominant influence; likewise, those fixed in the wrongness (*micchattaniyata*) are also so.

Thus it was said: "Similar to absorption... they do not arise. "Similar to absorption" means similar to those that have reached absorption. They consist of the obscurations of karma and defilements (*kamma-kilesāvaraṇa*).

And these are those states of wrongness fixed by nature (*micchattaniyata-dhamma*): those which constitute an obstruction of kamma (*kammāvaraṇa*), namely the defilements (*kilesa*) of the immediate (*ānantariya*) type; and those states of fixed wrong view (*niyatamicchādiṭṭhi*).

Herein, the associated volition (*sampayutta-cetanā*) should be regarded as belonging to the side of the obstruction of defilement, just as the resentment (*paṭigha*) associated with the volition of an immediate offense belongs to the side of the obstruction of kamma.
[This concludes] the section on the "Directly Opposed Course" (*paccakkhagati*).
It is said that [the predominance of the object] occurs even without immediate succession, as in the phrase: "even for the sense-sphere gods who have directly experienced the higher realms.
By this, he shows that among them, just like those with immediate succession (*ānantariya*), there are also impossible instances such as the insistence on causelessness (*ahetuka-abhinivesa*).
Regarding the threefold predominance of the object of action (*kiriya-ārammaṇādhipati*), here this "predominance of the object of action" has an internal object (*ajjhattārammaṇa*).
Showing that there is no possibility [of such a condition] whether it be intended as internal or external, he says: "But by way of the division into the sense-sphere and so forth," and so on.
Therein, the connection is: "there is no predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) for those dhammas with an object that belong to the mental continuum of another.

"Because of its non-existence" means because of its non-statement. For "non-statement" indeed signifies non-existence within the *Abhidhamma*, which is the teaching of dhammas according to their true nature.
Thus, by this very [reasoning], it should be understood that even though it has not been explicitly raised or stated, it is implied.
Since there is no dhamma possessing an object (sārammaṇa) that is exempt from the two categories of internal and external objects, one must say "it does not exist";

therefore, emphasizing that very fact of being understood, he said, "even when it is understood as 'it does not exist'. By this, it is stated: "in the external aggregates," and so forth. It must be in form (rūpa) alone...

The intention is that [the term "aggregates"] does not apply to such instances in the formless realm because they are impossible there. And it should be understood that this impossibility is to be known according to the aforementioned scriptural passage.

Why was it stated, “It has been investigated”? Is it not the case that, based on such statements as “one esteems and relishes past aggregates as objects, or future aggregates,” the word “aggregates” (khandha) indeed occurs even in the formless realm in such contexts? [This is so] because the functional process of adverting (āvajjana) exists there as well.
The word "pana" (but/however) is stated here with the intention of resolving the contradiction as seen in the cited text;

however, the non-statement [of certain points] occurs in some places due to the inclination of those to be trained (*vineyyajjhāsaya*) and in others by way of showing the underlying method (*nayadassana*). Thus, what occasion is there for a contradiction?
The commentary on the exposition of the dominant condition (*adhipatipaccaya*) is finished.

4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Condition of Immediate Succession (Anantara-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) The emptiness immediately following cessation as previously described consists in the attainment of cessation, the specific quality of making room, the capacity to produce a consciousness corresponding to itself, the causality for the determination of consciousness, and the capacity to produce [consciousness] immediately thereafter;
and because it lacks any fixed shape, it is most excellent in this regard.

The capacity for uninterrupted arising should be understood as a specific cause for the determination of consciousness (*cittaniyama-hetu*). "By way of element" means by way of the consciousness-element (*viññāṇadhātu*), the mind-element (*manodhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).
For it is only these elements that possess distinct intrinsic natures (*bhinnasabhāva*) and can be stated as such when determining them as immediate conditions (*anantarapaccayatā*);

however, those with non-distinct intrinsic natures (*abhinnasabhāva*) must be stated merely as preceding [moments], placing a distinction before them due to the absence of any further differentiation—namely, according to the classification of wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth.
It has been stated thus. Therefore, he said: "And by way of the wholesome, etc.

However, regarding that which must be stated as the condition of immediate antecedence (anantara-paccaya) by way of the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu), if it were stated there that the mind-consciousness-element is a condition for the mind-element by way of the condition of immediate antecedence, confusion might arise;
for it was previously stated [that the mind-element] exists as the condition of immediate antecedence for the mind-consciousness-element.

Now, if it were said that the mind-consciousness element is the mind element, the distinction between the condition and the conditioned would not be understood; however, when the state of being the immediate condition for the eye-consciousness element and the other elements is stated in relation to the mind element, there is no fixed restriction. Therefore he said:
"And [the mind element is] the eye-consciousness element," and so forth. "In the same way" means "in this very manner" because of the absence of a fixed restriction. "Therefore" [means]...

Because otherwise, in a teaching different from this, these faults would follow: the absence of distinction between conditions and conditionally arisen states, the interruption of the demonstration of specific types of consciousness, and the absence of a fixed rule;
therefore [it is said]. "By way of illustration" means by way of illustration according to the elements (*dhātu*).
"Having shown the method" means: "The mind-consciousness element and the states associated with it, and the mind-element and the states associated with it..."

Having thus shown the method for grasping the conditionality of immediate succession (*anantarapaccayatā*)—as in the passage beginning, “states are a condition for states by way of the condition of immediate succession”—the phrase “for the purpose of showing without remainder” means for the purpose of showing those arising of consciousness that possess the state of being an immediate condition without exception. “Of similar wholesome states” means of identical wholesome states;
and here, their identity should be understood as their inclusion within the same cognitive process (*ekavīthi*).

For this very reason he said: “The status of being a condition is stated even for those [factors] belonging to different planes. And because they belong to the same cognitive process (*samānavīthitā*)—since they possess the same feeling and the same roots—he said:
“Of wholesome [states] similar to the feeling or to the roots. Here, the word “or” (*vā*) has the sense of non-restriction;
by it, the inclusion of the various divisions such as knowledge (*ñāṇa*), formations (*saṅkhāra*), and so forth, should be understood through the method of optionality.

“Death-consciousness” (*cuti*) is included because it possesses that same nature. For it is the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) itself at its conclusion that is called “death-consciousness.

Furthermore, since it sometimes arises immediately after wholesome or unwholesome [consciousness], it should be understood that “registration” (*tadārammaṇa*) is also included; the intention is that registration arises immediately after functional impulsion (*kiriya-javana*).
To show that the meaning intended here is “of the functional [impulsion] of the sense-sphere and of the adverting [consciousness],” he says: “By the inclusion of adverting...”
He said, "It distinguishes the functional consciousness of the sense sphere. Indeed, in order to make that same meaning more clear, it was stated as "the resultant of the sense sphere," and so forth.
The intention is that the "determining consciousness" (voṭṭhabbana) is also included because it immediately follows the "investigating consciousness" (santīraṇa).
The commentary on the exposition of the immediate condition (anantarapaccaya) is finished.

6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Conascence Condition (Sahajātapaccayaniddesavaṇṇanā) "An ancient reading" (*porāṇapāṭho*) means an ancient reading from the Aṭṭhakathā. "Of this" (*imassa*) refers to this word. "Not stated" (*avuttassa*) means not stated in the Pāḷi.
Even though the word *sahagata* has the same meaning as the word *saṃsaṭṭha* in the commentary on its meaning, [it is used here].
In some instances, the meaning of another word is stated for the purpose of clarifying a specific nuance; nevertheless, [the author] says, “And yet...
is not [expressed],” showing that even so, the meaning of the root word has not been fully elucidated. Furthermore, regarding the term *aññamaññaṃ*:

where one should say *añña-aññaṃ*, this is a designation formed by the addition of the letter *m*; and this word is used in the sense of reciprocal action (*kammabyatihāra*), therefore it means “one another.”

This has been stated. Because it is accepted that the state of being a condition and a conditioned phenomenon belongs to both the condition and the conditioned at one and the same moment, "whatever is a condition for something at whatever moment, at that very moment it is also a condition for that"—this is what constitutes mutuality-conditionality (*aññamañña-paccayatā*) here.
For thus it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "One is [a condition] for another," and so on... [etc.]... "by this... etc.

It is said: "it illuminates. "Descent" (*okkamana*) means "entering" (*pavisaṇa*). For at the moment of sitting [in the womb], mental phenomena are as if entering this existence from a previous existence.
Therefore it was said: "Having come to this world from the other world, it arises as if entering.
Thus, with the intention that rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is, without distinction, denoted by the term "descent," [the text says...].

It was said: “The descent... [etc.]... was stated with this intention. “For the purpose of precluding that” means for the purpose of precluding the state of being a conascence-condition for material phenomena at other moments, by way of the statement: “At some times it is not a condition as a conascence-condition.
By those two phrases, he shows the specific distinction of the latter from the former among those related phenomena that are identical in their status as condition and conditioned.

And thus, with the intention that the meaning of the phrase "at some time" (kañci kāle) should be understood through a shift in case endings as either "at certain times" (keci kāle) or "at some [particular] time" (kismiñci kāle), he first showed the first alternative;

now, in order to show it by another method, he said: "The meaning is 'at some time' (kañci kāle) or 'at certain [times]' (keci) or 'at some [particular] time' (kismiñci kāle). By this, it is shown that "kañci" is a general designation (sāmaññaniddesa).

It shows this: for that meaning which is expressed by the plural form "keci" (some) and that which is expressed by the locative singular "kismiñci" (in something)—both of these, when the distinction between the time of the word and the time of the suffix is set aside, are combined together in the Pāḷi as "kañci" due to the commonality of what is to be expressed by the word *kiṃ*.
To demonstrate this by analyzing it, [the text says]: "keci kismiñci."

It has been stated [thus]. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated as “in something” (*kismiñci*) using the locative case. By that, [it refers] to the word according to the analysis of meaning as previously stated.
“Being the basis” (*vatthubhūtā*) means having the nature of a basis (*vatthusabhāvā*). He speaks with reference specifically to the heart-physical form (*hadayarūpa*).

“Of other forms” (*rūpantarānaṃ*) means of forms other than the heart-basis. Regarding the fact that immaterial [phenomena] are co-nascent conditions, it was stated previously: “At the moment of descent, name-and-form.”
Here, the construction is: "it prevents what was previously unprevented. Likewise, it prevents the immaterial [factors] from the basis at a time other than the moment of rebirth-linking.
By saying "And having done so," etc., he shows through the commentary on the meaning as stated that the grammatical case-terminations in the text indicate the nature of the material form.
Furthermore, he shows the distinction of the subsequent [moment] over the preceding one by way of accumulation (*upacaya*).

To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “And by the former” was stated. Therein, “by the former” refers to the statement defining the condition: “At the moment of descent, there is name-and-form.
It also refers to the textual readings of the Paṭiccasamuppāda-vāra and other sections, such as: “One aggregate and the physical basis [are conditions] for three aggregates,” and so forth.
For the entire seven great sections of the Paccayaniddesa-pāḷi constitute the exposition of the meaning. Regarding the necessity of discussing the physical basis (*vatthu*):
The construction is: "When [matter] has arisen, what is the condition?"—[the answer is] "for that name. By this: by the statement, "material phenomena are a condition for immaterial phenomena.
Of the sole: of the basis (vatthu) devoid of name. Likewise: by way of being a condition for the name. In some cases:
as in the statement, "material phenomena are at certain times a condition for immaterial phenomena by way of co-nascence-condition (sahajāta-paccaya)."
In this exposition. For here, the state of being a mutuality-condition and a co-nascence-condition is obtained.
By the word means: because by this word “mutuality” (*aññamañña*) the state of being a co-nascence-condition is not included in the Pāḷi [text], yet it is indeed obtained by way of meaning.
Therefore he said: “even though it is obtainable. Of that means: of the state of being a mutuality-condition. Thus means: “not by way of mutuality.”

"In this manner. Regarding the term "genitive case" (*sāmivacana*): it means the genitive case is used in the sense of a relationship between a part and a whole, either by way of denoting the whole or a portion thereof; that is, the genitive case is applied to the whole (*avayavin*) when there is a connection with its parts (*avayava*).
Alternatively, it is used in the sense of specification (*niddhāraṇa*), as in examples such as "the black one among cows.
The commentary on the exposition of the co-nascent conditions (*sahajāta-paccaya*) is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Support Condition (Nissaya-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) "8.
At any time whatsoever"—this [restriction] is not applicable here, because the state of being a support condition (nissaya-paccayatā) is obtainable at all times.

Indeed, the mere state of being a support, without distinguishing between the co-arisen (sahaja) and the pre-arisen (purejāta), constitutes the support condition. This refers to the materiality of the physical basis (vatthurūpa).

In the phrase "in the five-aggregate existence" (*pañcavokārabhave*), the word *ca* ("and") should be understood as having been elided after the term "materiality of the basis" (*vatthurūpaṃ*) and before "in the five-aggregate existence.

The phrase "of that" (*tassa*) refers to the establishment of the immaterial-sphere resultants (*āruppavipāka*). By the expression "because it must be made manifest," he shows that there is no room for objection on the grounds that the statement makes what was obscure clear.
The commentary on the exposition of the dependence condition (*nissayapaccaya*) is finished. 9.

Commentary on the Exposition of the Strong-Dependence Condition (*upanissayapaccaya*): Regarding "three strong-dependence conditions" (*upanissaye tayo*): there are three types of strong-dependence conditions, distinguished as the immediate-strong-dependence (*anantara-upanissaya*), the object-strong-dependence (*ārammaṇa-upanissaya*), and the natural-strong-dependence (*pakatūpanissaya*). Regarding "due to their having manifold groupings" (*anekasaṅgāhakatāya*):...

Because it comprises many conditioning states (*paccayadhamma*). They exist exclusively because they function as the cause for the restriction of consciousness and because they bring about the restriction of its occurrence.
"In which locations" means in which locations such as the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth. "Included" means having entered into inclusion;

the meaning is that among the words such as the wholesome, only certain words receive the proximity condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). Why was it not said of them, "of some"? Why?
It cannot be said that [this is so] because it is apprehended as an absolute rule. "Among them" refers to the categories of the wholesome and the unwholesome.

For the wholesome is not the proximity-strong-dependence (anantarūpanissaya) of the unwholesome, nor is the unwholesome the strong-dependence of the wholesome; however, object-strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya) and natural strong-dependence (pakatūpanissaya) are non-exclusive.
Therefore, in that context, it is stated: "of some. "Of the established conditioning states" means by way of their status as conditions.
“Of the previously produced wholesome and so forth” means of the wholesome or the unwholesome. “By the unwholesome and so forth” means respectively by the unwholesome or the wholesome.

“Without distinction” means without taking the aforementioned specific restriction regarding the unwholesome and so forth, [but rather applying it] to the unwholesome and wholesome among those [previously mentioned] by means of the phrase “of some,” and so on.

The construction is as follows: because it lacks an object (*anārammaṇattā*), and because it does not occur according to the fixed order of priority and posteriority, it does not obtain the object-strong-dependence condition (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*);
thus, it does not obtain the proximity-strong-dependence condition (*anantarūpanissaya*). “Of the natural” (*pakatassa*) means of that which has been produced or of that which has been cultivated.

For there is no production of faith and so forth by a material continuum (*rūpasantāna*), nor is the cultivation [of such qualities] through weather, food, and so forth possible. Therefore he said: “Just as... pe...”

"By means of the continuity of form. Now, one might suspect that since a distinction between earlier and later stages is indeed found within the continuity of form, and that this cannot occur without a cause of a similar nature, this must therefore be an instance of obtaining a natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*); anticipating this, he says "In which... and so forth.

Therein, "that" refers to the season, the seed, and so on, as well as karma and the like; by means of that, [there occurs] the production of that form previously produced, which is accompanied by an underlying intention (*sābhisandhika*).
It should be seen as follows. Among the dominant conditions (*adhipati*), "planning" (*pakappana*) is like a prior volitional formation (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*);

it is an arrangement or preparation. "Disposition" (*pakaraṇa*) is the persistence in the state of being a cause according to the definition already stated; from this, a specific cause is called "nature" (*pakati*).

If this is so, why is that [nature] denied in the case of material form alone? To this he says: "And just as... should be seen. In this way, [the role of] the season, the seed, and so forth, in relation to sprouts and the like—
To explain how there is a distinction among conditions, he said: "But the season, the seed, and so forth... by way of their state.
And since the term *upanissaya* (decisive support) intends a powerful cause, it is therefore not necessary here that a prior production must invariably occur.
If this is so, why is the word "prior" used in the Canon? To this he replied: "But only of those that are prior," and so forth. These too...
Or rather, they are called "previously established" by way of conceptualization (*parikappana*), for there is no occurrence of aspiration toward a basis whose mode is not yet cognized.
Therefore he said: "by virtue of having the same characteristics as that.

"Phenomena" (*dhammā*) refers to those phenomena which serve as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the designations (*paññatti*) of persons and seats. "This method" refers to it being presented by way of designation.

The method already stated is that the phenomena which constitute that [support] are to be understood as the objects of grasping (*upādāna*). Regarding the phrase "in this very [context]," it refers to the statement:

"Even a dwelling place (*senāsana*) is a condition by way of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*). In response to the objection, "How can there be the state of natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) for something present?", he will show the scriptural authority with the words "he will explain," etc., and then demonstrate the logical reasoning (*yutti*) with the words: "And even for such things that are present..."

It was said, "because they were previously natural. Regarding "of such [conditions]": whatever temperature and so forth have presented themselves, it is because those very conditions were previously—earlier than that—natural, having been brought to a state of fitness as a natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*).
Since the status of an object-decisive support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) is also possible for kasiṇas and so on, it was said with this intention: "of some."
"Yes, it does. For indeed, its status as a decisive support (upanissaya) has been stated in the Commentary by the passage beginning, "having seen the disk of the kasiṇa.

The intention is that even wholesome states of the formless sphere (arūpāvacara) serve as a decisive support, let alone wholesome states of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
To show how that serves as a decisive support, the passage beginning "in whatever kasiṇa, etc. was stated. Regarding the arising of jhāna not yet arisen:
This is said with reference to fine-material-sphere jhāna; however, there is nothing further to be said regarding immaterial-sphere jhāna.
"Of those wholesome states that produce it" means of those wholesome states that produce that fine-material-sphere resultant; the meaning is "of the fine-material-sphere wholesome states.

"Of the determiner of rebirth-linking" means of the fine-material-sphere determiner of rebirth-linking. "From death" means from the death-moment which serves as the immediate condition for the fine-material-sphere rebirth-linking.

"By way of death": this means by way of the state of being a javana proximate to death. Regarding the phrase "wholesome of the fine-material sphere is [the decisive support] for the fruition of the immaterial sphere," here too it should be connected by bringing in the words "of the wholesome states that produce that [fruition]," and so forth.

And just as it was stated that "wholesome of the fine-material sphere is the decisive support for the fruition of the immaterial sphere," so too should it be understood that "wholesome of the sense-sphere is [the decisive support] for the wholesome states that produce that [fruition]," and so forth.

It should be applied as follows: the state of decisive support (*upanissaya*) for supramundane fruition by way of being a foundation (*pādaka*) and so forth for the wholesome states of the three planes is indeed evident;

likewise, there is the state of decisive support for wholesome states of each respective plane by wholesome states of that same plane, for functional states of each respective plane by wholesome states of that same plane, for functional states of the fine-material and immaterial spheres by wholesome states of the sense-sphere, and for functional states of the immaterial sphere by wholesome states of the fine-material sphere.

Showing this meaning, he said: “Thus it should be understood individually... pe ... Since the reading for the decisive support as a natural condition (*pakatūpanissaya*)—beginning with “One gives a gift by relying on faith”—has come down in the text merely by way of enumeration and not by way of detailed analysis, he said:

“In the Pāḷi too... pe ... it is answered. The plural designation “in the question-sections” (*pañhāvāresu*) is used because they are divided into categories such as the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*), etc., according to their distinctions of direct order (*anuloma*) and so forth.

The brief point here is this: just as supramundane states act as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the arising of affection toward another by depending upon the production of the supramundane, so too it is possible for unwholesome states to serve as a decisive support for the supramundane that is yet to arise;

thus he said, "the intention is that this should not be regarded as essential. "Of wholesome states of the fine-material sphere, etc. refers to wholesome states of the fine-material, immaterial, and supramundane spheres.
The construction is: "of the wholesome [kamma] of the fine-material sphere that is being produced.

And as for how the resultant [consciousness] of the immaterial sphere is a decisive support (upanissaya) for the functional [consciousness] of the fine-material sphere, he says: "In those who have previously lived [in such states], etc., ... up to ... the Arahant.
One who aspires for this or that resultant state produces the wholesome [kamma] that serves as the cause for that respective resultant; thus, there is a wholesome decisive support for resultants.

He said: “The four planes... [etc. ...are the decisive support (upanissaya). However, showing that supramundane results (vipāka) are not the decisive support for mundane wholesome states, he said “even though,” and so forth.

For that very reason, the inclusion of the phrase “the result of the three planes” was made. In that context, “by him” means by the non-returner (anāgāmin). “That” refers to the fruit of arahantship. “Because of that” means because it has not been previously seen. Those...
It is like the fruits of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). "Of those" refers to worldlings (*puthujjana*) and others. "Of this one" refers to the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

This is what is meant: just as in the mental continuum (*santāna*) of worldlings and others, states such as meditative absorption (*jhāna*) are not a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the fruits of stream-entry and so forth because they have never been previously attained, so too, for a non-returner, the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*) is not a decisive support condition for states such as meditative absorption because it has never been previously seen.
Therefore it was said: “For even that which is yet to come is a decisive support (upanissaya) exactly like what was previously experienced.
However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), the wholesome decisive support for the lower fruits has already been stated.
Just as resultant states are a decisive support for wholesome states, so too is functional (kiriya) consciousness; in order to show this principle, [it is said]:
It was stated: “The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) and so forth are [the result of] action.

There is nothing further to be said regarding appropriate attention (yonisomanasikāra); thus, there is nothing here to be said that even wholesome states of the four planes have appropriate attention as their decisive support (upanissaya).
The meaning is: for one who brings about that appropriate attention for that purpose. “That” refers to appropriate attention. Regarding the unwholesome...
And the construction is: "appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the fruition (*vipāka*) of the four planes.

"In the same way, even for the functional (*kiriyā*)"—the meaning is that just as the decisive support was stated by way of appropriate attention for the wholesome (*kusala*), so too it should be applied by way of appropriate attention for the functional.
For, depending upon that [attention], it [the functional] gives rise to lust and so forth, according to the method already stated for the unwholesome (*akusala*).
By way of being a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for both the wholesome and the unwholesome, it certainly serves as a decisive support for the resultant states of the four planes.

If, indeed, that which is termed functional (*kiriya*)... [as before] ...certainly does so, then why was the functional not included in the analysis of the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*), while only climate, food, and lodging were included?
To this he says: "In the case of those things that are neither resultants nor of a nature to produce resultants... [as before] ...this is merely to show the method."

“*Evamādi*”: by the word *ādi*, it includes such passages as, “A wholesome state, having arisen together with an indeterminate state, does not arise by way of decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
It is stated thus because the term *upanissaya* is synonymous with the word *upanisā*:

“Name-and-form has consciousness as its decisive support; the six sense bases have name-and-form as their decisive support,” and so forth. For here, [it shows] that for consciousness, name-and-form...
The state of being a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for tangible form and so forth, as well as for the eye-base and so forth, has been explained.
The commentary on the exposition of the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) is finished.
10. Commentary on the Exposition of the Preceding-Arisen Condition (*purejāta-paccaya*).
10. The construction is: "It has indeed been shown by way of an illustration.
If it has indeed been shown, why was it said, "The teaching was given by way of what remains"? He replied: "Because it was not shown in its specific form (*sarūpena*).

"Whatever mental states and mental factors arise depending upon whichever preceding state as their object, those [latter] states [are related] to those [former] states by way of the condition of priority (*purejātapaccaya*)."
Because it is not shown in the text (*pāḷi*) by way of its specific form as "condition" (*paccayo*).

And by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and of the supernormal power of the modes of psychic potency" (*iddhividhābhiññā*), the inclusion of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (*cutūpapātañāṇa*) should also be understood.

For even that [knowledge], at the time when material phenomena are its object, has any one of the eighteen [types of] objects as a pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), because its object is present. [As it is said: "In those passing away, in those being reborn..."
For it has been said: "And there is nothing at all to be said regarding the knowledge of the divine eye and the divine ear.

As for the phrase "because of the non-existence of the other," the construction is: "due to the non-existence of even the object-prenascence (ārammaṇapurejāta), there is no apprehension of that which exists as rebirth-linking (paṭisandhibhāvin).

Even though for some [beings] there may exist an object-prenascence that constitutes rebirth-linking, because they do not make it an object by bringing it clearly into focus (vibhūtaṃ katvā), there is no apprehension.
It is said, "because of the absence of the other," treating it as something non-existent. For that very reason, he says:
"Because of the mere state of being an object for an indistinct object, just like [the object] of rebirth-linking. The construction is:

for the investigating mental-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) as well, the five objects such as visible form are exclusively a pre-arising condition (*purejātapaccaya*). And here, the phrase "of the mind-elements (*manodhātūnaṃ*)" and so forth [follows].
The phrase "tadārammaṇabhāvino" should have been placed before [the preceding term], but it has been written out of order.
The commentary on the exposition of the pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) is finished.
11. Commentary on the Exposition of the Post-arising Condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*).

11. "By way of showing the prior-born condition without remainder" means by way of showing the prior-born condition that has arisen as a condition for what was shown without remainder, namely, "the material body produced by four or three origins.

For here, the conditions are the resultant [consciousness] of the sense sphere and the fine-material sphere; among these, the sense-sphere resultant is [the condition] for the material body produced by four origins.
It is a condition, but not the other way around. For this very reason, he said: "But the resultant [consciousness] of the fine-material sphere is not [a condition] for that produced by nutriment.
Therefore, even when it is stated as "for that very [nutriment]," the meaning should be understood according to what is appropriate.
The commentary on the exposition of the postnascent condition is finished.

12. Commentary on the Exposition of the Condition of Repetition (Āsevanapaccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) "Skilled" (*paguṇa*) means multiplied by way of various modes; the meaning is that it has been cultivated through frequent occurrence.

"More skilled" (*paguṇatara*) means exceedingly skilled; for that very reason, it is more powerful. The state of being such is "the state of being more skilled and more powerful" (*paguṇatarabalavatarabhāva*); by means of that.

“Distinguished” means having attained distinction. Since this distinction does not exist in the case of karmic result (vipāka), he says: “By this, it is distinguished from the indeterminate (abyākata) that is a karmic result.
The commentary on the description of the condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya) is finished.
13. Commentary on the Description of the Condition of Kamma (kammapaccaya).
13. "Of such a nature" means having a nature that assists by way of the kamma-condition. "Capability" means power.

"Of that" refers to the fruit, which consists of the resultant aggregates and the kamma-produced matter. "The state of being a kamma-condition has been stated" means that its status as a condition by way of the kamma-condition has been explained.
"Even matter in the single-aggregate [existence]" means that even in the single-aggregate existence it does not produce matter, let alone in the four-aggregate existence.
The commentary on the exposition of the kamma-condition is finished.
14. Commentary on the exposition of the result-condition (vipāka-paccaya):
Just as in the form realm (rūpa-bhava), for those possessed of perception, the arising of form occurs solely through the volitional formations of merit produced therein, so too...

“Even for those without perception”: in that regard, while [kamma] acts as a condition for certain [beings]—namely, those for whom it accords with their maturation—it does so only for some and not for all, and only in certain places and not everywhere; but it is not so for the resultant [states]. Therefore, he said “absolutely.
“By way of them” means by way of those resultant aggregates which have obtained the condition for maturation. By the words beginning with “for it is not,”...

The phrase “exclusively” (ekantena) clarifies the stated meaning through contrast. The construction is as follows: “the result of two planes” refers to the result of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere;
it is not a condition for matter in the immaterial sphere.
The commentary on the exposition of the resultant condition is finished.

15. Commentary on the Exposition of the Nutriment Condition (Āhāra-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) Because there is no swallowing of pure nutritive essence (*ojā*) alone, it is said: "or swallowed together with the bases such as what is eaten and drunk.

Regarding what is eaten, which is divided into the categories of hard food (*khādanīya*) and soft food (*bhojanīya*), let it be admitted that the state of being a mouthful (*kabaḷīkāratā*) applies to the former; however, as for what is to be drunk and so forth—
He asks "How? and replies: "They are to be drunk... [etc. ...they become. Or rather, it should be understood that this was stated by way of the majority. "One who guards" means one who supports.

The fact that the mind-originated body has the state of being a nutriment-condition (*āhāra-paccaya*) for the physical body must be understood after having investigated the case of edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*).
If one asks why, he states the reason here with the words beginning "For not... (*na hīti* etc.). For if there were the state of being a condition...
One might have said, “Mind-originated edible food is a condition for the mind-originated body by way of the nutriment condition,” and so forth;
however, this was not stated, whereas it was stated for that which is not mind-originated. Therefore he said, “The threefold [nutriment]... has been explained.
The commentary on the exposition of the nutriment condition is finished.
16. Commentary on the Exposition of the Condition of the Faculties (Indriyapaccayaniddesa) 16.
"Because of being mixed" (*missakattā*): this is said with reference to the fact that the material and immaterial life-faculties (*rūpa-ārūpa-jīvitindriya*) have been taught together as one.
Therefore, "because of being mixed" means because of being mixed with the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*). [The term] "life-faculty" (*jīvitindriya*)...

The immaterial life-faculty (*arūpa-jīvitindriya*). "It is not to be excluded in its entirety" means that just as the immaterial life-faculty was not included in the *Pañhāpucchaka* because it is mixed [with other factors], so too here the immaterial life-faculty is not excluded; this is the meaning.

For the immaterial [consciousnesses] such as eye-consciousness and the rest, there is dependence on other conditions—namely, dependence on other conditions such as adverting (*āvajjana*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*).
By way of the faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya), there might be [a relationship] among the eye and other faculties, whether material or immaterial,

because they are never found in a state of inseparable existence from one another, and because they depend upon the convergence of other conditions. However, as for that which is "independent" (nirapekkha)—
unlike the eye and other faculties which are dependent upon other conditions— that which is independent therein is the faculty-condition.
There exists [a state] of inseparable phenomena, such as the two kinds of life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*); this is to be construed with "he does not have... and so forth, ending with "...there is none.

For even among those [phenomena] that are inseparable, such as gender (*liṅga*) and the rest, there might be the status of being a faculty-condition for those that are separable and arisen from conditions, since their lack of the status of a faculty-condition has not been seen.
Is it not the case that the status of being a faculty-condition belongs to the eye and so forth when they are separable?
"Is it seen? "It is indeed seen, but it is not of the same class," showing this, he said "no" and so forth.
"When there is" means when there is the state of being a condition for the faculties in that which is inseparable from what is of the same class as described above;
[it occurs] together with the female and male faculties. For this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*). Even though the female and male faculties...

The faculties such as the gender-faculty (*liṅga*) would not exercise their conditionality upon the sense-faculties during the stage of the *kalala* and so forth, because those [faculties] do not exist at that time.
As for those material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) that do exist then, why do they not exercise [their conditionality] upon those [faculties] that are inseparable from them? To this he says:
"But of others," and so forth. This is because of the absence of seeds (*abījabhāva*) and the absence of signs (*animittabhāva*). "Suitable to that" means suitable to the stages such as the *kalala*.
They maintain that [the distinction] exists, for their intention is that the natural differentiation of "woman" and "man" is thereby discerned.
In the phrase *kusalajātiyaṃ*, the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). However, for those who read it as *kusalajātikaṃ*, it is the nominative singular.

There is no separate single genus or plane, because it is merely a portion of that [genus]. In the expression "in the case of roots and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes "unwholesome nutriments" (*akusalāhāresu*) as well.

“‘The same method applies’ and so forth summarizes this. ‘This method’ refers to the method of meaning stated in the passage beginning with ‘When [states] are expressed by way of plane,’ which establishes the condition of faculty (indriya-paccaya) that is not found in the formless realm; that same method should be applied here as well.

Likewise, regarding ‘the root of wholesome states not included [in the mundane]’ and ‘likewise the roots of unwholesome states,’ here too, the first instance refers to the root of wholesome states not included [in the mundane].”

It should be connected thus: "Because the unwholesome root accompanied by displeasure (domanassa-sahagata-akusala-hetu) does not exist as a separate category, level, or plane, it is not established separately even though it is not found in the formless realm (ārūpa).
This same method applies to such passages as, "The same method applies to the unwholesome nutriments (akusala-āhāra) as well.

It was stated [that they are not included] because, although they possess the status of a co-nascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), they might also possess the status of a faculty condition (indriya-paccaya) at the moment of arising; therefore, [the faculties] were excluded on account of their lack of the status of a co-nascence condition.
“With reference to this,” it is said: “A phenomenon that, in arising, assists by way of its state of arising together is a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*).

Although the absence of its status as a co-nascent condition is explicitly shown in the Commentary with the words, “But it has no co-nascent conditionality,” nevertheless, not accepting that [view], he says, “In order to prevent [the idea] that... [arising]... and so forth.
With the words beginning “he will speak,” he establishes that meaning. For by this, its status as a condition at the moment of arising is shown to be similar to the kamma-condition.

And by the word “ca” (and) in the phrase “in the course of existence,” the construction is: “In rebirth-linking as well, there is no other faculty-condition for the materiality of the kamma-born (kaṭattā-rūpa) than the material life-faculty. The sections beginning with the “Dependent” (Paṭicca-vāra) and ending with the “Associated” (Sampayutta-vāra).

The intention is that [the formula] "dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises by way of root-condition" and so forth, applies only to the six instances occurring while grasping the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*), and not to the moment of presence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*). And "having done so" means because it occurs only by grasping the moment of arising.
"In these" refers to the six instances as previously stated. However, some [hold that] "in the case of the material life-faculty..."

They say: "Sustenance (anupālana) is not manifest and not strong at the moment of arising; however, because it attains a state of stability through the acquisition of conditions such as the postnascent condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) at the moment of presence (ṭhiti-khaṇa), it is manifest and strong then; therefore, it is stated [in the text] as 'at the moment of presence.
The commentary on the description of the faculty condition (indriya-paccaya-niddesa-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
17. Explanation of the Description of the Condition of Jhāna (Jhānapaccayaniddesavaṇṇanā) "Designated as joy and grief" means they are stated by way of the terms "joy" and "grief";
or, because of the distinction in their status as jhāna factors, it is only pleasure and pain that have become joy and grief which are the jhāna factors, not other types of pleasure and pain.

The inclusion of mental joy (*somanassa*) and grief (*domanassa*) was made for the purpose of showing that pleasure (*sukha*) and pain (*dukkha*), which are themselves factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*), possess the status of being factors of absorption.
Now, he elucidates in detail exactly what was stated previously with the words “in the two sets of fivefold consciousness,” and so forth;
that is indeed easy to understand. By the phrase “by that,” it refers to the inclusion of mental joy and grief, which serves as a qualification.

“Merely by way of striking” means by way of the mere state of making [the object] an objective support. It refers to the occurrence of reflection (*cintanā*) and the occurrence of close contemplation (*upanijjhāna*).
“By the very reason already stated” means by the reason given as “due to the absence of the mode of close contemplation. “Previously” means from the beginning.
“Four factors are excluded” means that when seven factors are being shown, four factors are excluded.
"Aṭṭhakathā hesā" (for this is the commentary) states the reason why it must be explained by way of a brief indication (*lesa*).

Although only one [of the three] would need to be mentioned, because the other three share the same characteristic, all three are included. "By the mention of the three," however, means by the statement intended to show that equanimity (*upekkhā*), pleasure (*sukha*), and pain (*dukkha*) are not factors of jhāna.
From that, [it follows that] there is no other state besides equanimity and so forth [that could be the object] of one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*).

It falls into the state of being unextracted as a jhāna-factor because it is not included among the jhāna-factors. "By the reason already stated" means by the reason stated as "due to the absence of the mode of close contemplation";

or else, it falls into the state of being unextracted for another reason, because it is not included along with those things whose nature is not that of close contemplation, and because it exists as a mode of close contemplation through a cause entirely different from that [other reason]—namely, in the case of one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) in the text.
One falls into a state of being unmanifested. "For the purpose of avoiding that fault" means for the purpose of liberation from the aforementioned fault.
"But those who... and so forth is merely a demonstration of the words of the author. "By means of joy and so forth" refers to joy, grief, and the equanimity that is a factor of jhāna.
"The state of being unmanifested" is equanimity (*upekkhanā*). For equanimity is said to have an unmanifested function. Of which things is it common? Of pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest.
By what [factors]? By joy (*somanassa*) and so forth. How? The construction is: "because it is associated with pleasure" (*sukha*), and so on. "Not by one-pointedness of mind" (*na cittekaggatāya*):

this refers to pleasure and the rest, as well as other factors such as directing the mind (*abhiniropana*).
