Because it does not perform the function of a faculty (*indriya-kicca*), nor does it perform the function of close contemplation (*upanijjhāyana-kicca*), and because it is not common [to all states], the reason why one-pointedness of mind in the fivefold sense-consciousnesses is not mentioned as a jhāna-factor must not be stated [as a separate cause].
“Sāti” means concentration of mind (*cittakaggatā*). “Therein” refers to the statement in the commentary, “equanimity, pleasure, and pain,” where it is not included.
“In the mind-element associated with doubt, etc. refers to the mind-element in a consciousness associated with doubt, and in the functions of receiving and so forth.
“Of that too” refers to its concentration of mind as well.
The commentary on the exposition of the jhāna-condition is finished.
18. Commentary on the Exposition of the Path-Condition:
Both types of intention—namely, right intention and wrong intention—are thus classified according to the distinction between the blameless and the blameworthy.
"Both kinds. The same method applies here as well for "energy and concentration.

"Having grouped them together" means having taken them along with [the others] by virtue of their commonality as factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*), and having taken each one individually. "By those" refers to wrong speech, action, and livelihood.

"Here" means in this exposition of the conditions for the path; it includes both those that are found [in the text] because they function as conditions for the path, and—by the word "and"—those that are not found there.
And because they lack the status of being path-conditions. If this is so, why were they mentioned? To this he says:

"By way of the commonality of the term 'path-factor'. Anticipating the objection—"What is the purpose of such a figurative description here?"—he says: "For in this way, the conventional usage of the Sutta is also shown.
By demonstrating it in this manner, [it is shown] how even those which are not path-factors in the ultimate sense are established as being called "path-factors" in the Sutta.
This is said by one who intends to show [the factors] together with the path-factors (*maggaṅga*). "Having extracted" means having performed the extraction of the words.
Now, the twelve factors together with wrong speech (*micchāvācā*) and so forth should not be shown; if it is asked why, he says: "For in the Canon... [etc. ...it should not be stated.

The intention is that they are called "wrong path-factors" (*micchāmagganga*) precisely because they are the opposites of those [right path-factors], and not because they possess an intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) like wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*) and the rest.

Showing that even when the purpose is to demonstrate the path through both the figurative and non-figurative methods (*pariyāya-nippariyāya*), it cannot be stated in this way regarding the word "meaning" (*attha*), he said:
"The figurative... [down to] ...legal issues" (*adhikaraṇāni*). Its meaning is as follows:

just as in the phrase "of a legal issue belonging to another category" (*aññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassa*), there is another word *adhikaraṇa* that is a counterpart to the word *adhikaraṇa* found in the Canon, because it is common to that other [category] not found in the Canon.
The meaning of both terms has been extracted in the passage, “A legal issue (adhikaraṇa) means the four kinds of legal issues.

Likewise, here too, one who wishes to show both the primary and the other [secondary] path-factors (maggaṅga) should have extracted the word *maggaṅga* as it occurs in the text, which is common to both;
yet it was not done so. Therefore—because only the word *maggaṅga* as it occurs in the text was extracted, and not that which is common to the others.
And since the intended meaning has not been restricted by way of a summary of the subject matter, therefore: "In those" means in those rootless consciousness-arising moments.
Regarding the passage "right view... right concentration," it is said that intention, effort, and concentration are stated having been distinguished by the terms "right" and "wrong";
thus he says, "right view and so forth exist as previously described. However, [the factors] consisting of intention, effort, and concentration—
In this context, some say "they certainly exist. Alternatively, it was said with reference to the entirety of right view and so forth, in the manner already described.
Therefore he said, "as previously stated. The intention is that [the term] serves to restrict the source of their arising, not to provide a qualification.
The commentary on the exposition of the path-condition is finished.

20. Commentary on the Exposition of the Dissociation-Condition “Becoming the basis for the suspicion of association” means becoming the locus (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for the suspicion of association. Therefore, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “For the immaterial aggregates arise as if they were emerging from within the bases such as the eye.”
The commentary on the exposition of the dissociation condition is finished.
21. Commentary on the Exposition of the Presence Condition:
"When something exists, another comes to be; when it does not exist, that other does not come to be"—this, in brief, is the characteristic of a condition.
With reference to this, it is said in the Sutta: “When this exists, that comes to be; when this does not exist, that does not come to be.
Demonstrating this by applying it to the condition of presence (*atthipaccaya*), he says “For whoever... and so forth.
Furthermore, to show that this principle does not apply to Nibbāna, and therefore Nibbāna is not cited as being a condition of presence, he says: “And Nibbāna... [etc.]”

"It is helpful," he said. By this, he shows that the state of being a condition for conditioned phenomena is particularly evident through the method of contrast (*vyatirekamukhena*). "Opposed to the helpfulness of non-existence" means opposed to the state of being a non-existence condition (*natthipaccaya*).
For the non-existence and existence conditions stand as direct opposites to one another, just like the disappearance and non-disappearance conditions.

Nibbāna is not a presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*) because it does not possess the quality of being an assistant to non-existence (*natthibhāvopakārakatā*), due to its non-opposition [to existence].
The intention is that those phenomena which are presence-conditions are indeed seen to be opposed to the quality of assisting non-existence.

And "while existing" (*sati*) is connected with "having arisen" (*uppannatta*). The construction is: "those for which nutriment and faculties are conditions. "The absence of those" means the absence of the conditions of co-nascence and so forth. "Of these" refers to the nutriment and the faculty as they occur by way of the condition of presence (*atthipaccaya*).

"By way of the individual essence of phenomena" means by way of their inherent nature (*dhammatā*). For this is the inherent nature: namely, that [the nutriment and the faculty] are [present] along with the phenomena produced by the conditions.
Food and the faculties, whether obtained prior to or subsequent to [a particular state], serve as the presence condition (*atthipaccaya*) for them, but not as co-nascent or other such conditions.
Or, just as in the case of the doors such as the eye and their objects such as visible forms—despite their fixed mode of operation—the consciousness becomes sixfold due to the doors and objects;

“Initial recitation” means the first recitation. And “that being so” means that even for hatred (*dosa*), when its status as a condition exists by way of the seventeen conditions, its status as a predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) is also admitted;

Regarding the statement, "In this case, the conditionality of dissociation from the faculties is not obtained," this refers to that specific instance or to the inclusion of the object-prenascence (*ārammaṇapurejāta*).
It should not be said that the basis (*vatthu*) possesses the conditionality of dissociation;

for the basis, when functioning as an object, does not become a condition of dissociation, but rather only when it functions as a support (*nissaya*). As for the phrase "furthermore than this" (*ito uttari*), here the word "this" (*ito*) refers to...
This refers either to the postnascent [condition] as a prior-born [condition] or to the object-prior-born condition. In that context, with reference to the first method, it is stated:
"also subsequent to the prior-born. By this, it is meant that one should understand what is obtainable and what is not obtainable even among the conditions such as kamma that will be mentioned later.
However, without reference to the second method, according to what has come down in the Aṭṭhakathā:

It was stated: "Or because it is dissociated from the faculties (indriya) from this [perspective]. However, according to the method stated by himself, it is "or because it is dissociated from the supporting faculty (nissaya-indriya). Regarding that, he himself says: "The object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati)," and so forth.

He will not explain what is obtainable or unobtainable among kamma and the others with the words "Beyond this," and so on, precisely because an extension (atidesa) has already been made; therefore, it is only the former [type] that is also "by way of prenascence" (purejāta).
Only the meaning already stated is intended.
By the phrase "without abandoning the status of being a path-condition," the path-condition is thus stated; therefore, it is said in the latter reading, "of the nine [factors] excluding the path.
However, in the former reading, because it was stated, "without abandoning the status of being a path-condition," [the path-condition is included].
Thus, since the conditions such as co-nascence (sahajāta) are to be understood along with the path-condition (maggapaccaya), it is stated as “of ten.
In that regard, in the latter reading, it should be said “in eleven ways,” while in the former reading, “in twelve ways.

This is because, although there is a specific distinction—namely, [the mind-element] existing as the immediately preceding ceased state and as an object-condition (ārammaṇa)—that distinction is not specifically mentioned, and only...
The meaning is: [it is] by way of being an object through its state of having just ceased, but not by way of the commonality of the state of having just ceased and being an object.

By the phrase "by this method," he shows that the two pairs of terms—namely, the demonstration of the similarity of conditions and the demonstration of the dissimilarity of conditions—have been extracted as a single unit; thus he says: "Of the co-nascent causes, etc...."
"...should be applied," he said. The construction is: "The state of mutual dissimilarity [arises] through the fact that causes, objects, and so forth, are either co-nascent or not co-nascent.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the following is included: the similarity of pre-nascent eye-faculties and visible forms by virtue of their being pre-nascent;
and during the course of existence, the similarity of the bases and aggregates, etc., which are pre-nascent and post-nascent, by virtue of their being pre-nascent and post-nascent.

The inclusion of terms such as "dissimilar" (*visabhāga*) and so forth should also be understood here. Furthermore, the analysis in this context is to be understood through pairs (*yugaḷaka*), based on the nature of being a cause (*hetu*) or not a cause (*ahetu*), and so on.
For the root-cause condition (*hetu-paccaya*) is a condition by way of being a cause, while the others are conditions by way of being something other than that.
Thus, in the case of the remaining conditions as well, they should be understood through their respective pairs.
"Both as a primary condition" means as a primary condition for both producing and supporting. "State" (*ṭhāna*) is a synonym for the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*);

thus, even without the abstract suffix (*bhāva-paccaya*), the meaning of the abstract suffix is understood. "By analyzing the decisive support" means by classifying it according to the distinction between the proximate decisive support (*anantara-upanissaya*) and the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*).
All three types of decisive supports should be mentioned because they constitute the classification of decisive supports. Only the mention of "decisive support" [is used here].

It should be done by means of the general form. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*): when [the relationship] is established in this way, the "breaking down" (*bhindana*) or analysis into immediate-proximity-decisive-support (*anantara-upanissaya*) and natural-decisive-support (*pakata-upanissaya*) is intended to show that natural-decisive-support lacks the status of being a condition for material phenomena (*rūpa*).
But surely, objective-decisive-support (*ārammaṇa-upanissaya*) and immediate-proximity-decisive-support are also not conditions for material phenomena? That is true.
"They do not exist, but they have been shown by way of method"—showing this meaning, he said, "The object...
should be seen," implying that by showing one part, the rest is also shown.

"Because they share the same course as those" means because of sharing the same course as those [conditions] mentioned immediately before, since only immaterial states function as conditions. "That" refers to the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*). "Therein" means having been recited among the immediate (*anantara*) and other conditions.
The commentary on the miscellaneous discussion of the exposition of conditions is finished.
Chapter on Questions: 1.
Commentary on the Positive Order of Conditions (Paccayānuloma).

"One by one, a triad and a dyad" means that within each of the twenty-two triads, such as the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*), and within the hundred dyads, such as the root-dyad (*hetuduka*), there is one triad and one dyad respectively.
"Not a triad-dyad" (*na tikaduka*) means that those which possess a common application are not [treated as] a triad-dyad.
However, a dyad distinguished by a triad and a triad distinguished by a dyad are taken as a basis, just as in the case of dyads distinguished by triads and triads distinguished by dyads.
Thus the teaching proceeds further.
Those wholesome and other states mentioned in such passages as, "Dependent on a wholesome state,
a wholesome state arises by way of the root condition," pervade the meaning of "dependent" with the meaning of the root condition and so forth.

The meaning is: "accomplishing both the wholesome and other conditions. For this very reason it was said: because the pervasion of the meaning of "condition" (paṭicca) by the conditioned phenomena occurs when there is a coexistence of both those [factors], and not otherwise;
for that same reason it was said, "And these are either co-nascent...
Here, "these" refers to the conditions such as the root-cause (hetu) and so forth. For among them, the root-cause, co-nascence, mutuality, support, and so on—
"Co-nascent conditions, such as the immediate and proximate conditions, are non-co-nascent conditions.
He says, "And thus skill in etymology is produced," referring to the teaching that proceeds by way of making known the mutual relationship through these two sections.
"Having raised those various questions" refers to [questions] such as, "Could a wholesome state be a condition for a wholesome state by way of the root-condition? and so forth.
Having extracted each and every question that receives an answer.
The statement "This is a careless scribal error" was said with reference to what was written as: "A wholesome root [is a condition] for the states associated with the root.

In the sections on "Dependent" and "Conascent," it is the conascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*); in the sections on "Condition" and "Supported," it is the supported condition (*nissaya-paccaya*); and in the sections on "Conjoined" and "Associated," it is the associated condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*).
He said, "Having spoken by making it exclusive," meaning "having restricted [the application] in the preceding sections...
and so forth. "Therein" means in those six preceding sections. They are not understood because they have not been extracted in their own form. By such questions as these.

"In the conditions and conditionally arisen states beginning with the cause" means in the causal factors beginning with the cause—divided into the associated aggregates and so forth—and in their respective conditionally arisen states. [The particle *tesu* is used] in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).

This is the locative case. "Because there is no determination of the conditions such as the root-cause (hetu) and so forth" means because there is no determination that "these indeed are those conditions such as the root-cause," since they have not been identified by their specific form.

For just as a creeper that is entangled in various other vines and situated within a thicket cannot be determined as "this is that creeper" when it is not visible by its specific form, even though one wishes to know it—so too [is it with these conditions].
A meaning that is not determined according to its own nature is neither "unrooted" nor "unbushy," because of the absence of certainty;

however, when that meaning has been determined according to its own nature, then—by virtue of the certainty regarding its object—the person does not fail to attain the state of one who has awakened [to it], and thus that question is called "unrooted" and "unbushy.
Therefore he said: "Because of the absence of certainty, those questions are unrooted and unbushy."
And it was said: "Having been made, they were not analyzed," and "Nothing was included in the questions... [etc. ...they were analyzed.

Regarding that, the state of being "without a root" (nijjaṭatā) was not stated with reference to the answering of the questions; rather, the intention is that it refers to the production of certainty.
Here, "establishment" (ṭhapana) means establishing within the mental continuum of those to be trained; furthermore, that is the illumination of that meaning.

He says "manifesting" because it is made manifest. "By modes" means by the modes of conditions such as cause (hetu), etc., or by the modes of the conditioned and the conditions arising from the wholesome (kusala), etc.
Having taken "arranging" to mean "constructing," he says: "A hypothetical question is a question concerning a procedure.
"Siyā" means "it might be. By the phrase "What is this procedure? the verb "might be" (siyā) functions as the statement of the procedure. Question.

However, it should be understood that [the meaning] is established by the sense of the sentence. Indeed, to demonstrate that very question established by the sense of the sentence, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"Could he, depending on a wholesome state (*kusalaṃ dhammaṃ*), exist? In that alternative, a hypothetical question (*saṃpucchanaṃ parikappapucchā*) is intended to mean that the question is made clear by the word for action itself. Thus: "Could he, depending on a wholesome state..."
In the passage, “Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state might arise by way of the root condition,” both parts—

“dependent on a wholesome state by way of the root condition”— are statements regarding the condition, while “a wholesome state might arise” is the statement regarding that which arises from the condition.
Among these, when the state of being a condition has been clarified for the conditioning factor, the arising of the conditioned factor is necessarily clarified by implication.

"Arises" refers only to the conditioned phenomena (*paccayadhamma*) that must be questioned. In this regard, the commentaries state that there are two possible alternatives for the meaning of the question: either the meaning of "dependent" (*paṭicca*) qualified by the conditioned phenomena, or the meaning qualified by the conditions (*paccaya*).
Showing that the first type of question is faulty, he says: "Whatever wholesome phenomenon might arise," and so forth.
In this context, "because of the occurrence of all the questions" means because of the occurrence of the seven sets of seven questions beginning with the roots of the wholesome (*kusalamūla*).

[The opponent] falls into the position that the arising of the wholesome is permitted by those conditions—namely, the postnascent (*pacchājāta*) and resultant (*vipāka*) conditions—but that is not tenable;
such is the intended meaning. "From their respective conditions" means from the respective conditions such as appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and so forth.
The fault in the construction "What might it be? is stated on the grounds that the existence of the state of being (*bhāvanām-atthitā*) is not questioned here.

And by doing so—meaning, because only its arising (*uppatti*) is questioned—in the alternative sense stated as "Or else," etc., [the word] "might arise" (*uppajjeyya*) is used in the sense of granting the possibility of its arising.
Having here admitted the arising of a wholesome condition (*kusalapaccaya*), [the text says: "of that" (*tassa*)—that is, of the arising.

"An inquiry into existence" (*bhavanapucchanam*) means that an inquiry into existence based on the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) is not appropriate; this is the connection. Again, "of that" (*tassa*) refers to the arising from the root-condition.
"An inquiry into existence" (*bhavanapucchanam*) means a mere inquiry into existence. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because, in the manner already stated, it applies to both cases.
It is inappropriate to inquire about arising by way of granting permission; therefore [the author says this].

Furthermore, the permission mentioned in the Commentary is implied in meaning within the two alternative interpretations of the sense [of the word]; not granting that permission, he said, "or without having granted permission," and so forth.
By the phrase "only in the case of inquiry," he shows that in the context of inquiry, "it might arise" (*uppajjeyya*) is a verb (*kiriyāpada*). If...
Regarding how this [term] "might be" (*siyā*) is used, he says: "'Might be'... [etc. ...he asks. This is the method (*naya*);
that is, the method of meaning just stated immediately prior by way of the word "might be" and so forth. It is not understood because no specific distinction has been mentioned.

Both questions—the question of possibility and the question regarding its specific qualities—are indeed one and the same question, because they share the nature of being a single inquiry and because they have a common subject matter.
"An expression of eagerness for going" means a statement of zeal for going.
Just as one becomes fit for a subsequent action to be performed after the act of going, so too standing is the "eagerness for going," and the word is the expression that makes it known.
And since such an action, in its actual meaning, is called dependent upon another action, therefore it is said:

“...there is a need for going... Having taken into account the objection that, in this section on the co-nascence condition (*sahajātapaccaya*) within the chapter on dependence (*paṭicca-vāra*), the word “dependent” (*paṭicca*) implies a sequence of times, he says “Even though,” and so forth. By this, he shows:
“Even though there is no difference in time between the dependent and the arisen [states], apart from the case of cause and fruit where a prior and subsequent time is observed elsewhere...”
“Having superimposed the state of cause and fruit here as well by way of their commonality, the conventional usage of ‘prior’ and ‘subsequent’ times is made by way of linguistic convention.
Therefore he said: “It should be understood by way of the mode of the occurrence of grasping... [etc] ...should be seen. Therein, “attainment of self” (attapaṭilābha) means arising (uppāda).
“Going” (gamana) is another synonym for the act of moving (ayanakiriya) found in the phrase “dependent on” (paṭicca). But that, in its actual sense, is—

Occurrence (*pavatti*) is simply the arising of phenomena according to their respective conditions. For in the world, all conventional expressions regarding action and agents pertain to the arising of phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
Therefore, regarding the term "dependent" (*paṭicca*), the "re-going" (*paṭigamana*) or "re-approaching" (*paṭiayana*) found here is, in actual meaning, "arising again" (*paṭiuppajjamāna*);
and since this occurs in relation to one who is going and so forth, he said: "for one who is going..."
"Returning," "arising again as it arises. This going and returning, this arising and arising-again, are identical actions.
How so? Because the meaning of the prefix *pati-* is "counteracting" (*paṭikaraṇa*).

Therefore—because the meaning of "dependent-arising" (*paṭicca uppajjati*) here is the "arising again" (*paṭiuppajjana*) of that which is arising while serving as a co-nascent condition; therefore. [It is called dependent-arising] because its arising is contingent upon that.
In the context of the term *saha* (together), it is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), or in the sense of the cause (*hetu*).

The meaning is: "having returned together with that [arising]," referring to an arising that is dependent and bound to the wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) as they arise. By this, he shows the simultaneity of the attainment of dependence and the attainment of the [wholesome] states.
For this very reason, he says: "It is as if it were said, 'making the co-nascent condition' (*sahajātapaccayaṃ katvā*)," and so forth. Is it not [so]?
And is it not the case that such verbal usage does not occur for an action at the same time, but only for an action at a prior time?
This is not an absolute rule, because it is accepted by some even in the case of simultaneous action.
For instance: "Having destroyed the darkness in the world, the thousand-rayed one has risen."
“Having become the eye of the world, the Sun has now reached his zenith.
Having first illuminated [the world] with the splendor of his beauty,
which reveals all loveliness, the Buddha is like another thousand-rayed sun.”
And these applications are seen.
35–38. *Tāsu* means "among those" in the method of the root-dyads; there are forty-nine questions in the dyad of root and object (*hetārammaṇaduka*).

Regarding "the dyad of root and object": this refers to the dyad of conditions that occurs by way of the root-condition and the object-condition, namely, "by way of the root-condition, by way of the object-condition."
"Because two questions have been shown" means that in whichever recensional path (vācanāmaggā) there are forty-nine questions—
beginning with those whose roots and conclusions consist of the wholesome terms, and those whose roots and conclusions consist of the triad of wholesome and so forth—

it is said with reference to the fact that only two questions, which constitute the beginning and the end [of each group], are shown therein. "In this" refers to this section on the formal rules (paṇṇattivāra) concerning the questions.
The meaning is: "not stated by way of conditions. For, according to the method of questioning, that which has a single root known as the root-condition (hetupaccaya) is "single-rooted" (*ekamūlaka*);
and this masculine designation is used in view of the word *naya*. The same applies to those rooted in the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and so forth.
Likewise, it should be applied in such ways as: "that which has two roots known as the root-condition and the object-condition is 'double-rooted' (*dvimūlaka*)," and so on.

However, if [the exposition] were stated by way of conditions (*paccaya*), the "single-rootedness" (*ekamūlaka*) of the first method would not be possible; for in that case, there would be no other condition (*paccayantaram*) which could be designated as the root.
Therefore he said, "But by way of conditions," and so forth. In the phrase "of the dyads beginning with cause and object" (*hetārammaṇadukādīnam*), the genitive case denotes a part of a whole;
it is connected with "the predominant and so forth" (*adhipatiādīnam*). Beyond that, because of the absence of a root, it is "rooted in all."
Because it is taken as the root-nature of all conditions without exception. For conditions that are taken by way of possessing a root are not themselves taken as the root-nature.
"The going of the conditions" is understood to mean "the going of the text," since gender, number, and so forth follow the nature of the referent. "Herein" refers to the direct order (*anuloma*).
The word *ca* has the sense of accumulation; it illuminates the fact that the twenty-three roots are being spoken of collectively as constituting the totality of the root-nature.
39–40. "This being so" means: when the sequence of recitation begins with "conditioned by object, conditioned by root" and proceeds as "conditioned by object, conditioned by non-disappearance;
conditioned by object, conditioned by root," one might occasionally say, "Let the course of the text follow the method of 'wheel-binding' (cakkabandhana);
what is the fault? To this he says: "And here in the Abhidhamma, by way of the lower purification..."
"...is found in the Pāḷi. For likewise, in the *Khandhavibhaṅga* and other such texts, the Pāḷi proceeds by way of the lower purification (*heṭṭhima-sodhana*).

To establish that meaning through the method of enumeration, it was said, "And having done so," and so forth. "In the object, etc. refers to the methods beginning with the root-object (*ārammaṇa-mūlaka*).
"In each respective one" means in each respective condition, such as the object-condition. "From the pure method" means from the *suddhika-naya*.

Therefore, because the pure method (*suddhikanaya*) is not obtainable among the methods beginning with the object-root (*ārammaṇamūlaka*), the intention is that the single-root method (*ekamūlakanaya*) is to be understood as the "object-root.

The passage beginning with “By way of the object-condition... or by way of the non-disappearance-condition,” etc., was stated with reference to such a textual path. Where [it says] “by way of the object-condition, by way of the root-condition; by way of the object-condition... [and so forth].
“By way of the predominance condition, by way of the object condition... [and so on] ...by way of the non-disappearance condition.
Thus, having shown that in the section based on the object condition, the single-rooted series—beginning with the proximity condition as its root and ending with the object condition—is presented;

then, starting from the remaining single-rooted sections above, it is condensed down to the disappearance condition in the section based on all conditions, and thus only the non-disappearance condition is shown. Therefore he said:
“*Ekamūlakesū*” and so forth. In all subsequent instances of this kind, this same method applies.

“Having shown only the root” means having shown the very beginning of the single-rooted [section] within the section on the predominance-root (*adhipatimūlaka*). “Not a showing of the pure” means not a showing of the pure method (*suddhikanaya*).
For it has been said: “The pure method is not found in the sections on the object-root (*ārammaṇamūlaka*) and so forth, because there is no distinction [in that case]. Nor...
The demonstration of a few conditions within the "all-rooted" [section] is because the "one-rooted" is presented later in the "all-rooted" section.

41. *Ekasmiñca* means in the method beginning with the "non-disappearance-rooted" (*avigata-mūlaka*). *Saṅkhepantaragato* means having entered into the midst of the summary—that which is to be summarized;
the meaning is "it should be condensed. *Majjhimānaṃ dassanaṃ* means from among the middle methods.
"Showing" (*dassana*) means, rather than showing the end, showing the course of the text (*pāḷigati*); and that is merely a partial showing from the beginning.

By that removal of the "dissociation" condition (*vigatapaccaya*), he shows the final tetrad in the section based on non-dissociation (*avigata-mūlaka*), because dissociation is the conclusion of the entire root-section.
By the final term, "conditioned by absence" (*vigatapaccayā*).

Just as the combinations of dyads, triads, and so forth were made according to the serial order of the conditions beginning with root (*hetu*), why was it not done in the same way there by skipping over the object (*ārammaṇa*) and other conditions? Even though [the text] does not exhaustively [list] all the conditions...
Because they are grasped as root-conditions (*mūla-paccaya*), there is no difference in meaning when some are joined with others;

however, in the case of the "root-object" (*ārammaṇa-mūlaka*) and other groups, there is indeed a distinction in meaning when those respective remaining conditions—such as the "object-dominance" (*ārammaṇādhipati*) dyads and so forth, or the "root-root," "root-dominance," and "immediately preceding" (*anantara*) triads and so forth—are joined.
Even so, since joining them in a non-sequential order is not easy to grasp, [the sequence is maintained].

And because it is possible for a person possessing superior knowledge to apply [the factors] according to the method as it has been shown, he stated the meaning with the words “In this regard, moreover,” etc., showing that they have been applied in their proper sequence rather than by taking the conditions out of order.
And that progression is logical; that is, the progression through the text by way of applying each couplet (duka) with all the triplets (tika).
That is appropriate because of the inclusion of the dyads within the triads. "Therein" means within the dyads. "In each one" means in each individual dyad-triad.
"Methods" refers to the four methods—such as the method of direct order (*anulomanaya*)—which occur in each section; however, there are twenty-seven questions.
If this is so, why are they said to be identical to the "reason-dyad" (*hetudukam*)? It is because that reason-dyad is found individually within each of the triad-locations.
This was stated by way of the commonality of the nature of the two factors (duka).

"By the method already stated" means by the method stated in the *Dukatika* [treatise] beginning with "Not indeed," and so forth. For in that context, there is no application of the *duka* as a whole;
rather, each individual *tika* is applied to each member of the *duka*. Therefore he said: "Each *tika* is joined with a hundred *dukas*."
"In each one" means in each of the triads and dyads.

"The six methods beginning with the triad" refers to the six methods—the Conditional Relations Triad (Tika-paṭṭhāna) and so forth—as stated in the verse beginning with "The excellent Paṭṭhāna, the triad...
"Even the sevenfold" means even when divided into seven ways according to the classification of sections. "In forward order" means in the forward order of conditions (paccayānuloma).
Having included [the factors] together by way of their commonality of being in the direct order (*anuloma*);

likewise, having included the fourfold *tikapaṭṭhāna* together by way of its commonality of being a *tikapaṭṭhāna*, and the four *dukapaṭṭhānas* and so forth together by way of their respective commonalities—having grasped this meaning, it was stated as "from the direct order" (*anulomamhī*) and so on, for the purpose of elucidating the intended sense of the verse: "The excellent *Paṭṭhāna* consisting of the *tikas*."
Having grasped this meaning: "In the sevenfold division" means in the sevenfold division by way of the "Dependent Chapter" (Paṭiccasamuppādavāra) and so forth. The construction is as follows:

it shows that these six [factors], though each divided fourfold by way of the triplets (tika) and so on, are to be extracted as six by way of the "conformable to the Dhamma" (dhammānuloma) and so forth.

This is the summary of the meaning here: although they are distinguished by the divisions of "conformable to the Dhamma" and so forth, they are [grouped] by virtue of their commonality as triplets and so on.

The six methods of dhamma, such as the "Triads" (tikas) and so forth—which are spoken of collectively under the designation of the *Paṭṭhāna*—when analyzed according to the "Dependent Chapter" (*paṭiccasamuppādavāra*) and other sections, and when extracted from their respective places, are called "conformity" (*anuloma*) by virtue of their commonality of being conformable. When taken together as the conformity of conditions (*paccayānuloma*), they are exceedingly profound.
However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it says: "In this context, moreover, this verse..."

"In that [passage], 'conformity with the Dhamma' (dhammānuloma) was stated with reference to conformity with conditions (paccayānuloma)," thus it was stated by defining "conformity with the Dhamma" as being a qualifier for "conformity with conditions.
This same method applies to the verses on the reverse order (paccanīya-gāthā) and so forth.

Since the meaning of the *Tika-paṭṭhāna* and the *Duka-paṭṭhāna* has already been explained previously, he says, "in the *Duka*, *Tika*-paṭṭhānas, etc. The phrase "the foundation (paṭṭhāna) by means of triads (tikehi)" means [the foundation] through various modes by means of triads.
The analysis of conditions (*paccayavibhāvana*), or the place where knowledge proceeds by means of triads (*tikesu*).

The *Paṭṭhāna* of triads connected with dyads, or the *Paṭṭhāna* of triads distinguished by dyads, is the "Dyad-Triad *Paṭṭhāna*. Showing this meaning, he said "of dyads," and so forth. "Of that which is distinguished by dyads, etc.
means that the state of being a dyad, etc., should be understood as being distinguished by the terms "dyad," etc., such as: "a wholesome state as a cause..."
This is because of such statements as: “dependent on a wholesome state that is not a cause,” and so forth.
The commentary on the positive order of conditions (*paccayānuloma*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Negative Order of Conditions (*paccayapaccanīya*).
42–44. Regarding the phrase "as many as the explanation of the meaning of the textual word," he says "the classification" (*pabheda*).

The meaning is: "there exists [a classification] for that which has twenty-three roots. "To that extent" means to that same extent of classification. "Therein" means it is presented in the section on the direct order (*anuloma*).
How is it shown? It shows the detailed exposition of each individual word. This refers to the remaining condition that has been included by virtue of its possessing a root.
The commentary on the Negative Enumeration of Conditions is finished.
3. Commentary on the Positive-Negative Enumeration. 45–48.
“Again, therein” refers to the positive enumeration. “Condition-terms” means that the conditions themselves are the terms; thus, they are condition-terms. “Herein” [refers to the following].

Regarding "in the positive-negative method" (*anulomapaccanīye*): the phrase "of the pure conditions" (*suddhikapaccayānam*) means with reference to the teaching of the positive-negative method that is about to be explained, which concerns conditions unmixed with other conditions.
The commentary on the positive-negative method is concluded.
The commentary on the Section of Questions is finished. 1.
The Triplet of the Wholesome.
1. Commentary on the Section on Dependence.
1. Positive Conditionality (Paccayānuloma) (1) Commentary on the Section of Analysis (Vibhaṅgavāra-vaṇṇanā): 53.
Since the difference between the triplets and the cross-triplet terms is indeed evident, it is stated: "Merely by way of the diversity of the triplets..."
"Without. "By way of the beginning and the end" means by way of the beginning and the end as stated in such passages as, "Nine [factors] have a single root and a single end," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase, "Not in the case of that same triad of feelings, etc.," he said, "It was stated 'not by that very same [similarity]' with reference to similarity," in order to show the similarity that was being rejected here.
"Yā" means "which" question. "The collection of all questions" refers to all [the questions].

The "comprehensive exposition" (*samuccayanakathā*) refers to the explanation of the forty-nine questions without omission. This is what must be done here in this presentation of the *paṭiccasamuppāda* (dependent origination).
For it is appropriate that after what has been stated from the beginning without omission, there should subsequently be a statement of one part thereof as required.
Indeed, those forty-nine questions do not receive their answers therein; therefore, in that [section], namely in the *dhammānulomapaccanīka* (the forward and reverse order of phenomena)...
The meaning is that in the *pītittika* (the triad of the yellow), forty-nine questions do not receive an answer, whereas in the twenty-eight [questions] they do.
"By way of being a co-nascence condition for that" means by way of that single dhamma classified as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, which acts as a co-nascence condition;
or the meaning is "by having attained, or reached, the state of being a co-nascence condition. "It is as if it were permitted" means...

Although in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it seems as if it is admitted that "a [dhamma] possessing the three moments arises" by such statements as "until its arrival at cessation," it is actually stated that "only that which possesses the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa) arises," because the six sections beginning with the section on dependence (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) proceed by taking up only the moment of arising.
For indeed, among those [six sections], the postnascent condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*) does not exist in the forward order (*anuloma*).
"Here, it is said with reference to the aggregates included by the term 'wholesome' (kusala).

This means that in this section on dependence (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), the statement "dependent on a wholesome phenomenon, a wholesome phenomenon arises" is said with reference to the aggregates included by the word "wholesome.
When all four wholesome aggregates arise together, as expressed in their general sense, [the relationship is established] by way of common conditions such as co-nascence (*sahajāta*).

Without distinction, it cannot be said that all [states] are conditions for all, nor can it be restricted by saying, "this alone is the condition for this," or "this is the condition for this alone. Therefore, it is stated in the Commentary: "of one only, or of two only," and so forth.
However, in such passages as "dependent on a state associated with pleasant feeling," the feeling and other factors function as qualifiers (*visesaṇa*).

Because they are taken separately, it is possible to say, "dependent on one aggregate (khandha), two aggregates [arise]," and so forth. Therefore, it was said: "But in the case of the triad of feeling (vedanāttika), etc.
By the word "tathā" (likewise), this phrase "and for each of the divisions such as the dyads (duka), etc. is brought forward.
"Etasmin" refers to the inclusion of the indeterminate resultant (vipākābyākata) and the indeterminate functional (kiriyābyākata), thus: "In all [these cases]..."
It was stated that [it] "should not be included. But where should it be included? He said: "Only here, namely, in the phrase 'matter originated by mind' (cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpaṃ).
Thus, having avoided the fault of over-extension (atibyāpita) in the first statement, he said "not only" and so forth, in order to avoid the fault of non-extension (abyāpita) in the second.
"Here" means: it should not be included in the passage "indeterminate as result (vipākābyākata) and indeterminate as functional (kiriyābyākata)."
Because even that [materiality] arising in the immaterial realm arises without materiality.

And here, just as the root-cause condition (*hetu-paccaya*) alone excludes the rootless (*ahetuka*), so too, by the mention of "matter produced by mind" (*citta-samutthāna-rūpa*), the kamma-resultant matter (*vipāka-rūpa*) arising there in the immaterial realm is not included along with the mental state that arises there; yet this is already established by the sense of the context.
In order to show [this] more clearly by not merely stating it as it is in the text but by making it manifest, the *Aṭṭhakathā* says,

"the resultant indeterminate," and so forth. However, it should be understood that here the rebirth-linking consciousness and the final consciousness are not included because, despite the non-arising of matter, there is an absence of delimitation [of the kamma-result].
Regarding the phrase "of that which has become a condition": this is said to preclude the charge that the physical basis (*vatthu*), which is a condition for the aggregates, has not been included.
How so? By way of being an arisen-from-conditions (*paccayuppanna*). Where? In the general statement, "And matter produced by karma" (*kaṭattā ca rūpaṃ*), it is stated:
"the bases in dependence upon the aggregates. For in this way, its state of being an arisen-from-conditions is demonstrated. This is a mutual dependence.
The "two statements" refers to the pair of phrases: "dependent on the aggregates, the [heart-]base; dependent on the base, the aggregates.
It is "taken by way of generality" means it is taken by this general statement, "and matter produced by karma," or by way of the generality of matter produced by karma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).
Without including derived matter (*upādārūpa*), and not taking it as "derived matter," mind-originated matter alone is simply called "matter produced by karma."

"Having taken" is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "in this demonstration," it refers to the demonstration of the meaning stated as: "for the purpose of showing that [matter] arises dependent upon the great primary elements.

"Accompanied by the conditions for the aggregates" refers to the matter produced by kamma (*kaṭattārūpa*) at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), and the matter originated by consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*) during the course of existence (*pavatti*).
"Unaccompanied," however, refers to the matter produced by kamma during the course of existence, and that originated by nutriment (*āhārasamuṭṭhāna*).
It is matter that arises from kamma, is not bound up with the faculties, and is included within the non-percipient existence (*asaññabhava*).

Regarding the phrase "also at rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhiyam-pi*), by the word "also" (*pi*), it should be understood that in the course of existence (*pavatti*) as well, kamma-born matter (*kaṭattārūpa*) and other derived matter (*upādārūpa*) arising there [at rebirth] are meant.
But how, in this context, does matter that arises dependent on the primary elements arise by way of the root-cause condition (*hetupaccaya*)?
“Matter arising in dependence on the aggregates by way of the root-condition (hetupaccaya) also arises in dependence on the primary elements (bhūta).
This is how this phrase is stated; or rather, it is so stated because [the matter] is produced from the primary elements by way of the root-condition.
For even the cause of a cause is called simply a “cause,” just as one says, “The village was burned by thieves.”
The phrase "dependent on the primary elements (bhūta), derived matter (upādārūpa)" is presented as a separate extraction;
however, the reading "derived matter dependent on the great primary elements" is what is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). This is the meaning:

according to the method explained in this reading, "derived matter dependent on the great primary elements," derived matter also arises dependent on the wholesome aggregates and the great primary elements.
In order to show what that method is, it was said: "With reference to the great elements... [etc.]... he spoke. Therein, this method is stated in terms of its meaning by the statement:

"Derived matter arises dependent on the great elements—mind-produced matter and kamma-born matter"—which, by speaking of the arising of derived matter dependent upon both the indeterminate aggregates and the great elements, [implies] the wholesome aggregates.
The meaning is that, in substance, the arising of derived matter (upādārūpa) in dependence upon the great primary elements (mahābhūta) has been stated.

54. By the statement "that which is conditionally arisen is not found apart from matter," he shows that those questions ending with the section on immateriality (arūpa) are not included here, let alone those ending with the section on matter.
57. "Having the same characteristics as that" means having the same characteristics as the rebirth-linking of one born from a womb, by way of being a rebirth-linking of the five aggregates.
"Of the complete phenomena" means of the five aggregates (khandhas), which are the phenomena classified according to the textual divisions.
"In this" refers to this exposition of the conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya).

"Matter produced by mind and matter produced by kamma" means matter produced by consciousness (citta-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa) and matter produced by kamma (kamma-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa). Again, "produced by nutriment" [is mentioned].
The repetition of the word "here" (*ettha*) refers to that which is temperature-originated (*utusamuṭṭhāna*). For that [matter] was not previously ungrasped by the inclusion of the external;
however, nutriment-originated matter was indeed not included. To the question, "Why is there a repetition regarding the temperature-originated?", he says:

"By these," and so forth. "Therein" means among the non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*). "Of that" means of the temperature-originated. "At the beginning" means by way of the external, nutriment-originated, temperature-originated, and non-percipient beings.

"By those who have arrived" means by those [who have arrived] on the first occasion. "A statement without distinction" (avisesa-vacanaṃ) refers to a statement spoken without making distinctions such as "external" and so forth;
the construction is: "including together with" that which, even though it is a non-material condition, obtains its meaning when it obtains conditions such as the *hetu* (cause) and others.
By the two words "of that" (*tassa*) and "therein" (*tattha*), one refers back specifically to the aforementioned first occasion. "Of the same grammatical status as that" (*taṃ-samāna-gatikaṃ*).
“Arising with the mind as its concomitant. Here too means in this exposition of the conascence condition.
“As in the analysis of the kamma condition” means as in the exposition of the asynchronous kamma condition. For it is said in the Commentary:
“By the phrase ‘arising together with that,’ even the kamma-produced matter at the moment of rebirth-linking is included. And this specific point here is certain.
Showing that [the term] is intended, he said: “For... there is,” and so forth.

“Without making a distinction” means without making a specific qualification such as “arisen from temperature” and so on. But why are they stated by making a distinction as “derived matter” (*upādārūpa*)?
This is the construction. In the phrase “in the root-conditions and so forth,” the word “and so forth” includes co-nascent conditions (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and others.
"Along with" means that mind-produced matter and kamma-produced matter are taken together as one. "Separately" means distinguishing mind-produced matter from kamma-produced matter.

In this context, "by means of the mention of 'external' and so forth," it is just as in such passages as "one external great primary," where the great primaries are distinguished by the mention of "external," "nutriment-produced," and "temperature-produced"; likewise here, [the phrase] "in the great primaries... [is used].

In this exposition [of the term] "dependent," because the great elements (mahābhūtāni) are not distinguished by any specific qualification, the construction is that they are stated only after having been distinguished by their states as mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa), matter that maintains [the body] (bhāvaka-rūpa), and matter consisting of kamma-formations (kaṭattā-rūpa).
Now, in order to show that they must also be distinguished by another reason, the passage beginning with "Moreover" (apica) was stated. Therein:

The statement "there is no condition whatsoever" is said with reference to the fact that, according to the system presented in the *Paṭṭhāna*, matter does not receive the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
Therefore, he says: "in the case of causes and so forth. However, because it is inseparable from that [mind], its status as the cause of those mental actions should be understood;

for this reason, it is stated that [those things] produced by supernormal power-mind (*iddhicitta*) are "conditioned by kamma" (*kammapaccaya*). But is it not the case that mind is [a condition] for those things originated by nutriment and temperature?

"Is it a condition? It is indeed a condition; however, showing that it is so by way of being a supporting factor (*upatthambhakattena*) and not by way of being a productive factor (*janakattena*), he says:
"Nutriment... [etc. ...not a producer. But what is their producer? He says: "The great elements themselves...
[etc. ...are the producers. The meaning is: of derived matter (*upādārūpa*) originated respectively by mind and by karma, which would be non-existent in the absence of mind and karma.

"Only those consisting of mind-originated matter and kamma-born matter" means only those produced from the great primaries (mahābhūta) originated by mind and kamma, because these [other types] are the proximate causes for those [two]. By "others," he refers to derived matter (upādārūpa) originated by temperature and nutriment.
The qualification is made thus: "mind-originated matter, kamma-born matter, and derived matter. This is done by way of what is of the same class.
The meaning is: "by means of material form, temperature, and nutriment.
The phrase "only those with manifest distinctions" is stated because those great elements by which they are produced have been distinguished as "produced by nutriment" and "produced by temperature.

They do not require further distinction nor should they be distinguished, because the specific difference is already established by the distinction of their causes, [as in the passage]: "dependent upon the great elements..."
The meaning is that they should indeed be called "derived matter" (*upādārūpa*).

These, moreover, are the types of matter born of mind and born of karma. To show the specific distinction by which they are distinguished, he says with reference to the mind: "by way of being a co-nascent and other conditions";
but with reference to the other [karma], he says: "by way of being the root cause," the meaning of which is "by way of being the kamma and decisive-support conditions."
"Others" refers to the derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*) originating from nutriment and temperature.

They are distinguished by the very qualification "great primary elements" (*mahābhūta*); thus, they are distinguished by the great primary elements themselves as the producing conditions—namely, nutriment and temperature—as in the phrase: "dependent on one great primary element originating from nutriment, [and] dependent on one great primary element originating from temperature. "Here" refers to "mind-originated..."
In this statement, "matter is kamma-born matter and derived matter," by the mention of the fact that derived matter is produced by consciousness and kamma,
the same status is indicated for its supports as well. An attribute qualifying one [of two] becomes an attribute qualifying both,
because both occur inseparably.

58. "In the past" refers to the root-conditions (*hetu-paccaya*) and so forth. "As a separate condition" means as a condition for the physical basis (*vatthu*) separately, according to such passages as:
"At the moment of rebirth-linking, dependent on one resultant indeterminate aggregate, there are three aggregates and the matter produced by kamma.
And here it cannot be said that they are shown only as separate conditions, because [the Suttas state]: "Dependent on the aggregates, there is the physical basis..."

Just as the state of being dependently arisen is shown by the phrase "the aggregates [arise] dependent on the physical basis," the state of being a condition for the aggregates is likewise shown from the perspective of the single [basis].
For that very reason, expressing his own lack of approval regarding that interpretation, he said: "It was said with this intention.
To show the interpretation that he himself approves of, he said: "But as for 'the physical basis [arises] dependent on the aggregates,' this... and so forth.

It has been stated. The connection is as follows: there is the demonstration of the pervasion of the sense of dependence (*paṭiccaṭṭha*) by the aggregates that serve as conditions, and the demonstration of the pervasion of the sense of dependence by the basis (*vatthu*) that serves as a condition; it is not [the case] for the aggregates alone. "In this very [instance]" means in this very mutual condition (*aññamaññapaccaya*).
This same method applies to the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) and the others as well, for therein the equality of the pervasion of the sense of dependence is demonstrated.
Because of the pervasion of the two meanings of *paṭicca*. And because the aggregates (*khandha*) and the bases (*vatthu*) have been shown:
thus, the pervasion of the meaning of *paṭicca* for both the aggregates and the bases together has indeed been shown.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "and so forth" (*evamādi*), such passages as "dependent on an unwholesome state" (*akusalaṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca*) are included. [The question is: "Is it not necessary [to state this]?"
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows. To show that this is an analogous example—just like the root-cause condition (hetupaccaya) and others—he says, "For not," and so forth.

The meaning is: "that class of conditions which was stated as 'dependent upon one, three, or two aggregates'. For the meaning of "condition" (paccaya) is indeed the meaning of "dependent upon" (paṭicca).
Therefore he said: "Those [aggregates] do not themselves become the root-cause condition. By this, [it is shown that] it does not extend to the meaning of "dependent upon" (paṭiccaṭṭha)...
This shows that the state of being a condition, such as the cause-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and so forth, is absolute. Therefore he said:

"This same principle applies to the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and the others. For a phenomenon that has become an object-condition does not exercise the sense of dependence (*paṭiccaṭṭha*).
And it is said: "Dependent on a wholesome phenomenon, a wholesome phenomenon arises by way of the object-condition."

Having grasped even the mere state of being an assistance by means of another condition, the conditions such as the root-cause (hetu) and so forth are shown in the section on "dependent upon" (paṭicca-vāra) and in other sections;
thus, clarifying the aforementioned [point] by way of accumulation (upacaya), he says: "And in the section on conditions," and so forth.

"That condition" (taṃ-paccayā) means the condition of the physical basis (vatthu-paccayā); the meaning is: having obtained the physical basis that serves as a condition as appropriate. "Those" (te) refers to the wholesome aggregates (khandhā).

"Dependent upon. "Of these" refers to the great elements (mahābhūta) and the aggregates (khandha). "By way of the presence or absence of the state of being a condition" is stated because the state of the aggregates as conditions—such as root-conditions (hetu-paccaya) and co-nascent conditions (sahajāta-paccaya)—is observed in the great elements.
If this were so, one might suspect that they [the great elements] would also be mutual conditions (aññamañña-paccaya) for those [aggregates];
thus, in order to dispel such a suspicion, he says: "For the word 'mutual'... and so forth. "Independent" means independent of anything else.
For a causal phenomenon does not become a cause-condition by being dependent upon another phenomenon; rather, the meaning here is stated from the perspective of the word.

"Dependent upon one or the other" (*aññatarāpekkha*) means that it depends on something else—either itself as a cooperative cause or any other thing whatsoever—which is why it is called "dependent upon one or the other.
"Mutually dependent as previously described" refers to the classification of the immaterial aggregates and so forth mentioned in the Canon.
It is called "mutually dependent" (*itaretarāpekkho*) because it depends upon that which has been described as being mutually a condition for one another.
Why was it said that the aggregates (*khandhā*) and the great elements (*mahābhūtā*) mentioned here might be [so related]?
For the aggregates and the great elements have not been stated to be mutual conditions for one another; rather, they are mentioned separately as "the aggregates and the great elements."
If they were so grasped, then it could not be said that "the great elements are not a condition for the aggregates.
Regarding the phrase "from that which is its own condition, or from that which is supported by it":

how can a phenomenon that arises from another phenomenon—which serves as its own condition—arise from that very phenomenon or from what is supported by it, by way of a mutuality-condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*)?

It has already been stated that such a class of phenomena deserves to be described as arising through mutual conditionality; this very point is now clarified by way of an illustration with the words beginning “Just as. Therein, “dependent on aggregates, aggregates [arise]” is the illustration for the phrase “arising by means of that mutual conditionality,” while “dependent on the basis, aggregates [arise]” is the illustration for the phrase “arising by means of that conditionality consisting in presence. Thus, it should be understood that all these classes of phenomena deserve to be described as arising through mutual conditionality. Furthermore, the meaning of the statement “dependent on the eye, eye-consciousness arises” should be understood in the same manner. The same applies to the remaining cases. Thus, it should be understood that the entire mass of phenomena deserves to be described as arising through mutual conditionality. This concludes the section on the exposition of the mutual conditionality of phenomena. Now follows the section on the exposition of the conditionality of presence. Herein, the exposition of the conditionality of presence is twofold: (1) the exposition of the conditionality of presence regarding the arising of phenomena, and (2) the exposition of the conditionality of presence regarding the maintenance of phenomena. Regarding the first, the following should be understood: “Dependent on ignorance, formations arise; dependent on formations, consciousness arises; dependent on consciousness, mind-and-body arises; dependent on mind-and-body, the six sense bases arise; dependent on the six sense bases, contact arises; dependent on contact, feeling arises; dependent on feeling, craving arises; dependent on craving, clinging arises; dependent on clinging, becoming arises; dependent on becoming, birth arises; dependent on birth, aging-and-death arises. This is the exposition of the conditionality of presence regarding the arising of phenomena. Now follows the exposition of the conditionality of presence regarding the maintenance of phenomena: “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; dependent on contact, feeling arises; dependent on feeling, craving arises; dependent on craving, clinging arises; dependent on clinging, becoming arises; dependent on becoming, birth arises; dependent on birth, aging-and-death arises. This is the exposition of the conditionality of presence regarding the maintenance of phenomena. It should be understood that this exposition of the conditionality of presence regarding the maintenance of phenomena is intended to show how the mass of suffering arises when there is no liberation from the round of rebirth. This concludes the section on the exposition of the conditionality of presence. Now follows the section on the exposition of the conditionality of non-disappearance. Herein, the exposition of the conditionality of non-disappearance is twofold: (1) the exposition of the conditionality of non-disappearance regarding the arising of phenomena, and (2) the exposition of the conditionality of non-disappearance regarding the maintenance of phenomena. Regarding the first, the following should be understood: “If ignorance were not to exist, formations would not come to be; if formations were not to exist, consciousness would not come to be; if consciousness were not to exist, mind-and-body would not come to be; if mind-and-body were not to exist, the six sense bases would not come to be; if the six sense bases were not to exist, contact would not come to be; if contact were not to exist, feeling would not come to be; if feeling were not to exist, craving would not come to be; if craving were not to exist, clinging would not come to be; if clinging were not to exist, becoming would not come to be; if becoming were not to exist, birth would not come to be; if birth were not to exist, aging-and-death would not come to be. This is the exposition of the conditionality of non-disappearance regarding the arising of phenomena. Now follows the exposition of the conditionality of non-disappearance regarding the maintenance of phenomena: “If the eye were not to exist, and forms were not to exist, eye-consciousness would not come to be; if the meeting of the three were not to exist, contact would not come to be; if contact were not to exist, feeling would not come to be; if feeling were not to exist, craving would not come to be; if craving were not to exist, clinging would not come to be; if clinging were not to exist, becoming would not come to be; if becoming were not to exist, birth would not come to be; if birth were not to exist, aging-and-death would not come to be. This is the exposition of the conditionality of non-disappearance regarding the maintenance of phenomena. It should be understood that this exposition of the conditionality of non-disappearance regarding the maintenance of phenomena is intended to show how the mass of suffering does not arise when there is liberation from the round of rebirth. This concludes the section on the exposition of the conditionality of non-disappearance. Now follows the section on the exposition of the conditionality of dissociation. Herein, the exposition of the conditionality of dissociation is twofold: (1) the exposition of the conditionality of dissociation regarding the arising of phenomena, and (2) the exposition of the conditionality of dissociation regarding the maintenance of phenomena. Regarding the first, the following should be understood: “Dependent on ignorance, formations arise; dependent on formations, consciousness arises; dependent on consciousness, mind-and-body arises; dependent on mind-and-body, the six sense bases arise; dependent on the six sense bases, contact arises; dependent on contact, feeling arises; dependent on feeling, craving arises; dependent on craving, clinging arises; dependent on clinging, becoming arises; dependent on becoming, birth arises; dependent on birth, aging-and-death arises. This is the exposition of the conditionality of dissociation regarding the arising of phenomena. Now follows the exposition of the conditionality of dissociation regarding the maintenance of phenomena: “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; dependent on contact, feeling arises; dependent on feeling, craving arises; dependent on craving, clinging arises; dependent on clinging, becoming arises; dependent on becoming, birth arises; dependent on birth, aging-and-death arises. This is the exposition of the conditionality of dissociation regarding the maintenance of phenomena. It should be understood that this exposition of the conditionality of dissociation regarding the maintenance of phenomena is intended to show how the mass of suffering arises when there is no liberation from the round of rebirth. This concludes the section on the exposition of the conditionality of dissociation. Now follows the section on the exposition of the conditionality of disappearance. Herein, the exposition of the conditionality of disappearance is twofold: (1) the exposition of the conditionality of disappearance regarding the arising of phenomena, and (2) the exposition of the conditionality of disappearance regarding the maintenance of phenomena. Regarding the first, the following should be understood: “With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, mind-and-body ceases; with the cessation of mind-and-body, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death ceases. This is the exposition of the conditionality of disappearance regarding the arising of phenomena. Now follows the exposition of the conditionality of disappearance regarding the maintenance of phenomena: “With the cessation of the eye and forms, eye-consciousness ceases; with the cessation of the meeting of the three, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death ceases. This is the exposition of the conditionality of disappearance regarding the maintenance of phenomena. It should be understood that this exposition of the conditionality of disappearance regarding the maintenance of phenomena is intended to show how the mass of suffering ceases when there is liberation from the round of rebirth. This concludes the section on the exposition of the conditionality of disappearance. Now follows the section on the exposition of the conditionality of absence. Herein, the exposition of the conditionality of absence is twofold: (1) the exposition of the conditionality of absence regarding the arising of phenomena, and (2) the exposition of the conditionality of absence regarding the maintenance of phenomena. Regarding the first, the following should be understood: “If ignorance were absent, formations would not come to be; if formations were absent, consciousness would not come to be; if consciousness were absent, mind-and-body would not come to be; if mind-and-body were absent, the six sense bases would not come to be; if the six sense bases were absent, contact would not come to be; if contact were absent, feeling would not come to be; if feeling were absent, craving would not come to be; if craving were absent, clinging would not come to be; if clinging were absent, becoming would not come to be; if becoming were absent, birth would not come to be; if birth were absent, aging-and-death would not come to be. This is the exposition of the conditionality of absence regarding the arising of phenomena. Now follows the exposition of the conditionality of absence regarding the maintenance of phenomena: “If the eye were absent, and forms were absent, eye-consciousness would not come to be; if the meeting of the three were absent, contact would not come to be;

This, however, refers to the phrase "arising by way of mutual condition dependent upon that. Therefore, the word *tasmā* (therefore) refers back to the very meaning already stated, treating it as the reason.

"Because of the absence of the state of being a condition for its own condition" means because of the absence of the state of being a condition for the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*) which constitute its own condition;
for the great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not [serve as conditions] for those aggregates from which they have arisen.

They are conditions. "Because of their mutual dependence" means because of their mutual dependence on the state of being reciprocal conditions. "Dependent upon the aggregates, and conditioned by the aggregates" means:

dependent upon the aggregates according to the rule stated in the section on "dependent upon" (paṭiccasutta), and conditioned by the aggregates according to the rule stated in the section on "conditioned by" (paccayasutta).
"And the reciprocal condition has been stated" means [a condition] other than the reciprocal condition, such as the support condition (nissaya-paccaya) and so forth.

The meaning is that the arising of the great primary elements (mahābhūta) has been explained. "Arising with the physical basis as condition" means arising by making the physical basis a prenascence condition (purejāta-paccaya).
And "by way of mutual condition supported by that" means they arise by way of the mutual condition (aññamañña-paccaya) constituted by the aggregates (khandha) supported by that physical basis;
therefore, for the reason stated, "with the physical basis as condition"... [and so forth].
By this method, however, the meaning is that there is a state of mutual conditionality (*aññamañña-paccaya*) between the bases (*vatthu*) during their direct occurrence.

59. “That has not been mentioned”: the meaning is that the status of the eye-base and so forth as a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), which was stated in the passage beginning “dependent on the eye-base,” has not been mentioned here in the section on “in dependence” (*paṭicca-vāra*).
This is because the sense of “co-arising” (*sahajāta*) is taken as the sense of “in dependence” (*paṭicca*). Therefore he said:

“‘The eye-base, etc.…’ … [as before] … ‘the intention. However, for those who maintain that the support-condition is sixfold by way of the immaterial aggregates, the great primaries, name-and-form, consciousness, mental factors, and material phenomena, it is analyzed here precisely according to their view.
If one asks, “How is it analyzed by way of matter?”—it is shown in its own form as “the aggregates depend upon the basis,” specifically by way of the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*).
By way of other [factors] as well, it is shown here in the statement: “Dependent on an indeterminate state, an indeterminate state arises by way of the dependence condition (nissaya-paccaya).

For just as in such passages as “Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises by way of the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya),” the status of being an object condition is shown for the visible-form base and so forth even though they lack the sense of pervading the meaning of “dependent,” so too is it here.
The state of being a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) for the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) and so forth has thus been demonstrated. Therefore it was said: “...the supports... are not included.
(60) Regarding the two kinds of decisive support (*upanissaya*): these are the proximate (*anantara*) and natural (*pakata*) decisive supports.

By the word “also” (*pi*) in the phrase “wholesome states that are sublime (*mahaggata*) also,” it draws in the indeterminate (*abyākata*) sublime states as well: “Wholesome states that are sublime do not receive the object-decisive-support (*ārammaṇa-upanissaya*).”
“Even more so, they are indeterminate. The meaning is that sometimes they are not obtained when they do not occur by way of being treated as weighty (*garu*).

61. “Elsewhere,” [meaning] in the sections on the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) and so forth. “Without specifying the condition” means without specifying the conditioned phenomenon (*dhamma*) in its own form.

For in the descriptions of the root-condition and so forth, the phenomena such as the root are not shown according to the specific distinctions of their own forms, such as non-greed (*alobha*) or the wholesome (*kusala*).

"In the wholesome, etc. (*kusalādīsu*): this is a qualification of non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth. By this, he shows that just as there is no fixed rule that this alone is the condition for non-greed and the rest, likewise there is no such rule for their specific instances, namely the wholesome (*kusala*) and so on.

However, here, regarding the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), [the phrase] "among the bases and the states that are not bases" (*vatthu-navatthu-dhammesu*) uses the locative case in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).
By the words "of those arising through the prenascence condition," [it is shown that] at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-khaṇe*) and in the formless realm (*ārūpe*)...

And it turns back the aggregates as they are arising. Now, having in mind the objection—"Why is only the *vatthupurejāta* (base-prenascence) included here, and not the *ārammaṇapurejāta* (object-prenascence)?"—he says:
"For even object-prenascence is not obtained when base-prenascence is absent.
"Of that" refers to the rebirth-linking result (*paṭisandhivipāka*). To make the meaning already stated clear, he says: "Neither-result-nor-non-result... etc."
It is said that "three" are mentioned. By the phrase "from non-acquisition," it is shown that if [the result] were to be acquired, "four" would have to be stated.

"Therein" refers to the triad of results (*vipākattika*). "Three" refers to these three: "dependent on a resultant state (*vipāka-dhamma*), a resultant state arises by way of prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*); dependent on a state with the nature of resulting (*vipākadhamma-dhamma*); and dependent on a state that is neither resultant nor having the nature of resulting (*nevavipākanavipākadhamma-dhamma*)."
63. "Of derived matter depending on those great primaries" means of the derived matter that arises depending upon those [great] elements.
"He speaks" refers to the kamma-condition, both simultaneous and asynchronous; for there is no distinction in the conditionality of those [derived matters] as they occur inseparably from their bases.

The qualification "of kamma-produced matter during its course" is intended to exclude kamma-produced matter at the moment of rebirth-linking, even though it too possesses a simultaneous kamma-condition.
Because it is intended [as such]. For that very reason, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, both types of kamma-condition are stated as:

"At the moment of rebirth-linking, of the great elements. 64. "Whatever is obtained at rebirth-linking": whichever sense-faculty-form (*indriyarūpa*) among the eye-faculty and so forth is obtained at rebirth-linking, by way of each of those, both the sense-faculty-form and the base-form (*vatthurūpa*) are called "kamma-produced form" (*kaṭattārūpa*).
69. "Of some": [this refers to] the aggregates of rebirth-linking and so forth in the five-aggregate plane. For their base is, by necessity, a dissociation-condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*).

It exists. "Common dissociation condition" (samānavippayuttapaccaya) means a similar dissociation condition.
