For wholesome and unwholesome aggregates, as well as certain indeterminate ones, are dissociation conditions for something else, yet they themselves do not receive a dissociation condition from that [other thing], because there is no dissociation condition for mind-originated [matter];
it is only by way of the physical basis (vatthu) that there is a dissociation condition.

Because they arise. However, some indeterminate states, for which [other states] serve as a dissociation condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*), themselves also receive that dissociation condition from them, just as the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the aggregates (*khandhā*) do at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Therefore it is said: "For some, the aggregates... [etc. ...are also various dissociation conditions.
It makes a condition for each condition; thus, it refers to the conditioned phenomena (*paccayadhamma*), namely the physical basis and the aggregates.

And it makes itself its condition; the meaning is that it proceeds having made the aforementioned conditioned phenomenon its condition. "From performing that function" means from performing the function of the dissociated condition.

"There is no arising in dependence" means there is no pervasion of the sense of dependence (*paṭiccaṭṭha*), because it is held that the sense of dependence is the sense of co-nascence (*sahajātaṭṭha*). [Regarding the phrase] "they arise in dependence":
He said only this much; on what basis? Because the meaning [of the aggregates] is well-known. Therefore he said, “But on what basis? and so forth.

Since a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding according to the principle of proximity (*paccāsatti*), he stated [the answer] in order to prevent one from taking it [as applying to that].
Thus he said: “Because of its immediate proximity... it is stated,” and so on.

71–72. "It is stated by way of those shown in brief" means that this statement beginning with "These twenty-three conditions," which is presented in the text (*pāḷi*) by those who show the path of recitation, was also stated in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) by way of the conditions shown in brief.
"Even by one" means even by a single word among the categories such as the wholesome (*kusala*), etc.; in that—
Or, in that description of conditions, even by a single word consisting of a complete sentence: "Three conditions" refers to the root, object, and predominance conditions.
Regarding the phrase "those four, excluding the postnascent": here, because the four conditions as previously stated have already been detailed, the word "excluding" is used;
however, the postnascent condition was not included at all. For there are only these nineteen [conditions].
"Excepting the conditions" means excluding the conditions already mentioned; "the rest" refers to those remaining. As for the phrase "but those which," he speaks of the makers of the words.
Regarding "having condensed," they explain the meaning as: "having included everything—both that which was expanded and that which was not expanded in the Pāḷi—the statement was made.
There should have been the reading "twenty-three conditions," because it is stated "having included everything. [The condition referred to is] only the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*).

"Indeed, it must be avoided. Having thus stated what ought to be said regarding the alternative arguments, he now says "But at the beginning... and so forth, in order to show the unerring meaning of the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
The commentary on the section on the analysis (*vibhaṅgavāra-vaṇṇanā*) is concluded.
(2) Explanation of the Enumeration of Terms 73.

As for the statement that "there is a distinction in the *aññamañña-paccaya* [mutuality condition] as found in the Vibhaṅga," this is said by way of the general nature of its distinctness from the analysis of the *hetu-paccaya* [root condition] and others;
for the kind of distinction found in the analysis of the *aññamañña-paccaya* is not the same as that found in the analysis of the *purejāta-paccaya* [pre-existence condition].
For in this way, rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) is obtained through the condition of mutuality (aññamañña-paccaya), not through the condition of prenascence (purejāta-paccaya).

By the passage in the Vibhaṅga beginning with “dependent on one resultant indeterminate aggregate,” he shows by way of illustration that very condition in which the resultant indeterminate is mentioned.
This is what is meant: just as in the case of the root-cause condition (hetu-paccaya) and others, [the phrase] “resultant indeterminate... [is used].

In the *Vibhaṅga*, the "resultant-indeterminate" (*vipākābyākata*) has been set forth by such passages as "dependent on one aggregate," and so forth; thus, it shows a distinction regarding the absence of the resultant-indeterminate in the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*). 74.

"In this accordance" (*etasmim anulometi*) means in this "accordance with conditions" (*paccayānuloma*) within the section on dependence (*paṭiccavāra*). "In the pure method" (*suddhikanaye*) means in the first method.
"From the enumeration shown" means from the enumeration shown in brief as "nine, three, one.
"In the methods following that" means in the second and subsequent methods following the first method. "Of another" means of another enumeration distinct from the division into nine and so forth.
"The state of having a common enumeration" refers to the condition of a multiple enumeration that is joined with a non-multiple enumeration; [the phrase] "by that non-multiple enumeration" [is used].

The particle *ca* here denotes exclusion (*byatireka*). By means of it, he illuminates that specific distinction which is stated in the positive sequence (*anuloma*) as opposed to the negative sequence (*paccanīya*). Therefore he said:
"They are to be seen only in the positive sequence. To show what is excluded by the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) "only in the positive sequence," he said:
"In the negative sequence... [etc. ...he will explain."

76–79. Regarding those methods beginning with the thirteen-rooted, when one takes only the "with-concomitance" (sāsevana) among the two types—namely, those with concomitance and those with result (savipāka)—and discards the other among the twenty-two rooted [methods], he says:
"Because the subsequently-arisen results have been abandoned. The phrase "provided there is no contradiction" is a hypothetical statement (*parikappa-vacana*), similar to such passages as:
"Could an unwholesome state arise dependent upon a wholesome state? and so forth.
This was said with intentional meaning (*saṇḍhāya*). Therefore, he said: "by the method shown in the question. And regarding that which has twenty-three as its root:

the term "name" refers to the name "having twenty-three as its root. By the phrase "twenty-two... is said," he shows that in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), only that which has twenty-two as its root is obtained, not that which has twenty-three as its root.

"Other factors" refers to the causal (hetu), dominant (adhipati), and other such factors. "The pure method" is the first method, which is called the "single-rooted" (*ekamūla*) in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
It is not found in the sections beginning with "rooted in the object" (*ārammaṇamūlaka*); that is, it is not applied to those starting from the "two-rooted" (*dumūlaka*) sections.
Indeed, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka proceeds by purifying each preceding section; therefore, [it says]: "In the object... [etc. ...the questions."
The word "said" (vutta) is the connection [to the context]. Regarding the phrase "there are only three questions":

since "the application of words conforms to the intended meaning" (*adhippāyānuvidhāyī saddappayogo*), he says, in order to clarify that intended meaning, "it precludes a number higher than that, but it does not reject a lower one.
This is because, by being designated as a specific number, it does not abandon the lower numbers already included within that enumeration.
Since a further enumeration is possible, he says: “And because one is included within the three, it is stated as ‘only three.
“His own statement” refers to his own statement beginning with “In this regard, this is the characteristic.
80–85. Even though [the factors] have been mentioned as “non-disappearance,” etc., the intention is that no permutation has been made. That [permutation] is thus shown.

If that [meaning] is shown without applying the reversal (*vipallāsa*), even though it is indeed shown, it is not shown by way of its manifestation because such a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) does not exist, as it would be in the case of the application of the reversal; this is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*).
Therefore he said: "The reversal... [is] not [present]. In the same way, the intended meaning should be applied thus: "Those... [he said] in order to show that."

Just as the intended meaning was applied there by the passage beginning with "even though [the state] has not yet passed" (*avigatānantara*), so too should the intended meaning be applied here in the phrase "therefore he makes this clear. What is meant?
Just as in that case, the point—that "when combining with those of fewer counts and those of equal counts, the count becomes both fewer and equal"—was shown for the purpose of making it known.

"Thus it is here as well. Therefore, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "In whatever way an object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) enters into combinations such as triads and dyads along with other conditions—whether by a greater number or an equal number—in all cases, exactly three answers to the questions are to be understood.
It is not only for the purpose of clarifying specific meanings that it is stated thus here.
The formal arrangement (*yojanā*) has already been made; however, in order to show that it is indeed the sequence of the teaching itself, he said:

“But even in the case of the reverse order (*paccanīya*), etc. Therein, “root term” (*mūlapada*) refers to the term that serves as the foundation in each respective method, such as the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and so forth. “Therein” (*tattha*) means in the case of the reverse order and so on.
“This characteristic” (*etaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ*) refers to the characteristic stated by the words “In this regard, this is the characteristic,” and so forth. “Therefore” (*tasmā*)...
Because the text proceeds in this very same manner from beginning to end, it is so.

By this, he shows that the teaching has come down according to the established method (ñāya), having placed the root-word right at the outset. If this is so, how can there be a manifestation of specific meanings through grammatical gender? To this he says:
"And when the meaning is already understood, there is no need for further verbal expression or for grammatical gender."
The commentary on the positive order of conditions (*paccayānulomavaṇṇanā*) is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the negative order of conditions (*paccayapaccanīyavaṇṇanā*) in the section on "dependent" (*paṭicca*).

86–87. Regarding the statement in the commentary, “It should be understood by way of the production of material phenomena alone,” this was said because the text immediately following reads, “and matter produced by consciousness.

However, since an application [of the definition] is also possible by way of the fivefold sense-consciousnesses and the rootless rebirth-linking consciousnesses, it was stated: “But this cannot be applied in a way that does not include everything.”

93. Regarding the phrase "co-nascence and pre-existence conditions" (*sahajāta-purejāta-paccayā*): this is stated to show that the condition characterizes the conditioned phenomenon. Having said, "Co-nascent causes and so forth... the meaning should be understood," he supports that very point with the words beginning "for it is not" (*na hi*).
94–97. "That condition" (*so paccayo*) means that condition which pervades the sense of dependence (*paṭicca-ṭṭha*).

99–102. Regarding "mind-originated and so forth" (*citta-samuṭṭhānādayo*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the categories of material phenomena such as external matter, nutriment-originated matter, and so on are included.
“They are grouped together. “Of that” means of the materiality that receives the path-condition (maggapaccaya).

“In the same way, moreover” refers back to what was said regarding the path-condition; it applies this same principle to the root-cause-condition (hetupaccaya) and others, meaning that for whatever receives the root-cause-condition, its [absence] is due to its having been lost.
Therefore he said: “The state of being conditionally arisen should be understood in the case of certain materialities.”
107–130. *Sabbattha* means in all the methods (*naya*), beginning with those rooted in the fifteen [factors].

Granted that there are dissimilar answers in the Pure Method (*suddhika-naya*) and others, nevertheless, the phrase "in some" (*ekesu*) and so forth was stated here in order to show the intended meaning.

*Iha* means in these methods rooted in nutriment (*āhāra-mūlaka*) and so on. "Only by way of number, not by showing the actual form" means that, as in the Pure Method, what is intended here is only the enumeration, not the demonstration of the specific forms.
The commentary on the negative exposition of conditions is finished.
Commentary on the Positive-Negative Exposition of Conditions (131–189):
"Of three" refers to these three conditions: root, predominance, and path. "Common" means...
Regarding the phrase "those which are common to those three": because it is stated by way of including them, [it refers to] those conditions which are not obtained from the contrary side.
"In the path condition" means when the path condition is present in the direct (anuloma) order. "By the others" means by the root and predominance conditions.
"The seven common ones" means the seven excluding the path condition. Thus, even the root condition is not obtained from the contrary side.
Because there is no predominance (adhipati) in those things that lack a cause. As for the phrase "but that," it is not stated because the root condition (hetupaccaya) is considered uncommon;

this is because what is being discussed here consists of conditions that are common and which have not yet been obtained [as such]. For the root condition is not common to the path condition (maggapaccaya). "By which" means by which conditions.

"Those" refers to the proximity condition (anantarapaccaya) and the others. "Because of exclusivity" means because of their inseparability (avinābhāvato). "Non-material bases" (arūpaṭṭhānika) means...
The conditions such as proximity (anantara-paccaya) and so forth are conditions only for immaterial phenomena, being themselves immaterial by nature.
"By that" means because it is intended here [in this context] that they are "exclusively immaterial-based. "By those" means by the pre-nascence (purejāta) and repetition (āsevana) conditions.

"By way of those" means by way of those lower numbers, beginning with the single [condition], etc. "Of each respective one" refers to whichever one has been applied in the negative formulation (paccanīya).
Of that [counting] consisting of pairs and so forth, which involves many numbers. "Counting" means a lower number.

By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "even for one who stands in direct order," it is shown that whether one stands in direct order or is engaged in reverse order, it is the same as the lower number.
By the statement "this characteristic is not absolute," it is shown that the aforementioned characteristic is stated by way of the majority (the general rule).
The commentary on the Positive-Negative (Paccayānulomapaccanīya) is finished.
Commentary on the Negative-Positive (Paccayapaccanīyānuloma): 190.
"In all" means in all conditions except for the postnascent (pacchājāta). For that [postnascent condition] cannot be obtained from the positive perspective.

The term “in all” (*sabbesu*) does not include what has been mentioned here. Because neither pre-nascence nor repetition conditions can be obtained for the immaterial-sphere resultant (*arūpāvacara-vipāka*) nor for the supramundane resultant (*lokuttara-vipāka*) that arises in the immaterial realms, he said, “showing by way of some illustration.
“Mere obtainment of the remainder” means the obtainment of certain remaining [conditions]. Therefore he said, “not of all, but of the remainder.”

“...is obtained. Since there is no possibility regarding what is posterior-born (*pacchājāta*), this possibility—that "the posterior-born stands in the manner of conformity" (*anuloma*)—does not exist at all.
Regarding the phrase "prior-born... is obtained," by this [statement], it follows by implication that the prior-born (*purejāta*) stands in opposition within the dissociated (*vippayutta*).
Having determined that, in order to show what must be said therein, [the text says] "the prior-born..."
"However, it has been stated: 'In the case of dissociation (vippayutta), that which stands as a negative (paccanīya) is obtained as a positive (anuloma),' and so forth.

In this context, the phrase 'if all the remaining ones were taken in the sense [of being included]' should be understood merely as pointing out the existence of such a logical consequence (atthāpatti);
the intended meaning here is that no such meaning is actually found. Therefore he said, "As for what some say," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "some [say] there," this refers to the authors of the *Padabhājaniya*. For they say:

"In order to make it known that for one passing away from the formless realm and being reborn in the sense-sphere realm, the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*) serves as an object-prenascence condition (*ārammaṇapurejāta*), this meaning—'there are nine non-dissociated conditions in the case of prenascence'—has been determined.
That is not tenable, because a mental state cannot arise in the formless realm directed toward a material form.

Likewise, some maintain that for the sense-sphere rebirth-linking consciousness following an immaterial-sphere state—just as it does following a non-percipient existence—the object is one that was previously established.
For this very reason, he says: "That too is merely their own preference," and so forth.
Or, by way of what arises from a compatible condition (*yujjamānapaccayuppannavasena*): in whichever condition is present in its natural order, whatever result is fit to arise from that condition.

The meaning is "by way of this or that. The intention is that it has not been analyzed because it is easy to understand. "Nine" refers to the object, proximity, contiguity, decisive support, prenascence, repetition, association, absence, and disappearance conditions.
That too [refers to] the fact that those nine conditions cannot be obtained in direct order (*anuloma*). 191–195.

"Of the root joined by mutuality" means that because the seventh root, which is joined by being established in the reverse order (*paccanīya*) through the mutuality condition, has been explained in detail. "All is similar" means that the entire course of the text (*pāḷi*) is similar.
Regarding the phrase "In this... [etc. ...should be understood": here, "in this" and "here" are two locative designations (*bhummavacana*).

Among these, the scope of the first has already been shown in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as being the "reverse and the conforming" (*paccanīyānuloma*); therefore, in order to show the scope of that which was not shown, the words beginning with "in these" (*etesu*) were stated.
By the word "also" (*pi*)—that is, by the word "also" in the phrase "of these also" (*imesampi*)—[it refers to] "in some condition" (*kismiñci paccaye*).
Although the eye and other [faculties], as well as resultant consciousness and so forth, receive the condition of kamma, they do not receive the status of a faculty;
therefore, it is said "for the most part" (*yebhuyyena*), which implies that a few do not receive it.

The same principle applies to the conditions of the path (*maggapaccaya*) and so on. "As previously stated" refers exclusively to the *kaṭattā-rūpa* (matter produced by past kamma) included within the five-aggregate existence and the non-percipient realm.
The intention is that it does not speak of the material phenomena originated by mind (*cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa*).

"Those which are conditions for material phenomena" means those conditions—such as root-cause (*hetu*), predominance (*adhipati*), and co-nascence (*sahajāta*)—that serve as conditions for material phenomena;

these very ones do not obtain the six conditions beginning with root-cause and predominance. By the expression "these very ones," it is established that other [conditions] obtain [them] to some extent.
Showing this, he said: "The postnascent... receives. And in order to show that this acquisition of conditions is not to be understood by way of being a producer, it was said:
"While being received... [omission] ...seeing. "By way of phenomena" means by way of the phenomena arisen from conditions.
"Faculty" means the faculty-condition. "If it were so" refers to whatever kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattārūpa*) does not receive [a condition], that very thing...

If it must be said [that this applies to all], then, since in the case of material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) only the primary elements (*bhūtarūpa*) obtain the condition of mutual dependence (*aññamaññapaccaya*), he says:
"The derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*)... [etc.]... must be stated. That statement, however, concerns the non-obtaining of the condition of mutual dependence by the derived material phenomena.
"Non-obtainment of immaterial faculties" means the non-obtainment of the faculty-condition (*indriyapaccaya*) by way of the immaterial faculties.
196–197. Since even a larger number, when combined with a smaller number, results in that same smaller number, it is said:
"Even though [the categories] begin with the triad, this [phrase] 'five by way of root' does not exist [therein]. It is profound because it is difficult to understand due to its non-obvious nature.
And just as the primary material phenomena do not arise through the condition of object or the condition of mutuality, so too at the moment of rebirth-linking...

He said "the physical basis" (vatthurūpa) because [it is stated] "but it also receives a physical basis. Just as below, where the "single-rooted" (ekamūlaka) was called "double-rooted" (dumūlaka), so too here they say that the "double-rooted" is "triple-rooted" (timūlaka).
203–233. Regarding "comprising mere volition": this refers to a question posed while taking only volition itself as the conditionally arisen (paccayuppanna).

For in that case, it would be possible to say, "by way of kamma-condition, by way of root-condition. By the phrase "in such a manner," he shows that this is an explanation of the meaning of the word "etc.
(*ādi*) in the expression "three, etc."; thus he says, "for the word 'etc. has the sense of 'manner' (*pakāra*) alone.
Matter (*rūpa*) is also included, because it is not excluded from being merely volition (*cetanā*).
The commentary on the Positive-Negative (Paccayapaccanīyānuloma) is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Dependent (Paṭiccavāra) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Chapter on Conascent (Sahajātavāra).
234–242. *Sahajātapaccayakaraṇaṃ*: occurring by making the co-nascent conditioning state (*paccayadhamma*) the condition.

*Sahajātāyattabhāvagamanaṃ*: the attainment of dependence upon the co-nascent conditioning state; that is, the arising of the conditioned phenomenon’s own existence being dependent on its co-nascent condition.
And here, it is called “co-nascent” because it makes that which is reckoned as the co-nascent condition.
A phenomenon arisen through conditions is "co-nascent" (sahajāta) when it proceeds in such a manner.

In this context, the word "co-nascent" is said to express that the phenomenon arisen through conditions proceeds by making its own co-nascent conditioning factor the condition, and that it enters into a state of dependence upon that [condition].
Therefore, it is stated: "by the word 'co-nascent'... [etc.]... is expressed. Of that act of going—
It applies to that aforementioned act of providing a co-nascent condition (*sahajātapaccaya*) or to the attainment of a state of dependence upon what is co-nascent.

Regarding the phrase "co-nascent with a wholesome phenomenon" (*kusalaṃ dhammaṃ sahajāto*), its meaning is: "having made a wholesome phenomenon—both co-nascent and cultivated together with it—the condition.
Thus he said, "because of the state of being karma for the wholesome and so forth. [This refers to] those things that coexist with the co-nascent condition.

In this context, the phrase "or reaching a state of dependence on what is co-nascent" is stated for the purpose of grouping the conditions together. "Because of their being karma" means because of the state of those aforementioned conditions acting as causes and reaching a state of dependence upon them.
In the Commentary, however, it says: "Co-nascent with a wholesome state" means having arisen together with that wholesome state in dependence upon it.
Having brought forward the word *paṭicca*, the meaning was stated; that was said by taking the sense of *paṭicca* to be the sense of "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*).
Regarding the connection with the word *sahajāta*, the grammatical justification for the accusative case in the phrase "a wholesome state" (*kusalaṃ dhammaṃ*) was not stated;

however, some maintain that because it was stated as "having become co-nascent with that," the accusative case is shown here in the sense of the instrumental. In the section on dependence (*nissaya-vāra*):

However, by one who says that "having made a wholesome state a condition in the sense of support," it should be understood that here too the meaning "having made a wholesome state a condition in the sense of co-nascence" has already been stated;
and the employment of the word *paṭicca* (dependent) should also be seen as making this very meaning known.
Furthermore, certain derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*) are both sustainers and supporters of the primary material phenomena (*bhūtarūpa*).
Even though it exists, it does not exist by way of the characteristic of being co-nascent; therefore, it does not pervade the meaning of "dependent" (paṭicca). Thus he said:
"The condition indicated by this word 'dependent' does not [itself] exist. It is stated "by way of illustration" means it is stated by way of an example, not as an exhaustive statement.
"As previously stated" means stated by way of pervading the meaning of "dependent. Just as...

Just as derived matter is not a condition for primary matter or for other derived matter, so too, with the exception of the six bases, the remaining types of matter are not conditions for immaterial phenomena;
demonstrating this, he said: "Matter, excluding the bases, is a condition for the immaterial.
The commentary on the section on co-nascence is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Section on Conditions (Paccayavāravaṇṇanā) 243.

The prefix *pati-* indicates the sense of "established," as in such phrases as "established in the core" (*sāre patiṭṭhito*). The word *aya* indicates "going" (*gati*), as in "it goes there, thus it is *ayo*.

Having included both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādārūpa*) together, it is stated that, just as with the derived matter, the primary elements serve as the support (*nissaya*).

[This was] having been done. If this is so, why is it that in the *Aṭṭhakathā* only derived matter (*upādārūpa*) is shown by the statement, “derived matter arises depending on the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*)”?
To this he says, “But in the *Aṭṭhakathā*,” and so forth. 255.
In the section on dependence (*paṭiccavāra*), regarding the commentary on the co-nascence condition (*sahajātapaccaya*), [the phrase] “born of karma and temperature” (*kamma-utujānaṃ*) refers to...

The construction is: "the meaning is stated by way of those born of karma (*kammaja*) and those born of the physical season (*utujā*). For it is said there: "It is stated by way of the primary elements (*bhūta*) originating from the two continuities (*dvisantati*).
And in the phrase "and in karma," "karma" refers to the condition of productive karma (*janakakamma-paccaya*). Regarding "those born of karma that are exclusively so and those not exclusively so":

this means those born of karma exclusively (*ekantakammaja*) and those not born of karma exclusively (*na-ekantakammaja*). Among these, in the non-percipient realm (*asañña-bhava*), it is called "exclusively born of karma."
The life-faculty, the other derived matter, and the primary matter are not exclusively born of kamma; both of these are mentioned there collectively.
However, the statement, "derived matter depending on the great primaries," is stated specifically by way of what is originated by kamma.
Therefore, that [meaning] which was stated in the section on dependence regarding the conascence condition as it was shown above is not intended here.
Therefore, that [meaning] is not intended here. If one asks why, he says: "Because of being produced... because it has been included.
"Leaving that aside" means leaving behind—that is, not taking—what was stated in the section on "dependent" (paṭicca).

"As it was taken" refers to what was taken in the text itself as: "Non-percipient... matter produced by kamma is derived matter. "Dependent" and "condition" (paccaya) are characteristics of both sections.

According to the method presented in the section on "Dependent" (paṭicca), it cannot be denied that great primary elements arise dependent upon great primary elements according to the method presented in the section on "Condition" (paccaya). Therefore,

by the inclusion of the term "derived matter" (upādārūpa) in the phrase "kamma-born matter reckoned as derived matter," one should exclude from among the derived matters those produced by temperature, mind, and nutriment, without specifically singling out kamma-born matter.
The construction here should be understood as follows: "Because of its existence, due to what has been performed... [etc. ...the qualification is to be seen. (286–287).
"Of certain material phenomena" means of those originated by rootless consciousness. The same principle applies to the mention of "certain material phenomena" in the subsequent sections as well.
"By way of the phenomena of the eye, etc. means by way of the material phenomena of the eye-base, etc. "By way of the categories such as mind-originated, etc. means...
By way of the categories of material phenomena such as those born of mind (*cittaja*), etc., everything is obtained.

Although this method is not rooted in causes (*na-hetu-mūlaka*), because there is nothing to be excluded among the twenty-five material phenomena existing according to the fourfold continuity, the enumeration of "all matter" by way of all matter is obtained;
that is, it is counted as one within the [categories] of "not-yet-arisen" (*no-natthi*) and "disappeared" (*vigata*).
The commentary on the section on conditions (*paccayavāra*) is finished.
4. Commentary on the section on support (*nissayavāra*). 329–337.

Regarding "the state of being a supporting condition" (*nissayapaccayabhāva*): this refers to the meaning of "support" (*nissaya*) as stated in the section on support, namely, that which is co-nascent (*sahajāta*) and pre-existent (*purejāta*).
The construction is: "to determine the state of being a condition for a phenomenon by means of the section on conditions. Likewise, the construction is:
"to determine the state of being co-nascent or pre-existent of the conditioning phenomenon spoken of as 'conditions' in the section on conditions by means of the section on support.
And here, this determination is shown to be without difference in meaning because the sense of condition and the sense of support are explained through different synonyms.

It should be understood thus. Therefore it was said: "The state of being a condition (paccayatta) is the state of being a support (nissayatta), and the state of being a support is the state of being a condition.
The commentary on the Section on Support (Nissayavāra) is finished.
5. Commentary on the Section on Conjoined (Saṃsaṭṭhavāra).
351–368. Rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) has a physical basis (savatthukā). "In this case too" means even in this section on associated states.

It is not found among the predominance, prenascence, and repetition conditions when they are established in the positive order (*anuloma*) but excluded from the kamma, resultant, jhāna, and dissociation conditions in the negative order (*paccanīya*).

However, it is found among the remaining [conditions] such as conascence and so forth when established in the positive order, and among the root and other conditions when established in both the positive and negative orders.
Therefore he said, "among the conditions that are obtainable. These [conditions] are extracted for the purpose of showing this specific distinction—that is, this aforementioned distinction.
Consequently, because there is no such distinction to be shown, rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) devoid of its basis (vatthu) is not extracted;

the meaning is that it is not excluded because it stands as a contrary to the dissociated (vippayutta) conditions. This is for the purpose of showing the mere absence of the root-cause condition (hetupaccaya).
By this, he shows that the statement of fact excludes the inclusion of rootless states, thereby precluding any deviation [from the rule].
It should read “by way of rootless resultant and functional [states],” because the Path has the roots as its limit.
369–391. Regarding the passage beginning, “When the roots stand in the forward order, the jhānas and the Paths are not obtained in the reverse order,” and so forth, which occurs here:

It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that there is no phenomenon arising by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and so forth that does not receive these eight conditions—namely, the four universals (*sabbaṭṭhānika*), nutriment, faculty, jhāna, and path.

This can be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the positive-negative section (*anuloma-paccanīya*) of the "Dependent" chapter (*paṭicca-vāra*). Thus he said: "In the 'Dependent' chapter... by way of the method."

Regarding the phrase "among the remaining": among the rootless states, excluding rootless delusion (*ahetuka-moha*), the fivefold sense-consciousnesses... [and so on] ...receive the condition of jhāna;
therefore, it cannot be said that "only rootless delusion receives the conditions of jhāna and the Path.

Furthermore, in the negative-positive method (*paccanīyānuloma*), there is no simultaneous conjunction of two conditions according to the positive method; rather, there is a conjunction for each one individually.
Because it has arrived [at the path], therefore only rootless delusion receives the condition of the path; thus should the construction here be understood.
The commentary on the section on "Conjoined" is finished.
6. Commentary on the Section on "Associated."

392–400. Regarding “similar and associated”: that which is called “what is similar is conjoined” (*saṃsaṭṭha*) is not what is meant by “associated” (*sampayutta*), as in such expressions as “the horses are conjoined and yoked. Regarding “unconjoined and mixed”:
that which is not conjoined, yet even when mixed by arising intermittently, is called “associated” due to its state of being blended; that is what is meant by “conjoined” (*saṃsaṭṭha*).
[This is] not the case in such passages as: "That investigation which... is associated with laziness," and so forth.

Thus, since there exists a figurative expression for "conjoined" (*saṃsaṭṭha*) even when [a factor] is not actually conjoined, and a figurative expression for "associated" (*sampayutta*) even when [a factor] is not actually associated, he said, "Both...
is a determiner," in order to show that both of these mutually determine one another. For the word *saṃsaṭṭha*...
There is no meaning of "mixed" (*vokiṇṇa*), and the word "associated" (*sampayutta*) has the sense of "similar.

Therefore, just as the word "conjoined" (*saṃsaṭṭha*), in relation to the word "associated," turns away from the meaning of similarity and makes known the meaning of having the same nature of arising together and so forth, so too the word "associated," in relation to the word "conjoined," turns away from the meaning of being mixed. Thus, regarding these two words which are mutually dependent:
The mutual determination [of the factors] is to be understood.
The commentary on the Section on Association is finished.
7. Commentary on the Analysis of the Section on Questions.
401–403. "Those conditions" refers to those conditions beginning with the root-cause (hetu).

Regarding the phrase "in succession," since there might be a doubt as to whether this means "in the sequence of conditions" or "in the sequence of the terms such as 'wholesome' (kusala)," the author first says "in due order" and so forth, demonstrating that the meaning is appropriate according to both ways.
Its meaning is as follows: "The root-cause condition, the object-condition," and so on.
"In order to show those conditions in accordance with the method, the sequence of teaching, and the specific order in which they appeared in the 'Dependent' (Paṭicca) Chapter,
the second [section] is shown by saying, 'The wholesome [is related] to the wholesome,' and so forth. Since this sequence of words is not fully demonstrated merely by showing the 'wholesome' term,
he now demonstrates the whole of it by way of the method, illustrating it through a single part."
He said: “‘The wholesome [is the condition] for the wholesome’... [etc. ...it is so.

By that means—that is, by the mere indication of the phrase “the wholesome [is the condition] for the wholesome”—“the entire classification” means the whole extent of the classification, such as “the wholesome [is the condition] for the wholesome” and so forth, which receives its answer in various places regarding the conditions;
all that is the “entire classification. These conditions are shown in their proper order.
In order to show those conditions, such as the cause-condition (hetu-paccaya),

in the sequence of terms beginning with "wholesome" (kusala), [the author] says, "having made it pure," meaning that those who desire a specific result give a gift in such a way that the offering is purified from the donor's side just as it is from the recipient's side. By the phrase "those who are worthy of being called 'theirs,'" [he indicates] the purification.

This demonstrates the unique status of the once-returner and others. Granted that purification (*vodāna*) is indeed the precursor to the highest path (*aggamagga*), it is not included here because one reviews it only after becoming an adept (*asekkha*). "That" refers to purification.

"Change-of-lineage consciousness" (*gotrabhucitta*) is the consciousness fit to be called "change-of-lineage" at the moment it arises for a person on the eighth stage (*aṭṭhamaka*). It is "similar to change-of-lineage."
Or, it should be understood here that the meaning is: "the mind that overcomes the lineage (gotra) of those such as stream-enterers," or "the lineage-mind" (gotrabhū-citta).
It defines the conditionally arisen state by way of its plane, as in the phrase "only wholesome [states] of the three planes," meaning it is not the conditioning phenomenon itself.
"Because of the difference in the teaching" means because it is distinct from the teaching that designates a person, such as "of one possessing a wholesome mind," and so forth; otherwise...
The intention is that one should not take up again what has already been taken.
(405) Just as for one free from lust, so too for one free from mental joy, there is no occurrence of lust toward an object by way of relishing;
thus it is said: "the function of relishing... [and so forth]... the task. This refers to that which occurs with the mental formation of agitation, having the nature of being elated.
Because craving that has been distinguished by rapture is called "delight in craving," it is said with reference to this: "the function of craving accompanied by the function of rapture.
And just as craving, which has been distinguished by rapture through its aforementioned specific functions, is "delight in craving," so too should "delight in views" be understood.
For in its actual meaning, that [delight] is simply view itself, distinguished by a particular condition.

Therefore it was said: “Delighting in views is just views themselves. Herein, however, regarding the word “delights,” among these two meanings stated by way of craving and views, the phrase “of one who delights” is said with reference specifically to delighting in views;
thus it is stated, “taking only the latter meaning. Of one who delights...
However, because it was stated without distinction, the intended meaning here is "of one who delights by way of craving and by way of views.
Therefore, the statement, "Delight... cannot be said [to exist]," finds no place here. Why?
Because delight is stated to exist even in a mental continuum devoid of views. One "delights by way of craving" means precisely by way of delight through craving.

The first meaning has already been stated. However, regarding the phrase "in two types of consciousness accompanied by joy," he speaks with reference to those types of consciousness accompanied by joy that are devoid of views.

"By means of the joy as it was described" refers to one who relishes [the object] by means of the joy described in the passage beginning "of joy in one possessed of lust," and who likewise relishes those same two types of consciousness as they were described by means of lust.

The application here should be understood as follows: in all four types of consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassasahagata*), when one delights with craving characterized by rapture (*sappītika-taṇhā*), and in all four types associated with views (*diṭṭhisampayutta*), when one delights through delighting in views (*diṭṭhābhinandanā*), a view arises.

Therefore, it was said: "It is possible to apply [the principle] in this way. Just as delighting in views arises from the supporting condition of a view (*diṭṭhūpanissaya*), [so too does craving arise].
Thus, it should be understood that from craving as a decisive support (taṇhūpanissaya), the delighting in craving (taṇhābhinandanā) also arises.
Regarding the statement, “Delighting, lust arises,” one might say that lust arises for one who delights in craving accompanied by rapture;
or alternatively, one might not say so, because the arising of lust is stated to occur precisely through the delighting in craving.
406. Regarding the statement "‘tadārammaṇatā’ is used where ‘tadārammaṇatāya’ should have been said," he says:

"Here, an elision of the case-ending has been made. He says this to show that in the term *tadārammaṇatā*, the meaning denoted by the word *tā* is called "state" (*bhāva*), and that there is no such state other than what is denoted by the word *tadārammaṇa*. By this, [it is shown] in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*).
This indicates that the word *taṃ* [is used here]. Therefore he says: "The meaning is that the result has become the state of having that as its object.
In this sense, "having that as its object" (*tadārammaṇatā*) should be understood as a nominative singular. Regarding the phrase "the base of infinite consciousness...

is not mentioned," although it is possible for even the results of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) to have karma as their object, that [sense-sphere karma] is [not mentioned] because it is [only] for the results of the base of infinite consciousness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...
This karma is not invariably determined as the object of this resultant consciousness because of the great variety of sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses;
therefore, the meaning is that although it is possible [for it to be its object], it was not mentioned. If this is so, one might suspect:

"Why then was it not shown even though it is possible? To address this doubt, he says: "But by way of the registration [consciousness]... and so forth. This refers to the case when entering [jhāna] in forward order (anuloma). For the most part...
The state of being the object for the proximate attainment is thus shown; otherwise, the statement "either in reverse order or by skipping one" would be purposeless—this is the intended meaning.
"It might be" means that even a non-proximate attainment could be the object, and it cannot be denied; for this very reason, the word "mostly" (*yebhuyyena*) was used. "This being so" means...

If it is intended that the indeterminate (abyākata) object-nature of wholesome aggregates is due solely to the status of the object for the adverting consciousness (āvajjanā), then this being the case, it ought to have been stated [in the text]:

“of the knowledge of supernormal powers (iddhividhañāṇa),” because that too serves as the object for adverting consciousness. Since that was not stated, that indeterminate knowledge of supernormal powers is [not included among] the wholesome...
It is not stated that "the aggregates are the object of the knowledge of the modes of psychic power. "Are" means they become the object. "Those" refers to the knowledge of others' minds and so forth.
"By whatever body" refers to the body by which one adverts through the act of making the knowledge of others' minds and other wholesome states its object. 407–409.

It should be understood that the arising of displeasure (*domanassa*) is to be connected with both the seeing of danger and the mere fact of its being undesirable by nature. The varieties of intolerance (*akkhanti*) are to be understood according to the classification of the bases for resentment (*āghātavatthu*) and so forth.
410. "Of all" (*sabbassa*): if taken in the sense of delimiting the treatise, it means "of all the indeterminate";
but if taken in the sense of a different meaning, it means "of all that is knowable. "Incapability" (*asakkuṇeyyattā*):
this is stated because of the infinity and immeasurability of what is to be described, not because of ignorance or opposition.
417. It is said that "emergence as purification does not occur from what is unprecedented" because it is stated:

"Emergence from the unprecedented stream of consciousness is simply the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). For that [purification] is the cleansing of a distinction already attained and the bringing about of proficiency;
thus, it is not called "unprecedented. Accordingly, it has been said: "For each lower jhāna, when made proficient, [serves as the basis] for the higher one..."
"It is the footing for the higher [state]; therefore, purification (vodāna) is also called emergence (vuṭṭhāna).
Because it is not to be omitted, there is nothing further to be said; since it is identical in its wholesome nature and lacks anything to be excluded, there is no need to speak by way of analysis.
Therefore, showing that which is obtainable as a qualification here: "The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... pe..."
He said, "Regarding attainment. Since this has already been stated in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*, however,

that which ought to be said regarding the state of having a resultant object (*tadārammaṇabhāva*) immediately following functional consciousness (*kiriyānantara*)— namely, "When the wholesome has ceased, the resultant arises as its object," and so forth—
has already been explained in the commentary to the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*.

“Both of them”: those two mind-consciousness elements (manoviññāṇadhātu) mentioned as “the wholesome-resultant rootless accompanied by joy and the accompanied by equanimity”—both of these are stated by way of the mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy.

Why? Because they serve as the proximity condition (anantarapaccaya) for the ten sense-sphere life-continuum (bhavaṅga) states at the time of their own object-referencing (tadārammaṇa), at the time of investigation (santīraṇa), and for the determining consciousness (voṭṭhapana). [The same applies to] those accompanied by equanimity.

However, it should be connected as follows: at the time of the ten aforementioned resultant mind-consciousness elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), [the consciousness] is associated with the functional determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbanakiriya*);
at the time of investigation (*santīraṇa*), with the functional mind-element (*manodhātukiriya*); and at the time of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), with the life-continuum itself.
423. "Having penetrated" means having known. "It should not be grasped firmly" means a firm grasp should not be taken. "Of one who is strong... etc.
By the phrase "in terms of ripening," it is shown that strength and weakness are not the measure [of the decisive support], whereas the granting of an opportunity is the measure.
And the granting of an opportunity should be understood as the state of being oriented toward fruition when the remaining conditions have come together.
The phrase "whatever" means whether it be strong or weak. Furthermore, even some karma that produces fruition does not constitute a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

It is indeed possible to say this. For if there were an inseparable connection between the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) and the kamma condition (*kamma-paccaya*), then when the decisive support condition is included in the triad of resultant states (*vipākattika*), the kamma condition would not need to be mentioned separately;

and in the triad of feeling (*vedanāttika*), it could not be said that the decisive support condition stands as its opposite while coexisting with the kamma condition. This is the intended meaning regarding these two conditions.
However, it can be maintained that even when the decisive support (upanissaya) is taken for the teaching which is currently being obtained, the kamma-condition must still be extracted.
For the extraction of what is obtainable is consistent with reason;
likewise, even though the decisive support stands as an opposing factor, the kamma-condition must indeed be stated because the decisive support has many divisions, [and] kamma produces its result.
It should be understood that it cannot be said that there is no decisive support (upanissaya) for the result (vipāka).
"Contempt directed at another" means a sense of inferiority directed toward oneself with reference to another person's continuum.
"Among them" refers to the relatives and friends of one who was previously killed by him. This is because of the prior volition (purima-cetanā) set in motion for the purpose of killing his mother.
There is similarity with the act of matricide; and just as this same principle applies to the command, it also applies to the blow. Therefore it was said:
"This method [applies] here also in two ways.
One who, while dependent on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), generates faith by means of giving and so forth, [does so] based upon greed (*rāga*) through the practice of giving and so forth.

It is said that [the text] "arouses" does not refer to [a state] dependent on turning away (vivaṭṭa), because it is stated without distinction; thus he says, "he speaks with this underlying intention.

"Of these" refers to bodily pleasure and pain. "Even on one side" is said considering that although there is no simultaneous arising of pleasure and pain within a single continuum at one moment, their conjunction of conditions can nevertheless occur even in the same place.

425. "As in the preceding sections" means as in the preceding sections such as the Section on Dependence (*paṭiccasamuppādavāra*). "In this [section]" refers to the Section on Questions (*pañhāvāra*).

"Arising by way of condition is stated" means that the arising of various things produced by conditions is not stated by way of each respective condition, such as the root-cause (*hetu*) and so forth.
"Of those respective phenomena" refers to those respective conditioning phenomena, such as the root-cause and so forth. "The state of being a respective condition" means...

The state of being a respective condition for causes and so forth is what is being stated. For that very reason, in the preceding six sections, the mention of "arising" was made in various places through such phrases as "a wholesome state arises";

however, here, the state of being a condition is taken up through such phrases as "it is a condition for a wholesome state by way of the cause-condition. "By that" means by way of the state of being a condition that provides support. "Here" refers to the section on questions.
427. *Patiṭṭhābhūtassa* means "of that which has become a support" (i.e., a basis). *Kammapaccayo* means "the co-nascent kamma-condition.

*Dukamūlakadukāvasānā* refers to the questions stated by making the "pair-based pair-ending" (*dukamūlakadukāvasāna*) formulation as follows: "Wholesome and indeterminate states [are related] to wholesome and indeterminate states.
*Tattha* means "in the section on conditions" (*paccayavāra*). *Kusalo ca abyākato ca dhammā* refers to the various classifications of wholesome and indeterminate states.

"Phenomena arisen by way of conditions" (*paccayuppannā dhammā*). By the phrase "from whatever [source] they arise," the intended meaning in that section on conditions is merely the fact of arising from either condition—whether wholesome or indeterminate—without establishing a fixed rule regarding the specific conditioning phenomena.

What is not intended is the status of being a condition for both types of aforementioned "condition-arisen" phenomena, nor the status of being a condition for both those aforementioned conditioning phenomena themselves.
The intention is that this teaching is because its primary focus is on arising (*uppāda*). "Those that have become the support, etc.

means that the conditioning states (*paccayadhamma*) which have become the support (*nissaya*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*) are not found [in this context]. Therefore, the construction is: "And the wholesome... is not stated.
The commentary on the analysis of the section of questions (*pañhāvāra*) is finished.
The forward calculation (anulomagaṇanā) for the composition of the section on questions (pañhāvāra):

439. “Therein” means in the section based on the indeterminate (abyākata). “If it were so” means: if [a state] which is not obtainable by way of wholesome or unwholesome roots were nevertheless obtainable [therein], that being the case. The intention is that this is due to a commonality in the mere number [of conditions], not a commonality in the specific conditions themselves.

440. It should be understood by way of illustration; for in most cases, the faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya), the path-condition (magga-paccaya), and the root-condition (hetu-paccaya) [function together].

Because they are of a different class (*visabhāga*). By the qualification "and because the faculty and path conditions are of a different class," it excludes whatever state of being of the same class (*sabhāga*) exists therein.
Likewise, "by way of presence and absence" means: by way of presence when that mode of the root condition exists;

that is to say, when the states that are roots exist as root-conditions, [the other conditions] exist as co-nascent and so forth. "Of the predominance condition, etc. refers to the predominance, faculty, and path conditions.
The dissimilarity of the root condition (*hetupaccaya*). "Of wholesome and other roots" means of wholesome, unwholesome, functional, and indeterminate roots.
"In the state of being a root condition" means in the capacity of a root condition, that is, in the state of being helpful by way of being a root.

"Due to the absence of the state of being a ripening condition" means because of the non-existence of the state of being a ripening condition; for there is no status as a ripening condition for those things that are already ripenings (*vipāka*). [This is so] because roots that are themselves ripenings possess the status of a root condition only in relation to other roots.
He said, "There is similarity," [referring to] "those excluding the cause.

There must be dissimilarity among the results (vipāka), for there is no similarity between those things whose nature is to produce a result (vipākadhamma), those that are themselves results (nevavipāka), and those whose nature is not to produce a result (navipākadhamma), because they belong to different categories;

this is the intended meaning. "Accompanied by both conditions" means accompanied by the conditions of cause (hetu) and result (vipāka). "In the case of a result when the condition of cause exists" means...
Regarding "in resultant phenomena occurring by way of the conditionality of root-cause":

because of the absence of the state of being a condition for resultants—that is, because of the non-existence of the presence or absence of the conditionality of resultants. For a resultant is not a condition for another resultant as a condition for resultants; therefore, the intention is that there is no dissimilarity between the conditions of root-cause and resultant.

Now, in order to support the very point just stated by means of an illustration, he says, "Just as," and so forth. "Accompanied by the cause-condition and the co-nascent condition" (*hetusahajātapaccayasahite*) means accompanied by both conditions;
this is the meaning. The term "of the causes" (*hetūnaṃ*) should also be connected with the phrase "the absence of the state of being a co-nascent condition.

For just as there is the state of being a cause-condition within a collection of causes that is accompanied by the cause-condition, [so too is there the state of being a co-nascent condition within a collection of phenomena accompanied by the co-nascent condition].

There is also the state of being a co-nascent condition (*sahajātapaccaya*). In that context, it is not said that there is a commonality (*sabhāgatā*) among co-nascent phenomena—excluding the cause—and the causal phenomenon itself, because they possess a common nature by virtue of the co-nascent condition.

"In the same way here" means that just as there is no dissimilarity (*visabhāgatā*) in the manner described regarding the cause and co-nascent conditions, so too there is no dissimilarity here between the cause and the resultant condition (*vipākapaccaya*).
The meaning is as follows. This same method applies to the dissociation condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*) as well;

that is to say, the method stated regarding the absence of dissimilarity (*visabhāgatābhāva*) in the root and co-nascent conditions (*hetu-sahajāta-paccaya*) also applies to the dissociation condition when accompanied by the root.

For there too, it is possible to apply the formulation beginning with, "In the group accompanied by the root-dissociation condition," and so forth. Only the present is the conditioned state (*paccayuppanna*), whereas the condition (*paccaya*) may also be past.
The phrase beginning with "Moreover" (*apicā*) demonstrates this point: that although a state is said to be "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) by way of its presence or absence at the present moment—

referring to its status as a cause-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) or a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) etc.— yet, when considering wholesome states (*kusala*) and so forth that exist at different moments,
as well as their results (*vipāka*), one cannot say that there is a lack of homogeneity (*visabhāgatā*) for that very same cause, even though it is also future and free from time.
With the intention that, because the distinction is not easily discerned from the general category alone due to the lack of a specifically grasped distinction, he said:

“It should be stated as ‘wholesome [states] dominated by investigation. (441–443) It is not possible to say, “The other two are obtained,” because those [cases] shown by the pairs of the root-dominance and the object-dominance—namely, “a wholesome state for a wholesome state,” “a wholesome state for an indeterminate state,” and “a wholesome state for a wholesome state... [are excluded].

Regarding the four answers—“a wholesome [state] for a wholesome [state],” “an unwholesome [state] for an unwholesome [state],” “a wholesome and indeterminate [state] for a wholesome [state],” and “an indeterminate state for an indeterminate state”—when the associated condition (sampayutta-paccaya) is included among the conditions of root, co-nascence, support, presence, non-disappearance, faculty, and path, one obtains these two:
“a wholesome state for a wholesome [state]” and “an indeterminate state for an indeterminate [state]. It is with reference to this that...
In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is stated: “If together with those... [as before] ...he obtains only those two.

However, by those [two], the other two—namely, “a wholesome state is a condition for an indeterminate state,” and “a wholesome state is a condition for both a wholesome and an indeterminate state”—would also be included.
For a wholesome state does not function as a condition for a wholesome state by way of dissociation-condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*). Therefore...
It is said: “The first reading states that ‘one obtains the other two,’ and so forth. Regarding “the other two”:

this refers either to the other two, which are the two answers based on the associated condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*); or else, in the introduction concerning the dissociated condition (*vippayutta*), there are two other answers of a different nature.
Referring to these, it was stated: “A wholesome [state] is related to the indeterminate; an indeterminate [state] is related to the indeterminate.”

‘He obtains two,’ they recite. In the phrase “among those,” it refers to those [conditions] with a lower count, such as resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*), mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*), and so forth.
“Resultants not included” means those for which the resultant condition has not been taken; this neuter designation is used in view of the connection [of the words].
They are not devoid of a resultant cause, because they are stated by way of their commonality. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: “By way of generality...”
[It is said: “They are stated by way of all nine causes,” and “The resultant cause is also found there.
Regarding the phrase “therein”: it refers to the five combinations starting from the fifth combination.

Furthermore, the meaning “that which has an arising (samuṭṭhāna) together with or simultaneously with that resultant” is also possible; thus it is said: “In rebirth-linking, the kamma-produced matter (kaṭattārūpa) also...”

“By the very mention of ‘arising from that,’ it includes it. By the phrase “the same method applies,” he extends this same point to show that even kamma-produced matter (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) is included by the very mention of “arising from that.
“Even so” means: even in the manner briefly stated by the passage beginning with “But among these...”. Therefore he said: “But among these... pe ...”
"Also by the method already stated": "Whichever condition" means whichever condition, such as the root-cause (hetu) and so forth, which stands as the primary basis for other conditions.
"Of those phenomena conditioned by that" means of those phenomena, such as the root-cause and so forth, which have become conditions through those conditions like the root-cause and so on.

"In the order of obtaining [them] without remainder, with remainder, less than that, and even less than that" means that those phenomena, in whichever questions they appropriately belong, [are treated] in that sequence.
They are obtained without remainder; those in which they are deficient, more deficient, or most deficient are obtained according to that sequence.

Because the statement of their combination follows that order, even those [factors] arisen through conditions are obtained in due order, following the sequence beginning with "without remainder. Therefore he said: "And in the obtaining without remainder...
it should be understood."
The section on the Root of Causes (*Hetumūlaka*) is finished.
445. Regarding the fifth [section], the phrase "one [root] with support" refers to the unwholesome root that has an indeterminate root as its support;

it is with reference to this that he says, "he will explain it with support by way of the basis (*vatthu*). The word "not this" refers to the fact that, although a basis is obtainable in this fourth [section], it is not [included here].
There is no synthesis by way of [other] factors because that will be explained later; therefore, the meaning is that the position is taken as "only by way of the object.

(446) By the statement "the co-nascent and prenascent [factors] are one supporting condition" (*nissaya-paccaya*), he shows that although there is a difference in the phenomena that serve as conditions, there is no difference in the nature of the condition itself;
likewise, this is also shown by the term "presence condition" (*atthi-paccaya*). Furthermore, the non-disappearance condition (*avigata-paccaya*) here is identical to the presence condition.
"He is included" is how it should be understood. The reading is "the presence-absence condition.

However, the co-nascent and object-predominance [conditions] are not merely a distinction in the types of phenomena that act as conditions; rather, there is also a distinction in their mode of being a condition.
Thus he said: "In this way... because of the absence... To make the very point already stated more clear, he said: "For the state of support," and so forth. Therein:
“Of the co-nascent, pre-existent, support, and so forth” means of the co-nascent support, the pre-existent support, and so on.

By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), it includes the co-nascent, pre-existent, presence, and non-disappearance [conditions]. Expounding upon the very meaning stated by the passage beginning with “But not even this,” he says “For that which is co-nascent,” and so on.

“Dissimilar in nature” (*bhinnasabhāvā*) means that although they are alike in being denotable by the term “predominance” (*adhipati*), they are dissimilar in nature due to their specific mode of being conditions.

It is not by its mere intrinsic nature (*sabhāvamatta*), as is the case with the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and others. "Precisely for that reason" means precisely because their intrinsic natures are distinct. Otherwise, one would have to state both together in a single instance, saying:
"The wholesome is a condition for the wholesome by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*); the indeterminate is a condition by way of object (*ārammaṇa*) and predominance (*adhipati*).
Since this was not stated, he said: "In the analysis of the Questions Section (*pañhāvāra-vibhaṅga*)... it was not stated."
447–452. "By way of commonality" means by way of the general nature of being a dominant factor (*adhipati*) and a faculty (*indriya*).
Having joined the six combinations in that very manner, he demonstrates them with the words beginning "the dominant factor" (*adhipati*).

"Two conditioning states" refers to two conditioning states by way of energy (*viriya*) and investigation (*vīmaṃsā*), while there is only one by way of mental dominance (*cittādhipati*). They should have been stated together previously according to the sequence of the dominant factors.
The intention is as follows: first, energy is predominant (*adhipati*), and afterwards, consciousness is predominant. Among those conditions of nutriment and path, those mentioned later are combined.
The phrase "because of similarity" is stated with reference to the subsequent statement beginning, "because of similarity to the combinations mentioned by way of root" (*hetu*).
457–460. "Rooted in two" (*dumūlaka*) means rooted in the wholesome and the indeterminate. Regarding the objection as to why that is stated among the wholesome roots:
He said: "By way of showing the state of being a condition for wholesome [states] accompanied by the indeterminate. "In this context" means in the forward enumeration (*anuloma-gaṇanā*).

"As stated" refers to those rooted in the co-nascent (*sahajāta*), mutuality (*aññamañña*), support (*nissaya*), result (*vipāka*), association (*sampayutta*), dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*)—that is, in those rooted in the co-nascent and so forth.
"Excluding those rooted in presence and non-disappearance" refers to the roots of presence and non-disappearance.
The connection is that, among the remaining [factors] excluding those [already mentioned], no combinations have been applied by way of nutriment or the nutriment-condition.

And the construction is that no combinations have been applied by way of predominance or faculties among the [conditions] beginning with co-nascence, excluding the support-condition and so forth. "In these" refers to the root-cause, kamma, jhāna, and path;

and to the nutriment, predominance, and faculties as they were described—being applied according to their respective combinations. "By that" refers only to the non-material phenomena such as the root-cause and so forth.

"From the point of being obtainable. "Conjunctions by means of those" refers to conjunctions when they are joined with causes and so forth. "Due to the absence of being mixed with material form" is a statement of reason for the similarity already mentioned.
But why are the root-conditions of presence and non-disappearance excluded here—namely, the conditions of support, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance?
To this he says: "But by means of presence and non-disappearance," and so forth. [This refers to] the predominance and faculty conditions when they are joined with support and the others.
The connection is: "They are not stated to be mixed with form.

If this is so, why has there been an application of nutriment (*āhāra*) to those based on the roots of existence (*atthi*) and non-disappearance (*avigata*), and of predominance (*adhipati*) and faculties (*indriya*) to those based on the root of support (*nissaya*) and so forth? Addressing this objection, he says: "In those based on predominance, nutriment, and faculties," and so on.

(473–477) In such instances, it is stated that the word *khandha* is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) only for the immaterial (*arūpa*), taking this into account, [it is said]: "not in the course of existence (*pavatta*)."
“...the aggregates themselves should be understood as having arisen through conditions.
By stating, “But even *kaṭattā-rūpa* (matter produced by past karma) is obtainable,” he rejects the statement that [the aggregates] were spoken of “by way of a single-moment kamma.
Making clearer the purpose for which it was asked, “Why was it not stated? he says, “Is it not so? and so forth, and then again, by means of an illustration:
The phrase beginning with "in whatever way" was stated in order to analyze [the matter].

"By way of being an object-condition and a support-condition" means by way of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and by way of being a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*). Since the fact that karma is a condition is indeed well-known, he said: "Karma also should be stated as being an object-condition.
"Of the two conditions" refers to the conditions of karma and the object. "Because of their mutual exclusion" means...
By this, he shows that because the two modes of conditionality are distinct, it is impossible for a single mode of occurrence to apply to a single conditioning phenomenon at one moment.
Demonstrating that what has been shown is not identical to what is to be illustrated, he says: "For the present...
it would be appropriate to say. Then, with the words "But as for kamma... and so forth, [he explains] because the modes of occurrence of the conditions of kamma and object are distinct.
Having become one, it demonstrates precisely the absence of occurrence.

Since those [factors] are stated to be mutual opposites, why is it that the very same object-base (*vatthu*) is both an object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), whereas the very same kamma is not both an object-condition and a kamma-condition?
This is not to be questioned; rather, showing that this is the intrinsic nature (*dhammasabhāva*) of phenomena, he says: "And this is its intrinsic nature," and so forth.
In this context, "of those occurring" (*vattamānānaṃ*) means "of those present.

The word "which" (*yaṃ*), being connected with the term "the state of being expressible" (*vattabbatā*), should be transformed into the feminine gender as "which" (*yā*). By the passage beginning with "just as," he clarifies that very meaning by showing an illustration.

(478–483) That consciousness which is not a dominant condition (*adhipatipaccaya*) should be understood as having its status as a dominant condition unaddressed. "By way of the physical basis" (*vatthussa vasena*) means by way of the physical basis that is to be excluded.

484–495. The construction is: "The immaterial faculties are obtained as conditions for material phenomena. Although it has been stated thus, since the material faculties are also obtained as conditions for the immaterial [phenomena], he says: "But the eye and so forth are obtained as conditions for eye-consciousness and so forth.
"Of the same course as that" means they share the same course as energy by way of being a condition for the path.

511–514. Regarding the section on dissociation (*vippayuttamūlaka*), the statement in the Commentary, “In the tenth [case], the wholesome and so forth [are causes] of mind-originated [matter],” was made by way of the course of existence (*pavatti*).

Therefore, he says: “But in the case of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), this is also applicable: ‘The aggregates [are causes] of the matter produced by kamma (*kaṭattārūpa*), and the physical basis (*vatthu*) is [a cause] of the aggregates.
“By way of seeing that” means by way of seeing that physical basis (*vatthu*).
It is not by way of showing the condition-dhamma in its entirety. Therefore he said: “The aggregates and the basis—this too is indeed obtainable.
They are not to be excluded because they must also be applied as being produced by conditions.
515–518. The meaning is: of the immaterial bases, objects, great elements, faculties, and nutriments, which are condition-dhammas. “Nutriment and faculty conditions...”
And it should also be stated thus: "Why? Because by way of the faculties (indriya) and nutriment (āhāra), [the conditions] such as conascence (sahajāta) and so forth are not obtained;

rather, by way of the faculties and nutriment, only the faculty-nutriment conditions (indriyāhāra-paccaya) are obtained. For after enumerating 'conascent, prenascence, postnascence, nutriment, and faculty,' the presence condition (atthi-paccaya) is analyzed. However, some here [hold that] by the inclusion of "nutriment" [in the enumeration],...
Only edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) has been taken [as the representative of food], and by the mention of the faculties (*indriya*), only the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) is meant;
the remaining faculties and foods are included within the categories of *sahajāta* (conascent) and so forth.

With reference to those which are included therein, the mention of "faculties and foods" was made in the commentary in the passage: "by way of non-material bases, objects, great elements, faculties, and foods."
They say it is stated that “the conditions of co-nascence, prenascence, and postnascence are obtainable.
In this context, the status of the immaterial states as conditions of co-nascence, postnascence, nutriment, and faculty should be understood accordingly.

The physical basis (vatthu) is both co-nascent and prenascence; the object (ārammaṇa) is exclusively prenascence; however, for direct-knowledge consciousness (abhiññā-ñāṇa), it is sometimes also co-nascent.

It certainly remains an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*). However, by the inclusion of the term "conascent" (*sahajāta*) here, only that which functions as a conascence-condition (*sahajātapaccaya*) is intended;
and since that is characterized by simultaneous arising and so forth, any state (*dhamma*) that becomes an object while being conascent is not what is meant here.
If even a conascent state can be an object, why is it not analyzed as such in the Canon (*pāḷi*)?

It is for the purpose of releasing [the mind] from confusion regarding that which is included within a single group and possesses the characteristics of simultaneous arising and so forth, as distinct from that which is included within a different group.
Furthermore, it is not included because of its rarity and its lack of manifestation. "From that" means "from the ninth," the intention being "not from the tenth";
for there is no dominant factor (*adhipati*) in the eleventh. Likewise, in the phrase "in the fourteenth,"...
By the word "thus" (tathā), he summarizes this point: that by the inclusion of the bases (vatthu), the bases such as the eye and so forth are also included.
"That very same" (tadeva) refers to the object (ārammaṇa) itself. 519.

"As if co-nascent" (sahajātāni viya) means as if they were combinations accompanied by the condition of co-nascence (sahajāta-paccaya). "By co-nascence" (sahajātena) means by the condition of co-nascence.

“Those” refers to the combinations mentioned as “miscellaneous combinations. For those which were not joined by way of the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) are here called miscellaneous combinations.
Regarding the phrase “by way of the prenascent...,” the construction here is as follows:
[the prenascent] is combined with the postnascent, nutriment, and faculties by way of the co-nascent, mutuality, and general conditions.
It is said that for those very [factors], there is non-identity (asāmañña) both by way of co-nascence and by way of mutual [non-identity].
Just as there is non-identity between the pre-nascent and the post-nascent due to their being of different natures (bhinnasabhāvattā) by way of co-nascence,

and for that very reason there is non-identity of the nutriments and faculties by way of that [co-nascence], so too there is mutual non-identity among all four— beginning with the pre-nascent— due to their being of different natures.
Thus, by way of non-uniformity and by way of inequality, the aforementioned combinations are scattered. However, just as the co-nascent conditions—
such as the immaterial aggregates and so forth— are not confused with others due to their mutual state of equality known as co-nascence,
and thus serve as conditions for their own conditionally arisen effects, so too [is it] by way of non-uniformity.

Their occurrence is thus: since the states that serve as pre-nascence and other conditions also [occur] in this way, those combinations—by virtue of their being conascent and mutually related, and according to the aforementioned commonality and non-commonality—are called "miscellaneous" (*pakiṇṇaka*) because they are scattered.
