If this is so, does it not follow that even the combinations of conascent factors would have the status of being "miscellaneous"? It does not follow, because of their state of being conascent.
This is because their state of being unscattered is established in this way. Therefore it was said: "The 'Miscellaneous' (pakiṇṇaka) are those mentioned without including the co-nascent [factors].

"Those" refers to the miscellaneous compositions. "Wholesome-resultants" (kusalavipāka) means both wholesome and resultants; the meaning is that those which, having identical characteristics, possess the nature of the wholesome and the nature of the resultant.
And such a nature belongs to only one faculty, namely, the final-faculty (aññindriya).
He said: “This... [etc. ...is obtained. But is this meaning not also obtainable by way of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) and the others?

Indeed, they too possess the nature of activity (*kiriya-sabhāvatā*). “Suffering” (*dukkha*) refers here to mental suffering. Therefore he said: “Only unwholesome (*akusala*). The construction is: “of the suffering that is result” (*vipākassa dukkhassa*). By this it is stated: “Because of not being a factor of jhāna.
[The term] “unwholesome-resultant-activity” (*akusalavipākakiriya*) applies to the doubt-consciousness, the fivefold sense-consciousness, and the activity-mind-element (*kiriyā-manodhātu*).
The meaning is that because it occurs [only] as a process, the stability of consciousness is exclusively unwholesome resultant (akusalavipāka) and functional (kiriya).

Since, if the meaning were taken as "unwholesome resultants," then just as in the case of the jhānas, this would apply by way of the stability of consciousness during suffering but not by way of others in other instances,
therefore, when the meaning is taken as "the resultants of the unwholesome," [it applies] to the faculty of suffering.
Showing that [the term] is obtained among the faculties by way of this [classification], he said: “Of the unwholesome... it would be obtained.

Showing the meaning that in this triad of the wholesome, only the result (vipāka) and the resultant-indeterminate (vipākābyākata) are included, and not distinguished by terms such as “unwholesome,” he said: “Wholesome-resultant... there is none.”
The positive enumeration in the application of the section on questions is finished.

527. Regarding the phrase "by way of the non-root condition" (*na-hetu-paccayena*), the word "not" (*na*) is shown here to have a distributive sense; thus it is explained as "by a condition other than the root condition."
He said: "By including what was not included"—that is, by including those [conditions] not already mentioned through the inclusion of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and so forth.

"There are eight" means that there are eight conditions, such as the object-condition (*ārammaṇa*) and others, as presented in this textual passage. "Among them" refers to those eight conditions. "By three" refers to the object-condition, the co-nascence-condition, and the decisive support-condition (*upanissaya*). "By two" refers to the object-condition and the decisive support-condition.
"In each respective condition" means in each respective condition such as the cause and so forth. "From that condition," meaning from the condition consisting of the cause and so forth.

"Should be applied as appropriate" means that whichever conditions, while standing in their reverse order, can be joined in their direct (anuloma) order within a given condition, those should be applied;
this is the meaning.
"Of two" refers to these two: the immediate decisive support (*anantarūpanissaya*) and the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*).
"Pre-arising" [condition] occurs by way of the object-base pre-arising (*vatthupurejāta*), because the object-pre-arising (*ārammaṇapurejāta*) is included within the category of the object.

"By another volition" refers to a volition that functions specifically as a asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kammapaccaya*). The immaterial nutriments (*arūpāhāra*) do not relinquish their state of being co-nascent (*sahajātābhāva*).

Thus they are nutriment-conditions; and since material nutriment exists only when it has reached the state of being established, it is said: "Nutriment by way of physical food other than that which is co-nascent.

The phrase "other than that which is co-nascent" is stated for the purpose of excluding immaterial nutriment, not for the purpose of excluding specific types of physical food, because there is no such thing as that [material nutriment] which is not of such a nature. For material nutriment is never a co-nascent condition.

It is neither a co-nascence condition nor a pre-nascence condition. Just as there is no co-nascence condition for those things that are co-nascent, so too there is no post-nascence condition for those that are pre-nascent, and no pre-nascence condition for those that are post-nascent. Why?
Because such a characteristic of a condition does not exist. For that which is the producer of something is not co-nascent with it.

There is no pre-arising (purejāta) status, nor is it endowed with the characteristic of the pre-arising condition; furthermore, because it is a material phenomenon (rūpadhamma), there is simply nothing that can be said regarding its status as a post-arising condition (pacchājātapaccayatā).
The same principle applies to its status as a supporting condition (upatthambhakatte).

Therefore, its nature as a condition should be understood as being devoid of the categories of co-nascence (sahajāta) and so forth. For this very reason, it is said: "Co-nascent, pre-arisen, post-arisen, nutriment, and faculty."
Here, material nutriment is taken separately, just as the material life-faculty is. Thus it is said: "Material nutriment...

is indeed a condition by way of nutriment. Regarding the phrase "of another material life-faculty, both by way of co-nascence and pre-nascence," the meaning should be understood in the same manner as explained for material nutriment.
And "having done so" means that because the subsequent ones are included by way of including those not already included by the preceding ones.
The meaning is that here the conditions of nutriment and faculty are included by way of material nutriment (*rūpāhāra*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*);
otherwise, it would have had to be stated as "conditioned by the nutriment-condition" and "conditioned by the faculty-condition.
That is why he said: "It is stated thus: 'object... etc. "From other than those" means from those conditions such as the object-condition and so forth.
Because there is no other condition here—such as the condition of kamma—that is intended [in this context] within the wholesome.

Therefore, since the decisive support (*upanissaya*) has been stated by way of two [types] other than the object-condition, it must be said that "object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*) is included within the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*)," and not that it is the "object-decisive-support" (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*);
such is the intention. If this is so, why [is it mentioned] in the section on the negative inquiry regarding the limited triad?

The object (ārammaṇa) was not mentioned. Anticipating the objection that it ought indeed to have been mentioned since it is not included within the decisive support (upanissaya), he says, "But as for that which...

and so forth. Therein, "stated by way of not being included among the preceding" means stated by way of not being included among the preceding conditions (paccaya) for the subsequent conditions. This is because there is no absence of exclusion from what is included.
Because there is no avoidance of a condition that is included by virtue of having a characteristic identical to itself; the meaning is that there is no reason for such avoidance.

"Because there is no other object apart from the decisive support" means that when an immeasurable state serves as the object for another immeasurable state, it is only an object-decisive-support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), in the sense that it possesses the status of an object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*). Just as with the object...
When the decisive support by object (ārammaṇūpanissaya) is taken, the object itself is already included because of its status as a powerful object;

likewise, when the decisive support by object is taken, the object is necessarily included because it is of that same nature. Therefore, it should be understood that the object is not mentioned separately therein.
Thus he said: "But it is not because the object is not included within the decisive support by object."
"Of the postnascent nutriment-factors" means: of the immaterial (arūpa) nutriments that are postnascent relative to the prenascent body which has arisen conditioned by themselves.
For these [nutriments] are co-nascence-presence conditions for the immaterial phenomena co-nascent with themselves, as well as for the material phenomena originated by them;
but they are postnascence-presence conditions for the prenascent bases (vatthu). "Of the postnascent faculties" means: of the postnascent...
Regarding the immaterial faculties: the remainder should be applied according to the method explained for nutriment.

Since these nutriments and faculties, at the very moment they receive the pre-arisen presence condition (*purejāta-atthipaccaya*), at that same moment become the conascent presence condition (*sahajāta-atthipaccaya*) and the post-arisen presence condition (*pacchājāta-atthipaccaya*) for those things arisen from their respective conditions, it is therefore said: "There is also the state of being a presence and non-disappearance condition simultaneously."
"Three" refers to the three [types of conditions], beginning with conascence (sahajāta). "By six modes" means by the six divisions of the presence condition (atthipaccaya):
namely, the five beginning with conascence when taken separately, and the division taken collectively as appropriate.

"Having grouped each one" means that the characteristic of the presence condition and the characteristic of the non-disappearance condition (avigatapaccaya) have been stated after grouping them individually according to those six divisions.

It should be stated that [the classification] is by way of the internal and external division because the eye-faculty and so forth, as well as the life-faculty, are intended here, whereas the faculties belonging to one's own and others' continua are not intended. The intention is:

"of those that are prior-born, supported, dissociated, present, and non-disappeared. For these are included within the category of the prior-born (*purejāta*). "Of a portion thereof" means of a portion of the object.

The meaning is: "of the object-predominance and the object-strong-dependence. "Of those" refers to the support-condition and the others. "In the strong-dependence and so forth" means in the strong-dependence, prenascence, and other conditions. That object which constitutes the prenascence-condition is what is meant there; that is, within the inclusion of the strong-dependence condition.
To show that the method already stated must be understood here as an absolute rule, the passage beginning with "But furthermore" was spoken.
The word *eva* (only) should be brought in and connected [to the text]; otherwise, it would imply that the arrival of the condition from those questions occurs as having only a single nature.
By the term *tena* ("by that"), that which was not grasped by the restriction "only one" is meant. By *tesu* ("in those"), the co-nascent and prenascent conditions are meant.
By *ukkaṭṭhavasena* ("by way of the highest limit"), it means by way of the maximum stated as "one, two," and so forth. *Te te paccaye saṅgahetvā* ("having included those respective conditions")...

Having grouped those conditions, such as the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*), together with the co-nascence conditions (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and others, [the text] presents the delimitation of the conditions shown.
"In the loss of the classification" means:
when there is a negation of this or that specific condition within the various classifications of conditions already grouped under the co-nascence condition and so forth.

The meaning is: "and in the case of the failure to answer a question. Regarding the phrase "not by way of the root-condition" (*na-hetu-paccayā*), since this includes conditions other than the root-condition, it is said:
"'Not by way of the root-condition' is stated with reference to the conditions found therein.
And having done so, because it was stated by way of the common characteristic shared by all opposites, it would not be right [to say] that it is not...
For when standing in opposition to the root condition (*hetupaccaya*), it can be said that a root-dhamma is a condition for a root-dhamma by way of the co-nascent condition (*sahajātapaccaya*).
"Twenty conditions" means twenty conditions including the root condition.
The construction is: "showing the detailed exposition of that which leads to decline."
“By those various conditions” means by those various conditions that serve as inclusive factors, such as co-nascent conditions (sahajāta-paccaya) and so forth.
“Those various conditions” refers to those conditions to be included—namely, mutual conditions (aññamañña-paccaya), root conditions (hetu-paccaya), and so on.
This was stated with reference to the absence of others; the intention is not that all of these [conditions] occur together. Therefore he said:
“Not so,” and so forth. In that context, the phrase “only two” is stated having set aside the predominance of the object (*ārammaṇādhipati*).
By the word “also” (*pi*) in the expression “of the indeterminate as well,” it is implied that not only the wholesome (*kusala*), but the indeterminate (*abyākata*) as well is included;

thus, the wholesome is brought together [with the indeterminate]. “Together with that” means together with the physical basis (*vatthu*). “Of the pure ones” refers to those taken exclusively, without the physical basis.
Regarding the wholesome aggregates (*kusalakkhandhānaṃ*). Although the meaning of "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*) does not apply to the physical basis (*vatthu*), he said "but by the physical basis...
and so forth, showing that the status of being a support (*nissaya*) and so on certainly exists.

This is because they are to be included under the presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*) among the co-nascent, prenascent, postnascent, nutriment, and faculty [conditions]. By means of the co-nascent and so forth...

In order to show that it is easy to include those things that are to be included by way of the *saṅgaha* (compendium), it was stated, "having included all conditions within the four," because the inclusion of those things to be included by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*) follows the method already described.

However, since there is also the possibility of karma not being included by way of co-nascent decisive support (*sahajātūpanissaya*), it was taken in its specific form; otherwise, one would have had to say, "within three conditions."
“Siyā” means: of that which is mixed and unmixed—that is, of that which is mixed by way of being co-nascent, pre-arisen, and so forth, as well as that which is not so mixed.
The passage beginning with “Na hi” was stated in order to demonstrate in detail the very meaning already mentioned.

By the phrase “tena,” there is the inclusion of the co-nascent factors and others which comprise the classification of the presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*). By the statement “of all conditions... it occurs,” [the author] refers to the section beginning with “In this enumeration of conditions.”
This shows the meaning that although the compendium of conditions was already stated [in the *Paṭṭhāna*], it is indeed demonstrated here by way of its meaning.
Why is the support condition (*nissaya*) not mentioned? The intention is that it can be analyzed as "co-nascent support" (*sahajāta-nissaya*) and "pre-nascent support" (*purejāta-nissaya*).

Or why is the dissociation condition (*vippayutta*) not mentioned? Because it can be analyzed as "pre-nascent dissociation" (*purejāta-vippayutta*) and "post-nascent dissociation" (*pacchājāta-vippayutta*).

The meaning is "it is possible. To show that which was stated as "because it cannot be predicated" with reference to the state of being mixed or unmixed, he said, "First, the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya)," and so forth.
It must be specified as "a condition by way of the dissociation-condition," because it is stated in the Canon without such specification.
"It is like that" means like the presence-condition (atthi-paccaya) or like the support-condition; this is because there is no distinction from the presence-condition.
The dissociation condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*) is indeed not to be mentioned [here], because it lacks the existence of the various classifications found in the case of two conditions.

Demonstrating this, he said, “Of the conascent and prenascents,” and so forth. To support with the canonical text the meaning already stated by the words “In that way,” etc., he said, “He will explain,” and so forth.
Therein, for the states of the Path and its Fruit, there is a conascent presence condition (*sahajāta-atthipaccaya*) by way of the materiality produced by the Path and its Fruit.

The construction is as follows: the post-nascence presence condition (*pacchājāt’atthipaccaya*) is stated with reference to the fourfold continuity of material form that is pre-nascent (*purejāta*) for those very [mental states], but it will not be stated that they possess the status of the dissociation condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*). "It" refers to the dissociation condition.
Since causes (*hetu*) and so forth are included within the category of co-nascence (*sahajāta*), causes and the rest are considered its specific types; thus it is said: "the co-nascence condition."
"And it is to be distinguished by causes and so forth. "It" refers to the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*).

"By contrary conditions" means by those conditions that are contrary to the co-nascent and prenascent [conditions] by virtue of their being co-nascent and so forth. Therefore he said: "by conditions contrary at the time of arising.
The commentary on the extraction of the opposites is finished.
Commentary on the Negative Enumeration;
Commentary on the Root of Non-cause (Nahetumūlaka). 532.

Regarding the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) which functions as the predominance-condition (adhipatipaccaya) and so forth: this refers to the object-object-predominance (ārammaṇa-ārammaṇādhipati) and the object-strong-dependence (ārammaṇūpanissaya).
It says [this]. And because those [factors] have precisely the nature of an object (*ārammaṇa*), it is therefore stated: "it simply falls away.

"In fifteen" means in the second [chapter], the "Conascence Condition" (*sahajāta-paccaya*), among the fifteen [conditions] stated beginning with "Root Condition" (*hetu-paccaya*). "By way of eleven" refers to: conascence condition;
predominance, support, kamma, nutriment, faculty, presence, non-disappearance, root, jhāna, and path—these being distinguished by their state of conascence.
[This is] by way of these eleven [factors]. The root-condition (hetu) and the others are included within the conascent (sahajāta).

When that [conascence] is excluded—that is, when that conascence is set aside as an opposing factor—those not included in the conascent are asked: "Which ones are they? He says: "The object-condition (ārammaṇa), predominance-condition (adhipati), prenascence-condition (purejāta), support-condition (nissaya), and so forth. "In the manner of object, etc. means in the manner of object-prenascence, support, asynchronous kamma, and so forth.
"When that is rejected" means when that co-nascent condition (*sahajātapaccaya*) is rejected. "These sections" refers to the sections answered as "co-nascent" and "pre-nascent.
"These, such as the support-condition (*nissaya*), etc. refers to the support-condition and so forth as distinguished by their co-nascence, not the others.
Therefore he said: "And because... [omitted] ...they are rejected by way of rejection."

"Excluding the condition of co-nascence (sahajātapaccaya) that functions as a support (nissaya), etc."—by this, it is shown that in the phrase "excluding the condition of co-nascence," only that which possesses the internal state of being a support, etc., is included as the condition of co-nascence. By the word "etc.

(ādi) in the term "support, etc.," the inclusion of the root-cause (hetu) and other such factors should be understood. "Because of the presence of occurrence by way of the phenomena of the mutuality-condition (aññamaññapaccaya)" means by way of the phenomena of the mutuality-condition.
Because of the absence of occurrence [of these conditions] due to their mutual exclusion by way of co-nascence and so forth,

the section stating "the wholesome [condition] for the wholesome and the indeterminate" is omitted. To dispel the apprehension that the general expression "of those respective conditionally arisen [states]" might—
on account of the statement "included within the mutuality condition"— be taken as referring only to those things that receive the mutuality condition, [the text specifies] "the wholesome..."
And so it is said: “...and of the wholesome,” and so forth. “Consisting of a collection” means consisting of a collection of the four aggregates.
“By those that consist of a single part” means by those very things that consist of a single part of that same [collection]. The passage beginning with “But the wholesome one...
is the explanatory statement that resolves the following words from the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “…does not decline through the condition of mutuality…. etc.

They are only a portion of the aggregate of material form (*rūpakkhandha*), by way of nutritive essence, material form, and the faculties; the factors spoken of as "states that are exclusively dissociated conditions" are referred to here as "they. Thus he says: "‘They’ means those states which are dissociated conditions.
Although it was stated, "in order to show the counting of the negative [analysis]," one might suspect that the counting of the positive conditions itself has been shown;
therefore, in order to dispel that doubt, he says: "For what is shown is the counting of the section on the negative analysis. Strong kamma.
"It is a decisive support (upanissaya) for the result (vipāka), while the other is a kamma-condition (kammapaccaya)"; thus he said, "But for the result as well... [it is] a kamma-condition.
The commentary on the section beginning with "not-root" (nahetumūlaka) is finished.
534. Regarding the phrase "limited enumerations" (paricchinnagaṇanāni): this does not refer to the number itself, but rather to the answers; thus he said.
“Enumerations with limited scope are the ‘releases’ (vissajjanā). Although the cause (hetu) stands even from the perspective of the reverse order, it stands as the very root of the methods (nayā);
therefore, he says “in the root-cause section” (*hetumūlake*). However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated simply as “not in the root-cause section” (*nahetumūlake*). 538.
“Having condensed the roots” means having condensed the seven-rooted, eight-rooted, and nine-rooted [sections]. “In two” means...

Regarding the three answers mentioned as "three": in the first two—namely, "a wholesome state [is a condition] for an indeterminate state" and "an unwholesome state [is a condition] for an indeterminate state"—it is said, "the result is arisen by way of conditions.

In the third—namely, "an indeterminate state [is a condition] for an indeterminate state"—it is said, "the body arisen from those [conditions]" (*tesamuṭṭhānikakāya*), which refers to the body arisen from those [conditions] by way of temperature, consciousness, and nutriment.
545. This was said with reference to these two cases: just as the immaterial is not a dissociation condition for the immaterial, so too the material is not a dissociation condition for the material.
"The indeterminate material for the indeterminate immaterial"—this was said with reference to the physical bases (vatthu) and the aggregates (khandha).
However, "the indeterminate immaterial for the indeterminate material"—this refers to mind-originated matter; thus, their relationship as a dissociation condition is absolute.
He said: “It is indeed [present] by way of the conascent... pe ... nutriment and faculty. By “by way of the conascent immaterial nutriment and faculty” is meant:

by way of the conascent immaterial nutriment and the faculties. (546) As for the statement that [conditions] from the single root up to the single peak are obtained by way of the immediate, natural, and decisive support conditions—this was stated according to what is appropriate;

therefore, it should also be shown according to what is appropriate by way of their exclusion or non-exclusion in the presence condition (*atthipaccaya*). “In the presence condition... [and so forth].

The passage beginning with “pana” has been stated. “In the preceding ones” means not in those beginning with the object-condition (ārammaṇa). “Nine” refers to the nine [combinations] ending with the single-rooted.
“Only two” refers to these two alone: “A wholesome state [is related] to an indeterminate state,” and “An unwholesome state [is related] to an indeterminate state.
The commentary on the Negative (Paccanīya) is concluded.
Commentary on the Positive-Negative (Anulomapaccanīya) [Exposition] 550.

“By these very same” means they are identical by virtue of the commonality of being wholesome and so forth, as in: “The wholesome [is the condition] for the wholesome; the unwholesome for the unwholesome. Therefore it was said:

“But because of the absence of the actual state [of being a condition], they are not corresponding. Although [the relationship] exists in the brief enumeration (*uddesa*) such as “the wholesome for the wholesome,” etc.,...
Since there might generally be a distinction in the analysis (vibhaṅga) regarding what is common, he said, “according to their application from the exposition.
551. *Hetunāmaṃ*: it is called *hetunāma* because it is both a cause (*hetu*) and a name (*nāma*). The construction is: “referring to that very thing which has become a condition (*paccaya*).
552. “Of both kinds of predominance”: by way of co-nascent predominance (*sahajāta-adhipati*) and object-predominance (*ārammaṇa-adhipati*); that [is] “wholesome for the wholesome...”
This should be understood according to the method stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) beginning with: "Both by way of co-nascence and by way of object.

The construction is as follows: "There are seven [conditions] in the object" is stated by way of the predominance of the object (ārammaṇādhipati), whereas "there are seven in co-nascence" is stated by way of the co-nascent predominance (sahajātādhipati).
"In this way" means just as it was stated regarding predominance, so it is in all cases for all conditions.

Having said, "In each of those... [etc. ...they should be extracted," he spoke the words, "In direct order... [etc. ...to be understood," showing that this extraction by counting is easy to perform and providing the method for it.
The commentary on the Positive-Negative (Anuloma-Paccanīya) is finished.
Commentary on the Negative-Positive (Paccanīyānuloma):

631. Regarding "by the calculation of those to be excluded" (*parihāpanagaṇanāya*), the intention is that the state of being common (*samānatta*) is not absolute, because there is also the possibility of a deficiency in number.
Therefore he said, "Of the dyads of non-cause and non-object" (*nahetunārammaṇadukkassa*), and so forth. Therein, together with that which is being joined...
The construction is: "even though they have fallen away by way of the dominant condition through a lower count.

Or, in the alternative reading "they have fallen away together with," the instrumental case in "by way of the dominant condition" (*adhipatipaccayena*) expresses a characteristic of state (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇa*). "This" refers to the characteristic.

"Non-abiding" (*aṭṭhāna*) means non-abiding or not remaining in accordance with the natural order (*anuloma*). "They abide" is to be construed as "they abide in accordance with the natural order. "Of these" refers to...
[This refers to] the root-conditions such as *hetu* and the rest. To show what is intended by "the others," the passage beginning with "dominant" (*adhipati*) was stated.
"These two" refers to these two: "wholesome and indeterminate [states] are conditions for the indeterminate, and unwholesome and indeterminate [states] are conditions for the indeterminate.
The commentary on the section based on the non-root condition (*nahetumūlaka*) is finished.
636. "By the three stated under the root-cause" means together with the three answers stated under the root-cause condition (*hetupaccaya*).

The intention is that he speaks of the commonality of the sequence (*vāra-sāmañña*) alone, not the commonality of the meaning (*attha-sāmañña*). Likewise, regarding "three under action" (*kamme tīṇi*), it is said "just as they were stated under the root-cause.
Thus, in this explanatory statement "just as they were stated under the root-cause" within the phrase "three under action," there is likewise only the commonality of the sequence.
The meaning is: "he speaks with intentional ambiguity. 644. "Each one alone" means each individual answer. 650.
"In its own place" means in the place where it itself stands. "Beyond that" means beyond that condition which was not grasped.

"From the negative perspective": regarding the nutriment condition (*āhāra-paccaya*), having applied the faculty condition (*indriya-paccaya*) from the positive perspective while the nutriment condition stands from the negative perspective, and having applied the nutriment condition from the positive perspective while the faculty condition stands from the negative perspective—this is the meaning of "how the question is obtained.
"In those" refers to the nutriments and faculties. They are divided in two ways: by way of the negative and the positive perspectives.
And [it is to be understood] by way of that which is to be applied.
The commentary on the Negative-Positive (Paccanīyānuloma) is finished.
The commentary on the Wholesome Triplet (Kusalattika) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Triplet of Feeling (Vedanāttika) 1.

Regarding the determination of "dependent" and so forth in the Triplet of Feeling: In the sections beginning with the "Dependent" (paṭicca-vāra), the determinations of "dependent," "conascent" (sahajāta), "foundation" (paccaya-ṭṭha), and so on—which would otherwise apply by virtue of their connection to the triplets—do not apply to feeling, material form, and Nibbāna. Why? Because they are excluded from the triplets.

Likewise is the expression "arisen by way of conditions. For it is not possible to say, with reference to feeling, form, and Nibbāna, that "dependent on a state associated with pleasant feeling, a state associated with pleasant feeling arises.

"Of the threefold states" means of the states belonging to the triad of feelings. "Therein" refers to the root-conditions and so forth. "According to what is appropriate" refers to feeling and the rest.
Whatever is suitable to serve as the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and so forth for a state associated with a particular feeling, it is [classified] accordingly.

In the phrase "object and so forth" (*ārammaṇādī*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipatipaccaya*), the object-strong-dependence condition (*ārammaṇūpanissayapaccaya*), and others.

In the "Triplet of the Wholesome" (*kusalattika*) as well, the term "abandoned" (*parihīna*) is stated with reference to the opposing side (*paccanīka*). [The phrase] "because of grasping material and immaterial phenomena" refers to their inclusion.
This is the statement of the reason for establishing [the object] at the beginning of that which is co-nascent, even though it has been without beginning.
By the word "beginning" (*ādi-saddena*) refers to the word "beginning" in the phrase "co-nascent and so forth" (*sahajātādayo*).

It is said, "of the objects and so forth that encompass all immaterial phenomena by way of their arising in dependence [on conditions]," because all immaterial phenomena become conditionally arisen states (*paccayuppanna*) by way of being directed toward [their respective objects] as appropriate.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), object-strong-dependence (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), and so forth.

By that—that is, by the statement beginning with "But those which comprehend all material phenomena" (*sabbārūpadhammapariggāhakā panā*)—the meaning is that the loss of [the condition] for those [states] existing in all bases (*sabbaṭṭhānika*) is shown by the demonstration of the co-nascent [condition].
For by the very demonstration of the loss of one part, the loss of the whole is demonstrated. Or alternatively, [the phrase refers to] "the co-nascent and the rest."

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), all four [types of relations] that exist in every instance are indicated. "Rooted in what is co-nascent" (*sahajātamūlaka*) means that they arise when the condition of co-nascence (*sahajātapaccaya*) is present;
they have not been set forth in the Canon by placing co-nascence first. Therefore he said: "The bond of co-nascence... it is thus stated. The connection is:
"But why does that which is subsequently arisen (*pacchājāta*) not fail? In that context, "therein" (*tattha*) refers to what has been stated.

[There are] two types: that which leads to decline and that which does not lead to decline. By the phrase "by means of co-nascent bonds," it is meant here that the causal factors (paccaya-dhamma) are the cause, by way of the characteristics of co-nascent phenomena acting as conditions.
"In this very [context]" means in the context of that which leads to decline; for that is what is emphasized here.

When it is said, "The decline belongs only to those things bound by co-nascence," one might suspect, "Does the decline belong to all of them? Anticipating this, he says: "By co-nascent... this is shown."

17. "It provides only a guide to the vision" means that just as it is permissible to say, with reference to rootless functional volition (*ahetuka-kiriya-cetanā*), "neither by way of root-condition nor by way of kamma-condition," so too is it permissible to say "nor by way of resultant-condition.
However, with reference to rootless delusion (*ahetuka-moha*), it is permissible to say "neither by way of root-condition nor by way of resultant-condition," but not "nor by way of kamma-condition.
Therefore he said: "And it is not a vision of the commonality between conditions and the phenomena arisen from conditions," and so forth.
25–37. Regarding the statement, “As with the wholesome triad (*kusalattika*), so should it be counted,” this was said in order to show what was intended by its inclusion in the *Pāḷi*:

“The commonality of non-counting for those rooted in causes... pe ... For the counts in the positive-negative method of the wholesome triad are not the same as those in the feeling triad (*vedanāttika*).
As for the phrase “even when applied by way of reversal,” here [the formula] begins: “Not-root condition, not-prenascence condition...”

Regarding the phrase "one [condition] in the object," they say that although the object should have been mentioned first, it was stated first by reversing the order of the "pre-arising" (purejāta) condition.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "three [conditions] in the case of kamma due to the non-root condition," they say that this very term has been reversed, such that it should instead be stated as "three [conditions] in the root condition due to the non-kamma condition."
39. *Taṃsampayutta* means associated with that mental distress (*domanassa*). Thus, the states associated [with it] are stated under the heading of mental distress.

*Saddhāpañcake* refers to faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. The construction *kattabbaṃ vā* should be understood as "it should be done. *Avasesesu* refers to greed and the other [defilements].
*Pāḷigatidassanatthaṃ* means for the purpose of showing the course of the text, [indicating] that "the text proceeds in this way."
For the purpose of showing its occurrence. "By means of lust and so forth" refers to those things that serve as decisive supports (upanissaya). "From non-arising" means from not arising.
Showing that this is the course of the text by means of the *Tikantarapāḷi*, he said, "In the *Kusalattika* also," and so forth.

"Here too" means even in this *Vedanāttika*. 62. "Non-otherness" means non-differentiation. For a state associated with pleasant feeling is [the cause] only for that which is associated with pleasant feeling.
It is a condition for the Dhamma by way of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*), but not for the others. This same method applies to the remaining phrases and to all instances where "three" occurs.
Therefore it was said: "All [the combinations] of the three should be understood by way of the three pure phrases.
It is logical that post-nascent states are not conditions for immaterial states; however, as for pre-nascent states, they [are conditions] for immaterial states...
Addressing the objection, "How is it to be understood that [these] are not conditions?", he says "arisen prior," and so forth;

the meaning is that they are not conditions while having arisen prior. For material phenomena, having arisen earlier and remaining, serve as the condition of priority for immaterial phenomena that arise later; however, this principle is not applicable to immaterial phenomena.
Therefore it was said: "Because of the absence of being pre-arisen. Likewise, "because of the absence of being post-arisen":

just as it was stated in this triad that because no state is pre-arisen, there are no pre-arisen conditions (*purejāta-paccaya*), so too, because of the absence of being post-arisen, they do not become conditions by way of being post-arisen;
the meaning is that there are no post-arisen conditions (*pacchājāta-paccaya*). For indeed, in a single [moment],...
In certain mental continua, after some immaterial phenomena have arisen and remained, other immaterial phenomena subsequently arise;
from this, the former would be the *pacchājāta-paccaya* (postnascent condition) for the latter.
83–87. Regarding the remaining eight, these refer to those beginning with "a phenomenon associated with pleasant feeling" and ending with the single-rooted and single-ended [formulas].

Among those [conditions] where nine or more instances are found—such as the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) and others—one should exclude one as previously stated, and [the co-nascent kamma-condition] is found in the remaining eight.
"In only three" means that the co-nascent kamma-condition is found only in the three pure [types of consciousness].
The commentary on the Triad of Feeling is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Triplet of Resultant (Vipākattika) 1–23.
"That very same" (*soyeva*): Whatever meaning is expressed by words that do not form a compound, that very same meaning is stated [here].
24–52. "That" (*taṃ*): This refers either to that statement or to that "matter produced by kamma" (*kaṭattārūpa*). Because of the derived matter (*upādārūpa*) originating from consciousness...
Just as there is arising in dependence upon the aggregates (khandhas), so too is there arising in dependence upon the great primary elements (mahābhūtas).
For its arising does not occur without both of these; however, such is not the case for the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa).

Since that [matter] arises in dependence upon the great primary elements while arising from the performance of kamma, therefore, in order to show this distinction of mind-originated matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) from derived matter (upādārūpa)—
In order to show this meaning— that only that [matter] was mentioned, whereas *kaṭattā-rūpa* (matter produced by karma) was not— he said, “dependent on the aggregates,” and so forth.
Although *kaṭattā-rūpa* was not included here in the passage, “dependent on the great elements, mind-originated matter is derived matter,” he said,
“but in the course of existence,” and so forth, showing that it is indeed included by another statement.
"And having done so" means precisely because there is no arising dependent upon the aggregates.

"Not as a nutriment-condition" means standing in opposition to the nutriment-condition. "That too" refers to the matter produced by karma (*kaṭattārūpa*). It is stated "at the moment of arising," taking into account that for matter produced by karma, nutriment is a support at the moment of its persistence.
The commentary on the triad of resultant states is finished.
4. Commentary on the triad of acquired states: 51.
Since among supramundane states only a dominant state arises without being a condition by way of dominance, he said: “not by way of the condition of dominance.”
"Because it itself has become the predominant factor. Anticipating the objection, "Does not a predominant state also arise by way of the predominance condition through the predominance of the object?
he says: "Not devoid... [etc. ...he shows. "In those not devoid of the predominance of the object" refers to the supramundane states;
for they are so called precisely because they have Nibbāna as their object. By the word "pi" (also/what need to say), what more need be said?
This shows [the distinction] between those with a dissociated object-condition (*ārammaṇādhipati*) and those with a non-exclusive object-condition.

72. Regarding the phrase "by way of preservation and support": just as the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) acts as a condition for the materiality produced by kamma (*kaṭattārūpa*) by way of preservation, so too does nutritive essence (*ojā*) act as a condition for that same kamma-born body by way of support, not by way of generation; such is the construction.

"But when this meaning is present" means: when this meaning is applicable—that the nutritive essence (*ojā*) within a group born of karma (*kammaja-kalāpa*) is a condition for that very same body born of karma by way of being its support—it may also be stated as "nutriment.
This is just as, by way of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), it is said:
"A state that is both acquired and subject to clinging is a condition, by way of presence-condition (*atthi-paccaya*), for a state that is both acquired and subject to clinging."
The meaning is that it should be stated in the same way regarding the aforementioned nutriment as well.
And here, the fact that the kamma-born nutritive essence sometimes acts as a supporting condition for that very same group [of material phenomena] is shown in the Aṭṭhakathā.
If the kamma-born nutritive essence were to function exclusively by way of supporting all other material phenomena, then—
Showing that there might be a contradiction with this textual passage (pāḷi), he quotes the commentary’s statement, “If...
[pe] ... it exists,” and then, in order to clarify the fault therein, he says, “This being so. In that context, *taṃ* refers to that statement.
“Not swallowed” means produced from its own condition; and here, the condition is specifically karma. Therefore, he says: “of that which has arisen as appropriated within one’s own continuity.”
The intention is that this question also [is to be considered], not only the nutriment mentioned previously. It ought to have been extracted, yet it was not.
Therefore, the word "tasmā" (therefore) is connected with the phrase "the doctrine is more powerful.

But why was nutriment not extracted from among the two questions stated as above? To this he says: "Of that which has been swallowed," and so forth. Therein, "the second question" refers to [the section] based on the dyad.
The construction is: "the second question. Regarding the phrase "and the second question was not extracted," here too one must supply and connect the passage:
"because of the absence of that which has been swallowed... [etc.]... "Of the other" means of that which has not been swallowed.

The intention is that it is precisely what has been swallowed, and not what has not been swallowed, as previously stated. Having said "more powerful," he demonstrates its state of being more powerful by saying: "not..."

He said, "Yes," and so forth. One should understand that for one who has swallowed a few [parts] and remains as if having finished eating, there is a specific benefit to the body from the mere act of swallowing, such as by frogs and other creatures.
"By what is stated here" means by what is stated in this triad of the clung-to (*upādinnattika*). "By the answers to questions ending in pairs and triads with a single root" means...
By means of question-and-answer explanations based on single terms, concluding with dyads and triads. These, moreover, are as follows:

"A state that is not-clung-to but subject-to-clinging is a condition, by way of presence-condition, for a state that is both clung-to and subject-to-clinging, and for a state that is neither clung-to nor subject-to-clinging.

A state that is neither clung-to nor subject-to-clinging [is a condition] for a state that is both clung-to and subject-to-clinging, for a state that is neither clung-to nor subject-to-clinging, and for a state that is neither clung-to nor subject-to-clinging..."
And it should be understood thus: "It is a condition for a state that is not acquired by clinging but is subject to clinging, by way of presence-condition.
Herein, "here" means in this section on the triad of states acquired by clinging. "As at the end of the second dyad" means as in the answer to the question at the end of the second dyad:

"A state that is not acquired by clinging but is subject to clinging is a condition for a state that is acquired by clinging and subject to clinging, and for a state that is not acquired by clinging but is subject to clinging, by way of presence-condition."

The meaning is: "as in the answer to [the question] 'conascent' and 'postnascent'. And this meaning is indeed found even in the questions at the end of the "Duka-trika" (groups of two and three) based on the third term.
However, if those questions are also found in the "Kusala-ttika" (the triad of the wholesome), then why were they not extracted there?
To this he says: "But there, for the sake of easy comprehension, the answer is given only by way of the conascent."
"Are stated. "By way of co-nascence alone" means by way of the condition of presence that is co-nascent. "Ending with the single-rooted dyads" refers to questions of this kind, such as:
"A wholesome state [is related] to both the wholesome and the indeterminate. These have been extracted there in the Wholesome Triplet.
But here, however, they are in this Acquired Triplet. By these aforementioned answers. "One state" means...

A single conditioning state, such as feeling (vedanā) and so forth; "by many" means by many specific types of presence conditions (atthipaccaya), such as conascence (sahajāta), post-nascence (pacchājāta), and others;
"of many states" means of many conditionally arisen states. "A single presence condition" is stated here from the standpoint of the commonality of the nature of being a presence condition.
Now, showing in detail the distinctions found within the presence condition—both those already mentioned and those not yet mentioned—[the author says]:
He spoke the passage beginning with “One indeed,” and so forth. Therein, “one” refers to one among the specific types of presence conditions (*atthipaccaya*).
“Of one” means of such a single [condition]. For otherwise, there is no such thing as one state being a condition for another state.

“By that very one” means by the co-nascent presence condition alone, as in the case of the physical base (*vatthu*) at the moment of descent [into the womb]; for that [base] is [the condition] for the mind (*nāma*) co-nascent with itself solely by way of the co-nascent presence condition.

It is a condition by way of co-nascence, not by way of pre-nascence and so forth. A single co-nascent immaterial aggregate is related to the multiple immaterial aggregates co-nascent with itself by one co-nascent presence-condition; it is related to the multiple mind-originated material phenomena co-nascent with itself by multiple co-nascent-post-nascent presence-conditions;
and it is related to the pre-nascent material phenomena originated by those [immaterial aggregates] by multiple co-nascent-presence-conditions, respectively.
Multiple pre-arisen material bases and co-nascent immaterial aggregates are related to a single immaterial aggregate respectively by way of the pre-arisen, co-nascent, and presence conditions.

Multiple immaterial phenomena are related to multiple co-nascent immaterial phenomena and pre-arisen material phenomena by way of the co-nascent, post-nascent, and presence conditions. Or, multiple types of nutriment and faculties [are related]...

It is a condition by way of presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*) for numerous material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) according to their respective roles—by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*), pre-existence (*purejāta*), post-existence (*pacchājāta*), nutriment (*āhāra*), and faculty (*indriya*). Thus, this meaning is possible even when the conditioned phenomena are dissimilar;
however, there is nothing at all to be said when they are similar. Therefore he said: "of the conditioned phenomena that are similar. Co-nascent (*sahajāta*).

The presence condition exists together with that which is pre-arisen; thus, a phenomenon that is a presence condition by way of co-nascence becomes a presence condition together with a phenomenon that is a presence condition by way of pre-arising.

Just as wholesome and other such phenomena, when receiving the presence condition by way of pre-arising from the [heart-]base, become a co-nascent presence condition for the co-nascent aggregates and for mind-originated matter, so too...
They are indeed also postnascent conditions for the prenascent body. Therefore he said, “And by the postnascent.

The connection is with the words “is a presence condition. This state of being a presence condition for both conascent and postnascent [states] is intended only when there is non-difference among the conditioning phenomena, not when there is difference.
Therefore he said, “… because they are not other phenomena… [etc. … when there is difference of phenomena.”
Now, demonstrating by means of the canonical text (pāḷi) that there is an absence of manifoldness in that [condition], he says, "If it were so," and so forth.

Therein, "there is no single state of being a presence-condition" means that there is no single state of being a presence-condition obtainable by way of a single conditioning phenomenon (paccaya-dhamma).
Why? Because of contradiction. Therefore it was said: "Conascent... not stated. And having done so:
Because of the simultaneous non-acquisition of co-nascent and post-nascent [states] by means of a single dhamma.

"By means of a single dhamma" means by means of one and the same conditioning state. Therefore he said: "Because of the contradictory natures of various dhammas. And this contradiction of nature should be understood in terms of the co-nascent and post-nascent;
however, in this context, it refers to the distinction between mundane and supramundane states, and so forth. "Otherwise" means...

Regarding the simultaneous acquisition of those conascent and postnascent [states] together as one. "Even when the faculty-condition is excluded" means even when it stands as an opposing condition to the faculty-condition.

"The acquisition of that question" refers to this question: "States that are both acquired and subject to clinging, and states that are not acquired but subject to clinging, are conditions by way of presence for a state that is both acquired and subject to clinging."

By way of gain: there are twenty-two [combinations], namely: nine ending with the single-rooted (ekamūlaka), five ending with the single-rooted dyad (duka), one ending with the single-rooted triad (tika);
four ending with the dyad-rooted unitary (eka), two ending with the dyad-rooted [dyad], and one ending with the dyad-rooted triad—thus, twenty-two.
Just as it was stated previously that co-nascence (sahajāta) is a presence-condition (atthipaccaya) together with pre-existence (purejāta), so too...
Showing that the pre-arisen [condition] is also [a condition] by means of that [simultaneously arisen one], he said: "The pre-arisen is a presence-condition together with the simultaneously arisen.
In this context, the phrase "together with the simultaneously arisen" means "together with the simultaneously arisen alone. For this word *eva* is used in the sense of exclusion;
the meaning is that there is no presence-condition of the pre-arisen without the simultaneously arisen. However, among the other phenomena that are presence-conditions...
There is no fixed rule that [the object] exists either together with or apart from those [other conditions]. Therefore he said, "not by others.

As for the statement, "That basis is also a presence-condition only when it is co-nascent with what is co-nascent," that too refers only to the basis as pre-nascent and the object as pre-nascent associated with it;
it does not refer to the object as pre-nascent alone. Therefore he said, "not the other."
Now, in order to clarify the aforementioned point by means of another reading, it is said: "In the *Kusalattika*... and so forth.

If that which is pre-arisen (*purejāta*) could be a presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*) even without its co-arisen (*sahajāta*) counterpart, then it would not be possible to state, "There are five [conditions] for the presence-condition excluding the non-dissociation-condition.
Yet this has been stated; therefore, it is understood that "the pre-arisen is a presence-condition only together with the co-arisen."
"...occurs. Regarding the twenty-two [factors] in the non-dissociation [section], the same method applies here as well.

"Therein" refers to the triad with visibility (*sanidassana*). "In the analysis of presence" (*atthivibhaṅge*) means in the exposition of the presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*). "Ending with the first of the root-triad" refers to:
"States that are both visible and impinging, invisible and impinging, and invisible and non-impinging, are a presence-condition for a state that is invisible and impinging..."

The question, beginning with the "triple-root" (*tikamūlaka*) and ending with the "single-conclusion," has thus been set forth. Regarding the "extraction of conditions" (*paccayuddhāra*), it is right there in the extraction of conditions that this question was posed.
To the objection—"How is this so? If the pre-arisen (*purejāta*) condition exists only together with the co-arisen (*sahajāta*) as a presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*)?"—he says:
"Because of its being a condition for that which is accompanied by the basis... etc. The meaning of this is: even if...
In this context, by the mention of "visible and impinging," the status of the object-prenascence as a presence-condition is stated;
nevertheless, because of the mention of "invisible and non-impinging," the physical basis (vatthu) is also included.

Thus, it is stated that the object-prenascence, together with its physical basis, functions as a presence-condition simultaneously with the conascent [condition]. Only the postnascent [condition] is a presence-condition together with nutriment and the faculties.

The intention is that [the condition] exists, but not as a pre-arisen condition (*purejāta*). "In the state of non-otherness" (*anaññadhammatte*) means in the non-difference of the conditioning phenomenon (*paccayadhamma*).

The construction is: "With the co-arisen, there is the presence condition (*atthipaccaya*). This same method applies to the other two phrases as well. In those cases too, the counterpart pre-arisen condition alone should be understood.
Regarding the investigation shown by himself in the passage beginning with "But among the specific types of presence conditions," one should accept it as "it is thus."
He affirms by way of conclusion.
The commentary on the triad of the acquired is finished.
6. Commentary on the triad of applied thought.

22. Regarding the "seven root-sets" in the triad of applied thought (*vitakkattika*): these refer to the seven sets of roots—consisting of three singles, three pairs, and one triad—as they appear in the sequence beginning with "dependent on a state accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakkasavicāraṃ dhammaṃ paṭicca*).
"In due order" means according to the sequence in which they are presented in the Canon. "Seven" refers to the first single-set; "five" refers to the second.
Five. These should be understood according to the method explained under the condition of cause (*hetu-paccaya*). However, here they should be applied solely by way of their occurrence (*pavatti*).
Regarding "three" and so forth: there are three in the third [clause], one in the fourth, three in the fifth, three in the sixth, and one in the seventh.
These, moreover, in their respective order, depend on the third clause: by way of the third clause, the second clause, both of them, and the first and third clauses.
By way of the third term in dependence [on the first], by way of both the first and second terms in dependence on the first and second terms,
by way of both the first and third terms in dependence on the second and third terms, and by way of the third term alone in dependence on the first,
second, and third terms— these are to be understood. By this same method, the twenty-eightfold [dependent origination] and so forth, in their mutual relations, are also to be understood.
The enumeration should be understood. "In this way" refers back to the enumeration as previously stated. Regarding those based on the second and third roots:
in the case of the second root, it should be joined as "one," and in the case of the third root, as "one. Likewise, regarding "by repetition":

the meaning is that just as there are eleven in the case of the pre-arisen condition, so too are there eleven by repetition. "In others" means in those other than the dominant, mutual, pre-arisen, and repeated conditions.
Regarding the enumerations of conditions: "similar to the root and object conditions" means they are similar to the enumerations found among the root and object conditions.
31. Regarding "without distinction": the construction is that no answer was given without applying the qualification "resultant.
To state the reason for this, he said "Why? and so forth. "Of the others" refers to mundane resultants (*lokiya-vipāka*). Having set those aside separately...

“Are stated”: those aforementioned mundane resultant states are stated separately by extracting them on the basis of their commonality of being “without applied thought and with sustained thought only.

The first section refers to the passage stated as: “Dependent on aggregates that are without applied thought and with sustained thought only, there are predominants that are without applied thought and with sustained thought only.
(38) “This”: this refers to the textual phrase that has come down as: “Accompanied by that which is without applied thought and with sustained thought only... proceeding together.”
To demonstrate its meaning, he said: "The root... [etc. ...is stated.

Therein, "by connecting" means by connecting the root-term, or specifically the term rooted in repetition (*āsevanamūlaka*), with the terms "without applied thought" (*avitakka*)—which are stated by way of the category of the "without applied thought" (*avitakkapariyāya*)—namely, the terms "without applied thought, with sustained thought only" (*avitakkavicāramatta*) and "without applied thought, without sustained thought" (*avitakka-avicāra*).
It is not like the "pre-arising" (*napurejāta*) condition, nor is it like the "repetition" (*nāsevane*) condition.
The meaning is that one should follow the canonical text (pāḷi) and recite it. However, in the manuscripts, it is seen as:
“*avitakkavicāramattaṃ vipākena saha gacchantenā*,” which means “by one who joins [the phrase] together with the resultant state (*vipāka*) acting as a qualifier.
For this very reason, he says: “One should join [the passage] beginning with ‘the resultant state without applied thought and with sustained thought (*avitakkavicāramatta-vipāka*)’ and so forth.”
Since it has already been applied in the text of the *Ekamūlaka*, it is stated: "In the first of the *Dumūlakas*.

49. Regarding the phrase "the root term itself as the final element": by means of such passages as "conditioned by a state with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakkasavicāra*), a state with applied thought and sustained thought arises, not by way of the root condition (*nahetupaccayā*)," the root term itself is applied as the final element. Seven.

The statement "delusion is to be extracted" was spoken with reference to the non-causal condition (*ahetupaccaya*). For in the section on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), non-causal delusion appears only three times;
however, here it appears in all four root-conditions, beginning with "conditioned by the physical basis" (*vatthuṃ paccayā*).
Therefore, it should be understood that the expression "seven delusions" is stated with reference to its appearance seven times.
"Because it is included by way of decisive support" means that the kamma-condition is included precisely by the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
Since all kamma pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres possesses strength, there is no absence of the state of being a decisive support; therefore, it is called "venerable" (*garu*).
However, as for kamma that brings about the exhaustion of kamma, there is simply nothing to be said regarding its state of possessing strength—this is the meaning.
It is stated, "In order to clarify this by means of the Pāḷi itself: 'Indeed, it is understood from the section on the counter-questions of the Upādinnattika'...
The commentary on the Vitakkattika is finished.
8. Commentary on the Dassanenapahātabbattika.

"It should be investigated according to the method analyzed in the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga*"—this was said with reference to the determination of the "Path whose Beginning is Unknown" (*amataggapatha-vinicchaya*) brought forward by himself [the author], beginning with the words:

"And it cannot be abandoned by the vision of ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), nor can it be asserted that for others there is no conditionality through any condition whatsoever. In that regard, whatever...
That which ought to be said has already been stated in the *Atthavivaraṇa* commentary on the *Paṭiccasamuppāda-ṭīkā*; therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained therein.
The commentary on the "Triad of what is to be abandoned by seeing" is finished.
The sub-commentary (*anuṭīkā*) on the *Paṭṭhāna-pakaraṇa* is completed.
Thus ends the *Anuṭīkā* (Sub-commentary), the Explanation of the Hidden Meaning,
within the *Mūlaṭīkā* (Root-Commentary) on the Five Treatises (*Pañcapakaraṇa*). The Sub-commentary on the Abhidhamma is completed.
